text:
4
           IDEAS FOR GETTING STARTED

The time has come to dive in and get started! Are you ready? Where will you begin? My
hope is that these projects will spark ideas that inspire you to take new directions in
your work and in your studio. Whether you choose the functional route or take a chance
with more sculptural pieces, the projects outlined in this chapter offer several different
ways to approach the surface of your ceramic creations. Take what you like and leave the
rest.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
SET OF COASTERS

It’s been a personal goal of mine to make more things just for fun and just for me. As a
full-time potter, I spend most of my time in the studio producing work for other people. I
love my job, and I love creating artwork that lives in the homes and the worlds of other
people. Somewhere along the way, I forgot the joys and pleasures of crafting something
special for my own personal gratification. A set of ceramic coasters became that
household object that I knew was missing in my life.
   Living with art every day can be as simple as a handmade set of coasters on your
coffee table or your nightstand. A coaster is practical and functional, and I think it might
as well be beautiful too. Coasters can be used in every room of the house, on any surface
area where you’d set a glass of water or an ice-cold beverage. They help protect your
household surfaces by preventing any ring marks caused by cups and mugs of your
various refreshments.
  When you’re starting your own set of coasters, take the opportunity to play around
with pattern and color. Working on a flat surface that won’t be used for serving food
means you can experiment with different glaze textures as well as intricate, colorful
designs. You have lots of opportunities to explore various shapes of coasters too. I went
with the classic circle and square coasters for the set I’m making, but you can go wild
with unique organic shapes if you like. Let’s get started!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired ceramic coasters (My circles are approximately 4 inches [10 cm] in
  diameter; my squares are approximately 4 inches [10 cm] square)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Pencil and ruler
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes, including fine tip and flat head, for applying glazes
Squeeze bottles with assorted tip sizes for applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil or pottery stamp
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Gently wipe clean any dust or debris from your bisque-fired ceramic
coasters. Using your pencil, start sketching out the design or pattern you’re
envisioning for the surface of your coasters. [A] [B] [C]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Using various fine-tip paintbrushes, start filling in your patterns on
the surface of the coaster with glaze. [D] If you’re brushing your glaze, it’s
important to make sure you’re applying multiple coats of glaze on each
section of the pattern, focusing on even coverage throughout the whole
surface. [E] Since you’ve already spent time experimenting with your glaze
testing, you should already know how many coats you need for each glaze
to achieve the desired finish.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 Using a small squeeze bottle is a quicker option since it only requires
one layer of glaze application, but it does require more controlled
movements and careful pressure so as not to release too much glaze and
mess up the pattern. Go slow and fill in your shapes and patterns following
the pencil lines as your guide. [F] Let the glazes dry in between coats and
when switching glaze colors.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 Once you’ve finished your glaze layers and patterns, use a damp
sponge to clean the edges and wipe off any drips of glaze on the underside
of the coaster too. Let the glazes dry, then sign your name or stamp your
logo and set each coaster aside for firing.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
BEADS

I have very busy hands! I like it best when I’m making things in the studio, but
sometimes, simple activities at home can do the trick too. Whether it’s cooking, washing
dishes, pulling weeds in the garden, or mending a piece of clothing, I like having a
creative task for my hands. As it turns out, having occupied hands is very good for the
brain and aids in stronger mental health. The handiwork is present in all stages of bead
making—from rolling the wet clay into small shapes and spheres to glazing small
designs and patterns on the beads and then stringing up your finished beads into
something unique. The palpable reward is there at each phase of the process.
  When you’re making your beads out of clay, don’t forget to use a needle tool or a
bamboo skewer to poke a hole through the center. The hole needs to be big enough so
that your bead will fit onto the bead rack you’re using during firing, as well as fitting onto
the cord you plan on using to string the beads, so keep shrinkage in mind as you’re
working on your beads.
   “What’s a bead rack,” you ask? It’s a kiln-safe rack with high-temperature rods that the
glazed beads are threaded onto for firing. It suspends the beads in mid-air so that you can
have a glaze all the way around the bead, without having it get stuck to the kiln shelf
during the glaze firing. Remember that glaze will fuse to whatever surface it touches in
the kiln, so it is important that the inner channel of the bead stays clean and free from
any glaze drips. Otherwise it will fuse itself to the bead rack and be stuck. You’ll only need
to use the bead rack for the glaze firing stage, not for the bisque firing stage.
  Handmade ceramic beads have such a tactile quality to them that just can’t compare
to store-bought plastic beads. Ceramic beads can be used for necklaces, longer wall
garlands, small key chains, ornaments, and the like, and making them offers a therapeutic
way to pass the time, giving your hands something creative to do to stay busy.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Clay for rolling and making the beads and a needle tool or bamboo skewer for poking
  holes in the beads or prepared bisque-fired ceramic beads (any shape and size)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes, including small detail brushes, for applying glazes
Bead rack for glaze firing
Cord for stringing beads
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Once you’ve determined what you want to create using your finished
beads, start making your beads with clay. If you’re making a necklace with
beads that match, make the beads about the same size using the same clay
so that they string up nicely. If you’re like me, and you love a bowl full of
mismatched beads, make them as unique and funky as you’d like! Don’t
forget to make the hole big enough so the beads fit on the firing rack (if
you’re glazing them) and on the string or cord you’re using for your
finished creation. [A] [B]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Allow your beads to dry completely. Refine them with a damp
sponge and prepare for bisque firing. I like to fire my beads inside of a cup
or a bowl so that they don’t roll off my kiln shelves. [C]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 Once you have bisque-fired beads, you can start thinking about color
and patterns and how you want to glaze your beads. I like to use a fine-tip
brush for layering in stripes or small polka dots or layered shapes. [D]





Beads are an excellent surface for playing with layering and texture, so feel
free to get adventurous. Be sure to keep the inner channel of the beads clean
and free from any glaze drips or smears. Glaze on the inside of the beads
will cause them to get stuck to the high-temperature rod of the bead rack
during firing.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 Once your beads are glazed, carefully clean them and slowly start to
fill the rods with beads one at a time, allowing ample room in between to
make sure that the beads don’t touch. [E] I use my bead rack at the top layer
of my kiln load. It’s much easier to fill and load this way if it’s near the top
instead of the bottom. Assemble the rack pieces first and then add each
filled firing rod one at a time to the rack. Once it’s loaded in the kiln,
double-check your spacing to make sure each bead has enough room and
isn’t touching the bead next to it or the rack itself. If you don’t want to
glaze your beads and prefer to keep the surface of the clay bead raw, you
can fire your beads directly on the kiln shelf instead, without the bead rack.
Fire to the proper temperature and let cool slowly.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 5 When the kiln is cool enough to be unloaded, carefully disassemble
the bead rack one rod at a time. [F] Some of the beads will slip off easily,
and some of the beads will take some wiggling to pry loose. If your bead
gets stuck, you can break the bead off of the rod or use a pair of pliers to try
to force the bead off. Make sure you don’t have any sharp bits of glaze
sticking off the surface of your beads.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text: STEP 6 String up your beads and build your creation! [G]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
SPOONS

A ceramic scoop or spoon can be a sweet little project for all kinds of uses. I like to make a
long skinny handled spoon as a cocktail stirrer. I also like making a small handheld scoop
for coffee beans or coffee grounds. A tiny spoon is a great sidekick to a small vessel for
sprinkling sea salt. The sky is the limit for all the ways a handmade spoon can be used.
  Because of their small size, these pieces will sit directly on the kiln shelves, so I have to
be careful where I add glaze. I like using underglaze designs for finishing my spoons so
that I don’t have to worry about any glazed surfaces laying against the kiln shelves. On
my spoons and scoops, the entire underside is left without glaze, and the spoons
sometimes just have the spoon head glazed and nothing else. If my spoon is little, I make
a hole at the end of the handle and slide it onto my bead rack for firing. This allows me to
glaze the entire surface of the spoon if that’s the finished look I’m going for. Keep in mind
that the spoon has to be small enough to be able to hang from the bead rack in the kiln
without touching the shelves.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Clay for handbuilding your spoons or finished bisque-fired ceramic spoons and scoops
  in various sizes and shapes
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes (underglazes and clear glaze)
Assorted paintbrushes, including small detail brushes, for applying glazes
Optional: bead rack
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Start by handbuilding your spoons. Which clay will you use? How
big will they be? Will you hang them from a bead rack or fire them directly
on the kiln shelves? These are important questions to ask yourself before
you begin to determine your design direction. A modest rounded spoon
head attached to a handle works great as a simple starting point. [A]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 After bisque firing and gently sponging off my spoon, I start adding
my colorful underglaze stripes. [B] I’m applying three coats of underglaze
with small detail brushes so I can make my lines extra skinny. I’m making
thinner lines so I can fit more colors on the spoon, but I could change my
line thickness for more of a color-block look instead. This is where pattern
work and layering can be really interesting with your underglaze colors.
Repeat your three-coat coverage with each color.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 Once I’ve finished my underglaze decoration, I let the colors dry
completely before I handle it too much and mess up my designs. I apply
three coats of a clear glaze on the head of the spoon, sponge off the edges
and the underside of the spoon for any glaze drips, and prepare my spoon
for firing. [C]





STEP 4 After your spoon is fired, gently clean it, and it’s ready to use! I like
to use my spoons for sea salt and spices in the kitchen, but they also make
lovely decorative objects when displayed on a small shelf of various
collectibles.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
WALL HANGINGS

Ceramic wall hangings have always been one of my favorite things to glaze when I’m
working in the studio. They allow me an opportunity to be spontaneous with my color
choices and get some funky shapes and textures in there that aren’t always suitable for
functional pieces. I like to emphasize the beauty of the raw texture of my clay in a lot of
these wall hangings. The dot pattern has become one of my go-to designs, and I love
when each wall hanging turns out one of a kind.
    I build wall hangings in all different shapes and sizes. I like to make irregular shapes
because I always have a small wall area in my home that needs a unique piece of artwork
—a narrow strip of wall where a framed painting or photograph won’t quite fit. I like
emphasizing the imperfect, torn edges on some. While certain wall hangings call for a
smooth and sharp rectangular or square shape, others have rounded corners. This body
of work really allows me to play with my materials and try new things. Those kinds of
projects are so beneficial to a creative mind!
  While you’re building your slabs from clay, there are a few things you want to
remember. Drying your slabs slowly and strategically so that they dry flat and aren’t
warped is ideal. Having a flat wall hanging means it’ll hang flush against the wall. And
don’t forget to include a hole toward the top so you can hang it up. If you do forget the
hang hole, I also like to set these pieces on a shelf and lean them against the wall. They’re
versatile and can add a unique pop of art and color to your home in almost any fickle spot.
  Ceramic wall hangings are a fun way to express yourself with a more painterly
approach to glazing. You can use a project like this to play around with patterns and
mark-making, as well as different brushing and squeeze-bottle glaze techniques. It’s a
flat, blank canvas ready for your artistic touch!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Flat, fired bisqueware, designed to hang on or lean against a wall
Sponge
Bucket of water
Pencil, ruler, and stencils or paper templates for tracing your designs
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Squeeze bottles with assorted tip sizes for applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Gently wipe clean your bisqueware with a damp sponge. Start
sketching or tracing your designs directly onto your flat, bisque-fired wall
pieces. Lead pencil marks will burn off in the kiln when they are fired, so
don’t stress if you change your patterns or make a mark in the wrong place.
[A]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Start choosing your glazes. [B] Some of my wall hangings have up to
twelve different glazes on them, so don’t be shy with your glaze choices.
Go with what feels right. [C]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 When you start painting or squeezing your glazes onto your designs,
keep in mind that the color of the liquid glaze will look totally different in
its current state than it will when it’s fully fired. [D] [E] So, you’ll have to
rely on your extensive glaze-testing knowledge, your sample library, your
glaze notes, and your sketchbook so that you can properly anticipate the
final results ahead of time. It’s a little bit like thinking and working
backward—you’re working with materials that will look different at the
end, and sometimes it’s challenging to paint using just your imagination.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 Once you’ve finished painting your wall hanging, use your damp
sponge to clean up the edges, wipe off the back side, and clean up any drips
or smears.

STEP 5 If you want, use an underglaze pencil to sign your name on the back.
Be careful not to smudge the freshly written signature or flake off any of the
glazes on the front. This piece is delicate at all stages, so handle it slowly
and load it into the kiln carefully.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 6 Once it’s been fully fired, proudly display your piece and admire
your handiwork. Either hang it up with a nail or a screw, [F] making sure it
has a solid hold, or position it prominently on a shelf or mantle, propped up
against the wall.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
ABSTRACT CHEESEBOARDS

I’m a big fan of a well-rounded snack dinner, and I’ve become very good at building a
proper cheeseboard. Whether it’s for myself or a group of friends I’m entertaining at my
place, I like to lay out a fabulous spread of cheeses on a beautiful cheeseboard because it’s
as much fun to focus on the presentation as it is to eat it.
   Starting from the wet clay stage, I’ve built my cheeseboards thicker than my wall
hangings because I want them to be used for serving and a thicker final slab feels more
durable for picking up and passing around the table. I’ve made a bigger hole at the top so
that my finger can rest in there when I’m holding it or passing it, and it can also be hung
on the wall in the kitchen when it’s not in use. An abstract, all-over pattern turns your
board into a lovely eye-catching piece of art when it’s not covered in fruit and cheese!
   Since this project idea is embracing a functional serving piece, it’s necessary to use
lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glaze. Unlike artwork intended for wall hangings, we want
to avoid heavily textured glazes or surfaces that are too porous for this project. Think
about what will come into contact with that surface—hard and soft cheeses, fruit, and
utensils. A high-gloss glaze will feel different from a matte finish, so think about this as
you pick your glazes. You’ll also want to think about ease of cleanup and how a cheese
knife will behave when it brushes against the surface of the glaze.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisqueware ready for glaze
Pencil, ruler, and stencils or paper templates for tracing your designs
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes
Assorted paintbrushes, squeeze bottles, and other glaze application tools
Sponge
Bucket of water
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Using a pencil, draw out your design or pattern on your bisque-fired
surface. You can trace objects or stencils for varying shapes on the surface
or fill it out with an allover pattern. [A] Decide if you want the surface fully
covered or if you want any raw clay showing around the edge of your
designs.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Start with your first glaze color and begin filling in your shapes or
patterns. [B] If you’re using squeeze bottles, you can do one pass of glaze. If
you’re brushing it on, don’t forget to think about how many layers you’ll
need for full glaze coverage.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 Alternate your colors and your glaze choices as you start to fill in
your patterns and designs. [C] [D] Once it feels complete, clean up and
prepare your piece for firing. [E]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text: STEP 4 Once it’s fired and ready to use, it’s time for a snack party! [F]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
SET OF CUPS

Ceramic mugs and tumblers are the “best sellers” when it comes to my studio inventory,
and I can barely keep enough of them in stock. I think it’s because everyone knows
exactly what to do with a cup or a mug, and whatever our preferred beverage is, a special
cup is a great way to elevate a daily routine.
  One of the most important things to remember when you’re glazing cups or any other
vertical ceramic work is to test your glazes on upright surfaces as well as flat surfaces so
that you know which glazes tend to run and which ones are stable. You want to avoid
glazes that will trickle down the surface and cause your vessel to get stuck to the kiln
shelf during firing.
    I like to leave a lot of the clay surface exposed on my cups and mugs because I have so
many different clay bodies that are just too beautiful to cover up. For this project
example, I’m using deep red stoneware, and I’ll be leaving some of the exterior surfaces
unglazed so that the beauty of the clay really shows through.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired cups or mugs (I’m making a set of four matching mugs)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes (I’ll be using 6 to 8 different glazes on this
  project)
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Wipe clean the inner and outer surfaces with a damp sponge,
removing any dust or debris from the surface before you glaze. [A]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Pick an interior glaze color. I’m using white on the inside of my
mugs, so I pour the glaze inside to approximately one-third of the way up,
do a quick rotation to fully coat the interior, and then I pour the glaze back
out. [B] I use a sponge to clean up any drips.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 I’m using the same white glaze to coat the handle of my mugs, and to
save time, I’m dipping the handle in the bucket of glaze. [C] One dip should
suffice, then I’ll clean up the area around the handle. [D] For the rest of the
surface, I’ll be painting shapes and patterns with various colored glazes.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 Starting with my planned pattern, [E] I pick my first color and start
painting my shapes. [F] I’m using either small-tipped detail brushes or
brushes with square heads, depending on the shapes I’m painting. I like to
embrace some drips and let my patterns blend in with one another, but I also
know to leave enough room at the bottom so that if my glazes drip, they
won’t drip all the way to the foot and run off the surface, sticking to the kiln
shelf. [G]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 5 I repeat my patterns and switch colors when necessary until the
patterns are complete. [H] I clean up the base of each mug and any
unwanted glaze spots and prepare them for firing. [I]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 6 Once fired, I gently hand-wash my cups before I use them and then
they’re ready. [J] A set of complimentary mugs or cups make a great set on
display in the kitchen, and your houseguests will love using your creations!
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
SET OF DINNER PLATES WITH INLAID CLAY DESIGNS

Inlaid clay designs are ideal for a finished surface that embraces patterns and natural
coloring and texture found within the clay. Using stoneware makes these a hearty option
for dinnerware, and a simple clear coat of glaze gives them a serviceable finish.
    I like to test my clear glaze on all of my clay bodies because sometimes the clear glaze
can take away some of the vivid colors of the clay. This helps me decide which clay will
look best when glazed clear and combined with other clay. For this project, I’m using
light, off-white, speckled stoneware clay with contrasting colors inlaid into the surface.
For these checkered patterns, I’m using black stoneware for the salad-sized plates and
white stoneware for the dinner-sized plates.
  Your patterns and shapes can change—they don’t have to be checkered. Play around
with dots and squares and have fun with organic shapes and blobs if you like as well!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

At least 2 different clay bodies that shrink at the same rate and fire at the same
  temperature
Rolling pin or slab roller
Silicone rib tool
Needle tool for cutting
Plaster hump or slump molds or drape molds
Sponge
Bucket of water
Ware boards or pieces of canvas for your work surface
Lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe clear glaze
Large paintbrush for applying glaze
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 I start by rolling a slab of my inlaid color clay (the slab that will be
cut and placed as the pattern) to a ⅛-inch (3 mm) thickness. [A] I compress
and smooth the surface with a silicone rib tool. Using my needle tool, I
handcut my shaped pieces, embracing the subtle differences and
imperfections in my cuts. [B] These shapes are cut small, and as they’re
pressed and rolled into the clay surface in the next steps, they’ll stretch out
and enlarge organically. I rarely aim for perfection with my cut shapes, but
you can if you like tight and clean designs. Set these cut-out shapes aside
with a sheet of plastic over the top so they don’t dry out too quickly.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Next, I use the other clay body to create the plate or the base color
that the shapes will be pressed into. I cut off a thick slab of this clay and roll
it out until it’s about 1-inch (2.5 cm) thick. [C]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 Using the shapes I handcut from step 1, I lay out my pattern on the
top surface of the 1-inch (2.5 cm) thick base clay. I gently set these shapes
on top in the desired pattern, knowing that they’ll enlarge and stretch. [D] I
rotate the slab so that the clay is being stretched to fit my plate molds and
not stretching the clay too much in one direction; this would create thin
spots and irregular stretching of the shapes. [E] I’m aiming for a finished
thickness of ¼ inch (6 mm) for my plates, so I’m careful not to roll them
out too thin.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 Once I’ve inlaid the shapes into the surface and I’ve reached my
desired thickness, I take my silicone rib tool and smooth any canvas texture
out, while also compressing my shapes and the inlaid clay. [F] Compression
is key to getting your inlaid clay to adhere. My smoothed slabs with the
inlaid patterns set up on ware boards for at least twenty-four hours, tightly
covered with plastic, before I cut the plates and press them onto their molds.
This allows the inlaid clay a chance to set up and be stronger when it comes
time to shape the plates.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 5 After my slabs have set up, I cut my plates out for draping over the
molds. Using a salad-sized plate mold, I trace it over the slab and cut it out
with my needle tool. I lightly smooth the cut edge with a damp sponge and
drape the plate over the mold, compressing down until the surface is
completely and evenly set over the mold. [G] I set the molds aside for the
clay to set and firm up a bit—usually an hour or two. I repeat this until I
have enough plates, alternating between larger dinner plates and smaller,
salad-sized plates.





STEP 6 Once the plates have set up, I can flip them off the mold and onto a
ware board. I cover them with plastic so they can dry very slowly, for about
a week in my studio.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 7 When the plates are in their greenware state, I use a damp sponge to
refine the edges and smooth out any fingerprints. [H] I bisque fire the plates
to their desired temperature.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 8 After the plates are cooled and cleaned after bisque, I apply three
coats of clear glaze and prepare the plates for their glaze firing. [I]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 9 Once they’re fired, I hand-wash the plates, and then it’s time to fix
my favorite meal and put them to use! [J]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
HANDBUILT VASES WITH HEAVILY LAYERED GLAZES

We’ve covered the importance of testing glazes already, and once you feel you have a good
idea of how your glazes behave, then it’s time to start testing what happens when you
layer multiple glazes on the same piece.
   Layering too much glaze on a single piece can sometimes be problematic, and we don’t
want our glazes running onto the kiln shelves. But having a chance to discover what
happens when glazes are overlapped and layered on thick can be an exciting experience
and can open the doors to new surface design ideas. If you’re concerned about the final
results, you should create a test tile and plan out which glazes you want to try layering
there first before you commit to your vase’s entire surface.
  The surface of this vase began with a layer of peach-colored underglaze ovals, painted
on by hand, and then a layer of clear glaze over the peach ovals. After that, I started
adding layers and heavy drips of a matte speckled brown glaze as well as a drippy light
green glaze and a textured white crawl glaze—all layered in the same direction so that
drips were encouraged, to an extent. I finished this vase with a few dramatic drips of gold
luster too, embracing a heavy luster application to encourage the gold to move down the
surface of the vase as well. It suddenly became a statement vase, layer by layer by layer,
and I love the way it came out! I’ll be demonstrating on a smaller vase that I’ve finished in
the same style as this larger vase.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired vases, any form will do (handbuilt, wheel-thrown, or slip cast)
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various underglazes for layering (be sure to pick glazes you have some experience
  working with)
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil or pottery stamp
Optional: gold luster or other overglaze
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Start by lightly sponging any dust off the surface of your bisque-fired
vase. Choose the interior glaze color and pour the inside, rotating the vase
so that the walls are fully coated, [A] and then pour the glaze out. [B] One
poured interior coat of glaze will suffice.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Starting with underglaze, lay your first layer of color and pattern
with one or multiple colors of underglaze. After the two to three coats of
underglaze have dried, you can start with your first glaze color. [C] Start
layering in a concentric pattern with controlled shapes or have fun with
organic drips and splatters if you’re going for a less arranged look.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 Keep layering your various colored glazes while also thinking about
varied textured glazes. Will layering a matte glaze change or affect the final
surface? Will adding four or more coats of glaze change the results you’re
used to achieving? Keep these design options in mind as you continue
layering your surface glazes. [D]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 Once you feel you’ve layered as much glaze as you’re willing to
carefully wipe the foot clean and add your signature or stamp to the bottom.
Prepare your vase for firing in the kiln. [E]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 5 You can opt for an additional layer of gold luster or other overglaze
[F], or you can call it good on its own.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
DRIP AND SPLATTER PLATTER

A serving platter is one of my favorite things to make. I imagine a table filled with people
who love one another sharing a meal and passing the platter around so that everyone
gets a bite. Serving platters feel significant because they’re often the pieces that get
pulled out for special occasions, and I’m a big fan of celebrating special occasions. A
handmade ceramic platter with unique and stylized splatters of glaze can make a
statement at the table and is sure to impress your guests.
  My platter is oval, but I also love a large circular platter or even a long rectangular
platter. Don’t forget to keep the size of your kiln in mind when you’re first building your
platter. You’ll want to be sure it fits soundly in the kiln on a single shelf without bumping
the kiln walls.
   I’m using chunks of dried clay that I’ve picked off the rim of my glaze pints. I first tried
this technique when I was irritated by the amount of dried-up glazes I had accumulated
in my studio. Multiple pints and jars of clay had dried-up bits stuck around the rim, and it
took a lot of work to remix them back into a workable glaze. Using my needle tool, I
scrape off some of those dried chunks of glaze and sprinkle them onto the surface of my
platter so that they’ll fire into these bright drips and dots on the finished surface.



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Bisque-fired ceramic platter
Sponge
Bucket of water
Various lead-free, nontoxic, food-safe glazes (I used a white base glaze with drips of
  navy blue)
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Needle tool for scraping dried glaze and applying glazes
Optional: underglaze pencil or pottery stamp
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 Starting with a damp sponge, gently wipe off the surface of your
bisque-fired platter to remove any dust.

STEP 2 Using a large paintbrush, lay down your base coat. [A] White is
usually a safe bet as it generally accepts drips of other colors on top without
changing too drastically. (If you want to get adventurous, test out a few tiles
with different base layers and other colors of glaze dripped on top—you just
might find your next favorite glaze combination!) I apply three coats of my
white base glaze. I also sponge off the edges to clean up any glaze drips
from the bottom at this time.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 Since we’re adding a more intricate glaze finish on the surface of the
platter, now is also a good time to go ahead and stamp or sign the bottom of
your platter (if you haven’t already). That way, you can ensure the surface
design won’t get messed up by flipping the platter over to sign it later. If
your platter was already stamped or signed when the clay was still wet, you
can skip this part.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 I chose a deep navy blue glaze for my splatter drips, so using my
needle tool, I started by scraping off any dried pieces of glaze off the rim of
the pint and sprinkling those dried bits of glaze onto the platter’s surface.
[B] [C] Once you’re finished scattering the flecks of glaze, use a small brush
or your needle tool to dip into the wet glaze at the bottom of the pint jar.
Hold it over the platter and let the glaze fall in heavy drops onto the surface.
If you want more of a streaky splatter pattern (think Jackson Pollock), wave
your arm and brush or needle tool. A splatter design pattern looks very
different depending on your movements and the tool you use to apply the
glaze, so play around to uncover whatever splatter configurations are
calling your name on this project.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 5 Once you’ve finalized the splatter look you’re going for and you’re
done treating the surface, you can set your piece aside for its kiln firing. [D]
As you move your platter or load it into the kiln, be careful to keep it flat
and not to tip the platter. Your loose glaze chunks might fall off, and you
don’t want those falling into the kiln or onto the kiln shelves.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 6 Once your platter is cooled and out of the kiln, clean up any kiln
shelf debris from the bottom. Hand-wash your new serving tray and find an
occasion that calls for plentiful platters and people you love gathered
together! [E]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
PLANTERS WITH ADDITIVE DESIGNS

A planter is one of the best functional pieces that allow you to get wild with shaped
attachments and additive designs on the outer surface. You won’t be using this piece in
the same way you would use a plate or a cup, so an intricate design attached to the outer
surface is suitable for things like planters that sit on a shelf or a plant stand. Not to
mention, it’s a beautiful way to embellish your ceramic pieces.
  One of the more important things to keep in mind when you’re attaching two pieces of
clay together is making sure both pieces are at the same stage of drying or have the same
level of moisture. If the attachment pieces are drier than the clay they’re being attached
to, they’ll shrink at a faster rate than the other piece, causing the attachment to crack at
the point of contact. You want the attached pieces to dry at the same rate as the pot
they’re attached to.
  For my planters, I’ve used a simple rectangular shape that I’ve cut and repeatedly
attached all around the exterior wall. I call them tabs. I use a different-colored glaze for
each tab and embrace the raw red texture of the rest of the clay. The finished result is a
colorful rainbow planter that becomes a statement piece no matter what plant lives in
there!



TOOLS AND MATERIALS

Clay for handbuilding your planter
Rolling pin
Needle tool for scoring and making attachments
Slip brush
Various glazes
Assorted paintbrushes for applying glazes
Sponge
Bucket of water
Optional: pencil, ruler, and stencils or paper templates for tracing your designs
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Instructions

STEP 1 I’m a handbuilder at heart, so I’m starting by coil building a large-
sized planter. [A] [B] [C] Once I’ve built the planter to my desired size, I can
cut my shaped attachment pieces.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 2 Next, I roll a small slab to cut my shaped attachment pieces out of. I
roll my slab to about ⅛ inch (3 mm) thick and start cutting out rectangular
tabs that I’ll attach in a line all the way around the planter. I want my rolled
slab to be the same consistency as the planter, so make sure the attached
pieces aren’t too dry or too wet in comparison to the piece they’ll be
attached to. To make things easier, I score an entire side of the slab, and
then I use templates to trace designs or cut shapes freehand out of the slab.
[D] [E] Pull up your shapes and cover them in plastic so they don’t dry out
too quickly while you’re working.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 3 I’m attaching the rectangular tabs all around the center portion of the
planter, so I size up my first tab and score the planter where the tab will
attach. With a small amount of slip, I adhere the shaped piece to the planter
with careful compressions, and I use my slip brush to clean up my
attachment. [F] [G] Repeat until all of your shapes are attached in the
desired pattern and cover your planter with plastic to slowly dry over the
next several days. Slow drying is key.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 4 Once your planter has been carefully dried and refined, you can
prepare it for bisque firing. [H]
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 5 Now, it’s time to glaze. Your attachment pieces can be finished in
whatever color palette and combinations you dream of. I went for a rainbow
effect, painting each rectangular tab in a different color. You could pick a
single color glaze or alternate colors on each tab like I have. Pick your own
designs and colors. I’m brushing the glazes on with a paintbrush that is
about the same width as my attachment shapes. [I] Most of my glazes need
three coats of application.





STEP 6 Clean up any drips or glaze from around the edges of your glazed
attachment shapes with a small sponge and prepare your piece for the kiln.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
STEP 7 Once your planter is fired, find the right plant that needs a new home
and admire your handiwork! [J] [K]

text:
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Emily Reinhardt is a ceramic artist
and designer whose work focuses on
beautiful, functional ceramic objects
for the home. In her studio in the
Crossroads Arts District of Kansas
City, Missouri, Emily designs and
builds by hand a variety of one-of-a-
kind art objects, including plates,
vases, wall hangings, tumblers,
mugs, goblets, and trays. Her
modern, unfussy aesthetic features
perfectly imperfect shapes and
stunning surface design techniques,
such as striking glazes, touches of
gold luster, bold patterns, texture,
and raised effects. Emily founded
The Object Enthusiast in 2011 and
continues to grow a loyal community of customers and students, teaching
classes online through Skillshare as well as in person at her studio. She is
also the cofounder of her shop, Duet, and of The Ekru Project, an art gallery
and curatorial project, both of which share a space with her Crossroads
studio. Emily lives in Kansas City, Missouri. To see more of her work, visit
theobjectenthusiast.com and @theobjectenthusiast on Instagram, Facebook,
and Skillshare.

text: Hello, I’m Kara.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
I’ve been making pottery for nearly 20 years, and at the time of
writing this I’ve been a full-time potter for 9 years. That doesn’t
even seem possible, but  it’s true. I’m predominantly a self-taught
potter. I’ve had my work stocked in Fortnum & Mason. I’ve made
plates for a Michelin-starred restaurant. I’ve taught hundreds of
people pottery via workshops both in person and online via my
Pottery Club. And I’m the author of Pottery for Beginners.
A few years ago, I was searching for a good pottery notebook but
couldn’t find one, so I created my own. Here it is. This notebook
began as a way of keeping notes of my own kiln firings. Originally it
was just in digital format, but as time went on, I knew how much
my fellow potters would benefit from this tool and how useful it
would be to make it into a real-life book that you can hold in your
hands. It has evolved to include a ton of information on how to
make your firings more successful, as well as an area to record your
making processes too.
This notebook is a companion tool for all your pottery adventures.
Keeping a pottery notebook doesn’t just help you get excellent,
repeatable results; it’s also a lovely way to look back at your skill
progression. Treat it like an artist’s sketchbook or diary with added
useful data. I hope this will always be your go-to notebook and a
place to keep your notes for reference and posterity.




    TIP FOR ELECTRIC KILN OWNERS
     In this notebook there are 120 pages to record 120 firings. The
    average set of kiln elements lasts 100 firings. It’s a great idea to
     start a new notebook when you get a new kiln or a new set of
    elements. When you’re nearing the end of your notebook  is
   when your elements might be wearing out and need changing.

This section is designed for you to keep sketches and notes of your

PRO TIPS
• Sketch out designs in clay as well as on paper. This will help you

• Keep a prototype of each design you are happy with. This will help

text:
Calculating Shrinkage Rates
Everything you make will shrink approximately 10 to 20 percent on
average from the wet raw clay to final firing. It’s important to know
how much. Most manufacturers list the shrinkage rate of the clay on
their packaging, but you can also calculate it by making a shrinkage
ruler.
Roll out a slab of your clay ¼ inch (0.6 cm) thick. Using a plastic
ruler as a template, cut out two ruler shapes. Mark on them the
inches or centimeters. Then leave them to dry. Pop one ruler in the
glaze firing and one in the bisque. Then measure your fired rulers
and compare them to the original to see the shrinkage rate of your
clay  at  the  different  stages  of making. When recording the
dimensions of your greenware, make sure you record whether
it is freshly thrown, leather hard or bone dry.
Formula
100% - [(Fired Ruler Length / Original Ruler Length) × 100]% =
shrinkage percentage
Example
Original Ruler Length: 30 cm
Fired Ruler Length: 27 cm
27 / 30 = 0.9 × 100 = 90
Shrinkage rate = 100% – 90% = 10%

state—fresh out of the bag. The ruler next to it shows the clay in its bone

on  the  far  right (though not  glazed) has been  fired  to glazeware

text:
Calculating Specific Gravity
Measuring the specific gravity of your glaze is a way of checking
you have the correct  ratio of water to glaze material. This  is
especially relevant for dipping glazes and for those who make their
own glazes from raw materials based on a recipe.
Specific gravity has to do with the “fit” of the glaze. Imagine the
glaze is like clothing that the clay wears. If there is too much glaze
material in the glaze, the clothing may become too tight. Put stress
on the clay (such as pouring in hot water), and the clothing may
tear. This can create faults in your pottery, such as a crack. Too
little glaze material in the glaze and it may become too weak. This
may make  it very powdery before  it’s fired and chip easily. The
color of the glaze may also come out wishy-washy or brown.
Most glazes work best between 1.4 and 1.6, but there are exceptions
to this. Only by testing will you find the correct specific gravity of
your glaze. You can measure specific gravity using a graduated
cylinder and a digital scale. Note: Make sure you  stir the glaze
really well before measuring.
Specific Gravity Formula
Weight in grams of glaze / Volume in ml of the glaze
Example
700 grams / 500 ml = 1.4
Keeping the specific gravity of your glaze consistent at a ratio you
know works well will help you to reproduce good glaze results.
 • If your specific gravity is too high, you need to add water. Do this
  gradually, recalculating the gravity in between.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
•  If your  specific gravity  is too low, you can add more glaze
  material or you can allow the glaze to settle overnight and syphon
  off some of the water.
                      OceanofPDF.com

text:
Calculating Cost of Firings
If your kiln controller does not give you information on KW usage or
cost,  here’s a formula  to help you!  You’ll need the following
information:
 • Cost of electricity per kilowatt hour (kWh) – These vary from
  location to location, so make sure to look up your local electricity
   tariff.
 • Kilowatt rating of the kiln – This is normally written on a metal
  panel on the side of the kiln.
 • Program duration in hours.
 • Duty cycle of the kiln – The elements are not on for the entire
  firing cycle. A duty cycle of the kiln  is the amount of time
  electricity  is actually passing through the elements, when the
  relays are turned on. You will hear when the relays turn on and
   off by the clicks. A duty cycle is typically 60%. You would express
  this value as a decimal, e.g., 0.6.
Formula
(Cost of electricity per kilowatt hour) × (kilowatt rating of the kiln)
× (program duration in hours) × (duty cycle of the kiln)
Example
$0.35 × 7.5 × 8 hours × 0.6 = $12.60
   PRO TIP
    Take photos of your pots and put them into a digital folder
     labeled with the corresponding number of your firing and the
     date. It’s a great idea to take a photo of your cones too so you
    can have a visual reference of the heat work without needing to
    keep all your cones.

text:
Firing Glossary
Heat work: Heat work is the combined effect of heat over a period
of time. As potters, we are much more concerned with heat work
versus purely temperature. It takes the accumulation of heat over a
period of time for clay and glaze to absorb the heat work it needs to
become ceramic. A bit like in your home oven, we can either cook
something at a high temperature for a shorter period of time or at a
low temperature for a longer period of time.
Top temperature: This  is the highest temperature the kiln will
reach during your firing.
Schedule: This is the temperature you want your kiln to get to and
how fast you want it to get there. It can be slow, medium or fast on
a manual or gas kiln, or it may be done in ramps (see below for
explanation of ramp) on a digital controller.
Ramp: This refers to how many degrees per hour your kiln will heat
up as programmed into its digital controller (e.g., 212°F [100°C] per
hour).
Soak: This refers to holding the top temperature for a period of time
(normally in 15-minute increments) to help even out the heat work
throughout the kiln. The middle of a kiln tends to be hottest, with
cooler shelves at the bottom. You may want to add a soak to a glaze
firing to even out the temperature, making sure all shelves reach the
same cone. Or pack the kiln more heavily in the middle. This is
especially useful in larger kilns. For example: For my large 117-liter
kiln,  I add a 15-minute soak at 2183°F (1195°C) for my cone 6
firings. This evens out the temperature throughout my kiln before
the firing then climbs to its final temperature of 2232°F (1222°C).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Vitrification (or maturity): Clay and glaze remain porous and
relatively weak until they are fired to their vitrification temperature.
You need your pots to be glazed, fired and vitrified or fired to
maturity in order to hold your coffee. It is important to note the
firing temperature of your clay and glazes when you buy them, as
this will inform the temperature the kiln must be fired to. Your clay
and glaze temperatures must always be within the same  firing
range.





Element wear: Elements generally last between 50 to 150 firings
(average being 100), but this varies depending on things such as the
temperature you fire to and the glazes you use. Hotter firings wear
elements quicker. A potter using cone 10 porcelain may need to
change their elements sooner than a potter using cone 6 stoneware.
As the elements in a kiln age, your firings will likely take longer,
and it will take more energy to pass a current through the element.
Eventually, they might not even be able to reach temperature at all!
The longer your firings take and the longer elements spend at a
higher temperature, the more they wear. Certain materials in glaze
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
recipes will also wear your elements more than others. Keeping
peepholes open until 1112°F (600°C) can help elements last longer
as this allows corrosive vapors to escape. Having a downdraft vent
will help pull vapors out of the kiln and away from elements,
making them last longer.
Using cones and keeping accurate notes of how long your firings are
taking will help you predict when you need to change your elements
—which is much better than getting caught out a week before your
next craft market! Other parts of a kiln can wear out too such as the
thermocouple and relays. Keeping a record of how many firings
your kiln has done will help you maintain your kiln’s health and
ensure it keeps firing consistently.

text: What Are Cones?
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Cones are made of ceramic material just like your clay and glazes.
They are designed to melt and bend at very specific temperatures
according to how much heat work they have been exposed to during
a firing.
In most modern digital kilns, temperature is measured by the kiln’s
thermocouple  at a  single spot  in the  kiln and  is displayed  in
Fahrenheit or Celsius on your kiln’s digital controller.
As we know, heat work takes things a step further and  is the
accumulative  effect that temperature has over a period  of  time.
Pyrometric cones are the only real way of reading the heat
work your pottery has absorbed. They may sound technical, but
they are a useful little tool for all potters.
Some clays and glazes have a wide firing range, while others need
much more accuracy to get the desired results. So many issues we
encounter as potters have to do with what goes on inside our kiln
(e.g., if your glazes ran during a firing, this could mean the glaze
was applied too thickly or your kiln overfired). Cones help us
understand if we have underfired, overfired or reached our desired
heat work. If the cones look good, we can rule out the firing as an
issue. By using cones in all our glaze firings, accurately recording
our processes and results, we can identify issues and replicate good
results next time.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Small cone on the left compared to a large standard cone in the middle
and a self-supporting cone on the right.





A cone pack consisting of cone 4, cone 5 and cone 6.
Types of Cones
Cones range from cone 022 very low temperature to cone 14 very
high temperature. See cone charts here for equivalent temperatures.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Small Cones and Bar Cones: These are used in a kiln sitter in a
manual kiln. These bend and drop the lever to shut off the kiln
when    it  has  reached  temperature.  They  cannot  be  used
interchangeably with standard or self-supporting cones. Note: I won’t be
referring to these throughout this book as they bend differently than
standard or self-supporting cones. If you use a manual kiln, I still
recommend using standard or self-supporting cones to record the
heat work in your firings.
Standard Cones: These are referred to as witness cones, as they are
literally  “witnessing  the  firing.” These can be  stood  in  small
sausages of clay to create a cone pack. (See How to Use Cones to
learn how to make a cone pack.)
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Three cone 7 self-supporting cones.
Self-Supporting Cones: These are also referred to as witness cones,
but they have a small additional triangle at the base, which means
they stand up on their own and do not need clay sausages. They are
a little more expensive, but you can always be sure they are at the
correct angle, and they don’t need to be placed into clay.
I  will be  referring  to both standard and  self-supporting cones
interchangeably throughout this notebook.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text: How to Use Cones
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Always use the cones that match the temperature of the glazes and
clay you are using.
Be careful: Cone 06 and cone 6 are very different!
 • A cone 6 will bend at around 2232°F (1222°C) depending upon the
  speed of the firing. This is a mid-fire or low stoneware.
 • Cone 06 will bend at around 1830°F (999°C), so it is for low-fire or
  earthenware.
To use cones, you normally use three. This is called a “cone pack.”
For a cone 6 firing you would use cone 5, cone 6 and cone 7.





The above image is a 6 cone pack.
 • The Guide Cone (cone 5) is the one to the left.
 • The Target Cone (cone 6) is the middle cone—the heat work or
  cone you are aiming for.
 • The Guard Cone (cone 7) is the one to the right.
Making a Cone Pack
You can put standard large cones into a little sausage of soft clay
(no bigger than the thickness of a pencil). Gently push the cone all
the way through the clay until the base is touching the surface of
the table. This ensures they are sitting at the correct angle, which is
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
determined by the slope of the base. You can squash the clay back
around the base to keep them in place if need be.
Poke the clay with a needle tool (as shown in the image above) to
ensure  any  water  quickly  escapes  in  the  firing  and  avoids
explosions. You can wait until the clay is bone dry before putting it
in the  kiln.  I normally make a whole bunch of cone packs in
advance so they are ready and dry when I need them.
If you are using specifically made cone holders, like the one on here,
make sure the falling face always goes next to the dot. (If you stand
a cone on a table, the falling face is the direction the cone falls.)
   NOTE
      If you try to stand a standard large cone up on its own, it will
      fall over. This is due to the specific angle of the base which,
    with the help of gravity, ensures the cone bends correctly.
    Ensuring the cones are at the correct angle is important. If you
    stand a cone on a table the falling face is the direction the cone
      falls.





The cone pack on the left is correct; note the slight lean to the left. The
cone pack on the right is incorrect; note they are pointing straight up and
won’t bend properly in the firing.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Cone Placement
With gas and wood firings, potters put cone packs near the vents or
peepholes so they can be observed during the firing. This must be
done wearing welding goggles or there is a risk to the eyesight. In
my experience with electric kilns, and certainly those new to firing
their own kilns,  it  is very awkward to get cones in the correct
position and difficult to see them when the kiln is white hot. It’s
best to look at cones retrospectively—that is after the firing.
We need to put the cones far enough away from our work so when
they bend they don’t stick to it. The middle of a kiln shelf is best
and is the most accurate representation of heat work. For larger
kilns, it’s best to put a cone pack on the bottom, middle and top
shelf. For smaller kilns, you shouldn’t get a lot of difference in heat
work between shelves, so one cone pack on the middle shelf will
normally suffice.
   NOTE
    Be careful when handling cones as they are fragile and can
    break easily. Hold the ends and twist them apart. Or hold one
    on the end, flush to the edge of a table and push down on the
     other. See the image below for reference.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Good to know:
 • Cones lose their color after they’ve been fired and turn white. This
   is so that even if the cones haven’t bent, you know they’ve been
  used.
 • You can only use cones once.
 • Specifically made cone holders, like the one on here, are single
  use. As a reminder, the falling face always goes next to the dot.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
How to Read Cones (Have You
Had a Successful Firing?)
You know you have the perfect heat work when the guide cone
(left) melts  first and  likely melts completely. The  target cone
(middle) will bend over next in an elegant arc. The guard cone
(right) will remain straight or only start to bend slightly.





This firing has reached a perfect cone 6.





Contrary to popular belief, the tip does not have to touch the kiln shelf.
Example of Overfiring
Image 1 shows that the firing was too hot. These cones absorbed too
much heat work. The glazes and clay in this kiln load may show
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
signs of overfiring (e.g., running, blistering, bloating, etc.).
How to fix:  I’ll need to reduce the temperature of the kiln next
time, speed up the firing, remove the soak or a combination of all
three.





Overfiring: All the cones, including the guard cone, have melted and bent
all the way over.
Example of Underfiring
Image 2 shows the work on  this  shelf  didn’t  quite reach the
temperature I wanted. This tells me my pottery and cones did not
absorb enough heat work to vitrify cone 6 clay and glazes.
How to fix: I’ll need to increase the top temperature of my firing
schedule, slow down the firing or add a soak onto the end of my
firing next time.
The key is in the tip of the cone. If the tip is still angled up, it hasn’t
quite reached the temperature range required. Once the  tip  is
pointing down, the melt of the cone is quite rapid.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Underfiring: Note that the middle cone, cone 6 which is the target cone,
has only bent a little bit. This was more like a cone 5.5 firing.
PRO TIP
The difference between the bend in these two cones represents only
about 35 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius)!





Note the tip is touching the table.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Note the tip is pointing down but hasn’t quite touched the table. As long
as your tip is angled down you are within the target cone tolerance.
You will need to put cones in  all glaze  firings to ensure your
adjustments have had the desired effect and maintain consistency.
Don’t forget to record what you did and your results straight away
in your notebook!
   GOOD TO KNOW
    You don’t need to put cones in all your bisque firings. Our goal
      is not to vitrify our pottery during bisque firings, so it’s not as
     critical    to   ensure  we   have   reached   a    specific
    temperature/amount of heat work.





Variables that can affect heat work:
 • The peak temperature the kiln reached.
 • The period of time the work is in the kiln.
 • The amount of work in the firing. Tightly packed kilns take longer
  to heat up so the time variable needs to increase, but the top
  temperature will need to be adjusted lower to reach the required
  heat work value.
 • How the shelves are placed. Ensuring shelves are well distributed
  throughout the kiln will help it to heat evenly.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
• Some kilns tend to be hotter in the middle. Stacking the middle of
  the kiln more densely with work will help to even out the heat
  work.
Glaze only starts to melt in the final 212°F (100°C) of a firing. Note
the Heating Rate on the cone chart here. This refers to the ramp
used ONLY during the final 212°F (100°C) of the firing.
Slower firings can give more interesting glaze results as it has given
the glazes more time to “mature” (when all the ingredients in the
glaze melt and mingle together). Remember a slower firing will use
more energy.
To get the benefit of a slow firing while also using less energy, it’s
possible to use a relatively fast-firing schedule and then slow the
ramp in the final 212°F (100°C). Alternatively, you could add a soak
period onto the end of your firing. A 15- to 20-minute hold  is
roughly equal to one cone’s worth of heat. You may need to lower
the top temperature to compensate for the additional time, but not
always.
To recap:
 • Putting cones in every glaze firing will help you best understand
  how your kiln is firing.
 • Always refer to the cone chart here to make sure you are using the
  correct cones for your glazes.
 • Cones will always bend in a consistent way in reaction to the heat
  and time they are exposed to in the kiln. From batch to batch they
  are carefully tested by the manufacturer for accuracy.
 • Commercial glazes and clays will always have the cone or firing
  temperature displayed on the packaging.
A quick note about glaze and food safety:
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
One major way (but not the only way) to ensure pottery is safe to
use with food is to make sure the clay and glazes you use become
fully matured (or cooked) during the firing. This means colorant
oxides become chemically bound into the glaze and are unlikely to
leach out. Keeping accurate notes and using cones in your firings to
ensure you reached the desired heat work are two due diligences
that potters can employ.
Other ways include but are not exclusive to:
 • Only use commercial glazes labeled as lead free and food or
  dinnerware safe.
 • Do not use glaze with lots of texture for surfaces which come in
  contact with food.
 •  If you make your own glazes,  it’s best to steer clear of toxic
  ingredients such as lead, cadmium, barium and lithium.
 • Use color oxides in low percentages (<3%).

text:
Kiln Schedules
There are no one-size-fits-all kiln schedules. The heat work achieved
in your firing relies on many variables. You will need to test some
schedules out to determine the correct firing for your work.





It is to be expected to need to test a new kiln or any new glazes to find
the best schedule for your desired result.
Most firings in an electric kiln (except for luster and decal) take
between 8 to 12 hours and then at least an additional 24 hours to
cool down depending on the size of the kiln. Small kilns tend to cool
faster.
For safety reasons, it is always best to wait until it has cooled to
room temperature before unloading.
New kilns come with a manual and recommended firing schedules.
If you bought your kiln secondhand or don’t have the manual, here
are  some  suggested  general  schedules  for  kilns  with  digital
controllers. These should be used as a starting point as all kilns fire
slightly differently. Even kilns of the same brand and of a similar
size can vary. You may need to adjust these schedules depending on
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the clay and glaze you are using and your desired results. For
example, my small 45-liter kiln is so well insulated, it achieves a
cone 6 firing with a top temperature of 2183°F (1195°C).
   NOTE
   A slower firing schedule with a lower top temperature can have
     similar  heat  work  as  a  fast  schedule  at  a  higher  top
    temperature. Which works best for your work depends on the
    type of kiln you use, the clay, glazes, how the kiln is packed
    and the aesthetic you are looking for.





Fast firing





Slow firing
For example, both of these pots were fired in my kiln in two
separate   firings  on   different  schedules  with   different  top
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
temperatures and ramps. They are the same glaze and the same
clay. They have produced a similar result. Both are vitrified, but the
glaze on the right (in the slower firing) has a slightly better result
(in my opinion) as the glaze ingredients have had more time to
mingle and mature.
The mug on the left
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 392°F (200°C) per hour to 2264°F (1240°C) (top temp)
   • No soak
   • 7¾ hours approximately (depending on the age of your elements
   —see here)
The mug on the right
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 392°F (200°C) per hour to 2057°F (1125°C)
   • Ramp 3: 140°F (60°C) per hour to 2228°F (1220°C) (top temp)
   • 20-minute soak
   • 9 hours approximately (depending on the age of your elements—
    see here)
Kiln Schedule Examples
Ghost Firing
This is a firing for a new kiln or a new set of elements. This includes
furniture—shelves and stilts—but without any pottery. This helps
oxidize the elements and protect them from fumes and water vapor
damage during  future  firings. Note:  Please  refer  to your  kiln
manufacturer’s manual in the first instance as recommended ghost
firings can vary by brand.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
• Ramp 1: 176°F (80°C) per hour to 1112°F (600°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 1922°F (1050°C)
   • 1½-hour soak
   • Vents open throughout
Bisque
For bisque firings, you want to take it slow as there may be residual
moisture left in the clay. With the bisque firing we do not need to
vitrify the clay, but only make it less brittle so it is easier to handle
while glazing. Normally, potters will bisque to between 1652 and
1940°F (900 and 1060°C).
   • Ramp 1: 176°F (80°C) per hour to 1112°F (600°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 1922°F (1050°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Vents open throughout
Earthenware Glaze Firing
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 2102°F (1150°C)
   • No soak
   • Close vents at 1112°F (600°C)
Fast Stoneware Glaze Firing—Cone 6
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 2228°F (1220°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Close vents at 1112°F (600°C)
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Slow Stoneware Glaze Firing—Cone 8
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 2050°F (1121°C)
   • Ramp 3: 140°F (60°C) per hour to 2246°F (1230°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Close vents at 1112°F (600°C)
Slow Cool Schedule for Crystalline Glazes
Add this ramp to the end of either a Fast or Slow Stoneware Glaze
Firing.
   • Drop: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 1940°F (1060°C)
   • Hold: 1.5 hours
   • Cool naturally
Gold Luster Firing—Cone 018
Always refer to luster manufacturer instructions.
   • Ramp 1: 392°F (200°C) per hour to 1274–1292°F (690–700°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Vents open throughout
Over Glaze Decals Firing—Cones 011–012
Always refer to decal manufacturer instructions.
   • Ramp 1: 338°F (170°C) per hour to 788°F (420°C)
   • Ramp 2: 392°F (200°C) per hour to 1616°F (880°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Vents open throughout

text:
Pottery, Efficiency and the Environment
Pottery has an impact on the planet. Keeping accurate notes using
this notebook for all your firings ensures your work will be more
successful. Fewer dud pots means happier potters but also fewer
refires and less waste. Here are some tips to maximize our efficiency
and minimize our environmental impact.
   • When buying a kiln, choose one with the thickest insulation; it
    will be more energy efficient.
   • Firing a full kiln is more energy efficient than firing a half-empty
     kiln. Always fire your kilns full. Tumble stack your bisque. As
    the pottery is unglazed, work can touch and be stacked together
    in the kiln. Make sure you leave a little wiggle room so pieces
    don’t crack each other. Glazed work cannot touch each other, or
      it will stick together!
   • Ensure your work is fully dried before putting it in your kiln.
    This includes after glazing. I always wait 24 hours after glazing
    before loading my kiln.
   • Excess moisture wears your elements quicker and as a result
    they use more energy (not to mention may cause explosions).
   • Fast glaze firings are more energy efficient. When it comes to
    kiln schedules,  it’s a balancing act of using the most energy-
    efficient firing schedule possible while still getting your desired
     results.  There  are  critical  points  of  the  firing where  it’s
    important to go slow, e.g., at the beginning and at the end. Start
    slow, speed it up and slow down again at the end.
   • Your  pots could be around  for  the next 1,000  years! Be
    discerning. Bad work equals landfill. Not every pot needs to be
     fired. Only chose your best work to  fire. Reclaim the  rest.
   Encourage your students to do the same.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
• Clay and glazes are mined. Their production has an impact on
  the planet. Ask your pottery supplier where your clay and glaze
  materials come from. Ask  if oxides are responsibly sourced.
  Choose clay sourced from within your country, if possible.
• Use a “three bucket glaze reclaim system.” Rinse all your glazing
  tools in one bucket, then dip a second time in the next bucket. A
  dip in the third bucket should come out clean. Once the first
  bucket  is full of glaze material, use this as a mystery glaze.
  Alternatively, evaporate all the water, fire it in a sacrificial pot
 and throw it away.
• Ensure your local energy is from 100% renewables. This is not
  the same as “backed by” 100% renewable energy.
• Vacuum your kiln every few firings. Dust and debris which
  inevitably build up over time will make the elements work
  harder.

Preface
From the perspective of the anthropology of art, and embedded in a global
academic context, this work allows one to recognize that “history is, in
large measure, the record of human activity which spreads from the local to
the regional, from the regional to the global, and from the global to the
universal.” From reading The History of Chinese Ceramics, you will find it
evident that China was not only the first country to create porcelain but also
the first to export it to the world—both the product and its technology. The
History of Chinese Ceramics thus relives the history of China’s foreign
trade while at the same time depicting the expansion of Chinese ceramic
technology and culture. This expansion was a learning process in which
different nations were able to grow by absorbing and disseminating each
other’s civilization and culture. It demonstrates that China was not a closed
and isolated country but rather interacted with many other nations.
Moreover, China’s multiple ethnicities contributed to the various cultures
that made Chinese ceramics what they are today. In China, ceramics were
not simply tableware but played an active role in ritual, religion, the
scholar’s studio, and many other cultural institutions. Hence, they are
utensils as well as symbols of culture. Understanding the use, production,
and international export of Chinese ceramics is invaluable for the
comprehension of the history of China’s society, art, aesthetic ideology,
technical expertise, lifestyle, foreign trade, and civilization itself. As a
result, a knowledge of the history of Chinese ceramics is of great
importance to grasping the essence of Chinese culture and aesthetics.
    Translated by
                                          Andrew Maske
                                                           Beijing, China

text:
Introduction—Viewing Ceramics History
Through the Lens of the Anthropology of Art: A
New Approach

Overview
To view arts and crafts history and theories from the perspective of the
anthropology of art has long been my aspiration. This aspiration was the
reason why, after gaining my Ph.D. in history at the Central Academy of
Craft Art (now the Academy of Arts and Design at Tsinghua University) in
1996, I applied for a postdoctoral position at the Institute of Sociology and
Anthropology at Peking University, where I received basic training in
anthropology. The postdoctoral program ended in 1998, and since, then I
have been engaged in research on the anthropology of art. I undertook an
extended period of field research in Jingdezhen, where, with the ceramics-
making history and production practice of craftsmen as case studies, I
examined the transformation and restructuring of traditional crafts in
modern society. Later, I took on a national key research project on folk
culture resources in Western China. I studied the folk arts of Shaanxi
Province on-site, including the folk ceramics of Chenluzhen, and visited
Guizhou Province to study how the hmongb rongt people’s cultural life and
arts heritage were appropriated as resources.1 Long periods of field research
gave me new understandings of and new theoretical approaches to the
relation between arts and socio-cultural development, the interaction
between arts and people’s modes of production and lifestyles, the
relationship between arts and the social and aesthetic values of different
eras, and the mutual promotion between the Great Tradition and the Little
Tradition in art.
   That was when the idea of rewriting arts and crafts history using the
perspective of the anthropology of art occurred to me. Naturally, I would
not be so ambitious as to take on the task of rewriting the entire history of
arts and crafts. My intention was to focus on the history of one particular art
and craft form, and the one I was most familiar with was the history of
ceramics. I studied at the Arts Department of the Jingdezhen Ceramic
Institute, gained my Ph.D. in the history of arts and crafts in the History
Department of the Central Academy of Craft Art, and then did postdoctoral
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
studies at the Institute of Sociology and Anthropology at Peking University,
where I chose Jingdezhen folk kilns as the subject of my research and
produced the report Traditions and Changes—Field Research on the Old
and New Folk Kilns of Jingdezhen as my graduation thesis. Later, I wrote
Jingdezhen Folk Kilns and Old Town Gone—Past Stories of the Ceramics
Capital. These three works totaled nearly one million words. Since the
Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties, the development of China’s ceramics
industry has been centered on Jingdezhen; especially since the Ming and
Qing dynasties, since after that Jingdezhen has basically been the sole
leading kiln center while all other kilns remained secondary. The research I
conducted on the history and status of Jingdezhen ceramics laid the
foundation for my compilation of The History of Chinese Ceramics.
Professor Tian Zibing, my Ph.D. supervisor, decided to compile The
Complete History of Chinese Craft Arts in 1997 and assigned me to
document ceramics history as part of that work. It took me three years to
finish the first draft. But for a number of reasons, The Complete History of
Chinese Craft Arts was never published. Then in 2007, Qilu Publishing
House invited me to submit a manuscript on ceramics history. At that time,
I had just completed the research project on folk culture in Western China,
so I spent years revising and modifying the first draft which I wrote during
my doctoral studies before submitting this final version.
     I relate the above story to make two points: that this history of Chinese
ceramics is written from the perspective of the anthropology of art, and that
the work was initially intended to be part of The Complete History of
Chinese Craft Arts. The latter is also why the book, viewing ceramics
primarily as one major craft art in Chinese history, examines the artistic
characteristics of ceramics in different historical periods and the
contributing factors to those characteristics, notably, how emperors, literati,
and craftsmen in different dynasties expressed their spiritual pursuits and
aesthetic preferences through colorful ceramic ware.
    In writing this work, much of my attention and effort was concentrated
on how to observe and understand ceramics as a craft art using the approach
of the anthropology of art. In art anthropological studies, “one needs to
know where the art was made, who made it, what its use was, what its
