concepts of “Great Tradition” and “Little Tradition.” Great Tradition refers
to the tradition of the introspective minority in a civilization, and Little
Tradition refers to the tradition of the non-introspective majority. Great
Tradition is nurtured in the school or the church, while Little Tradition
grows and exists in the life of village communities. This pair of concepts is
similar to the concepts of “elite culture and mass culture,” “refined culture
and popular culture,” and “sacred culture and secular culture.” Using these
concepts, we can see that over time, Chinese ceramics basically progressed
from elite culture to mass culture, from refined culture to popular culture,
and from sacred culture to secular culture. I believe there are two reasons
for this.
    Firstly, urbanization and commercialization promoted the development
of a market economy and the rising urban popular culture, and the arts were
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
liberated from divine ceremonies and rituals enabling them to enter people’s
everyday lives as objects of appreciation. Redfield stresses the impact of
Great Tradition on Little Tradition. He believes that in modern civilizations
urban, areas represent Great Tradition while rural areas represent Little
Tradition, and that with the progress of civilization, the countryside is
inevitably “eaten away” and “assimilated” by cities.29 Following such
views, it could be said that Chinese society began moving toward
modernity after the Yuan Dynasty, and the secularization of ceramic art was
one of the signs of this migration.
   Secondly, the inflow of Western culture also contributed to the
secularization of ceramic art. European porcelain traders started placing
orders with Jingdezhen folk kilns in the mid to late Ming Dynasty. In
addition to purchasing varieties, Jingdezhen was already making, these
traders requested the craftsmen to design a large number of new models and
patterns suited to the culture, customs, and aesthetic tastes of Western
customers to better cater to foreign market needs. Craftsmen in Jingdezhen
had to create, based on the required shapes and decorative patterns, which
in turn gave rise to new styles and varieties of Jingdezhen ceramics.
   European culture also influenced the aesthetic preference of China’s
imperial court. For instance, Emperor Qianlong of the Qing Dynasty not
only invited European artists to serve the royal family in the palace and to
participate in the architectural design of the Yuanmingyuan imperial garden
but also gave orders to set up an “Enamel Workshop” in the “Zaobanchu”
(Office of Manufacture) where European artists created porcelain-body
enamel together with Chinese painters and craftsmen. Additionally, many of
the porcelain wares fired by the Jingdezhen imperial kilns were made
following the drawings and designs provided by painters of the
“Zaobanchu,” the “Ruyiguan” (Institute of Indulgence, an agency tasked
with investigating Western scientific achievements) and the “Qintianjian”
(the Imperial Board of Astronomy) in the palace. European artists in the
imperial palace worked with Chinese painters and craftsmen daily,
influencing and inspiring each other. It was partly due to the impact of
European art that Chinese ceramics, with Jingdezhen at its center, assumed
a flowery, ornate, and overly elaborate style, which after the mid-Qing
Dynasty replaced simple and natural beauty to become the main pursuit of
Chinese ceramic art and remained the mainstream trend until the end of the
Qing and even into the Republican era.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Anthropological research has traditionally aimed most of its attention at
remote Indigenous tribes. In such isolated communities with little contact
with the outside world, cultural evolution probably only involves the
ideological component, the sociological component, and the technological
component. But for an open and civilized society, there is yet another
component, namely, external information, and influences. The earlier we go
back in history, the more closed human society has been and the less
intercultural communication has occurred. Back then, the effect of the
information component was weak and social mobility was low. As mankind
approached modernity or the modern era, communication between countries
or regions became more frequent and social mobility speeded up. From the
Ming and Qing dynasties, with the development of foreign exchange and
trade, the development of China’s ceramic art inevitably accelerated and
moved toward commercialization and secularization, a transition in which
the role of the information component could not be ignored.

Understanding Chinese Society Through Ceramic History
Ancient China as a Plebeian Society
Influenced by Western evolutionary theory, previous researchers, especially
those around the founding of New China, mostly believed that all societies
progressed along the same line from primitive society to slave society,
feudal society, capitalist society, socialist society, and ultimately communist
society. When looking at Chinese society, however, people found that such
an historical progression did not always apply. The traditional view is that
from the Qin and Han dynasties to the end of the Qing Dynasty China was a
feudal society. Yet scholars represented by Qian Mu believe that in the Qin
and Han dynasties China began a transformation from ancient aristocratic
society to a plebeian society rather than a feudal society, a view that is
evidenced in the study of the history of Chinese ceramics.
   One example is the maturity of Chinese porcelain in the Eastern Han
Dynasty, which I believe was not the arbitrary result of technological
advances but was more closely related to the cultural trends at the time, and
specifically, the social emphasis on the literati and the general social disdain
for luxurious lifestyles. Before the Han Dynasty Chinese society was
centered around the aristocratic class who led extremely extravagant lives
and used bronze, gold, silver, and lacquerwares as daily utensils, while
ceramics, used only by common people as daily necessities or ritual objects,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
did not occupy a significant position in aristocratic life and was therefore
not taken seriously by the court. But when it came to the Han Dynasty,
especially the Eastern Han, the life of the rich was constrained, and the use
of luxury objects as daily utensils was no longer encouraged. This is where
porcelain wares came in. Simple, mild, but noble, with a jade-like texture,
porcelain accorded perfectly with the aesthetic of the Chinese literati. The
earliest porcelain wares were mainly used as burial objects, but as firing
techniques matured, porcelain products grew to be more pleasing to the eye
and more practical. Thus, they became more common in the everyday lives
of the royal family, aristocrats, dignitaries, officials, and common people.
They entered every corner of the Chinese people’s lives and became the
most important daily utensil in Chinese history.
  A more important factor influencing the development of ceramics was
the Imperial Examination System created during the Tang Dynasty. The
examination system offered grassroots men an opportunity to enter the
supreme political realm through study and examination. Most of these men
were from the countryside. Qian Mu states: “That is because the rural
environment was the best breeding ground for ideal talent, one that had
genius, knowledge, aspiration, and good ethics. Urban society, bustling with
industry and commerce, was not an ideal place for the nurturing of such
people. They entered the government from the countryside and then
returned to the countryside from government. Many famous figures across
different dynasties, having accomplished outstanding achievements in
politics, retreated to the rural quiet to enjoy the rest of their lives
surrounded by beautiful landscapes and fertile lands. Such choices resulted
from the literary and artistic edification they received during their early
years in the countryside. Even those who remained in cities after retirement
somehow turned their surrounding environments rustic and country-like. It
was almost mandatory that retired scholar-bureaucrats would incorporate in
their residences some small garden architectural feature with vivid rural
overtones and a strong interest in nature.”30 In this way, the seeds of
traditional culture remained in rural areas across the country, with its roots
growing deeper and deeper and its branches reaching higher and higher.
With the Imperial Examination System as the motivation, all villages in the
country produced aspiring men who studied hard, and as a result now
almost every place in China boasts famous historical figures and historic
sites. The countryside became the incubation chamber of Chinese culture.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
The significance of the Imperial Examination System to ceramics was
amplified by the fact that before the Ming Dynasty, when ceramic
production became a specialized urban profession, potters were also
farmers and their lives involved both ceramic production and farming.
Thus, the abovementioned rural-incubated culture was bound to influence
the artistic creation of potters at the time, which was beneficial to the
development of the ceramics industry because ceramics were not only
practical commodities but also handicraft works that embodied the thought,
interests, and philosophies of the Chinese literati. Progress of the handicraft
industry and commerce promoted the production and circulation of ceramic
products while progress in literature and the arts elevated their artistic taste.
    Inscriptions first appeared on the porcelain wares of the Changsha kilns
in the Tang Dynasty. The inscriptions included ware names as well as words
and poems promoting the ware, with poems being the most prevalent. For
products of the Changsha kilns, poems were mostly inscribed below the
spout of bell mouth pots, and some on amphora bellies, saucer centers, or
pillow surfaces. The poems or sentences, mostly originating from folk
poetry and proverbs, and rarely containing allusions, were easy to
understand. The inscriptions, engraved by craftsmen for the use of the
common people, also led to the plebeian trajectory of the written language
and calligraphy, the mastering of which were no longer the privilege of
imperial aristocrats or the cultural elite. This makes the following statement
by Qian Mu much easier to understand: “Ancient literature was more used
by the aristocratic society, followed by religion; ancient arts were more used
in religion, followed by the aristocratic society. This all changed in the Tang
Dynasty, when literature and arts started serving the everyday lives of
common people. This was a major leap forward in the history of Chinese
culture.”31 This statement is fully reflected in the porcelain art of the Tang
Dynasty.
    Porcelain had always been favored by the literati, aristocrats and
common people for its simplicity and jade-like texture, and in the Song
Dynasty, it replaced metal wares in the royal family’s sacrificial ceremonies
to Heaven and Earth as it was deemed to represent “quality and sincerity.”
This shows that the Chinese people chose to use ceramic wares not by
chance but based on certain values. In fact, an artificial creation is never
solely technological; there are always cultural reasons behind it.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
After the Qin and Han dynasties, China was transformed from an
aristocratic society featuring a hereditary system to a plebeian society.
Then, the inception of the Imperial Examination System gave common
people a chance to become government officials through study and
examination, a system which was quite advanced for the time. From its
inception, a dedication to study became the focus of Chinese parental
instruction for succeeding generations. The ancient Chinese aspiration for
and stress on study was well expressed in porcelain decorations, such as the
typical images of “Reading while grazing the cattle with one’s book hung
on the bull’s horn” and “Fishing, woodcutting, plowing, and reading.”
These images also depicted the basic lifestyle of the early Chinese. They
chose to do farm work while studying because on the one hand they
yearned for the simple and free pastoral life, while on the other they aspired
to enter the government and fulfill their political ambitions. From a
sociological point of view, although the social structure of ancient China
was strictly stratified, the examination system served as a mechanism for
common people to ascend the social ladder and to change their fortunes
through study. While studying, they appreciated artistic performances, craft
arts and decorative images, which were also edifying experiences.
   Through the above examination of ancient Chinese ceramic art, it can
be seen that ancient China was a society of civic-minded individuals, a
society which held simplicity, morality, and knowledge in high regard. This
makes it a much more advanced culture compared to the aristocratic culture
of Europe of the same period.

The Early Maturing Chinese Culture
Liang Shuming believed Chinese culture was an early maturing culture, and
Qian Mu was of the same opinion. He argued that Chinese society had been
an early maturing society from as early as the Qin and Han dynasties when
China had built comprehensive institutional systems. Then in the Sui and
Tang dynasties, China completed the basic systems for all humanistic
creativity in literature and arts.
   This is true of the development of Chinese ceramics. Porcelain
production matured in the Han Dynasty. In the Tang Dynasty, while celadon
kilns were not as widespread as they would later become, Southern kilns
represented by the Yue kilns and Northern ones represented by the Yaozhou
kilns laid the groundwork for the emergence of the many celadon kilns,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
each with their own characteristics, in the Song Dynasty. In addition, the
white porcelain firing technique of the Xing kilns laid the foundation for the
appearance of the Ding kilns’ white porcelain and Jingdezhen’s qingbai
porcelain, egg-white porcelain, and white porcelain after the Song Dynasty.
If not for the emergence of the white porcelain, the polychrome porcelains
of the Yuan, Ming, and Qing would not have flourished. The colorful glaze
ware and black glaze porcelain of the Tang Dynasty laid the foundation for
the flambé glaze wares of the Song Dynasty such as Jun ware, hare-fur
porcelain, oil-spot porcelain, and tortoiseshell glaze ware. Then there is the
tricolor glazed earthenware of the Tang Dynasty, which, though not suitable
as tableware since it was low-fired lead-glazed pottery, but it still aided the
development of glazed tiles which were used in later generations for
building temples and palaces. Products of the Changsha kilns deserve
special attention because their underglaze color painting, inscriptions, and
decoration combining calligraphy and painting, sowed the seed for the
black and white porcelain of the Cizhou kilns in the Song Dynasty, for the
blue and white porcelain of Jingdezhen in the Yuan Dynasty, and for the
blue and white doucai porcelain, wucai porcelain, and famille-rose
porcelain of Jingdezhen in the Ming and Qing dynasties. From all this, it
can be seen that the decorative means and expressive techniques of various
porcelain varieties in later dynasties found their beginnings in the Tang
Dynasty. These beginnings not only refer to technology; it also involved the
formation of cultural ideas and artistic aesthetics. Chinese culture before the
Sui and Tang dynasties, featuring bold and heroic values, lauded the
bravery of soldiers, while after Sui and Tang it moved toward elegance and
gentleness and featured more of a literatus temperament. It could be said
that though ceramics during the Tang Dynasty were not as prosperous as
they were in the Song, the Tang Dynasty, marking the beginning of a new
style, was an important turning point in the history of Chinese ceramic art.
   Liang Shuming believed that the standard of a culture achieving
maturity is the inner rationality of its individuals and in this regard Chinese
culture matured much earlier than Western culture. Western culture has its
roots in religion while Chinese culture, taking a different path, focuses on
morality rather than religion and maintains customs, discipline, and order
through morality.32 Westerners generally believe that religion is the
inevitable experience of a society, yet China has never had a religion in the
real sense apart from primitive religious activities. What happened is that
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
early in Chinese history Confucianism transfigured primitive religions into
rites and music, from which art was born to edify people’s sentiments and
improve people’s self-cultivation. Ceramic wares, as a part of this process,
were both ritual objects and works of art.
   The two major philosophical schools in China, Confucianism and
Taoism, both non-religious, regarded life as their foundation and
emphasized nature rather than artifice. This philosophy is reflected in
Chinese ceramic art’s preference for bringing out the natural beauty of the
material itself, which is considered to be real ingenuity. Chinese pursue the
“union of Heaven and man,” which in artistic practice became the “union of
the object and the soul.” Chinese craftsmen avoid impairing the inner
quality of the object. Rather, they endeavor to bring out the beauty of the
object itself and add radiance to it. Such is the ideal of Chinese craft arts. It
is also why Chinese people often praise craft work as the “secret workings
of nature” or “Heaven’s workings through man’s hand.” These sayings
show that the Chinese refuse to tamper with natural objects through
artificial work. This does not mean that Chinese people are unwilling to
apply human effort. It is just that they do not wish to damage, conquer, or
replace nature with human effort. The goal is always to improve nature
through human effort. Such philosophical thinking started to manifest itself
in the ceramic art of the Tang Dynasty and reached its peak in the Song
Dynasty. During this time, the craftsmen ingeniously took advantage of
material properties themselves to achieve natural beauty effects. These
effects included the glaze colors of azure, light greenish blue and plum
green, the ice crackle pattern, “golden threads and iron lines,” the crab claw
pattern, “purple rim and iron feet,” the flambé glaze of the Jun kilns, and
the earthworm trail pattern.
   The Ancient Chinese liked surrounding themselves with calligraphy,
paintings and poetry and used every opportunity to edify people’s
sentiments through art. Thus, close attention was paid to the decorative
images even on daily utensils made of porcelain, which were often flowers,
birds, fish, and insects, which created a serene and peaceful atmosphere.
Even wares of a single color without decoration were not entirely blank.
They often featured more intricate pursuits in terms of texture. Different art
forms permeate each other, and different philosophies have been expressed
in literature and the arts throughout history. Ceramic art has always been a
critical vessel for philosophical ideas. From Chinese ceramic works we can
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
observe the cultural pursuits of the Chinese people. It can also be seen that
Chinese culture is one that integrates everyday arts with moral concepts and
uses art instead of religion to express a moral orientation. It was an early
maturing culture that was once admired by European society.
   At a certain stage this, early maturing of Chinese society hampered the
country’s pace toward industrialization and as a result, the once strongest
nation in the agricultural era lagged behind when the Western world entered
the industrial era. But today, as mankind enters post-industrial civilization,
material production has reached a certain degree of saturation and the
ecological environment has been seriously damaged. Under these
circumstances, it is being realized increasingly that the artistic ideal of
ancient China, one that advocated nature, worshiped life, and pursued truth,
may offer valuable inspiration for the future development of humankind, a
quest that invites further examination.

Ancient China as a Manufacturing Power
The early maturing of Chinese society contributed to China’s highly
developed handicrafts in the ancient past. Yet China’s industrial
backwardness in the last century has led to many people’s fallacious
perception that ancient China was merely an agriculturally advanced
country. They fail to realize that China was once also a major
manufacturing power. China started exporting handicraft products to
surrounding countries in the Han Dynasty and expanded the market to East
Asia, Southeast Asia, West Asia, Africa, and Europe in the Song and Yuan
dynasties. From the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries, the geographical
discoveries of the Europeans accelerated globalization and at the same time
pushed Chinese handicraft exports to its zenith. Of China’s exported
handicrafts across different dynasties, porcelain has always been one of the
most important.
   The scale and volume of the porcelain trade alone shows that China was
once a manufacturing power similar to what it is now. What is different is
that now China manufactures and exports low-cost daily goods while
previously the porcelain, silk, furniture, gold and silver wares,
lacquerwares, etc. China made and exported were the most expensive
luxuries in the world. From 1700 to 1820, the average annual growth rate of
China’s economy was three times higher than that of Europe and China’s
GDP accounted for one third of the world’s total. One contributing factor of
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
this economic success was that at the time porcelain and other handicraft
products from China were luxurious and trendy commodities, heavily
demanded by many countries. As the products were exported, silver flowed
into China, especially from European countries. Behind the popularity of
Chinese handicrafts at the time was not only the strength of China’s
manufacturing, but more importantly, foreign countries’ admiration for
Chinese values, aesthetic tastes, and the Chinese culture in general. In
European countries at that time, the most sought-after household
decorations were Chinese style ornamental objects, including porcelain,
lacquerware, furniture, gold, and silver ware, with porcelain being the most
popular. These porcelain wares, embellished with various scenes of Chinese
life, with dramatic and fictional stories, with flowers, birds, fish, and
insects, and with Chinese landscapes, filled Europeans with curiosity and
fascination for Chinese culture. China became the exotic ideal land of the
European imagination. The sweeping popularity of Chinese culture
influenced European aesthetics and arts and had a considerable impact on
the Enlightenment which was taking place at the time. What China
exported, then, was more than commodities—it also exported ideas,
philosophy, and values embodied in those commodities.
   The year 1820 was the 25th year of the Jiaqing era in China’s Qing
Dynasty. In that year, China was still the largest exporter and the leading
economic power in the world, exporting large volumes of porcelain to
Europe and America. Then, only 20 years later, the Opium War broke out,
in an instant driving the Chinese empire to the verge of collapse.
Subsequently, China lost its status as a manufacturing and exporting power,
and even domestic manufactured products began to be imported from the
West. Handicraft products such as ceramics and textiles, once China’s
strong suit, started to be replaced by Western machine-made items. It is still
a vivid memory for many that until the 1960s the Chinese market was
pervaded by imported industrial products whose names all started with the
character yang, meaning foreign. Kerosene was called “foreign oil,” cotton
cloth “foreign cloth,” and matches “foreign kindling.”
   This change fits well A. R. Radcliffe-Brown’s description: the unity of a
culture will be in serious turmoil because of a collision with a very different
culture and may even be destroyed and replaced; such cultural
disintegration is very common in today’s world—from the Americas or the
South Pacific to China and India.33 The impact of the new industrial
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
civilization turned China from a major exporter into an importer, from a
strong country into a weak one, and from a culturally advanced country into
a backward one. It was against this background that we forgot our history.
Many major museums in Europe and America display various refined
porcelain wares, furniture, gold and silver wares, lacquerwares and silk
shipped from China that represent the highest manufacturing standards of
ancient China, while in Chinese museums we mostly see luxury objects of
the imperial palace and aristocracy but not such exquisite works. This has
led many current young Chinese to overlook the fact that China was once a
manufacturing powerhouse. They only regard her as once a backward
agricultural civilization. Now China has again become a major exporter, but
what we export is mostly cheap goods rather than fashion or luxury
products. We lack design capacity and our own brands. In most cases we
only manufacture based on foreign designs. The fundamental reason for the
difference is that in ancient times China was a culturally developed country.
Its cultural system and values were a model that the rest of the world
admired and learned from. Thus, at that time China was exporting culture
and values as well as goods, and this culture and these values are the most
important thing a country can offer to the outside world. All commodities
are essentially carriers of culture and ideology. This, in another way, shows
that the determining factor of social transformation is the ideological
component rather than the technological. Currently, China will achieve
breakthroughs in technological and cultural innovation only if she produces
thought and ideas that represent the new era.

The Contemporary Value of Chinese Ceramic History
Research
Historical studies are more than explorations of the past. They are to benefit
the present and the future. As an anthropologist, I have examined and
written about the history of Chinese ceramics to gain and share with readers
a deeper understanding of the origin and development of Chinese society
and culture, namely, the yesterday of our country, which hopefully will
benefit its today and tomorrow.
   As Benedetto Croce argued, while history is not contemporary, if it is
not regarded as a mere hollow echo and is given true meaning, all history is
contemporary history. “Like contemporary history, the precondition of its
existence is that the stories it tells must reverberate in the mind of
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
historians.”34 Past history reverberates in our minds because of its close
relation to present-day life. “Contemporary history no doubt comes directly
from life, and history which is not called contemporary history must also
come from life because it goes without saying that the only thing that would
motivate people to study the facts of the past is an interest in the present
life. Hence, past facts are looked at by historians with a mind to not a past
interest but a current interest.”35 It is also for this that while I am writing
about ancient history far removed from the present day, every step along the
way I cannot resist comparing the past with today, for I know that present-
day China grew out of the past and that we will understand the root of many
current phenomena only if we know their past. This is exactly how Lucien
Febvre put it: “It is a need every human group recognizes at some point of
its evolution: people look for value in or attach value to “past” behaviors,
events, and trends. These behaviors, events, and trends indicate reality,
make people understand reality and help people live in reality.”36
   Karl Popper believes the usefulness of history lies in its close
relationship with present reality. Some of the questions that arise from
contemporary life require the historians’ input of a past perspective. “We
need to know how our difficulties are related to the past so as to know
which path we shall take to go forward and solve the main tasks we face
and choose.”37 Therefore, in a sense, all history is “contemporary history,”
for all history researchers rethink and rewrite history from the standpoint of
life today.
   The writing of this book is in a sense influenced by the concept of
Cultural Self-consciousness championed by Fei Xiaotong. Cultural Self-
consciousness means that people living in a certain culture should have
adequate knowledge of that culture, of is origin, formation, characteristics,
and development trends. Such knowledge is necessary if a culture is to be
more strongly independent in its cultural transformation and to achieve
autonomy in the task of making cultural choices that are suited to the new
environment and new era.38 My purpose in writing this book is similar, that
is, to understand Chinese culture and Chinese society through a study of
China’s ceramic history and to explore the future path of Chinese culture.
    Fei Xiaotong’s Cultural Self-consciousness requires us not to think
about Chinese culture and history in isolation, but to perceive Chinese
culture and history from a global perspective and from the standpoint of the
interests of all human beings. Fei Xiaotong argues: “The cultural contacts
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
following economic globalization will inevitably bring huge changes, and
we should be prepared for this worldwide cultural contention. On the one
hand, we should recognize the goodness in traditional Chinese culture and
study our own history from a modern scientific approach in the mission of
achieving Cultural Self-consciousness and creating a splendid modern
Chinese culture, and on the other hand we should learn about and
understand other cultures in the world, learn to handle and resolve problems
arising from cultural contacts, and contribute to the common future of all
humanity.”39 It is with such a mission in mind that I adopt a global vision
when studying the history of Chinese ceramics, always accommodating its
interaction with Western culture, thought, economy, and trade.
   This book is also intended to contribute answers, albeit incomplete, to
broader questions raised by Fei Xiaotong, namely, “Why are we living this
way? What is the meaning of living this way? What results will such living
bring us? That is to say, having developed to this stage, the human race
needs to know where our cultures came from, how they took their present
form, what is their essence, and where will they take human beings.”40
Examining the history of ceramics with these questions in mind, my
research yields some new understandings about traditional Chinese culture.
Naturally, arising from my personal research, these understandings are not
automatically validated or comprehensive.
   As mentioned above, all history is contemporary history. History is not
the dead past. It is alive. What it has to offer is not some sealed treasure
inviting us to take it as it is. It requires us to search for and assemble
numerous fragments in order to truly embrace it. It takes constant re-
visiting and re-understanding. People in different eras have different ways
of understanding and obtain different nutrients from history, according to
the needs of their respective times. That is why people in different eras
interpret and write history in different ways and from different standpoints.

Writing Ideas
The knowledge and insights the history of Chinese ceramics is able to offer
is far beyond what has been mentioned above. Since the birth of pottery, the
production of ceramics has been in existence for about 10,000 years.
Throughout this long history, ceramic wares have accompanied the entire
course of the development of the Chinese nation, including its culture,
politics, economy, and science and technology. It would be a daunting task
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
for anyone to attempt a comprehensive discussion of this huge and complex
subject through individual effort.
    Therefore, in this book, I restrict myself to my own field and examine
the history of Chinese ceramics purely from the perspective of the
anthropology of art. My focus is on the contributing factors to the aesthetic
and artistic styles of ceramics in different dynasties and on the interaction
between the ideological, sociological, technological, natural, and
informational components of Chinese culture as reflected in the process of
ceramic production development. And the study seems to point to the
following conclusions: art is born of a range of factors including material
and spirit, religion and labor; the ideological component acts on the
technological component to bring changes to the sociological component;
Chinese history should not be divided along mechanical evolutionist lines
into primitive, slave, feudal, capitalist, and socialist periods but should be
reexamined from an anthropological viewpoint, and the history of ceramics
shows that after the Qin and Han dynasties China was a plebeian society
rather than a feudal society; attention should be given to spatial diffusion in
addition to temporal evolution in the study of the history of Chinese
ceramics. Another research result is the realization that not only do the
ideological, sociological, and technological components as suggested by
White contribute to the historical changes of a civilization, but so also do
nature and information, and that in modern times, the information
component, which represents diffusion and communication, is playing an
ever more significant role. As the dissemination of information speeds up,
so does the tempo of social change.
   This work gives more weight to the information component, i.e., to the
global ceramic trade and cultural exchange. Previous work on the history of
Chinese ceramics has often spent more time on the Song Dynasty as that
period boasted more kilns than any other period in Chinese history. This
work, however, devotes its most comprehensive and richest chapter to the
Qing Dynasty, because that was when Chinese ceramics enjoyed their
widest distribution and the broadest contact with other countries. Selling not
only in China, but also to Asian, African, and European countries as well as
the emerging American market, the ceramics trade at that time was an early
model of trade globalization. By then, countries around the world were no
longer isolated from each other. They all joined a collective historical tide
in a complex and changing era, and the development of China’s ceramics
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
industry was one wave in that tide. With the rise of the Western world, the
acceleration of information, communication, and exchange around the
globe altered the political, economic, cultural, and social development
modes in every country.
   “The other culture” and “the other” are among the most important
concepts of anthropology. The general idea is to use the exotic culture of
“the other” as a mirror to look at one’s own culture and to reflect upon it to
facilitate improvement. While “the other culture” in traditional
anthropology is defined in terms of geographic distance, I believe temporal
distance may also cause cultural estrangement and “otherness.” To us, the
ancient world and culture are also “the other” and “the other culture.”
   Another important anthropological concept is the idea of the “field.”
Fieldwork is how anthropologists obtain first-hand research materials and
the field is where they meet cultural groups face to face. When our research
object is history, the “field” in this sense, namely, living groups with whom
we may interact and talk, is no longer present. But the “field” of ancient
culture is not entirely absent. It remains in the silent wares, ruins and relics
that have survived. To explore such a “field” is like talking to the ancients.
In this manner, we can use ancient culture as a mirror to look at our present
culture and reflect on it, which may help us find a correct path to the future.
   Anthropology as a discipline originated in the West. I have long
pondered how best to apply it to the study Chinese culture and history and
how to develop anthropological theories with Chinese characteristics. As a
venerable civilization, China has immense volumes of historical literature,
rich tangible archaeological resources, and historical relics, which, if fully
explored, well utilized, and carefully studied in combination with the
present reality would certainly open a new door for anthropological studies
in general and for branch studies including art anthropology and historical
anthropology. This would remove many of the limitations on previous
anthropological research, draw worldwide attention to Chinese
anthropological studies, and promote the reconstruction of specialized
historical studies in China such as cultural history, art history, and economic
history. These are some of my objectives while writing this History of
Chinese Ceramics.
   The above are some of my ideas about the writing of this book. They
are mostly about underrepresented aspects of previous ceramic history
studies and problems I have been exploring. As this is perhaps the first
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
attempt to look at the issues from an anthropological perspective,
immaturity and limitations are bound to exist and further studies will be
required to address the questions in more depth.

1. Earthenware of the Neolithic

Lili Fang1
(1)  Chinese National Academy of Arts, Beijing, China



   Lili Fang
  Email: zhongzl@fltrp.com

1.1 Introduction
1.1.1 Origin of Earthenware
Pottery making is the earliest complex human handicraft. It is also an
important marker for the classification of human cultures in the Neolithic
period.
   The invention of pottery making was closely related to the use of fire.
Human understanding and use of fire began in the Paleolithic, as confirmed
by evidence unearthed in China. Traces of human beings using fire has been
found in the Xihoudu Paleolithic culture ruins in Shanxi and the discovery
site of the Yuanmou Man fossils in Yunnan. These traces date from 1.7 to
1.8 million years ago. The harnessing of fire marked the transformation of
human beings from adapting to nature to making use of nature. Pottery
making is particularly significant because by molding clay into certain
shapes and then firing it into wares, humans changed the external look and
internal molecular structure of the natural material. Meanwhile, prior to the
advent of pottery, although humans were already making tools with natural
materials such as stone and wood, they merely changed the shape of natural
objects, not the molecular structure. Thus, pottery was the first human
invention that transformed one substance into another through chemical
reaction.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
It is believed by some scholars that the invention of pottery occurred
when early humans noticed how earth or clay that accidentally fell into fire
became hardened after being burnt and realized that they might make wares
which they needed by molding clay into desired shapes and then firing
them. If this was the case, early humans in different places would in all
probability discover or invent pottery in the course of their own lives,
without the need for learning from other groups. Existing evidence shows
this might indeed be the case. Pottery works of the Peiligang and Cishan
cultures in the Yellow River basin and of the Hemudu Culture in the lower
Yangtze River, all in the early Neolithic period, varied in terms of form,
variety, craftsmanship and decoration. They thus apparently developed in
isolation from each other.
   Concerning the earliest pottery technique used by human ancestors,
many agree with what Fredrick Engels said in The Origin of the Family,
Private Property and the State: “In many cases it has been proved, and in
all it is probable, that the first pots originated from the habit of covering
baskets or wooden vessels with clay to make them fireproof; in this way it
was soon discovered that the clay mold answered the purpose without any
inner vessel”.1 But the conjecture was challenged by many scholars on the
grounds that if the technique was used to fire pottery the size of a basket, it
would only result in a pile of earthen pieces. It was more likely that humans
started by burning hand-kneaded small objects and utensils, which might be
successfully fired even under the simplest conditions. Encouraged by some
successes with these small objects, they would then explore more
possibilities in clay material selection and processing, try better molding
methods, improve firing conditions, and even design special kilns for firing
greenware, which would then lead to the successful firing of larger pottery.2
   Early pottery remnants have been found in China in multiple sites since
the 1970s. The remnants from the early and middle Neolithic demonstrate
traces of clay layers stuck together and earthen layers peeling off. The
phenomenon was first identified in pottery shards of the fourth level of the
Hemudu Site in Yuyao, Zhejiang Province, namely, Hemudu Culture Phase
I. Then it was also found in the lower floor of the Zaoshi Site in Shimen, in
the Dadiwan Site Phase I, in the Peiligang Culture in Henan, and in even
earlier sites, mainly cave ruins, such as the 10,000-year old Fairy Cave in
Jiangxi and the Zhenpiyan Site in Guilin. These remains date even earlier
than the cultures of Yangshao, Hongshan, Daxi, Dawenkou, and Hemudu
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Phase II, and feature a molding method that was earlier and more primitive
than coiling. Archaeologists name it “the sticking technique”. The coiling
technique, namely, rolling clay into a long roll and placing one coil on top
of another to form large vessels, appeared and was popularized later in the
middle Neolithic, and was probably inspired by basket making.

1.1.2 Significance of the Emergence of Earthenware
The introduction of pottery marked the beginning of the Neolithic, or
barbarism. Pottery has since become an indispensable utensil in the daily
life of human beings. The emergence of pottery in the Neolithic was
directly related to advances in agriculture at the time since pottery wares
made it possible to process various grains into cooked food. The need to
cook grains drove the development of certain pottery shapes, which in turn
facilitated the effective use of food. The consumption of cooked food
allowed humans to take in more nutrients, which was beneficial to their
physiological and intellectual development. The emergence of pottery also
contributed to the stabilization of human life. “A precondition for the
prevalence of pottery use was long-term residence because pottery wares,
cumbersome and fragile, were not suitable for a lifestyle featuring frequent
mobility. In turn, the production of pottery promoted the transition of
human lifestyles from wandering to settling down, hence the formation of
villages, and this enabled early humans to better engage in agriculture.3 So
it is believed by some that pottery appeared with the emergence of settled
life, with agriculture at the center, and at the same time it promoted the
stability of this settled life and accelerated the growth of productivity. A
recent suggestion regarding the introduction of pottery associates it with
early humans cooking snails and mussels. The evidence for this is the
remains of snails and mussels found in many early pottery relics.
Nevertheless, this author believes that agricultural production and a settled
lifestyle played a more pronounced role in the invention of pottery. West
Asia, China, and Central America, all birthplaces of human agricultural
civilizations, are also the earliest places to start making pottery.
   The introduction and development of pottery has played a significant
role in human history and to this day has been an integral part of human life
and production. The development of pottery helped lead humans into the
metal era, because pottery served a fundamental function in the
development of metallurgical technology. Besides using pottery for
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
cooking, early humans also took advantage of its excellent fire resistance
and used it as vessels for metal smelting. The vessels found in the remains
of early copper-smelting works are mainly of two types. The first type was
large pottery containers like vats and large-mouthed zun, some of which
were plastered with a thick layer of grass-mixed clay both inside and out.
The second type was made entirely of grass-mixed clay. Pottery made such
a significant contribution to metallurgical technology that it is no
exaggeration to say that the appearance of pottery accelerated the progress
of human civilization and elevated human existence to a new level. Besides,
pottery remains are the richest evidence found among ruins of primitive
cultures. From these remains we are able to get an idea of the lifestyle,
material possessions and cultural level of Neolithic humans. In archaeology,
pottery is one important factor for differentiating between various cultures
due to the significant role it played in primitive human culture and its robust
and widespread preservation.

1.2 Pottery of the Early and Middle Neolithic
1.2.1 Site Locations
China is an ancient civilization with a long history, and it has been a highly
developed agricultural civilization from ancient times. Highly developed
pottery techniques and culture made their appearance in China at the dawn
of agricultural civilization in the Neolithic.
    Neolithic cultural sites can be found in many parts of China, including
northwest China, northeast China, the central plains, central and southern
Shandong and northern Jiangsu, Taihu Lake and northern Zhejiang, both
sides of the Yangtze River with the Ningzhen Mountains at the center, as
well as southern and southwest China.
   The earliest pottery found in China is that which was unearthed at the
Fairy Cave4 and the Bucket Handle Site in Dayuan, Jiangxi, which date to
over 10,000 years ago in the early Neolithic. Early pottery has also been
found at the Zhenpiyan Site in Guilin, Guangxi, the Jade Toad Rock Site in
Daoxian, Hunan, the Fairy Cave in Lishui, Jiangsu, the Nantouzhuang Site
in Xushui, Hebei, and elsewhere. Extremely early pottery shards were
found at the Jade Toad Rock Site. The shards are blackish-brown, loose in
texture and mixed with coarse sand grains, the largest of which reaching
two centimeters in diameter. The roughly made shards were decorated with
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
rope patterns on both inside and out. Restoration shows they are from an
open-mouth cauldron with a pointed spherical bottom,5 which according to
the latest dating was created about 16,000 years ago.6 In addition, pottery
shards from 17,000 years ago were discovered at the Miaoyan Cave Site in
Guilin, Guangxi.7 In the mid-1970s, remains from the early Neolithic were
discovered in many places including Xinzheng, Mixian, Dengfeng,
Gongxian, Weishi, Zhengzhou, Xuchang, Chang’ge, Wuyang, Xiangcheng,
Hengchuan and Qixian in Henan and Wu‘an in Hebei.

1.2.2 Materials and Forms
Pottery unearthed at early Neolithic cultural sites was all made from
common soluble clay, a material early humans had easy access to. All
shards contain coarse grains, indicating the clay was not carefully washed.
The fracture surface shows structure from mud patch plastering. The body
texture is crude, and the bodies are all hand-kneaded and thick. No remains
of kilns have been found. Presumably the pottery was burnt with a bonfire
at relatively low temperatures, about 600 to 800 degrees Celsius, which
would explain the high fragility of the products. The pottery is mostly
reddish brown, grayish brown or blackish brown. The surface is mostly
plain. Some have stripe patterns resembling ropes or baskets. Pottery at that
time, mostly jars (cauldrons) with spherical (or pointed spherical) bottoms,
lacked variety. This form continued well into the middle and late Neolithic.
    Representative pottery of the early Neolithic has been found in Cishan
(Hebei), Peiligang (Henan), Pengtoushan (Lixian, Hunan), Xinglongwa
(Aohan Banner, Inner Mongolia), Beishouling (Baoji, Shaanxi),8as well as
Laoguantai and Yuanjun Temple (Baoji, Shaanxi).9 Some wares have even
been found in later sites such as Hougang (Anyang, Henan),10 Miaodigou
(Shaanxian, Henan),11 Jieduanying (Cixian, Hebei)12, and Xiapanwang
(Cixian, Hebei)13. This indicates that such pottery existed for an extended
period. The colored pottery and fine line pattern which is frequently
observed at Yangshao Culture sites indicate these pottery remains were
closely related to the Yangshao Culture. (Fig. 1.1).

   The most distinctive of these pottery works are those of the Laoguantai
Culture, represented by the Laoguantai Site on the east bank of the Xisha
River, a tributary of the Weihe River to the southwest of the county town of
Huaxian, Shaanxi Province and the Baijia Village Site in Lintong,
Shaanxi14. Pottery unearthed at these two sites bore characteristics of the
Yangshao Culture, but their era preceded that of Yangshao. Thus,
researchers sometimes term the period of these two sites Pre-Yangshao. The
pottery unearthed includes spherical bottom bowls, tripod bowls, circular
foot bowls, tripod swollen belly jars, tripod cylindrical jars, and swollen
belly urns. The wares are decorated on the outside with various rope
patterns, the most distinctive of which being interlaced line patterns. Also
discovered at these sites is the earliest colored pottery in the Yellow River
basin, dating back 7,330 to 7,050 years. The colored pottery, mostly bowls
and tripod wares, is brownish red and some of the bowls are drawn with
simple symmetrical geometric symbols on the inside. (Fig. 1.2).

   Pengtoushan Culture is represented by the Pengtoushan Site and the
Bashidang Site in Lixian, Hunan. Pottery unearthed there is mostly
adulterated with rice husks and blades of grass. The body is black, vessel
walls are thick and cumbersome, and the outer surface has reddish brown
mud coating mottled with different shades all over, resulting from an
uneven firing temperature. Decorations are mainly disorderly interlaced
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
lines, fingernail prints, poking and scratching marks. The model is simple
and rough. The size is relatively large. Spherical bottoms are prevalent and
most wares do not have a rim around the mouth. Varieties include big-
mouth deep belly jars, small-mouth deep belly jars, round belly jars, long
necked amphorae, plates, pedestals, bowls, basins, saucers and tripod ware.
   Earthenware from the Cishan and Peiligang cultures is mainly red
pottery, including clay wares and sandy wares. All are handmade with
uneven wall thickness. When first unearthed, the pottery texture was loose
and soft, probably due to serious dampness resulting from being buried
underground for so long. Testing shows that the firing temperature of red
pottery is 900 to 960 degrees Celsius. The wares mostly feature a plain
surface with a few decorated with scratch marks, comb point patterns,
fingernail prints and bump patterns. There are not many varieties, only
bowls, jars, ding, etc. The double-handled tripod red pottery pot is unique in
shape with a round or oval belly, slight outward extension of the mouth,
spherical bottom, symmetrical vertical handles on the shoulders with small
holes, and three solid feet (Fig. 1.3). Other representative wares include
spherical bottom bowls, deep belly jars and ding. At the Jiahu Site in
Wuyang, Henan, a site belonging to the Peiligang Culture, pottery kilns
with vent holes were discovered along with a large amount of pottery
including horn-shaped handle jars, square mouth basins, chisel-shaped leg
ding, and pots with angular shoulders.15 Pottery unearthed at the Cishan
Site was also hand-kneaded. Most are brownish red sandy pottery, and
some are red clay pottery. The firing temperature was about the same as
that of the pottery unearthed at the Peiligang site. The surface is polished
and decorated with scratch marks, comb point patterns, fingernail prints,
thin rope patterns, and bump patterns. Varieties are richer, including bowls,
plates, pots, jars, dou (long stem vessels), yu (wide-mouthed jars or pots),
and four-legged ding. Yu, the most common variety, include round and oval
models, all with vertical walls and flat bottoms. The pedestals are in the
shape of an inverted boot with a solid or circular foot. In addition, several
colored pottery shards from the Cishan Culture were found, indicating the
Cishan Culture to be a predecessor of the Yangshao Culture.16

   Despite notable differences between the pottery of the Peiligang and
Cishan sites, the two are basically identical in terms of body material,
molding method and firing temperature. They both include varieties like
spherical bottom bowls, tripod bowls, and small-mouth double-handled
pots, and share common decorative patterns including scratch marks, comb
point patterns, fingernail prints and bump patterns. This shows that the two
sites are closely related. In addition, some pottery of the two sites, such as
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
fake circular foot bowls, tripod bowls and deep belly jars, have certain
connections with remains of the early Yangshao Culture.
   The Xinglongwa Culture from northeast China was from the same time
period as the Peiligang and Laoguantai cultures of the central plains.
Pottery unearthed at the Xinglongwa site is mostly hand-molded. Mainly
sandy cylindrical jars and bowls, the wares are fully covered with patterns
on the outside. The printed patterns, predominantly continuous lines in the
shapes of X and Z, are pressed with flake-shaped tools point by point.17
(Fig. 1.4).

1.2.3 Shape and Decoration
The early and middle Neolithic was an early stage of primitive human
culture. Nevertheless, pottery of this period did not appear out of nowhere.
Their models mostly derived from the shapes of the objects the pottery was
scheduled to replace, namely, melon or fruit shells and woven objects that
human beings used as water vessels, food vessels and storage containers
prior to the invention of pottery. For instance, pottery mostly had spherical
bottoms (including spherical bottoms with three feet), even though it might
seem obvious to us that flat bottom wares would be easier to make and
easier to place on a surface. All inventions come from life or tradition, and
this is also true of the spherical bottom, the prevalence of which at the time
was due to the fact that pottery then was made in imitation of the existing
natural and manmade containers. Melon and fruit shells all had spherical
bottoms. For vessels woven with vines, bamboo or ropes plastered with
clay, because of the limits of the technical conditions at that time, it was
much easier to make spherical bottoms than flat ones. Since spherical
bottomed vessels were not sufficiently stable, people started placing support
below the vessels and gradually discovered the mechanical principle that
maximum stability could be achieved with three supporting points. This
also laid the foundation for the appearance of the bag-shaped foot that was
about to make its debut.
    Pottery decorations were also drawn from life and tradition. Pottery
decorations in the early and middle Neolithic included basket, mat and rope
patterns, which were inspired by early woven objects. There were also
printed patterns pressed with tools. The pressing was on the one hand to
make the pottery more aesthetically pleasing and on the other hand to help
the clay stick more solidly together. In addition, there were string patterns
and net patterns carved with thin wooden planks. Such patterns were
inspired by net-shaped woven objects and came from early human
understanding of intersecting and parallel lines. Such perceptions and use of
lines opened the door for China‘s painted pottery and all arts in general. As
Lei Guiyuan attests: “The line was an extraordinary invention in primitive
life. With the line, early humans had clothes on their back, had mats to sit
and lie on, had cords to catch beasts and birds, and had ropes to bind
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
bamboo and timber to build sheds. The making and using of the line was a
special skill of primitive humans, a skill that after practice and perfection
became an art”.18 Used in pottery decoration, the line grew to embody great
creativeness and became an indispensable image of beauty in human life.
    Often, the practicality and beauty of a form is inseparable. Intersecting
lines, the most beautiful decorative pattern of early pottery, were also the
most useful in life. They were used in making fences, binding tool handles,
weaving objects, knitting nets, splicing ropes and tying up wooden frames.
These intersecting lines were used on pottery wares to make the pottery
aesthetically more appealing and to bind the clay more solidly together. In
fact, the fingernail prints, comb point patterns and bump patterns that
appeared at the time were originally also intended to compact the pottery
clay. Their aesthetic value was discovered later in practice and thus their
patterns were also used for ornamental effect which heralded the beginning
of decorative ceramic art. The next major developmental stage of ceramic
art occurred when people began painting various patterns on pottery with
brushes and mineral pigments, marking a qualitative change in ceramic art
and endowing it with deeper cultural connotations. All innovations are
rooted in tradition and life. The painted pottery that developed in the late
Neolithic occurred on the foundation of the early Neolithic. Early human
understanding of molding, of decoration and of various lines in the life of
the early and middle Neolithic all constituted bases for the later
development of painted pottery art.

1.3 Pottery of the Late Neolithic
Over the 3,000 to 4,000 years following the beginning of the Neolithic,
about 12,000 years ago, several cultural systems came into existence in
different parts of China. In about 8000 BCE, millet and rice growing
appeared in the middle reaches of the Yellow and Yangtze rivers
respectively. Different natural conditions in different regions gave birth to
different agricultural systems in the north and south. With a vast territory of
about 10 million square kilometers, China has a complex variety of natural
landforms including mountains, plateaus, deserts, basins and river valley
plains, of which river valley plains obviously offered the best geographical
conditions for the early development of farming. These valleys, located at
different latitudes, experienced different climatic conditions and bred the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
following primitive cultures in the middle Neolithic: the Yangshao Culture
in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, the Dawenkou Culture in the
lower reaches of the Yellow River and Huaihe River basin; the Daxi,
Shanbei, Majiabang cultures and the Hemudu Culture in the middle and
lower reaches of the Yangtze River; the Shixia Culture centered around the
Pearl River basin; and the Hongshan Culture in the Liaohe River basin.19
   Humans at that time lived in concentrated settlements, engaged in
farming, animal husbandry, and food collecting and hunting. They had
developed regional characteristics in architecture, pottery and burial
customs, all of which can be seen from the remnants of their utensils,
artifacts and residences. Nevertheless, primitive cultures were not isolated
from each other. Trade and other exchanges among them gradually led to
the unity of traditional Chinese culture across regions. In northern China,
the most influential were the Yangshao and Dawenkou cultures while in the
south the Daxi and Hemudu cultures exerted the largest impact on
subsequent cultural development. The Yangshao Culture evolved from
earlier cultures along the Yellow River and its tributaries such as the
Cishan, Beilinggang and Laoguantai cultures. The region was later called
“the cradle of the central plains culture and Chinese culture”. The Yangshao
and Hongshan cultures along the coast of the Bohai Sea influenced each
other. Later, the Hongshan Culture evolved into the culture systems of
Panshan, Majiayao, Machang, etc. The representative objects of these
cultures are painted pottery, which were shaped using the coiling technique
and lacquered with red or black patterns. The Yellow River and the lower
reaches of the Yangtze River were known for gray and black pottery. They
were the earliest regions in China to use the potter’s wheel and their wares
mostly had three feet.20

1.3.1 Emergence of Painted Pottery
One of the most remarkable events in the middle and late Neolithic was the
appearance of painted pottery in most of the cultures in different parts of
China. The development of production and arts in an area invariably
depends on its natural environment and the natural materials it has access
to. Thus, in different places different pottery clay was used. In the lower
reaches of the Yangtze River and the southeast coastal areas, black clay
deposited by rivers and ponds was used. Such clay had a fine texture and
often contained clamshell fragments and plant fiber. The pottery fired from
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
it was grayish brown and was not capable of easily exhibiting colored
patterns. Nevertheless, the fine texture made it easy to display printed
patterns. As a result, pottery in these areas quickly developed printed and
carved patterns but lagged in terms of colored decoration. In contrast, red
clay rich in iron was used in the middle and upper reaches of the Yellow
River. Such clay turned brownish red or orange red after being fired in
semi-closed oxidizing flame kilns. Since the clay contained few impurities,
the pottery could be polished to become relatively smooth and shiny,
making it easy to exhibit painted color patterns. As a result, the ceramic art
in these areas were focused on color decoration, and painted pottery art
developed quickly.
    Painted pottery came into existence only when pottery making
techniques had reached a certain level. Specifically, the creation of painted
pottery required three conditions. The first was the understanding and
application of colors to decorate pottery along with the skills in choosing
and processing colorings. Spectral analysis of painted pottery pigment from
the Yangshao Culture shows the main coloring element of brownish red
pigment was iron, that of black pigment was iron and manganese, and there
was barely any colorant in white pigment except a small amount of iron.
Based on this, researchers estimate that the brownish red coloring was
ochre, the black coloring was a type of red earth rich in iron and the white
coloring was probably a kind of porcelain clay with a solvent added.21
Painted pottery could not have developed if early humans had not grasped
the skills of selecting and processing colorings. The second condition was
more advanced firing techniques. If the firing temperature was not high
enough, colors painted on the pottery would peel off. Good kiln airtightness
and high firing temperatures were necessary to make sure the colors stuck.
The third condition for the rise of painted pottery was the use of smooth-
textured fine clay, without which it would be impossible to show the
brightness of the colors or to draw smooth strokes on the wares. Most
pottery wares in the early Neolithic were grayish brown mixed with fine
sands. Only later in areas of the Yangshao Culture did red sandy pottery
appear. There also appeared a small quantity of red clay pottery. The use of
red clay to make pottery was a prerequisite for the rapid development of
painted pottery.
   The invention of the ink brush was of great significance to the history of
Chinese civilization. It could be used for both painting and writing. Western
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
scholars often use three criteria to determine if a society has entered the
civilized stage, namely, the emergence of copper smelting, of written
language and of cities. Gauged against these criteria China entered the
civilized stage in the late Yangshao to early Longshan Culture periods
(3000 to 2500 BCE), because at that time the ink brush and cloth already
existed, and were probably writing tools. Pottery written with character-like
symbols with the ink brush have been unearthed in formations of the same
period.

1.3.2 Painted Pottery Archaeological Sites
1.3.2.1 Dadiwan Phase I Culture
Primitive painted pottery of the Neolithic was found in the most abundance
in the Helong region. Helong, a short name for the ancient Gansu Corridor
and the Longyou (west of Longshan Mountain) area, lay in the upper
reaches of the Yellow River and is roughly equivalent to present-day Gansu
Province and parts of Qinghai, Ningxia and Xinjiang in northwest China.
Located at the intersection of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the Neimenggu-
Xinjiang Plateau and the Loess Plateau, Helong is a belt-shaped region
extending about 1,600 km from the central point of China‘s territory to the
northwest with a north-to-south width of tens up to 100 km. The special
geographical location of the region, namely, the meeting of the Guanzhong
(present-day middle Shaanxi Province) area to the east and the western
Regions, gave the region the special function of being a bridge for
economic and cultural communications between the ancient eastern and
western areas.
   The Helong region has been a multi-ethnic area from ancient times.
Throughout history, different ethnicities came into contact with each other
on this land. They coexisted, connected and intermingled to form the unique
Helong cultural landscape featuring intertwined yet independent cultures.
Helong is not only one of the breeding grounds for the Yellow River
civilization, but also a grand stage where multiple ethnic cultures
blossomed in radiant splendor.
   The Helong region has been the habitat of three representative Neolithic
cultures, namely, the Dadiwan Phase I Culture, the Yangshao Culture
(including the early, middle and late phases) and the Majiayao Culture
(including the Shilingxia, Majiayao, Banshan, and Machang types). The
three emerged in successive periods. The sites of the Dadiwan Phase I
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Culture and the Yangshao Culture were both in the mythical birthplaces of
Fuxi and Nüwa, that is, in the east and central areas of Gansu Province
which was part of the central plains. The two cultures also had close
associations with the central plains culture: Dadiwan Phase I Culture
belonged to the same system as the Laoguantai Culture of Guanzhong; and
the Yangshao Culture of central and east Gansu Province lay on the western
edge of the broader Yangshao cultural circle. In comparison, the Majiayao
Culture evolved into a relatively independent local culture due to its
continuous expansion to areas west of the Yellow River and integration with
indigenous cultures (Table 1.1).

                                       Majiayao type      5,100 to 4,700 years ago

   The earliest known Chinese painted pottery appeared in the Dadiwan
Phase I Culture. Some of the color symbols painted on the pottery might be
records of events. Chinese civilization began as agricultural, and the site of
the Dadiwan Phase I Culture was one of the earliest places to grow crops in
northern China. The Dadiwan residential site of Yangshao culture was on a
larger scale than any other residential ruins in China of the same period. It
is undeniable that we must understand the significance of these ancient
ruins for Chinese culture in order to explore the origins of Chinese
civilization.
   When painted pottery of the Yangshao Culture was first discovered at
the beginning of the twentieth century, some suggested that Chinese painted
pottery was introduced from the West because the unearthed wares were
already mature in form. Subsequently, the discovery of the painted pottery
of the Dadiwan Phase I Culture helped us discover the roots of Chinese
painted pottery art.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Dadiwan Phase I Culture was of approximately the same period as the
early Neolithic cultures of the Yellow River basin, including the Laoguantai
Culture in Guanzhong, the Peiligang-Cishan Culture in the central plains,
and the Beixin Culture in Shandong. They were all early agricultural
cultures along the Yellow River. Dadiwan Phase I Culture was one of the
earliest ancient cultures to make painted pottery and was of the same period
as the Jarmo and Hassuna culture in the Tigris-Euphrates river system,
which were also the earliest cultures to make painted pottery in the world.
The pottery of Dadiwan Phase I Culture was still at the stage of initial
creation, yet there were already painted wares. Since the slow wheel had
not been adopted at the time, all the wares were handmade. The simple and
rough forms of the painted pottery served as evidence that it originated and
developed in the area rather than having been introduced from elsewhere.
   At this point painted pottery accounted for only about one quarter of all
pottery wares. The shapes, patterns and lines were relatively simple. A
broad red line was drawn on the outer surface of the mouth of spherical-
bottomed bowls and the inner side of the mouth rim was drawn with a thin
line or with short or zigzagging slashes. These simple patterns give rise to
at least two observations. Firstly, the painted pottery expressed confidence
and enthusiasm in the life of the residents of the Dadiwan Phase I Culture.
They used red as the earliest decorative color because in their eyes it
symbolized life. Secondly, in terms of artistic skill, the broad line pattern
drawn along the outside of the mouth rim resembles a belt when looked at
from the side while resembling a circle when seen from above, showing that
the “multi effect decoration method” had its debut in the earliest painted
pottery of China. The simple pattern embodies extraordinary wisdom and
rich imagination. Dadiwan Phase I painted pottery marked the development
of ancient pottery craftsmanship and decorative art and evidenced the
aesthetic value of ancient pottery (Fig. 1.5).

1.3.2.2 Yangshao Culture
Yangshao Culture got its name because specimens which later came to be
identified as a distinct culture were first discovered at Yangshao Village in
Mianchi, Henan, in 1921, after which similar discoveries were made in
Shanxi, Henan, Shaanxi, southern Hebei, eastern Gansu, Xinjiang and Inner
Mongolia. Carbon-14 dating shows that early Yangshao Culture specimens
dated at 4430 to 4150 BCE, that is, about 6,400 years ago.23 Ruins were
found in large numbers and with a wide geographical distribution. Over
1,000 sites have been excavated for research purposes, including the
relatively larger sites of Banpo in Xi’an, Laoguantai in Huaxian and
Jiangzhai in Lintong, Shaanxi Province, Miaodigou in Shaanxian, Dahe
Village in Zhengzhou, Henan Province, and Xiapanwang in Cishan, Hebei
Province. In archaeology these ruins are collectively termed “Yangshao
Culture.
   Yangshao Culture pottery developed from the pottery of Dadiwan Phase
I Culture along with that of the early Neolithic cultures in different
locations, notably Cishan Culture, Peiligang Culture and Laoguantai
Culture. The pottery of early Yangshao Culture may be classified into
Banpo and Miaodigou Types and that of the late Yangshao Culture into Late
Banpo, Xiwangcun, Dasikong, Quanhu Phase II, Miaodigou Phase II,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Taikou Types and more. Yangshao Culture featured red pottery and painted
pottery. It is dominated by red clay pottery, followed by sandy red pottery
and a small amount of gray pottery. Black pottery and even white pottery
have also been found at a few sites but are extremely rare. These wares are
characterized by pure and fine body texture, washed clay, and smooth
polished surfaces. Hand molding still prevailed, but there were signs of
perfecting with a slow wheel. Firing temperature was generally higher,
reaching 900 to 1,000 degrees Celsius. The ware surface was mostly plain
or polished, and decorated with scratch marks, string patterns, additional
stacking patterns, stamped patterns resembling ropes or baskets, etc. The
surface of some fine-textured wares had pottery coating applied to their
surfaces, and were painted with black, white and red patterns to produce
distinctive multicolored pottery.
   The Banpo Type of Yangshao Culture is so named because it was first
discovered in Banpo Village in Xi’an, Shaanxi. Sites of the same type are
mainly distributed in the Wei River basin and the eastern part of Gansu in
the Guanzhong Plain.24 Most painted pottery featured black patterns in the
shapes of bands, triangles, waves, nets, human faces, fish, deer, or frogs.
Some drawings are on the inner surfaces of the ware, which was rare in
Yangshao pottery. Symbols are often carved along the mouth of painted
pottery bowls on the inner side. The fish pattern is the most representative
decoration of Banpo painted pottery. (Fig. 1.6) It is often painted on the
shoulder or inner wall of rolled-rim spherical-bottomed basins and is of two
types, namely single fish pattern or multiple fish pattern, the latter
containing from two to four fish in one image. The fish pattern was mostly
single fish in the early stages but was dominated by multiple fish patterns in
later stages. Moreover, the fish pattern gradually evolved from realistic
images in the early stage, to adopt an abstract, geometric and styled mode
later. The fish bodies are segmented and regrouped to form decorative
patterns composed of transverse triangles and lines.

   The Miaodigou Type of Yangshao Culture is so named because it was
first discovered at Miaodigou in Shaanxian, Henan. Developed on the basis
of the Banpo Type, its distribution was centered in Guanzhong, Shaanxi and
radiated into the surrounding areas, reaching southern Shanxi and western
Henan to the east and to Gansu and eastern Qinghai in the west.25
Representative wares include open-mouth bent-belly flat-bottom basins,
big-mouth spherical-bottom bowls, deep-belly pointy-bottom bottles, small-
mouth spherical-bottom jars, jar-shaped ding, small-mouth flattened-belly
fu (cauldron), and basin-shaped triangular stoves. Surface decorations are
mainly black patterns on a brownish red body or in rare cases on a white
coated body. Patterns include images of birds, frogs, flower petals, and
abstract geometrical patterns of stripes, dots, leaves, arc triangles and
curves. (Figs. 1.7, 1.8).
