1.3.2.3 Majiayao Culture
Majiayao Culture was named after the Majiayao Ancient Culture Relics site
in Lintao, Gansu where it was first discovered in 1924. A Neolithic culture
developed under the influence of Yangshao Culture in Guanzhong. It
featured pottery characteristics similar to those of the Yangshao Culture, but
it had its own distinctive local features.
   Majiayao Culture was mainly distributed in Gansu, Ningxia, the
Minjiang River basin in Sichuan, and northeast Qinghai. Carbon-14 dating
indicates the Shilingxia Type, the earliest type of Majiayao Culture,
flourished in 3813 ± 175 BCE, roughly corresponding to the middle and
later Neolithic age in the middle reaches of the Yellow River. Relics of the
Majiayao Culture seem to have emerged in an east-to-west progression over
the course of about 1,000 years. The Zongri Site that was excavated only in
recent years in Tongde, Qinghai also has many characteristics of the
Majiayao Culture. Some researchers term this site the Zongri Type for its
many unique features.
    Sites of the Majiayao Culture that have been excavated are numerous,
including Caojiazui in Lanzhou, Gansu and Liuwan in Ledu, Qinghai. Most
pottery wares unearthed are molded by hand and some with models. Red
clay pottery and sandy red pottery account for the majority and gray clay
wares are relatively few. Painted pottery was highly developed, often
making up 30% to 50% of the total wares unearthed. They have distinctive
molding characteristics. There are bowls, basins, jars, pots, urns, dou,
bottles, yu (wide-mouthed jars/pots), zun and cups. Sandy pottery is mostly
decorated with rope patterns over its surface, and some are decorated with
several parallel lines, polygonal lines, triangles or interlacing additional
stacking patterns. Most of the painted wares are clay pottery that is usually
more finely made. Black is still the main coloring and painting on the inside
is more advanced than wares of other culture types. The patterns, soft and
smoothly drawn, include stripes, broad bands, dots, arcs, waves, checks,
parallel lines, human faces, and frogs. The pottery is beautifully shaped and
the bowls and rolled-rim shallow-belly basins are similar to those of the
Yangshao Culture‘s Miaodigou Type which indicates that the Majiayao
Culture was deeply influenced by the Yangshao Culture in the central
plains.
   The painted pottery of both Banpo and Miaodigou types are dominated
by big-mouth basins and bowls. The painted pottery of Majiayao is mainly
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
small-mouth pots and jars. One typical example is the “Painted Pottery Pot
with Swirl Pattern“(Fig. 1.9), a red clay pottery ware with a bell-shaped
mouth, flared rim, long neck, broad shoulder, slanting belly, flat bottom,
two ring ears on the belly, and black patterns. The neck is painted with
parallel lines and the whole body with vortices composed of concentric
circles. The pattern resembles ripples spreading outward in all directions
when a water surface is struck by a pebble, producing a strong rhythm with
the curving lines. Another feature of Majiayao Type painted pottery which
is rare in other culture types are the decorative patterns which often cover
the entire ware surface, both inside and out.





Fig. 1.9 Painted pottery pot with swirl pattern,
Majiayao Type, height: 26 cm, top diam.: 7.2 cm, in the Gansu Provincial Museum

   The Banshan Type of Majiayao Culture is so named because it was first
discovered in the Banshan area of Guangtong, Gansu. The most common
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
painted pottery wares of this type are long-neck swollen-belly double-
handled pots (Fig. 1.10) and extended-mouth short-neck swollen-belly
double-handled urns. These wares feature round bodies which narrow
downward to form a small bottom. They are relatively short, with the belly
diameter equaling or exceeding the height. The decorative patterns are
mostly black and in some cases red. The patterns have complex
compositions which can be roughly divided into two types. The first is
composed of swirls or vortices (Figs. 1.11, 1.12), which in some cases are
independent of each other and in other cases linked together. With the
second type, the ware surface is divided into several decorative units with
gourd patterns. Apart from the two types there are also patterns of
rhombuses, circles, triangles, weaves, continuous arcs, nets, and serrations.

Banshan Type, height: 42 cm, top diam.: 10 cm, in the Qinghai Provincial Institute of Archaeology

   The Machang Type painted pottery of Majiayao Culture was found in a
late Neolithic tomb in Machangyuan, Minhe, Qinghai. The Machang Type
developed from the Banshan Type but the area of distribution expanded
further westward, reaching the west end of the Gansu corridor.
   The Machang painted pottery inherited the characteristics of the
Banshan Type and developed new features. Compared with that of Banshan,
the pottery was more roughly made. Black and red colors were still used for
painting, and there emerged a new drawing technique featuring one black
line flanked by two red lines. The decorative patterns, in addition to those
inherited from Banpo, also included the human figure (also called frog)
pattern, polygonal lines, square spirals (a fret resembling the Chinese
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
character 回), shell patterns, large triangles, continuous square spirals and
symbolic frog patterns. Relief and kneaded sculpture on wares were
developed. For instance, on one painted pottery jar unearthed in one tomb
in Ledu, Qinghai, there is a sculpture of a naked woman.26 Most of the
wares were of the same or similar design to those of the Banshan Type.
There were also new varieties such as the four-handled basin, single-
handled cylindrical jar with knob on the belly, painted pottery jar with
human-head-shaped mouth27, and painted pottery pot with human figure
relief. Many jars are drawn with various symbols on the lower belly or the
bottom. Over 50 types of such symbols have been found. (Fig. 1.13).

1.3.2.4 Dawenkou Culture
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
The Dawenkou Culture is so named because it was first discovered in
Dawenkou, Ningyang, Shandong in 1959. It was mainly distributed in
Shandong and northern Jiangsu. Carbon-14 dating shows that it existed
from 4040 to 2240 BCE, lasting about 2,000 years. It coincided
approximately with the middle and late Yangshao Culture in the central
plains and more than 10 ruins and tombs have been excavated.28
   The period from the Dawenkou Culture, which existed 6,000 years ago,
to the Longshan Culture, which existed 4,000 to 5,000 years ago, was the
most glorious period of prehistoric civilization in modern-day Shandong.
The culture, spreading to northern Jiangsu and Anhui in the south and
reaching eastern Henan in the west, exerted tremendous influence on the
Yangshao Culture in the central plains and the Longshan Culture in Henan.
     It is argued by some scholars that the characters written on Dawenkou
pottery “are already highly developed and are remote ancestors of the
Chinese characters in the Shang and Zhou dynasties”, and that “Dawenkou
Culture was already a civilized period with a written record”. Though this
view is controversial, the advanced nature of the Dawenkou prehistoric
civilization can certainly be observed.29 During the Dawenkou Culture,
double burial of men and women was common, indicating humans had
entered a paternal society stage. It can also be deduced that from 3500 to
3000 BCE, society had become quite complicated, evidenced by such
findings as the appearance of settlement, worship activities involving
pottery, specialized production of stone and jade wares, and widespread
interregional trade and exchange. Nevertheless, these activities still seemed
to be collectively carried out by one settlement as a unit rather than being
organized and managed by individuals.30
   The pottery of the early Dawenkou Culture was dominated by red sandy
pottery and red clay pottery. In the middle and late Dawenkou Culture, red
pottery was still the most common, but gray and black pottery also
increased significantly. More clay types such as kaolin and porcelain clay
started to be used to make white pottery in addition to ordinary pottery clay.
Rich color varieties became a major feature of Dawenkou pottery. There
were red, gray, bluish gray, brown, yellow, black, and white. The black
pottery, however, was actually black-skinned since its body was red or gray.
(Fig. 1.14) A small number of wares resembled the eggshell pottery typical
of the Longshan Culture in Shandong.

Tai’an, Shandong

   Red coated pottery and painted pottery accounted for a small portion of
Dawenkou pottery, but the painted pottery had distinctive features. There
were three colorings, namely red, black, and white, all three of which were
sometimes painted on one ware. The paintings were mostly on the outer
surfaces. Some patterns were drawn after the wares were fired and so were
prone to falling off. Some of the wares were painted with a red or white
coat before color patterns were drawn. The patterns include dots, triangles
(Fig. 1.15), circles, ripples, rhombuses, swirls, arcs, octagons, petals,
polygonal lines in parallel, running curves and convolutions, and ribbon
grids (Fig. 1.16). These last two were very similar to the Yangshao Culture
(Miaodigou and Qinwangzhai Types), indicating the two cultures had close
exchanges.

1.3.2.5 Daxi Culture
The Daxi Culture, named after the town where it was first discovered in
Wushan, Sichuan in 1958, was mainly distributed in the Three Gorges area,
Hunan, and Hubei. Daxi Culture is divided into early and late periods, with
the later period lasting from 3825 to 2405 BCE according to Carbon-14
dating, coinciding approximately with or slightly earlier than the middle
period of the Yangshao Culture in the middle reaches of the Yellow River.31
   Chinese civilization originated in the Yellow River basin and the
Yangtze River basin. The former has long been known to the world, while
the Yangtze River basin as one of the originating places of Chinese
civilization has only been gradually confirmed since the twentieth century
with the progress of anthropology and archaeology. It is characterized by
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
widely distributed sites, diverse cultural types and rich cultural remains. A
clear developmental sequence can be drawn from Daxi in Wushan, Sichuan,
Qujialing in Jingshan, Hubei, and Shijiahe in Tianmen, Hubei to the
cultures in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River including Hemudu in
Zhejiang, Qingliangang in Jiangsu and Liangzhu in Zhejiang.32
   Ancient human activities in the Jianghan area (the plain where the
Yangtze and Hanshui rivers merge) can be traced back to the early
Paleolithic period. Many ancient human fossils and early Paleolithic
cultural relics have been discovered in the area (Table 1.2).

   China entered the Neolithic age about 10,000 years ago. During this
period, which lasted for more than 6,000 years, the Jianghan area bred in
succession four main indigenous cultures, namely, the Chengbeixi, Daxi,
Qujialing and Shijiahe Cultures. These cultures were distributed across a
wide area and their centers were not constant, probably due to the migration
of the indigenous population.33
   The Daxi Culture mainly featured red pottery, most of which was
orange red. (Figs. 1.17 and 1.18) There were also wares which were red on
the outside and grayish black on the inside, a process which required
relatively meticulous craftsmanship. Late Daxi Culture featured slightly
more gray and black pottery. A small amount of white pottery was also
found in Hunan. The wares were mostly shaped by hand. Some had rims
trimmed with a slow wheel. A few of the wares still had traces of coil-
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
forming. The pottery was mostly made from common clay. Few were from
fine or sandy clay. Those made from sandy clay were mixed with crushed
husks in addition to quartz sand, so that after firing the clay turned into
black coal or gave rise to many pores. The body of the red pottery was
orange, gray or black. For the black pottery, some had thin walls with both
the surface and body black, while some had black surfaces but gray bodies.
Most wares had plain or polished surfaces, with only a small portion
decorated with string patterns, scratch marks, tile patterns, basket patterns,
comb patterns, poke marks, additional stacking patterns, through-carved
holes, etc. Poke marks, imprinted with small punches of various shapes on
the circular feet of plates, bowls and dou, were a pattern unique to the Daxi
Culture. Daxi Culture also produced a small volume of painted pottery,
mostly fine red clay pottery painted with black coloring, (Fig. 1.19) some
intermingled with red coloring. The paintings were mostly on the outer
surface. In a few wares both the outer and inner surfaces were painted. The
patterns were relatively simple, including arcs, broad bands, rope patterns,
parallel lines, horizontal herringbone, rhombus checks, and deformed
swirls. Some black pottery was painted with scarlet coloring.

1.3.2.6 Qujialing Culture
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Qujialing Culture was named after the site where it was first discovered in
Jingshan, Hubei in 1954. Developed directly from Daxi Culture, the
Qujialing Culture was distributed in roughly the same areas as Daxi
Culture, namely, in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, albeit a little
more to the east of Daxi Culture and extending further to the north reaching
the Hanshui and Danjiang River tributaries at the junction of Hubei, Henan
and Shaanxi. Carbon-14 dating shows Qujialing Culture to be from 2550 to
2195 BCE, roughly the same period as the late Yangshao and early
Longshan cultures in the middle reaches of the Yellow River.34
   Very few remains of the early Qujialing Culture have been found and
the Qujialing Culture as commonly described is based on remains of its
later period. Early Qujialing Culture featured many black pottery pieces and
some red, while the late period was characterized primarily by gray pottery
and some yellow. The wares were mostly shaped by hand with plain
surfaces. A small portion is decorated with string patterns, shallow basket
patterns, carved and scratched marks, additional stacking patterns, through-
carved holes, etc. There is also painted pottery. The firing temperature of
the painted and gray pottery was about 900 degrees Celsius.
   The shape of the Qujialing Culture pottery designs displays distinct
features. Those with basically the same shape were made into wares with
different functions by adding three feet or one circular foot of different
heights to suit different purposes. For instance, the “long-neck circular-foot
pot, a black clay pottery ware, has thin walls, smoothly polished surfaces,
straight mouths, round lips, long necks, broad shoulders, and an oblate
belly. The lower part of the belly sharply narrows inward to form a circular
foot, which is decorated with through-carved holes. It was unearthed with
an upside down flat-bottom thin-wall black pottery cup covering its mouth.
Other representative wares of the Qujialing Culture seldom found in other
cultures include the high circular-foot cup (Fig. 1.20), tripod plate, circular-
foot bowl, yu-shaped wares, ding with flat chisel shaped feet, and zeng (rice
steamer) with lid and short circular foot.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 1.20 Long stem black pottery cup,
Qujialing Culture, height: 19.5 cm, top diam.: 7.5 cm, in the Henan Museum

    Painted pottery making is a worldwide phenomenon, yet it has seen
different artistic expressions in different regions and cultures. In the
Jianghan area, painted pottery became popular during the Daxi and
Qujialing Cultures. Daxi Culture painted pottery featured swirl patterns,
wave patterns and horizontal herringbone, which were inspired by the shape
of flowing water. These expressed the deep feelings towards water of the
early Jianghan residents owing to their long physical association with it.
   Jianghan residents were able to skillfully make pottery about 9,000
years ago, albeit only as an auxiliary production activity within individual
households. When it came to the Qujialing Culture period, the introduction
of the potter’s wheel precipitated the development of pottery making as an
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
independent handicraft industry. By the middle of the Shijiahe Culture,
there emerged commercial pottery production for exchange purposes, which
marked the separation of the pottery making industry from agriculture.
    Textile production appeared later than pottery making. The Hanjiang
area was among the regions that had a flourishing primitive textile industry.
People started making textiles during the Chengbeixi and Daxi Cultures, but
not many textile tools from the two cultures have been unearthed, indicating
that at the time textile production was not yet common. In addition, spindle
whorls unearthed from the two cultures are all large and cumbersome,
indicating that the rotational inertia of the spindle was strong, making it
only suitable for producing coarse fiber and thick yarn.
   The Qujialing Culture was an important period for the development of
the primitive textile industry in the Jianghan area. The spindle whorls of
this period were small and light, and the size, weight and rotational inertia
of the spindles had also decreased, indicating that thin and soft fibers could
be spun and then woven into fine cloth. Large numbers of pottery spindle
whorls of the period have been unearthed which shows that textile
manufacture had become a daily activity of women at the time. All these
demonstrate the great progress of textile techniques during the Qujialing
Culture. Painted pottery spindle whorls of the period are decorated with
more than 10 pattern types including straight lines and swirls. When the
whorl spins, the patterns change and produce different aesthetic effects.
    Still another type of ware representative of the Qujialing Culture was
eggshell painted pottery (Fig. 1.21), whose walls were relatively thin, about
one centimeter in thickness. The main varieties of this product were cups
and bowls. The body was orange-yellow and the surface was coated to
become gray, black, red, orange-red, etc., and then painted with black or
yellow coloring. Cups were mainly painted on the inside while bowls were
painted on the outside. Some wares were painted on both sides. Patterns
include dots, arcs, stripes, nets, rhombus checks, and spots in boxes. Some
wares were painted with a unique smudging technique to create cloud-like
patterns with different shades of black, gray and brown, which were then
dotted with rows of spots. The unique features of Qujialing Culture painted
pottery reflected the superb craftsmanship at the time.

1.3.2.7 North Yinyangying Culture
Located in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River, specifically Zhenjiang
and Nanjing in Jiangsu to northeastern Anhui, this culture is so named
because it was first discovered at North Yinyangying in Nanjing in the
1950s. No dating result is available so far, but studies estimate the culture
existed 6,000 to 5,000 years ago.35 Red sandy pottery was dominant,
followed by red clay pottery. There are also small amounts of clay gray
pottery, sandy gray pottery and painted pottery. Most wares are hand-
molded with thick walls. Apart from plain surfaces, some are decorated
with pressed and scratched marks, string patterns, as well as additional
stacking patterns or engravings.
   Most are circular foot and tripod wares with some flat bottom and
spherical bottom wares, and ware with bag-shaped feet are absent. The
main varieties are ding, dou, bowls with tight mouths and circular feet,
spherical bottom bowls, amphorae, pots, zun, and he (round vessels with a
spout). The pottery he was especially developed, with unique and varied
forms; one type included a flat bottom and the other, three feet. Some have
decorative designs on their mouths. Circular foot bowls were especially
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
prevalent. All the feet of the tripod wares are solid and wedge-shaped, and
many have horn-shaped handles and the bodies are mostly thick.

1.3.2.8 Hemudu Culture
Hemudu Culture is the earliest primitive culture found in the Wu Yue area
(roughly present-day Jiangsu and Zhejiang). Located in south China, it was
concurrent with but geographically far removed from the Peiligang Culture
in the north, the earliest culture in the Yellow River basin, indicating that
there were at least two sources of prehistoric Chinese civilization, one in the
north and one in the south.36 So named because it was first discovered at
Hemudu in Yuyao, Zhejiang, Hemudu Culture was located around the Bay
of Hangzhou in Zhejiang, including the Zhoushan Islands, opposite the
Majiabang Culture on the north bank. It existed 7,000 to 5,000 years ago,
with its early period belonging to the middle Neolithic and concurrent with
the Peiligang and Cishan Cultures on the central plains.37
   Hemudu Culture was one of the earliest cultural systems in the world to
cultivate rice. Researchers have found astonishingly large quantities of rice
remains at the Hemudu Site. Piles of rice, straw and husks covering an area
of 2,800 square meters, some places one meter high, indicate rice yields
were already considerable at the time.
   Besides bone and wood objects, the Hemudu Culture ancestors also
made pottery and jade wares. Pottery was dominated by a type of coal-
mixed black pottery, which is believed to have been fired with low-oxygen
reducing flame from pottery clay mixed with organic matter such as plant
fragments and husks.38 The pottery texture was loose and soft. (Fig. 1.22)
There was also some sandy gray pottery and clay gray pottery. It has been
ascertained that the firing temperature of the black pottery was 800 to 930
degrees Celsius and that of the gray pottery was 800 to 850 degrees Celsius.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 1.22 Coal-mixed black pottery fu with scratch mark,
Hemudu Culture, height: 26 cm, top diam.: 12 cm, in the Zhejiang Provincial Museum

   The pottery surface is often decorated with dense rope patterns and
various carved and scratched marks. Rope patterns, found mainly on the
spherical bottoms of cauldrons and jars, are composed of small patches of
interlacing rope lines. Somewhat messy, they seem to have been patted onto
the ware with a bat twined with ropes. Carved and scratched marks were
also extensively used. The marks, mainly plant images and various other
patterns derived from plants, were mostly applied to tight-mouthed fu
(cauldrons). In addition, some wares are decorated with animal patterns.
One representative is the black pottery oval bowl with a swine pattern (Fig.
1.23), a coal-mixed black pottery ware with a tight mouth, rounded
rectangular belly, flat bottom, and swine patterns carved on both front and
back sides. The swine has a long snout, pointed ears, wide-opened eyes,
erect mane and four feet apart as if walking. Its body is decorated with
whorls and leaf patterns. The image has a simple yet bold style, with some
exaggeration indicating more than simple imitation. Some bowls and basins
are carved with patterns of waterweeds or the phoenix bird. Some basins are
carved with ears of rice as well as the swine image. There have also been
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
discovered painted wares which were first believed to be painted pottery but
later proved to be lacquer painting instead.

1.3.2.9 Majiabang Culture
The Majiabang Culture paralleled the Hemudu Culture yet developed
independently from it. Like the Hemudu Culture, it also featured primitive
rice cultivation. Three cloth pieces were unearthed at its site, whose raw
material was most probably wild Kudzu. The cloth was made with the leno
weave using the weft to create patterns, a technique more advanced than
plain weaving. These were the earliest textile specimens to be found in
China.
   Majiabang Culture is so named because it was first discovered at
Majiabang in Jiaxing, Zhejiang in 1959. Carbon-14 dating shows it existed
from 3670 to 2685 BCE. Distributed in areas equivalent to present-day
northern Zhejiang, Shanghai and southern Jiangsu, Majiabang Culture
lasted about 1,000 years before developing into the Songze Culture. Its
pottery was quite influential in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River with
its distinct features. Nevertheless, due to its early age, the craftsmanship
was somewhat rough and the production techniques were not well
developed. When it came to the Songze Culture period, pottery wares saw
significant improvement and there emerged small quantities of clay red
pottery and black-skinned pottery, which were not found in the Majiabang
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Culture. By that time, wares with coating became rare. There were also
small quantities of colored and painted pottery. Varieties included ding, fu,
jars, basins, pots, dou, gu (goblets with broad lips, long narrow stems, and
flared bases), zeng (rice steamers), and filters, some of which appeared only
after the Majiabang Culture. There was a considerable increase in ding
pottery and a decrease in fu pottery.

1.3.2.10 Liangzhu Culture
Liangzhu Culture was first discovered at Liangzhu in Yuhang, Zhejiang in
the 1930s. Developing directly from the late Songze Culture, a later type of
Majiabang Culture, it existed in roughly the same areas as the Majiabang
Culture, albeit extending southward to the Ningshao area (in northeastern
Zhejiang). It flourished about 4,000 years ago, roughly coinciding with the
Longshan Culture on the central plains.39
   The pottery of the Liangzhu Culture was dominated by sandy black
pottery and clay gray-bodied black-skinned pottery, complemented by some
thin-walled black pottery and a small number of sandy and clay orange red
pottery pieces with a black coating. The wares were all shaped with the
potter’s wheel. A typical piece is a black pottery pot with zigzag patterns
and a broad handle, a clay black pottery ware with outwardly extended
mouth, arc-shaped spout, thin neck, deep and swelling belly, and dented
bottom foot. It has a broad handle on the belly and is decorated with parallel
vertical stripes. The outside surface of the mouth is decorated with five
parallel strings that symbolize flying birds and the belly is fully covered
with fine zigzag lines. Apart from most wares sporting a plain polished
surface, some are decorated with string patterns, carved and scratched
marks, bamboo patterns, drill pricks and openwork. (Fig. 1.24) Carved and
scratched marks are mostly patterns of lotus, polygonal lines, nets, clouds,
vortexes, circles and triangles. Images of birds and fish are also eye-
catching. Colored, painted or lacquered pottery was rare. Painted pottery is
usually decorated with simple stripes of red and yellow. Lacquered wares
were found at the Tuanjie Village Site and the Meinian Site in Wujiang,
Suzhou. A coat of brown lacquer was first applied to the black pottery pots
and then skein patterns were added with golden and brownish red lacquer.
The lacquer was identified as raw, indicating that in areas around Taihu
Lake raw lacquer was already used to decorate pottery in the late Neolithic.
Representative varieties included tight-mouthed rolled-rim deep and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
swelling belly jar-shaped long-legged ding and big-mouthed shallow-
bellied basin-shaped long-legged ding. The feet are in the shape of fish fins,
triangles or “T”s. There are also thin and long necked high-crotched gui (鬶,
cooking vessels with three hollow feet) with slim bag feet, short-necked
low-crotched gui (鬶) with fat bag feet, oblate sphere bellied he with three
solid feet and a handle, short or long stemmed dou with bamboo patterns,
large plates with circular feet and deep or shallow bellies, big-mouthed gui
(簋, food vessel) with three handles and a circular foot, long-necked
swelling-bellied pots with circular feet, pots with pierced lugs (Fig. 1.25),
bell-mouthed circular-footed zun, high-collared broad-shouldered (or open-
mouthed thin-necked) deep-bellied jars, large cups with broad handles and
spouts, sandy tanks with big mouths and pointed spherical bottoms, and
vessel lids.

1.3.2.11 Hongshan Culture
Hongshan Culture is so named because it was discovered behind Hongshan
Mountain in Chifeng in eastern Inner Mongolia in 1935. Its range reached
the Olji Moron River in Inner Mongolia to the north, Lingyuan in
Chaoyang, Liaoning and northern Hebei to the south, and the Jirem League
and Jinzhou to the east. Carbon-14 dating determines the age of Hongshan
Culture to be about 5,000 years, that is, in the middle and late Neolithic.40
In the half century after its naming, archaeological circles only regarded
Hongshan Culture as one of the regular primitive cultures of the Neolithic
until the 1980s when researchers, based on a series of new historical and
archaeological studies and discoveries, found that this era, some 5,000 years
ago, was a major transformative age in ancient Chinese history. It was an
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
era of intense social change and frequent cultural clashes when China
gradually moved on from the clan society towards the embryonic nation.
Hongshan Culture then, due to its important position and significant role in
this historic change, became an essential object of archaeological study in
the Liaohe River basin of northeast China.
   The populace of the Hongshan Culture, following those of Xinglongwa
and Zhaobaogou, dominated the entire Xar Moron River and wide areas
surrounding it. The civilization of Hongshan Culture was, in some respects,
even more advanced than the cultures of the Yellow River basin during the
same period and occupied a very important position in the history of
Chinese civilization. Focusing on crop growing and complemented by
animal husbandry, Hongshan Culture maintained prolonged contact with the
farming cultures of the Yellow River basin to its south, constantly clashing
with them and absorbing from them, and quite possibly also assimilated
cultural elements from west Asian civilizations through the nomadic
cultures to its north. Such intense cultural contact in both form and range
gave birth to not merely a simple compounding of cultures, but the initial
architecture of Chinese cultural traditions itself.
   The settlement sites of Hongshan Culture were much larger in scale and
more numerous than the preceding Xinglongwa and Zhaobaogou cultures.
The introduction of large stone si, a spade-shaped farm tool used to turn the
soil, indicated the development of deep plowing and the expansion of
cultivated land. The large numbers of unearthed tools for harvesting and
processing grains, such as stone knives, sharpening discs and sharpening
rods, showed that Hongshan Culture was an agriculture-based economy.
Pottery production also saw great progress. The mastery of clay washing
techniques, the improvement in kilns, and the raising of firing temperatures
enabled the production of clay red pottery vessels in large quantities. In
addition, the appearance of rich varieties of painted pottery reflected the
early human love for the beauty of shapes and colors, and opened up a vast
artistic world to the pottery industry.
   The pottery of Hongshan Culture is mainly sandy brown pottery and red
clay pottery with a small amount of gray clay and black pottery. All were
made by hand. The surfaces are decorated with patterns pressed with tools,
scratch marks, additional stacking patterns and color painting. Patterns
pressed with tools are mostly horizontal Z-shaped lines with somevertical
Z-shaped lines and Z-shaped comb point patterns. The scratch marks are
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
mostly parallel straight lines. T painted pottery was red clay that was etched
with black or purplish red colorations before being fired. One typical
example is the “painted pottery cylindrical ware”, a red clay pottery article
painted with six black rings of leaf pattern encircling the body, a decorative
pattern common to Hongshan Culture pottery (Fig. 1.26). Other decorative
patterns of painted pottery include straight lines, oblique lines, triangles or
triangular patterns made of parallel lines, rhombuses, scales, swirls,
tadpoles, etc. Varieties include various forms of big-mouthed deep-bellied
flat-bottomed jars, small-mouthed long-necked deep-bellied jars, straight-
mouthed folded-bellied flat-bottomed bowls (and some “red top bowls”),
cylindrical wares, big-mouthed bowls, and small-mouthed long-collar urns.
A special feature is that some sandy big-mouthed jars have flat mouths
while some have slanting mouths. The “Z” shaped pattern is a decoration
distinct to Hongshan Culture pottery.

1.3.2.12 Qijia Culture
Qijia Culture is so named because it was first discovered at the Qijia Ping
Site in Guanghe, Gansu. Based on Majiayao Culture, it was distributed
from the upper reaches of the Wei and Jing rivers in the east to the Huang
River in east Qinghai and the Gansu Corridor in the west, and from
southern Ningxia and southern Inner Mongolia in the north to the upper
reaches of the Han River in the south. Flourishing 4,200 to 3,900 years ago,
it roughly coincided with the late Longshan Culture in the middle reaches
of the Yellow River and was one of the Bronze Age cultures of the Helong
area. Bronze smelting can be deduced to have developed locally from the
fact that people used only red copper in the early stages of the Qijia Culture
and began making axes, knives and mirrors with bronze later. As for
pottery, painted pottery declined during this period, but the craftsmanship
remained meticulous.
    Qijia Culture pottery was dominated by sandy and clay orange pottery,
complemented by some gray pottery. Decorative patterns included rope
patterns (Fig. 1.27), basket patterns, scratch patterns, drill pricks (Fig. 1.28)
and color painting. There was less painted pottery than before and the
patterns included rhombus checks, triangles and butterflies. Varieties
included single handled li (cooking vessels with hollow feet), flowery rim
jars, three-handled jars, double-handled jars, jars with two large handles,
long neck amphora, extended mouth amphora, open mouth bowls, long
stem dou, open-mouth flat-bottom basins, tight-mouth basins, single-
handled cups, pots and zun. Painted pottery wares were mainly small-mouth
round-belly amphora, of which some thin-wall polished jars with two large
handles and long neck amphora were extremely exquisitely made.41 One
representative pottery ware of the Qijia Culture is the painted amphora with
triangle pattern unearthed in Datong, Qinghai in 1976. It is a clay orange
pottery ware with a bell mouth, high collar, swelling belly, and flat bottom.
It has two large, broad handles with triangles and dots carved through,
which in combination resemble a human face. The upper part of the belly is
painted with triangle patterns with red coloring. The wall is only 0.15 cm
thick, i.e. thin as eggshell. The surface is smoothly polished and the whole
ware is light and delicate. (Fig. 1.29) Researchers believe the Qijia Culture
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
had entered the phase of class society since many bronze tools have been
unearthed, and more importantly, the phenomenon of men being buried
alive with the dead has been found in tombs from the time. Its age was
probably equivalent to the Xia Dynasty in the central plains.

   More culture types than those discussed above existed during the
middle and late Neolithic, and for each there have been pottery of diverse

1.3.3 Cultural Connotations of Painted Pottery Patterns
It can be seen from the distribution of pottery in the middle and late
Neolithic described above that 7,000 to 6,000 years ago, painted pottery of
Yangshao Culture‘s Banpo Type which developed on the back of the
Laoguantai Culture in the Wei and Jing River reaches, grew rapidly, and
subsequently, under the influence of the early Yangshao Culture, saw
painted pottery art flourish in most regions across the country, each with its
own characteristics, ushering in a flourishing period for Chinese painted
pottery. The painted pottery of Yangshao Culture in Gansu and Shaanxi was
the most developed. Originating from Laoguantai Culture, the pottery had
generally the same features as the early period of Yangshao Culture, and
then gradually developed along two branches, one spreading eastward and
one westward. The center of the first branch moved eastward to the
Guanzhong Plain and the area of convergence of present-day Shaanxi,
Henan and Shanxi provinces. It developed quickly amid frequent cultural
exchanges with the central plains and disappeared relatively early. The
branch developing westward spread to the central Gansu plateau. It
developed relatively slowly due to the restrictions of the natural conditions
and diverged increasingly from the other branch. For a very long time it
maintained the tradition of painted pottery craft and its characteristics grew
increasingly distinct. Majiayao Culture developed from this branch.
    Painted pottery was an extraordinary achievement of late Neolithic
pottery craft. The paintings were drawn on the pottery body before it was
fired and then the firing made the paintings adhere firmly to the ware
surface. The paintings were mostly in black, with the occasional red. In
some areas a white background coating was applied before color painting,
meaning the painted patterns stood out better. The patterns included
flowers, geometric shapes and animals. They were mostly drawn on the
mouth and belly of fine clay pottery bowls, basins and jars, and not on the
lower sections of wares. Such a design was for a reason—the patterns were
drawn on these sites because these sections of pottery vessels were most
easily exposed to the sight of Neolithic people who often sat or squatted on
the ground. Painted pottery was made for practical purposes and apart from
a small portion used as burial objects, almost all were used in some aspect
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
of people’s lives. They can be classified into two categories based on
purpose, namely, utensils for living and production tools, among which the
former, which included water, food, storage and cooking vessels accounted
for the majority. (Fig. 1.30).





Fig. 1.30 Red pottery bottle with small mouth and pointy bottom,
Banpo Type, height: 54 cm, top diam.: 6.5 cm, in the National Museum of China

    Painted pottery drew the wide attention of archaeologists, craft artists,
historians and anthropologists because the rich color paintings covering
them were also a record of information from primitive times, a feature not
possessed by regular plain surface pottery such as red, gray, black, and
white pottery, or pottery with only imprinted patterns. The paintings
comprise more than aesthetic value: they are also records of early human
values, religious views and understandings of the world, and even
reflections of the production conditions and social structures at the time. In
these paintings we may trace the origin of Chinese culture and art.
    All art forms are influenced by the production modes of their times and
the world views, values and aesthetics formed based on such production
modes. These views and values are often expressed through religious
beliefs, and this was especially so in primitive times. Primitive religion
represented early human questioning of the natural world and the effort to
understand themselves and perceive the world through such questioning.
The earliest form of religion was totem worship and animism. In primitive
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
societies everything had something to do with religion, and painted pottery
decoration was no exception. The pottery vessels were made for practical
use, but their decorative patterns were created for more than beauty. They
related to religion, and especially totem worship. Indeed, many of the
pottery wares at the time were purpose-made sacrificial objects rather than
practical objects.
   The low production level of the Neolithic Age determined that the
primary task of people at the time was to survive, and naturally the first
factor people considered in pottery making was whether it would be
favorable to their survival. Since at that time to survive individuals had to
rely on the collective strength of the clan and, since enhancing solidarity
within a clan was conducive to survival, behaviors that promoted the sense
of solidarity within a clan were considered important and desirable. The
totem was a symbol or emblem of a clan. Primitive people might regard an
animal such as a bird or an object as the ancestor of their group, or they
might believe that they formed certain relations with such an animal or
object. Hence primitive totems were mostly animals, sometimes plants, and
in rare cases lifeless objects or natural phenomena. There were even
primitive groups who took humans as their totem. Totemic consciousness
was the earliest common consciousness of mankind, totemic belief was the
earliest religious belief of mankind, and the totem system was the earliest
social system. A totem was a materialized symbol of the unity and
solidarity of a primitive clan and totem worship was essentially “group self-
worship”. Totem consciousness was the common consciousness of the clan
and the spiritual pillar supporting and consolidating relations among clan
members. Totem consciousness strengthened the unity within the clan and
strengthened the clan organization. In primitive times human survival was
constantly threatened by fierce beasts and natural disasters. Against such a
backdrop a strong and unified group was not only necessary for human
survival but also a precondition for social development. Worshipping a
common totem was a means of consolidating the consanguinity-based
relations among clan members and a means of organizing them to engage in
production in a collective manner. When expressed in arts, such means was
the totem pattern people used to decorate their bodies, their residential
spaces, and their vessels and utensils. Their dance and music were also
themed around the totem. Today the bodies of primitive people are gone,
many of the objects they used have decayed, and their dance and music
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
have left no record. The only totem art preserved is paintings on rocks, and,
more abundantly, decorative patterns on painted pottery. (Fig. 1.31).





Fig. 1.31 Painted pottery basin with dancing pattern,
Majiayao Type, height:14 cm, top diam.: 28 cm, in the National Museum of China

     It is believed by scholars that if animal-themed patterns were found
throughout the painted pottery system of a particular culture type, such
patterns could be deemed to be totem-related.
  Common images found on Yangshao Culture painted pottery are fish,
birds, frogs, and deer. There are also a small number of flower and deity
images. Fish patterns dominate the pottery in the Jing and Wei River basins,
notably the painted pottery of the Banpo Type, while bird patterns dominate
in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, for instance on the
painted pottery of the Miaodigou Type. Patterns combing birds and fish
have also been found in these areas. Traces of primitive people in these
areas taking fish or birds as clan totems can be found in ancient Chinese
mythology. For instance, the legend of the birth and death of Hou Ji,
ancestor of the clan originating in the Jing and Wei River reaches that
became the ruling family of the Zhou Dynasty, involves fish and birds. It is
recorded in the Huai Nan Zi: On Terrain that: “Hou Ji had his tomb west of
Jianmu. He returned from death, half turned into a fish. Hou Ji turned half
fish and half human following his death. Being human and fish in one
embodies a return to the ancestral form of fish. Seven instances of such
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
patterns have been found on painted pottery of the Banpo Type, and most
were drawn on the inner walls of basins with big mouths, rolled rims,
shallow bellies and spherical bottoms. The wares have a brownish red
coating and the paintings are black. (Fig. 1.32) One representative basin is
painted with alternate human faces and fish on its inner wall. The human
faces are round, with the part above the eyes painted with black or blank
triangles. The ears are in the shape of two fish. The fish bodies are long
triangles filled with rhombus checks as scales, and the heads are also
triangular, with round eyes. The mouth area of the faces is also flanked by a
fish pattern on either side. Such decorative imagery is in line with the
above-mentioned “combined human and fish“legend. One poem titled
“Qian“about the sacrificial activities of the Zhou Dynasty in the Book of
Songs mentions the great abundance of fish in the Qi and Ju rivers, both of
which merge into the Wei River, and that only fish was used as a sacrifice
to the Zhou ancestors. The poem “Fish and Pondweed“of the Xiao Ya
(Minor Odes of the Kingdom), also in the Books of Songs, makes an
analogy with the king of Zhou, happy and at ease with fish, roaming freely
among pondweed. Such recurrent associations of fish with the Zhou
ancestors and the king was probably not coincidental—perhaps fish were
the totem of the ancestors of the Zhou clan. As for the pattern combining
fish and birds seen in Banpo Type painted pottery, some scholars believe
that its conception was probably because the ancestors of the Zhou clan
once received help and protection from a clan holding the bird as totem,
which is indeed a plausible theory. (Fig. 1.33).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

The main decorative imagery of pottery in the middle and lower reaches
of the Yellow River was the bird. Bird patterns were one of the dominant
patterns of Miaodigou Type painted pottery. Similarly, there are also
legends and records about birds as local clan totems in the region. (Fig.
1.34) For instance, “Black Bird“in Shang Song (Odes of Shang) in the Book
of Songs opens with “Sent by Heaven, the black bird descended and gave
birth to Shang”. A recurrent pattern on painted pottery of the late Yangshao
Culture was a double-headed multi-legged bird with a long body, which
often appeared together with the sun pattern, indicating that the clan taking
the bird as its totem probably worshipped the sun. Indeed, many ancient
myths and stories associate birds with the sun. For instance, The Classic of
the Great Wilderness: East (Dahuangdong jing) of the Classic of Mountains
and Seas (Shan Hai Jing) includes: “The sun comes, and the sun goes,
carried by the Crow”. The image of a bird residing in the sun is frequently
seen in silk paintings and stone sculptures of the Han Dynasty. Many of the
“Golden Crow in the Sun“images have three legs like the bird pattern on
Miaodigou Type painted pottery. It can be deduced therefore that the three-
legged bird was a symbol of the sun.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 1.34 Painted pottery urn with stork and stone axe pattern,
Miaodigou Type, height:47 cm, top diam.: 32.7 cm, in the National Museum of China

   Other patterns derived from everyday life are frequently found in other
cultural types, for instance, the salamander pattern of the late Yangshao
Culture in eastern Gansu, the human-face fish-body pattern of Majiayao
Type, the human figure pattern of Banshan and Machang types, and the
lizard pattern of Siba Culture. All of these patterns could be associated with
totem worship.
   Modern people are not able to know for sure the purpose of ancient
people in decorating painted pottery with such totems, but some theories
have been advanced. In ancient times, as society developed, contact
between clans and tribes grew increasingly frequent. Members of different
groups mingled together, and it became difficult to tell them apart. Totem
symbols enabled people to easily and accurately distinguish one group from
another, so as to avoid the outflow of members of their own clan to other
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
groups. In this way the strength of their own group was preserved. Pottery
wares as daily utensils also needed to bear some mark to indicate which
clan they belonged to, and many such marks were in the pattern of the
clan’s totem.
   Decorative images of painted pottery may be classified into two major
styles, life imitating styles and abstract geometric styles. Earlier periods
often featured the first style but the focus gradually shifted to the latter in
later times. The reasons probably include the following. In earlier times
totem culture was more prevalent and so concrete and life-like portrayal of
the totem was required. In addition, the earliest painted pottery was made
entirely by hand, and so it was more convenient to draw a single realistic
pattern than patterns that cover the entire ware. As time moved on totem
culture declined and there was less imperative for realistic and life-like
totem images. Later, the introduction of the slow wheel made it convenient
to paint the whole ware with abstract and regular geometric patterns. In
fact, the geometric patterns drawn in this manner were beautiful and rich,
and the technique was easy to master and impart. The totem images on
pottery wares also served both marking and worshipping purposes in the
first place. Later their significance as marks grew while their value in terms
of totem worship waned. As marks, it is natural that they developed to
become simpler, clearer, yet richer in meaning. This course of development
was similar to that of hieroglyphics.
    Naturally, even the earliest so-called life-like images were already two-
dimensional and regularized decorative patterns. The Banpo Type human
face and fish patterns and the Miaodigou Type bird pattern of the early
Yangshao Culture, the Machang Type frog and human figure patterns of the
Majiayao Culture, the Zhangjiazui Type canine pattern of the Xindian
Culture, the Huoshaogou Type lizard pattern of the Siba Culture, etc., all
shifted gradually from realistic to abstract geometric style. The
transformation of the fish pattern of Banpo Type painted pottery is a typical
example. The earliest patterns were mostly made of a single minutely and
realistically depicted fish with little exaggeration and were generally
painted on the upper part of the wares. In the middle stage, the fish patterns
began shifting towards a more liberal style. The fish heads and bodies
started evolving from their irregular natural shapes to regular geometric
shapes, taking on a stronger decorative effect, until in the late stage they
became complete geometric patterns with barely any reference to the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
original fish. A pair of facing heads first evolved into a square with four
black (yin) and blank (yang) triangles with only two eyes remaining to give
the suggestion of a fish. Then the eyes also disappeared and the two heads
were simplified into a square with diagonal lines. The fish body, fins and
tail also underwent a series of changes to form symmetric yin and yang
patterns of right-angled triangles with arc hypotenuses, which further
evolved into slanting and then horizontal lines. (Fig. 1.35).





Fig. 1.35 Evolution of the fish pattern on Banpo Type painted pottery
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
The bird pattern on Miaodigou Type painted pottery also went through a
similar process from the realistic to the abstract. There are two types of bird
patterns, namely frontal and lateral. Those from the frontal perspective used
a dot to represent the bird‘s head, a triangle with curved sides to represent
the body of a bird about to fly, as well as three vertical lines representing
three legs. Subsequently, the three legs were omitted and only the dot and
curved triangle were retained as a geometric pattern to represent the bird.
The lateral bird image was initially also realistic, basically the silhouette of
a standing bird. A blank point represented the eye on a head in the shape of
a triangle. Two wings pointed upward and two parallel lines represented the
two legs. Later the head morphed from triangular to circular, the legs and
beak were omitted altogether, the body was transformed into a long line and
the wings and tail became several upward arcs. In the end the lateral bird
pattern was simplified into one dot and three arcs which evolved into a
variety of continuous geometric patterns composed of dots, straight lines,
arcs, and crescents. Such geometric patterns lost all suggestion of the shape
of a bird whilst preserving the dynamic sense of flying. (Fig. 1.36).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

Fig. 1.36 Evolution of bird pattern on Miaodigou Type painted pottery

   The Banshan and Machang Types of painted pottery of the Majiayao
Culture features a pattern that resembles a frog or an erect human with both
arms raised and legs apart. Some scholars believe it is a frog pattern while
others believe it is a human figure. Some researchers believe that the pattern
depicts wizards praying to Heaven by imitating the appearance of a frog,
probably by clans taking the frog as their totem. Still others believe the
pattern depicts people in the action of sowing seeds and associate it with
Shennong (a mythical agricultural deity). In any case, the pattern, initially
depicting the complete form of a frog or a human, later lost the head and
retained only the limbs and fingers. Then even the fingers were omitted,
and they became continuous polygonal line patterns consisting of thick and
thin lines. (Fig. 1.37).

   Many Neolithic painted pottery patterns experienced a similar
evolution. The lizard pattern of Huoshaogou painted pottery developed
from single realistic lizard images to rhombus checks and polygonal lines.
(Fig. 1.38) The lateral canine pattern of Xindian Culture eventually evolved
into a type of curve pattern. As for the various swirl patterns of Majiayao
Culture, some scholars believe they evolved from images of flying birds or
salamanders while others believe they evolved from images of snakes or
water waves, which are all possible.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 1.38 Double shoulder handled jar with lizard pattern,
Xindian Culture, height: 15 cm, unearthed in Lintao, Gansu Province

     It could be inferred that the painted pottery patterns of the Neolithic
followed strict rules. They were more than marks using totems to
distinguish between clans, or mere decorations for religious worship—they
were probably also a pictorial language that conveyed various cultural and
lifestyle information. They bordered on a system of linguistic symbols that
made sense to the people at the time like the written language we now have.
The geometric patterns on the pottery wares might be relating the legends
and stories of a tribe or clan, describing a certain life scene or sacrificial
ritual, or expressing or displaying some sort of collective wish. Since these
patterns and our present language belong to completely different cultural
systems, modern people are not able to comprehend their meanings, while
people back then would have understood them perfectly and used them as
one of the means to record, transmit and exchange information.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
These ancient painted pottery patterns might also offer a glimpse into
the origin of Chinese philosophy. Besides realistic decorative images,
primitive pottery patterns in other countries included geometric patterns that
were symmetrical or stratified. Some were arranged at fixed points with
equal intervals. The patterns were mostly static. Chinese painted pottery
patterns, on the contrary, were often organized in a dynamic format.
Composed of curved lines, arc shapes and round dots, they often had a
strong sense of motion, indeed, infinite motion. For instance, the painted
pottery of Majiayao Culture, and its Banshan Type in particular, as well as
Dawenkou and Daxi Cultures, were often decorated with swirling patterns
like infinitely revolving spirals. (Fig. 1.39) Jars, basins and bowls of the
Majiayao Culture were often painted with circles or lines revolving around
more than three central points, creating a feeling of continuous rotation.
(Fig. 1.40) The painted pottery of Qujialing Culture also featured pairs of
whirling patterns, one up and one down and linked in the middle, which
were subsequently simplified into a pattern resembling the Taiji Diagram.
Such patterns, describing a sort of infinite motion that shattered the
restriction of finite space with repeated and endless rhythms, represented
the Chinese ancestors‘ macroscopic perception and overall grasp of the
chaotic external world. Additionally, many painted pottery pieces of the late
Banpo Type had dualistic patterns composed of yin (black) and yang
(blank) sections. Such patterns not only exhibited a strong decorative effect,
but also expressed the artistic conception of contrast, the combination of
nihility and reality, and the unity of opposites. The Banpo regions were also
the residence of the ancient Zhou people and the birthplace of the yin and
yang theory. Thus, it might not be accidental that yin and yang style
patterns were often found on the painted pottery of these areas. The painted
pottery spindle whorls of the Qujialing Culture (Fig. 1.41) also featured yin
and yang patterns. These patterns, while varied, all derived from a basic
framework similar to the Taiji Diagram which is characterized by an “S”
shape drawn at the diameter of a perfect circle to divide the circle into two
parts, one yin and one yang, both revolving around the core of the circle.
The centrosymmetric motion expressed how nihility and reality, negativity
and positivity, and nonexistence and existence revolve around the same
center, eating into each other and becoming each other. Such motion
represented the unity of all opposite things, including heaven and earth, the
sun and moon, men and women, left and right, and above and below. The I
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Ching (Classic of Change) holds that “yin and yang is the Way. Such an
idea stemmed from our ancestors’ simple understanding of the nature of the
universe. They already realized that the world we live in is one that is
constantly moving, and that everything is opposed to but also dependent on
the other. It was such understandings that gave rise to the yin-yang and Wu
Xing (five elements, namely, water, soil, fire, wood, metal) cosmology, the
Taiji Diagram, the Eight Trigrams, as well as Taoism and Confucianism.

1.3.4 Artistic Value of Painted Pottery Patterns
Besides rich cultural connotations, painted pottery patterns, as one of the
earliest human primitive arts, also have significant artistic value. They
indicate that the origin of art was more associated with religion and
practicality than with aestheticism and entertainment. The religious value of
arts lie in the fact that they express primitive humanity’s raw and
imaginative understandings of the universe and nature. With animism as the
earliest religious thought, patterns or totemic images painted on pottery
wares were imputed with some sort of spirituality and were even considered
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
protectors of their owners. Some pottery wares were burial or sacrificial
objects in the first place. One example is the thin-neck painted pottery pot
with hole-shaped mouth of the Banpo Type. This liquid vessel is found
throughout the development of the Banpo culture, but it was mainly
unearthed in tombs and rarely in living spaces. Some scholars thus believe
these wares were almost solely used as burial objects. Another instance is
the small water vessels of the late Banpo Type, mainly calabash-shaped
painted pottery bottles whose smaller upper section was often painted black
and lower belly drawn with totem images of fish, human faces or the two in
combination. These vessels are also predominately unearthed in tombs.
     It is believed by some that before the pottery age there had existed a
calabash age when humans used dried calabash as various utensils. This is
plausible because many rural areas in China still use ladles or liquor vessels
made of calabash. Legend has it that calabash was the savior of mankind.
After the primeval flood, when everything was submerged in water, a boy
and a girl emerged from a calabash that had kept them safe throughout the
flood, and so human beings were able to survive and reproduce. The poem
“Mian“in the Da Ya (Greater Odes of the Kingdom) section of the Book of
Songs opens with an analogy extolling the multitudinous early Zhou
population replete with countless calabash. These all suggest that there was
some primitive worshiping of calabash at the time. (Fig. 1.42) The calabash
theme was used not only in shaping pottery wares, but also in the painted
pottery patterns of Majiayao Culture.

   One practical value of the patterns might be to help distinguish between
different tribes. As primitive humans did not have names, the pottery
patterns and their body tattoos could all serve as marks of individuals and
their respective groups. In an age without written language, the rich abstract
images were very probably a means of recording and communicating
information. Composed of straight lines, curved lines, squares, circles, arcs,
waves, swirls, dots, etc., the pictographic patterns are rich in meaning;
brilliant creations of the Neolithic ancestors. They are also similar to the
earliest Chinese characters inscribed on tortoise shells and bronze objects
which were also made up of simple dots and lines.
   Since these patterns were not solely for the purpose of visual
entertainment or aestheticism, their creation was not random. It must have
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
followed certain rules and a linguistic system of symbols. Each abstract
geometric pattern came from a concrete entity. When developing a pattern,
the painter preserved and integrated the main characteristics of the entity
and left out most of the details. The resultant pattern might be far from the
appearance of the entity on which it was based, but it preserved and
highlighted its spirit. This approach of reconstructing, processing and
refining abstract images based on real life and natural entities is still used in
the present-day teaching and practice of art design.
   Another feature of late Neolithic painted pottery was the artful use of
coloring and blankness in decorative patterns. Specifically, dots, curved
lines and triangular arcs were drawn and painted black to form intricate and
beautiful patterns, and in such an ingenious way that the space left blank
also formed unique patterns. The black and blank sections, interrelated,
mutually conditional and echoing one another, when combined, generate
more numerous and much richer visual effects. This technique embodies the
Chinese philosophical idea of “mutual generation and mutual restraint”.
(Fig. 1.43).





Fig. 1.43 Painted pottery basin,
Miaodigou Type, height: 18 cm, top diam.: 38 cm, in the Palace Museum

   As totem-associated symbols, abstract geometric patterns on late
Neolithic painted pottery had to be recognizable and identifiable by
members of the same cultural type. Thus, their design must conform to
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
certain rules. The art of pattern design is in itself different from painting.
One difference is that it is subject to the restrictions of “guiju“(literally
“compass” and “setsquare”, or rules). On picture bricks of the Han Dynasty,
the Fuxi and Nüwa were depicted standing side by side with their tails
entangled. One holds a compass and the other holds a setsquare, indicating
the importance of geometric instruments in ancient times, which is echoed
by the ancient Chinese saying, “one cannot draw a circle or square without
a compass or setsquare”. The painted pottery patterns in the late Neolithic
were almost all geometric patterns. In fact, this was the earliest period of
large-scale geometric pattern design in China. The patterns revealed the
richness of early Chinese culture. The rules, order and discipline regulating
social activities probably took shape in the same period. The decorative
pottery patterns in the late Neolithic laid down most of the pattern design
rules that were used in later periods. The period saw fully developed
patterns including band-shaped decoration and scattered dot decoration,
mature rules and techniques including the principles of symmetry, balance,
contrast and change within unity, the creation of independent and integrated
patterns, and the artful use of dots, lines and surfaces, as well as the colors
black, white and gray. All these made the late Neolithic a peak period in the
history of Chinese pattern decoration.

1.3.5 Emergence and Development of Black Pottery
Though other pottery categories such as gray, red and white pottery also
appeared in the late Neolithic, this book focuses on the painted and black
pottery because the two were the most representative and the most prevalent
pottery categories of the period and incorporated the richest cultural
connotations. While painted pottery was mainly distributed in Yangshao
Culture, black pottery was a main feature of Longshan Culture.
    Originating in Longshan in Zhangqiu, Shandong, Longshan Culture
expanded across China and blended with different local cultures to form a
wide cultural system. Its wide distribution also resulted in different parts of
the country experiencing the Longshan Culture at different times. In the
middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, Longshan Culture ran from
2600 to 2200 BCE, while in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, it
started in the early days of Qujialing Culture and lasted from 3000 to 2500
BCE. Meanwhile, in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River its period
stretched from 2600 to 2200 BCE. During this time all these regions in
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
China began to display features common to the Longshan Culture which
went beyond the characteristics of pottery, stone wares and weapons, and
included remarkable developments in religion, agriculture and the
handicraft industry, as well as the more significant appearance of obvious
class stratification and the emergence of a large number of small states
across China.
   Longshan Culture was first discovered at Chengziya in Longshan in
1928. Following this, a number of similar cultural sites were discovered in
Henan, Shaanxi, Shanxi, Hebei, Anhui, Jiangsu and Gansu. Developed on
the basis of several Yangshao Culture types as well as the Dawenkou and
Qujialing Cultures, Longshan Culture represented a new historic period, a
transition between the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, a period during which
both stone wares and bronzewares were used. Longshan Culture developed
in different regions from different cultures and local conditions, and
therefore varied markedly despite many commonalities. To distinguish
between the different variations, people named them “Shandong Longshan
Culture, “Henan Longshan Culture, “Hubei Longshan Culture, “Shaanxi
Longshan Culture, and so on. Later researchers found such province-based
naming did not accurately reflect the nature of the different culture types
and began using terms like the “Keshengzhuang Type“(also known as
Keshengzhuang Phase II Culture), “Taosi Type”, “Hougang Type“(also
known as Hougang Phase II Culture), “Wangwan Phase III Culture, and
“Sanliqiao Type, and these were collectively called the Central Plains
Longshan Culture. They also marked off Hubei Longshan or Qinglongquan
Phase III Culture from Longshan Culture and renamed it Shijiahe Culture42,
and called “Shandong Longshan Culture” “Typical Longshan
Culture.Longshan Culture started and ended in different regions at different
times. The end of the later ones overlapped with the Bronze Age in the
central plains. Carbon-14 dating shows that Longshan Culture in the central
plains existed from 2010 to 1810 BCE, and Shandong Longshan Culture
existed from 2010 to 1580 BCE. Hence some scholars termed the historical
period represented by Longshan Culture in different regions the “Longshan
Age“due to its considerable longevity. It constituted the late stage of the
Neolithic or the end of the prehistoric era. Very soon human society entered
the civilized age and class society.
   Chinese scholars have not yet reached agreement as to whether the
Longshan Age following the Yangshao Culture and preceding the Xia
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Dynasty had entered the city-state era of the “nation” stage. Zhang
Guangzhi believes that the Longshan Age still belonged to clan society and
specifically, the clan alliance stage of late clan society, and that the nation
did not come into being until the Xia Dynasty.43 During the Longshan Age,
stone shovels appeared and quickly increased in number. Meanwhile, many
stone tools became transformed into ritual objects symbolizing power and
status, particularly the yue (battle-axe), bi (a round flat piece of jade with a
hole in the center) and axes, many of which featured delicate polishing and
carved decorations (though these features already existed in the late
Neolithic, they were not as prevalent). The development and
professionalization of stone art also contributed to the emergence of the
jade industry. Large numbers of jade objects have been unearthed from
large tombs. The carved decorations are exquisite and there are artifacts
with sacrificial functions and functions representing political and military
power such as dragon-shaped objects. The superb workmanship and high
manufacturing cost of these artifacts indicate a considerable concentration
of wealth and control by certain individuals over large labor forces across
wide areas at the time.44
   Longshan Culture pottery was represented by black pottery as well as
thin walled “eggshell pottery, and representative varieties included tripod
food vessels (such as ding) and wine vessels (such as dou). These wares
mainly served as sacrificial objects rather than daily utensils, and in this
period, specialization appeared in the pottery industry. Most of these
exquisite pottery wares can only be found in large settlements and large
tombs and are distinctly different from those produced by small kilns in
small settlements. Tens of thousands of small red pottery cups and small
pottery angler statues were found in the southwest corner of the Shijiahe
Ancient Town Site. These were probably used for religious sacrifices and
daily use by ordinary people, yet regular Longshan Culture settlements had
only comprised hundreds or thousands of individuals. The number of
products far exceeded the demands of a single settlement and should
therefore be assumed to be aimed at supplying the regional market, a
market which ranged beyond even a large city-state and covered some
2,000 square kilometers. In addition to confirming that religious worship
had become a part of our ancestors’ everyday consciousness, these findings
also helped prove the existence of an interregional economic division of
labor and long-distance trade.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Courtyard style houses have been found in the earliest Longshan
Culture sites. They include workshops and food storage rooms, indicating
the beginning of handicraft activities with the household as the unit.
Economic development naturally led to a further disintegration of clan
society and the development of class society. Unprecedented rivalry among
tribes and regions also began. The behaviors and features of the elite class
displayed increasing alienation from clan traditions. The elite class
monopolized wars, religious activities, and the manufacture and use of
ritual objects to realize a concentration of power and wealth.
     It is for the above reasons that a considerable number of Chinese
scholars subscribe to the view that China had become a complex class
society in the Longshan Age. In this Age there were not only
handicraftsmen, professional soldiers, farmers, administrators and slaves,
but kings also appeared for the first time in prehistoric China. The kings
seemed to have evolved from the military or administrative leaders of
previous clan tribes, and they continued to rely on religion to ensure the
legitimacy of their social status.45
    Pottery expresses the cultural ideals of the time. As the social system
and social structure changed in the Longshan Age, the black pottery of the
Age grew to be remarkably different to the painted pottery of the previous
period both in terms of shape and artistic approach. The pottery of different
Longshan Culture types in different parts of the country exhibited different
features. Following are the major types.

1.3.5.1 Hougang Phase II Culture
Also known as “Henan Longshan Culture Type”, Hougang Phase II Culture
existed in eastern and northern Henan, southwestern Shandong and
southern Hebei. Its pottery was dominated by gray pottery, complemented
by red, black and white pottery. In its late stage red pottery decreased and
black pottery increased and the characteristic eggshell black pottery
emerged. Representative varieties included tripod ding with tight mouth and
deep, round belly, straight-mouth shallow-belly ding with three flat legs,
tight-mouth deep-belly flat-bottom jars, and tight-mouth deep-belly li with
handles. There were also open-mouth flat-bottom plates, small pots with
flat bottoms and a single handle, filters and circular-foot plates with their
inner walls engraved with grooves, dou, gui (鬶), jia (tripod wine vessels), gu
(goblets with broad lips, long narrow stems, and flared bases), cups, urns,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
etc., among which li (cooking vessels with hollow feet), flat-leg ding, and
gui (鬶) with arc-shaped spouts were typical of the culture type.46 The
surface decoration was dominated by rope patterns, followed by basket
patterns and checks, and some fingernail prints.

1.3.5.2 Shandong Longshan Culture Type
ALso called Typical Longshan Culture due to its representativeness,
Shandong Longshan Culture was distributed in areas with Shandong at the
center and reaching the Liaodong Peninsula in the north and northern
Jiangsu in the south. Over half of the pottery wares were made with a
potter’s wheel. Most were black pottery, followed by gray pottery and small
numbers of red, yellow and white pottery. The latter three types were
mostly gui (簋). The firing temperature of the black pottery has been
measured to around 1,000 degrees Celsius, the red pottery 950 degrees, and
the white pottery from 800 to 900 degrees. The black pottery was made
from fine clay, regular clay and sandy clay, and of these, fine-clay thin-wall
black pottery demonstrated the highest workmanship. The wares were made
from fine clay that had been carefully washed and molded using a potter’s
wheel, resulting in highly polished walls that were only 0.5 to one
millimeter thick. The large number of such eggshell black pottery pieces is
a prominent feature of Shandong Longshan Culture. The main eggshell
black pottery varieties include long stem cups with broad rims which
featured a fine body texture, exquisite workmanship and elegant shape.
Production of such thin-walled pottery required rich and prolonged
experience and considerable skill, indicating that by this time the pottery
industry had become highly specialized and mastered by a handful of
experienced families.
  An eggshell black pottery goblet was unearthed in Rizhao, Shandong in
1973. (Fig. 1.44) It has an extended mouth, deep and slightly swollen belly
whose mid-section is decorated with several dented strings and whose
lower part is spherical. The long, thin stem is tubule-shaped in the upper
and lower sections, yet the middle section is swollen for easy holding and
placement. The swollen section is hollow and decorated with tiny through-
carved holes. Below the stem is a pedestal-shaped circular foot. Formed
with a potter’s wheel and fired at an optimum temperature, the ware has a
hard body, excellent impermeability, a bright black surface and eggshell-
like walls, with the thinnest part less than 0.5 mm. Of delicate shape, plain
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
but elegant color and exquisite decoration, the goblet is both a practical
utensil and a piece of art. Other wares such as eggshell black pottery goblet
sets, and black pottery tripod ding also reflect the superb pottery
workmanship in the lower reaches of the Yellow River. (Fig. 1.45).
