1.3.5.3 Keshengzhuang Phase II Culture
Also known as “Shaanxi Longshan Culture Type, Keshengzhuang Phase II
Culture was first discovered in Keshengzhuang in Chang’an, Shaanxi and
was distributed in the Wei River basin in the Guanzhong area of Shaanxi.
Its pottery was mainly sandy and clay gray pottery, complemented by small
amounts of black pottery and red pottery. Coil-forming was the most
prevalent manufacturing technique, and some were molded with a model or
wheel. Apart from plain and polished surfaces, some objects were decorated
with basket and rope patterns, a few with check patterns, and some painted.
The Li with a handle on the neck displayed the most distinctive local
feature. There are also a tripod ding with a tight mouth, folded rim, and
deep and rounded belly, a tight-mouthed single-handled deep-bellied li with
bag-shaped feet, straight-mouthed double-handled cylindrical-bellied jia
with bag-shaped feet, single-handled jars, amphorae, three-handled round-
bellied flat-bottomed jars, slanting-walled flat-bottomed bowls, small-
mouthed high-collared angular-shouldered urns, vessel lids, etc.47 The ding
and gui (鬶) were similar to those of the Wangwan Type, the li and jia were
similar to those of the Sanliqiao Type, and the amphorae, small amphorae
and small-mouthed angular-shouldered urns were close in form to those of
the Qijia Culture, which shows that there were frequent interactions and
mutual influences between Keshengzhuang Type pottery with the
contemporary Longshan Culture types in surrounding areas.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
1.3.5.4 Shijiahe Culture (Qinglongquan Phase III Culture)
Also known as “Hubei Longshan Culture Type, Shijiahe Culture was first
discovered in the Qinglongquan Phase III (upper layer) site in Yunyang,
Hubei, and is therefore also called Qinglongquan Phase III Culture. It is
distributed in roughly the same areas as Qujialing Culture, namely, the
Jianghan Plain as the center and surrounding areas. Carbon-14 dating shows
it existed about 4,000 years ago.48
   The pottery of Qinglongquan Phase III Culture was mostly sandy and
clay gray pottery, complemented with small amounts of brownish gray and
black pottery. Surface decorations are mainly basket patterns with some
additional stacking patterns, checks, rope patterns and scratched marks. The
main varieties are tight-mouthed shallow-bellied ding with broad flat feet,
tight-mouthed rolled-rim long-necked jia with bag-shaped feet, jars with
small mouths, folded rims, and deep, round bellies, gui (鬶) with bag-shaped
feet, open-mouthed circular-footed dou, circular footed plates, open-
mouthed basin-shaped circular-footed zeng (rice steamers), goblets, long
necked pots, small-mouthed high-collar jars, small-mouthed high-collar
urns, flat-bottomed cups, big-mouthed thick-walled vats, funnel-shaped
filters and vessel lids. The shapes and decorations indicate that the culture
type obviously developed on the basis of the local Qujialing Culture and
was also influenced by the Longshan Culture in the central plains.49

1.3.5.5 Shanxi Xiangfen Taosi Longshan Culture Type
This culture type was first discovered in Taosi Village in Xiangfen County,
Shanxi, and covered the lower reaches of the Fenhe River and the Linfen
Basin along the river. More than 70 similar sites have been found but not
entirely of the same period.
   The pottery of the Shanxi Xiangfen Taosi Longshan Culture Type was
dominated by sandy and clay gray pottery, accompanied by some brown
and black pottery. Early and late periods of the culture type featured
different pottery forms. Notably, pottery of the early period was thicker and
was mainly decorated with rope patterns. Basket patterns and checks were
rare. The main varieties included cylindrical cookers with connected
cauldron and stove, flat-leg ding, small-mouth long-neck deep-belly flat-
bottom jars, big-mouth slanting-wall flat-bottom zeng with through-carved
holes, dou with open mouth, shallow basins, high circular foot, big-mouth
folded-belly flat-bottom basins, and big-mouth urns. Pottery of the late
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
period had thinner walls. Surface decorations were mainly basket patterns.
Rope patterns and checks were less common. Some of the early pottery
wares resemble those of the Miaodigou Type and some are similar to those
of the Wangwan Type, while pottery of the late period is closer to that of the
Sanliqiao Type, which shows that the Taosi Longshan Culture was slightly
later than the Miaodigou.50

1.3.6 Elements Contributing to Black Pottery Style
In summary, it can be seen that painted pottery started declining and that
black pottery took its place. Indeed, the Longshan Culture Age featured
other pottery types apart from black pottery, especially in its early stage
when gray pottery was produced in the greatest quantity. Then in the middle
period, black pottery appeared in large quantities, which was dominated by
sandy and clay blackish gray pottery, followed by clay black pottery
(including black-skinned pottery). The black pottery art of Longshan
Culture arose based on painted pottery art. The black pottery was made
from good quality fine clay as was painted pottery. Though hand-forming
still continued, for some wares fast wheels started to be used in place of the
slow wheel of the painted pottery period, and the use of the jigger wheel
became prevalent. The most remarkable was the pottery industry of
Shandong Longshan Culture, which developed on the basis of the
Dawenkou Culture. By that time, apart from some wares and accessories
such as handles, knobs, spouts, and feet, almost all ware bodies were
formed with the potter’s wheel, which led to a more perfect body shape and
a more even wall thickness and made possible the making of eggshell black
pottery. In terms of surface decoration, polishing was applied. Specifically,
gravel or bone tools were used to press and polish the surface of greenware
when it was about to dry, so that the ware would have a certain luster after
being fired. This technique first appeared in the Peiligang and Cishan
Cultures while the painted pottery of Yangshao Culture was also decorated
with patterns after polishing. The black pottery art of Longshan Culture
inherited this decorative technique and succeeded in creating eggshell black
pottery that had a brightness resembling lacquer.
   The emergence of black pottery was also associated with the
improvement in firing techniques and kiln atmosphere. Pottery clay rich in
iron would create red or brown pottery when fired in an oxidizing flame and
black pottery in a reducing flame. The earliest method for making black
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
pottery was to block the vent when the temperature in the kiln reached a
certain level, so that there was a significant shortage of oxygen in the kiln.
Iron oxides were thus reduced, which, together with the smoking effect, led
to the black color of the resultant ware. Such a method required a high kiln
temperature and the skills to control kiln atmosphere. It would be
impossible without improved firing skills and more diversified firing
techniques.
   The new techniques outlined above developed on the basis of previous
traditions, namely, meticulous washing of pottery clay, the application of
the fast wheel, improved surface polishing skills, and the use of the
reducing flame for firing. This contributed to the birth of black pottery and
endowed it with features different to previous pottery. First, improved firing
techniques raised the degree of sintering and therefore resulted in a higher
density and hardness of the pottery. Second, the use of fast wheels not only
led to even wall thickness and perfect body shapes, but also, and more
importantly, to more diversified ware forms and shapes. A lot of new
varieties unseen in painted pottery came into being. These new varieties on
the one hand met the new needs brought on by improvements in the
people’s livelihoods, and on the other hand were made possible by the
technical conditions brought about by the application of the fast wheel.
   The change in firing and shaping techniques naturally led to a change in
decorative approaches. The black color and the more complex shapes and
structures of pottery wares made painting an unsuitable decorative
approach. Thus, during the black pottery dominated Longshan Age, the
practice of painting on pottery surfaces declined, retaining a certain degree
of popularity only in a few local cultural systems. In its place the approach
of painting after the wares were fired was adopted, but this was for ritual or
religious purposes rather than practical aesthetic appeal. Black pottery
wares for practical use were mostly plain and polished, which was also a
decorative means, and indeed, an elegant and exquisite one. Apart from
polishing, the surface was decorated with a rich variety of string patterns,
some concave and some convex, pressed down or stacked up with the
convenience of the fast wheel. The string patterns as aesthetically pleasing
decoration constituted a major stylistic feature of the black pottery in this
period.
    In terms of shaping, the use of the fast wheel also brought more intricate
changes and fluctuations to the outline of the wares. Painted pottery wares
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
mostly have simple and rounded outlines as people usually focus on the
paintings rather than the ware shape itself. In this respect, black pottery is
different. Since it carries no painting, all the decoration lies in the ingenuity
of the shape. Therefore, particular care was devoted to the ups and downs of
the ware’s outline, especially at turning points between the mouth and
shoulder, shoulder and belly, and belly and foot. While the glamor of
painted pottery lies in the beauty of its decorative patterns, that of black
pottery lies in the beauty of its shape which is rich in diversity.
    In the age of painted pottery, everyday varieties were limited to jars,
basins, pots, bowls, bottles and cups, and by the age of black pottery,
varieties increased greatly thanks to the introduction of the fast wheel. In
addition, pottery of this age was not limited to black pottery. There was also
gray, white and red pottery. In terms of decoration, besides plain polished
surfaces, there were also scratch marks, string patterns, basket patterns,
checks, additional stacking patterns, fingernail prints, circles and through-
carved holes. Since Longshan Culture developed based on middle Neolithic
cultures, its pottery varieties were not entirely new, but also featured
innovations based on previous traditions. One example was the great
popularity of tripod wares, which first appeared back in the early Neolithic
and took on new characteristics during the Longshan Age. Most previous
tripod wares had solid feet, but by the Longshan Age, bag-shaped feet
became popular. It was an age of wide popularity for wares with three bag-
shaped feet, including li, urns, gui (鬶), and he. (Fig. 1.46) The appearance of
li presaged its great heyday during the Xia and Shang dynasties. Ding was
also quite popular during the Longshan Age, and common varieties were
various long-legged jar-shaped ding and long-legged basin-shaped ding.
Circular footed wares also increased, especially circular foot dou. Other
wares not frequently seen in previous times included flat-bottomed or
spherical-bottomed sandy jars, goblets, shallow basins, circular footed
plates, flat bottomed bowls, flat bottomed basins, and flat-bottomed zun.
(Fig. 1.47).

   One feature of the Longshan Age was the dramatic increase in pottery
liquor vessels such as the jia, gu, cups and small pots, which shows that by
this time there was considerable surplus grain enabling it to be made into
alcohol. The white pottery and imprinted hard pottery of Longshan Culture
boasted a fine texture and exquisite workmanship. White pottery wares
were dominated by gui (鬶) and dou with bag-shaped feet. There were also
smaller numbers of white pottery bowls and yu. The firing temperature of
white pottery was high and some wares when struck would give off
powerful and clear sounds resembling that of porcelain. The raw material
for the white pottery was like that of porcelain and was called porcelain
clay in northern China with some bearing a close affinity to kaolinite. Such
clay contained much less iron oxide than pottery clay and therefore would
take on a white color after firing. China was the first country in the world to
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
use porcelain clay and kaolinite, and the appearance of white pottery and
the rise in kiln temperatures lay the groundwork for the later transition from
pottery to porcelain.

1.3.7 Primitive Pottery and Emerging Chinese Values
In previous sections of this work, the reasons behind the rise of black
pottery art and the decline of painted pottery art during the Longshan period
were explored from the perspective of workmanship and materials. Apart
from these, there were also cultural reasons. Longshan Culture closely
followed primitive culture and was a transition period from primitive
society to slave society. In the study of painted pottery art, a carrier of
primitive totem consciousness, totem beliefs and totem systems, we are able
to trace back to the earliest social systems and religious forms in China and
at the same time, probe the source of Chinese philosophy. It has been
mentioned above that there were already early forms of the Chinese Taiji
Diagram in the painted pottery patterns of Qujialing Culture, and there were
many yin and yang associated patterns on the Banpo and Miaodigou Type
painted pottery. I therefore believe that the Chinese yin and yang
philosophy had probably already taken shape during the Neolithic Age.
     It is believed by some scholars that the Tao was the principle of Chinese
totem society and that “the concepts of yin and yang developed from the
Tao”. The philosophical concept of the Tao was created by neither
Confucius nor Laozi since “such a principle of totem culture came into
being long before these philosophers”. Rather, it is believed that “the
philosophical systems of Confucianism and Taoism can be regarded as the
direct product of the great principle of the totem system—the Tao, and that
“Confucius‘ ideological system centered on filial piety (孝) and rites (礼) also
grew from the Totem Complex.51 Some scholars also believe that the rites
(礼) and music (乐) that matured during the Western Zhou were developed and
derived forms of primitive totem singing, dancing, sorcery and ceremonies,
and that they originated from the unwritten behavioral rules ancient clans
and tribes required individual members to follow and abide by.52 By the
time of the Longshan Culture, totem culture was on the wane, but the
philosophical ideas, social organizational forms and various ritualistic
activities such as joining, reproduction, and ancestor worship rituals, which
came into being during the totem culture period, did not disappear. Rather,
these rituals and rules were improved, institutionalized and standardized to
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
gradually form the “li“(礼) system. People at the time had to undertake the
various trainings in li (礼) to grow into mature, humane individuals in which
humanity is essentially the sociality required by primitive groups, clans or
tribes.
   This is also reflected in pottery. The lively, exciting, and imaginative
patterns of painted pottery were replaced by rigorous, orderly and highly
regulated string patterns, and the vibrant contrasting colors of red, black and
yellow were replaced by solemn and monotonous black. The string patterns
frequently seen on black pottery wares, especially on goblets, were full of
rhythm and boasted a refined stylistic beauty. People are born with emotion,
but li (礼) restricted such emotion. It symbolized the remolding of people
with reason. Therefore, if the painted pottery art represented passionate
beauty, then the black pottery art represented rational beauty.

2. Ceramics of the Xia and Shang
Dynasties

Lili Fang1
(1)  Chinese National Academy of Arts, Beijing, China



   Lili Fang
  Email: zhongzl@fltrp.com

2.1 Introduction
2.1.1 Pottery in the Bronze Age
The Xia Dynasty was the earliest of the three founding dynasties (Xia,
Shang and Zhou) of Chinese civilization. The Records of the Grand
Historian (the Shiji) includes the Annals of Xia which records the kings and
major events of the Xia Dynasty. Records of the territory, capital location,
major events, etc. of the Xia Dynasty can also be found in other ancient
books including the Book of Documents (the Shangshu, also known as the
Shujing) and the Book of Songs.
   Apart from some marks on pottery wares, no written language of the
Xia Dynasty has been found to date. Important cultural remains of the
dynasty began to be discovered only in the 1950s and it was only after
about four decades of excavations and research, namely by around 1990,
that scholars began to form a relatively concrete picture of the Xia Dynasty.
Thus, it is not surprising that many Western researchers believe that the Xia
Dynasty is only legendary and that Chinese history began with the Shang
Dynasty.
    Cultural remains of the Xia Dynasty were found mainly in the Erlitou
Sites, in the site of the capital of the Xia, Zhenxun. Thus, in Chinese
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
archaeology, the culture of the Xia Dynasty is also known as “Erlitou
Culture”.The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project commissioned by the
Chinese government in 1996 concluded that the Xia existed between 1970
and 1600 BCE.
   By 2000, some 150 Erlitou cultural sites were identified, among which
67 were concentrated in the Erlitou area of central Henan, the cultural
center of the Xia Dynasty, and 35 were in modern southwestern Shanxi and
eastern Shaanxi, mostly concentrated around Dongxiafeng, the geographical
center of the Xia Dynasty. Only seven sites are in modern northern Henan,
and several are in southern Henan. Branches of the Xia culture have also
been found in southwestern Shandong, northwestern Anhui, Hubei, and
northern Jiangsu, covering a large area extending 1,000 km from end to
end.1
   Henan Longshan Culture existed from 2200 to 2000 BCE and Erlitou
Culture succeeded it. The discovery of Erlitou Culture in 1959 filled the gap
in the Huaxia Culture, in other words the culture of Chinas central plains,
between the Longshan Culture and the Shang Dynasty. Xia society
exhibited many advancements compared to the Longshan Culture. Stone
farming tools were carefully polished and excavation tools were widely
used. Bone tools and shell instruments appeared in large quantities. Stone
blades and scissors for harvesting crops had sharp edges, and knives for
cutting were introduced. Pigs, cattle and sheep were raised in large
numbers. Fishing also made advances, evidenced by the unearthing of large
numbers of hooks carved out of bone and pottery or jade sinkers. Jade
began to be used to make daily utensils and decorations instead of mainly as
ritual objects in previous times. The unearthing of sewing needles and
spindle whorls in many areas indicate that the textile industry was
flourishing at the time. Bone product workshops produced large quantities
of tools and decorative accessories including knives, needles, shovels,
hairpins and beads. Lacquer also became common in daily use products,
including gu, bowls and musical instruments such as drums. The pottery of
the Xia was dominated by gray pottery and tripod wares. The shapes and
styles displayed an obvious inheritance from Longshan Culture. The
appearance in large numbers of wine vessels such as gu, jue (ancient wine
vessels with three legs and a loop handle), jia and he, indicate the rise of
wine culture thanks to the progress in agriculture.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Archaeological excavations over the past five decades have offered new
data on the Xia Dynasty besides that contained in ancient historical texts.
Most of Sima Qians narrative on the Xia Dynasty in his Records of the
Grand Historian has been proven to be true by today’s archaeological
findings, especially the existence of a cultural system termed Huaxia at the
time in the central plains of China, a culture that was based on centralized
power and whose influence reached modern Hebei and Inner Mongolia in
the north and Henan and Jiangsu in the south. The Xia Dynasty marked the
beginning of the Bronze Age and slave society in China. During the
Longshan Culture before the Xia, society was built on the basis of
numerous independent regional political bodies or states, above which there
was only a loosely confederated alliance and whose leader was elected
based on their virtue and concrete contributions to the states, such as
inventing new agricultural techniques or preventing floods. Such was the
ideal time described by Confucius as the society of “Great Unity“(Datong, 大
同), where the passing of the throne was not based on family or blood ties,
but on the Abdication System.
   Major handicraft industries in the kingdom were controlled and mass
production was organized. Regional culture was gradually unified and
standardized. The central areas of the kingdom, namely the capital, became
the main urban settlement, which featured a stratified society, large numbers
of handicraftsmen and slaves, and a complex and organized controlling
institution with highly centralized powers. It cannot be denied that Erlitou
Culture or the Xia Dynasty was already a civilized society, a large country
with a capital at its center, and that that capital featured centralized power
and a complex structure.2
   The above describes in general terms the Xia Dynasty in time and
space. Next, the Shang time and space will be briefly reviewed. The Xia–
Shang–Zhou Chronology Project placed the Shang at 1600 to 1046 BCE. It
was divided into early and late Shang, with the former lasting from 1600 to
1298 BCE, and covering 17 kingly reigns. In terms of political systems, the
Shang inherited the tradition of familial rule and the Hereditary System that
had formed by the end of the Xia Dynasty.
   The birthplace of the Shang clan was in the ancient Zhang River Plain
east to the Taihang Mountains, that is, the present-day border area between
Henan and Hebei. The Zhang River was the ancient Shang River, and that is
why the clan was named “Shang”. The predynastic founder of the Shang
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
lineage was Qi (契), son of Emperor Ku (喾, one of the Five Emperors of the
Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors in Chinese mythology), who was
granted a place called Shang as a fief during the time of Yao and Shun.3
   The Huainanzi records that “King Zhous rule reaches the East Sea to
the left, Liusha to the right, Jiaozhi in the front and Youdu at the back”.
(King Zhou was the last king of the Shang Dynasty) Archaeological
materials have proven that the early Shang capital occupied roughly the
same area as the Erlitou Culture of the Xia Dynasty. By late Erligang
Culture, Shang’s rule had expanded to present-day Shandong, northern
Jiangxi, northern Hunan, southern Inner Mongolia, central Shaanxi and
southern Hebei.4
   The Shang Dynasty inherited the four-tier settlement system of the Xia
to govern its vast territory. The center of the kingdom was still the central
plains, where the Xia and Shang clans gradually merged over the two
centuries. The middle reaches of the Yellow River with a high agricultural
production efficiency and the main tributaries of the Yellow River with
fertile soil became the solid foundation for the Shang’s success.5
     It can be seen from the above descriptions that as Chinese civilization
entered the era of the Xia and Shang, cities and states took shape. The
development of private ownership gave rise to a gap between rich and poor,
and primitive society gave way to slave society, a class society mainly
composed of save owners and slaves. In terms of the handicraft industry,
Xia and Shang marked the transition from the Stone Age to the Bronze
Age. The production methods and tools (stone blades, wooden balls with
short handles) of class society seemed to exhibit no major difference from
those of the Neolithic, but the social structure, status of the citizenry, etc.
underwent significant changes. The walled cities, war chariots and bronze
sacrificial objects found in archaeological excavations were all owned by
the nobility, the existence of whom can be clearly identified from their
sacrifice and war activities, while little distinct archaeological evidence
remains of the peasant class. The court was the center of all activities of the
aristocratic class and the locus of all religious, administrative, military and
economic functions. The royal family sat at the top of all clan organizations
and the leaders of different clans also led the sacrifices of different families.
The dominant status of religion and religious activities was the most
distinctive feature of Shang civilization that set it apart from later
civilizations.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Ritual objects and food vessels were an essential part of all aspects of
aristocratic life and sacrificial activities in the Shang Dynasty. The
appearance of bronzewares meant pottery wares were no longer the most
beautiful utensils used in daily life or the most beautiful ritual objects used
in sacrificial activities. Bronze had yet another advantage over pottery—
that it could be used to make parts for weapons. As bronze became the most
important material for making daily utensils, ritual objects and weapons for
the Shang aristocratic class, pottery, while still developing and being used
by the common people, had lost much of its religious significance and was
therefore no longer as radiant or culturally rich as the painted and black
pottery of previous eras.

2.1.2 Development of Pottery Production in the Xia and Shang
Dynasties
Few ancient records have been found of the development of the pottery
industry in the Xia Dynasty. The article “Gengzhu” in Mozi mentions that
the Xia’s Kunwu clan was good at firing pottery and smelting bronze.
Though no bronzeware has yet been uncovered at early Erlitou Culture
sites, remains of bronze smelting have been found at a late Longshan
Culture site in western Henan, which slightly pre-dates Erlitou Culture.6 In
late Erlitou Culture sites and tombs, bronze tools including knives, cones,
chisels, and adzes, and bronze vessels such as the jue, have been found.7 It
could thus be deduced that bronze smelting was probably introduced back
in the early Erlitou Culture of the Xia Dynasty, or even earlier, during the
middle or late Longshan Culture. The invention of the bronze smelting
furnace might have drawn upon progress made in pottery kilns, while the
technique of smelting bronze with high-temperature furnaces in turn created
conditions for improving pottery kilns so that white pottery and early
porcelain with high thermostability could be fired.
   The Xia culture developed directly from the late Longshan Culture and
as a result the pottery of early Erlitou Culture in western Henan had
basically the same characteristics as the pottery of the late Longshan
Culture in the same area, except for minor differences in variety, shape and
surface decoration. Sandy and clay gray pottery (deep gray and grayish
black) (Fig. 2.1) still dominated, and there were also black pottery
(including black-skinned pottery), brownish gray pottery and red pottery,
with a scattering of white pottery and hard pottery wares. Design still
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
followed the previous style, mainly featuring the folded rim, flat bottom,
three solid legs and circular foot, but a small number of spherical bottomed
wares have also been found in the region. Most wares were formed with the
potter’s wheel and some were shaped by hand or with a model. Prevalent
surface decorations include scratch marks, string patterns, basket patterns,
checks, rope patterns, and additional stacking patterns, while square spirals,
yunlei (literally “cloud and thunder”) pattern (round and square spirals),
swirls, leaf vein patterns, petal patterns, herringbone, etc. can also be seen.
(Fig. 2.2).





Fig. 2.1 Gray pottery jue,
Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture, top diam.: 11.5 cm × 4.5 cm, height: 17 cm, unearthed at the
Dadianzi Site in Aohan Banner, Inner Mongolia
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 2.2 Painted cylindrical jar,
Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture, unearthed at the Dadianzi Site in Aohan Banner, Inner Mongolia

   Copper wares appeared on the Inner Mongolia prairie in the late
Neolithic. With the rise in production capacity and the improvement in
bronze smelting technology, most of the areas in present-day Inner
Mongolia entered the Bronze Age in a real sense about 4,000 years ago.
The emergence and development of bronze civilization on the prairie was
basically concurrent with that on the central plains. The difference was that
most of the bronzewares in agricultural zones in the central plains were
ritual objects for sacrificial purposes, while those in the northern grassland
were mainly for making weapons, production tools and everyday utensils.
The forerunners of the Bronze Age were the residents of Xiajiadian Lower
Layer Culture in eastern Inner Mongolia, who, using bronze tools, small
decorative accessories and small amounts of ritual objects with distinct
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
features, and building walled cities, had entered the “state” era. Xiajiadian
Lower Layer Culture was contemporaneous with the Xia and early Shang
Dynasty in the central plains. Also from the same period was the Zhukaigou
Culture in central and southern Inner Mongolia.
   The Xiajiadian Lower Layer and Zhukaigou cultures were two branches
of the early Bronze civilization. Records of these cultures can be found in
oracle bone inscriptions discovered at Yinxu (literally “the Ruins of Yin,
site of the ancient city of Yin, the last Shang Dynasty capital) and in ancient
historical texts. By the time of the Shang Dynasty, Xiajiadian Lower Layer
Culture had probably developed into the “Guzhu State(literally, “State of
Lonely Bamboos”) in the northernmost part of the Shang kingdom, which
was the remote “northern wasteland” of the four wastelands as recorded in
the Shidi (literally, Explaining Earth) chapter of Erya, the oldest surviving
Chinese dictionary written in the Han Dynasty. Xiajiadian Lower Layer
Culture was closely related to the Shang culture. The beast face pattern on
the painted pottery of Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture resembles the taotie
on bronze vessels from the Shang, and some ritual bronze vessels
resembled the copper wares of the Shang Dynasty.
   People of the Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture lived in tribal clusters,
were buried in tribal clusters after death, and maintained the traditions and
customs of the clan society stage. In some cemeteries, different clans or
families can be identified from the layout of tombs and the differences in
burial pottery. This indicates the dominant position of patriarchal clans.
Though social stratification had appeared, members of the same clan, old or
young, rich or poor, were still buried together. In general, under city-state
rule, the gap between classes was not wide, members of society were
relatively equal, and the slave system was not yet developed.
    Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture also had the funerary custom of
sacrificing livestock. A limited number of burial objects were used. The
dead with a high social status might be buried with ritual objects such as
pottery jue and gui (鬶), which were made by imitating similar objects from
the central plains, indicating that the deceased had economic and cultural
contact with the central plains when alive. Burial painted pottery was used
only for those with an especially high social status and tombs with painted
pottery were rarely found. The painted pottery had a unique style that was
not found in other cultures of the same period. They were completely
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
indigenous and the unique invention of Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture
residents.
   The Dadianzi Tomb was a typical Xiajiadian Low Layer Culture painted
pottery site. The wares were thickly and intricately painted with beautiful
and ingenious images, mainly in red and white. Most of the patterns were
composed of curly lines resembling the yunlei pattern frequently seen on
bronzewares, and some look like feathers. A small number of vessels were
decorated with animal faces as the main image complemented by other
decorative patterns to cover the entire surface of the vessel. The means of
partitioning the paintings and some of the images bears a strong similarity
to bronze decoration. Since the time of the pottery preceded that of
bronzewares, it is safe to say that the mature pottery paintings had a
profound influence on the decorative patterns of bronzewares.8 (Figs. 2.3,
2.4).





Fig. 2.3 Painted pottery jar,
Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture, top diam.: 16.5 cm, belly diam. at its largest: 19 cm, base diam.:
15.2 cm, height: 34.5 cm, unearthed at the Dadianzi Site in Aohan Banner, Inner Mongolia
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 2.4 Painted tripod jar with lid,
Xiajiadian Lower Layer Culture, top diam.: 9.5 cm, belly diam.: 15.2 cm, height: 19.5 cm, unearthed
at the Dadianzi Site in Aohan Banner, Inner Mongolia

    Handicraft production in the early Shang Dynasty had evolved from
agriculture to become an independent industry. In addition, different crafts
began developing along their own course. Due to the progress of pottery
technology in the early Shang Dynasty, the regular gray and white pottery
of the Shang featured increased varieties, higher firing temperature and
better quality when compared with the Xia. The most outstanding was the
exquisite white pottery which represented the peak of white pottery
workmanship throughout history. The imprinted hard pottery that first
emerged in areas south of the Yangtze River and along the southeastern
coast was a variety with a unique local style. (Fig. 2.5).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 2.5 Pottery ding,
Xia Dynasty, top diam.: 25.5 cm, height: 29 cm, in the Henan Museum

   By the mid-Shang, while gray and white pottery continued to be
produced, the earliest form of porcelain as it is known in China today
appeared. The appearance of primitive porcelain represented a leap in the
history of China’s ceramics industry and laid the foundation for the
development of Chinese porcelain. Primitive blue glazed porcelain has been
discovered in many of the mid-Shang sites across a wide region in the
middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, indicating that the skills and
techniques of firing primitive blue glazed porcelain was disseminated to
many areas of China after they were invented. The production quantity and
development speed were the highest in areas south of the Yangtze River.

2.2 Gray Pottery of the Xia and Shang Dynasties
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
2.2.1 Materials and Shapes of Xia and Shang Gray Pottery
Chinese pottery was dominated by painted pottery during the Yangshao
Culture, by black pottery during the Longshan Culture, and then by gray
pottery when it came to the Xia and Shang dynasties. It is not that there was
only gray pottery in the Xia and Shang, as there were other types apart from
painted and black pottery in the late Neolithic. It is just that during the Xia
and Shang gray pottery was produced in the largest quantities and was the
most prevalent vessel used by people on a daily basis. This situation
continued into the Han.
   Black pottery gradually declined as society developed from the
Longshan to the Xia and Shang. The black pottery of Longshan Culture,
especially eggshell black pottery, was mostly used as ritual objects and was
therefore exquisitely made, so when the more exquisite bronzewares
appeared in the Xia and Shang, they soon replaced black pottery for ritual
purposes. Black pottery as daily utensils was also quickly forsaken due to
its fragility and difficult production process.
   Gray pottery included clay pottery fired from “easily soluble clay” (i.e.,
pottery clay) and sandy pottery fired from soluble clay mixed with certain
proportions of sand or clamshell powder. Clay and sandy gray pottery were
the dominant pottery types of the Xia and Shang dynasties. These were
complimented by clay red and clay black pottery as well as sandy brown
and sandy red pottery. Gray pottery was fired with a reducing flame as was
black pottery. Compared with pottery wares fired with an oxidizing flame,
those fired with a reducing flame were harder, more durable, and deeper in
color. Compared with black pottery, gray pottery making was easier and
saved fuel since it required shorter reducing time, making gray pottery
wares economical and practical daily utensils. When the reduction time was
insufficient, the pottery turned out to be brown or red, and when reduced for
too long, they turned out to be deep gray or black. (Fig. 2.6).

   Sandy gray pottery was harder and hence was mostly made into cooking
pots, large and thick-walled containers, and sometimes drinking vessels,
while clay pottery, due to its fine texture and exquisite workmanship, was
mostly made into drinking vessels, food vessels and storage containers. The
production of gray pottery inherited modeling with a potter’s wheel from
Longshan times. Wares with simple shapes such as bowls, jars, basins and
urns were modeled entirely with the wheel. More complex wares had their
main bodies shaped with the wheel and accessory parts kneaded by hand or
shaped with a model and then stuck onto the main body. During the Xia and
early Shang, gray pottery inherited the characteristics of Longshan Culture
pottery in terms of shape design, and featured spherical bottoms, circular
feet and bag-shaped feet. Gray pottery of the late Xia and early Shang,
while still dominated by clay pottery, included a remarkably larger number
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
of sandy wares, including red and brown pottery with a coarse sandy
texture, and clay black or clay black-skinned pottery were no longer so
prevalent. This indicates technological progress in reducing firing. The
main varieties of Xia and Shang pottery were ding, jars, zeng, yan (cooking
pots composed of a li below and a zeng on top), li, jia, gu, jue, he, dou, gui
(簋) (Fig. 2.7), tripod plates, basins, urns, big-mouthed zun, vats, etc. There
were also pottery grinding wares with open mouths, slanting walls,
spherical bottoms and grooves on their inner walls, pottery lids with
mushroom-shaped handles, etc.





Fig. 2.7 Pottery gui (簋),
Shang Dynasty, top diam.: 27 cm, height: 18 cm, in the Henan Museum

    In terms of surface decoration, a small number of wares had plain
polished surfaces and some had polished surfaces decorated with raised
string patterns and stamped bands or striped images such as the yunlei
pattern, double curve pattern, and circles. Apart from these, most pottery
wares were fully decorated with deep rope patterns complemented by some
additional stacking patterns and dented string patterns. Rope patterns
covered at least 80% of the ware surface while additional stacking patterns
were much less frequent than previously. Full check decoration was used
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
only on a few vats with coarse sandy texture and thick walls, and basket
pattern was used only on a few pottery basins. Some exquisitely made
wares with smoothly polished surfaces were carved with shallow patterns of
fish, kuilong (an ancient mythical dragon-like creature), cicadas, etc. During
the Xia and Shang dynasties animal patterns were frequently seen on
bronzewares but were rarely used for pottery wares. (Fig. 2.8).





Fig. 2.8 Pottery jia with taotie pattern,
Shang Dynasty, top diam.: 19 cm, height: 27 cm, in the Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural
Heritage and Archaeology

2.2.2 Changes and Development in Shang Gray Pottery
The gray pottery varieties of the early Shang Dynasty differed from those of
the Xia. In the early Shang, pottery ding as a type of cooking utensil was
gradually replaced by pottery li, and the pottery cauldron appeared. Once a
major cooking utensil during the Xia Dynasty, pottery ding were used much
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
less for cooking during the Shang, and some basin-shaped pottery ding
evolved into fine-clay polished vessels used as food containers. Another
change is the significant increase in wine vessels such as gu, dou, he and
jue. Big-mouthed zun containers appeared and became one of the most
important types of container at the time. In addition, most big-mouthed zun
were carved with inscriptions and marks on the rim, which was of
significance for understanding the purpose of the zun. As far as food vessels
are concerned, dou with a shallow plate and long stem decreased and
circular footed dou and gui (簋) appeared. For other pottery types there were
also different degrees of change, reflecting the obvious differences between
the Shang and Xia in terms of pottery.
   By the mid-Shang, clay and sandy gray pottery still dominated,
accounting for over 90% of all pottery wares of the time, with sandy pottery
slightly less common than clay pottery, though sandy pottery was still more
popular than earlier. There was also some coarse sandy red pottery, black-
skinned clay pottery and clay red pottery. Folded rims were rare and most
gray pottery wares had rolled rims. Spherical bottoms and bag-shaped feet
dominated, circular feet were more common than previously, while flat
bottomed wares decreased dramatically. Rough counting shows that of the
various pottery wares unearthed at the Erligang Site in Zhengzhou, Henan,
those with spherical bottoms accounted for more than 46%, those with three
bag-shaped feet accounted for about 30%, circular feet for about 7%, and
flat bottoms for about 11%. Pottery li increased exponentially to account for
about two thirds of all cooking vessels and 23% of all pottery wares.
Pottery cauldrons increased considerably while sandy pottery jars
decreased. Sandy pottery ding became extremely rare. The few that were
occasionally found were copies of contemporaneous bronze ding and served
as ritual objects. It could be concluded that pottery li and pottery cauldrons
were the main cooking vessels used in the mid-Shang Dynasty. Of the
drinking vessels, the numbers of pottery jia and jue increased considerably
while pottery he became rare. Of food vessels, pottery gui (簋) and dou
increased dramatically while flat-bottomed tripod plates became extremely
rare. Of containers, pottery basins, big-mouthed pottery zun and coarse
sandy red pottery vats all increased. Compared with big-mouthed zun in the
early Shang, whose mouths were slightly smaller than their shoulders, those
from the mid-Shang had bigger mouths and theirs shoulders were no longer
note-worthy.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Regarding surface decoration, most pottery wares of the mid-Shang
were ornamented with thin rope patterns, with the only exception being a
small portion of sandy thick-wall red pottery vats decorated with checks,
basket patterns or yunlei patterns. Wares including li, cauldrons, jars and
shallow bellied basins were often comprehensively printed with rope
patterns. Urns, deep bellied basins, big-mouthed zun, jia and gui (簋) were
usually fully decorated with rope patterns on the lower belly and bottom
and brightly polished on the upper body and shoulder. Some basins, gui (簋)
and pots were stamped with a band circle composed of various images on
the polished area of the upper belly or shoulder. Plain or completely
polished wares were few. On rope patterned and polished plain pottery, a
combination of raised string patterns and shallow dented patterns prevailed
while additional stacking patterns decreased when compared with the early
Shang Dynasty. (Fig. 2.2–2.9) Band circles composed of images was often
applied to the belly, shoulder and circular foot of gui (簋), dou, basins, pots,
lei, and some urns. (Fig. 2.10) Common images making up band circles
were taotie, kuilong, checks, herringbone, petals, yunlei, swirls, zigzags,
continuous rings, bumps, tadpoles, circles and flames. Band circles
composed of taotie were the most common. Usually three sets of taotie
patterns formed one band circle. Heavy use of the taotie pattern on pottery
wares was most common during the mid-Shang Dynasty. Some of the
pottery wares decorated with taotie were identical in terms of design with
contemporaneous bronzewares decorated with taotie.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

   By the late Shang Dynasty, though clay and sandy gray pottery was still
the main material for daily use utensils and vessels, gray pottery started
declining as bronzewares, white pottery, imprinted hard pottery and
primitive porcelain developed and enjoyed wider application because of
their harder texture. Gray pottery wares were no longer decorated with
exquisite patterns, pottery workmanship became crude, and the varieties of
pottery for daily use also decreased. Only a dozen were still used on a daily
basis, such as li, gui (簋), yan, dou, jars, urns, lei and lids. With the large-
scale production and use of bronze ritual objects, pottery wares imitating
bronze ceremonial vessels appeared, among which there were gu, you (wine
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
containers), ding, and zun. The workmanship of these wares was very
variable.

2.3 White Pottery of the Xia and Shang Dynasties
2.3.1 Origins and Development
White pottery is pottery whose surface and body are both white in color. Its
material is different from that of clay and sandy pottery represented by gray
pottery. Researchers examined the white pottery unearthed at Chengziya in
Longshan, Shandong and Yinxu in Anyang, Henan, and found their
chemical composition to be very close to that of porcelain clay and
kaolinite.9 This indicates that the Chinese ancestors started using porcelain
clay and kaolinite to make pottery back in the Longshan Age and the Xia
and Shang dynasties, or even earlier, making China the first country in the
world to fire vessels with kaolinite. As the iron content of porcelain clay
and kaolinite was only 1.59% and 1.72% respectively, much lower than that
of other pottery materials, pottery fired with these materials does not
change color due to changes in the iron element and thus remains white.
The firing temperature was usually around 1,000 degrees Celsius, not high
enough to realize full sintering and produce porcelain, but the technique
made possible the later invention of porcelain.
   White pottery wares printed with complex patterns have been unearthed
at the Neolithic cultural site dated to 7,000 years ago at Luojiajiao in
Tongxiang, Zhejiang.10 During the middle Neolithic, white pottery making
was already advanced in some areas in China, with that of the Sanyuangong
Type of Daxi Culture particularly prominent and prevalent. Small numbers
of white pottery pieces also featured in the Hougang Type, Dasikong Type
and Dahecun Type of late Yangshao Culture, as well as the Banshan Type of
Majiayao Culture.
   White pottery accounted for 18% of all pottery remains at the middle
Neolithic Dawenkou cultural site.11 (Fig. 2.11) White pottery of the
Dawenkou Culture made its appearance in its middle period and thrived in
its late period. Made from white kaolinite mixed with fine sand, the pottery
had a hard texture, white or slightly yellow or pink color, and a smooth and
bright surface. Mostly modeled with the potter’s wheel, the wares included
gui (鬶) with bag-shaped feet, tripod he, wide shouldered pots, and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
cylindrical dou, of which gui (鬶) was of especially high artistic quality with
rich varieties, simple but elegant shapes and a beautiful presence. The white
pottery of the Shandong Longshan Culture was a direct descendant of that
of the Dawenkou Culture. It was not as prevalent as it was in the Dawenkou
Culture, but it inherited the shape design of the Dawenkou Culture, and
especially the white pottery gui (鬶) (Fig. 2.12), a prominent representative
of Shandong Longshan Culture whose influence continued into the Xia and
Shang dynasties.





Fig. 2.11 White pottery gui (鬶) with two-level mouth,
Dawenkou Culture, height: 36.8 cm, unearthed at Dafanzhuang, Linyi, Shandong
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 2.12 White pottery gui (鬶) with two handles,
Dawenkou Culture, height: 34.1 cm, unearthed at Lingyanghe, Juxian, Shandong

   White pottery was also unearthed at the sites and tombs of the late
Longshan Culture in Yuxi, Henan as well as the Xia Dynasty’s early Erlitou
Culture. The white pottery of the early Erlitou Culture probably developed
from the Yuxi Longshan Culture. White pottery from the early Shang
Dynasty has been discovered at some sites and tombs in Yuxi, Henan.
White pottery of the mid-Shang Dynasty has been discovered at a number
of sites in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, but most of the
findings were only fragments. The late Shang was a prosperous time for
ancient Chinese white pottery. White pottery vessels have been discovered
at most late Shang sites and tombs in Henan, Hebei, Shanxi, Shandong, and
elsewhere, with those unearthed at Yinxu in Anyang, Henan the most
numerous and highly exquisite in terms of workmanship.
   White pottery won favor with the ruling class with its advantages of
hard body and clean finish in comparison with regular gray and other types
of pottery. In the Xia and early Shang, it was mainly used to make exquisite
wine vessels. The wine vessels of the Xia Dynasty included gui (鬶) (Fig.
2.13), he and dou. Some of the white pottery gui (鬶) were decorated with
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
serrations on the mouth rim, triangular through-carved holes on the handle,
and two symmetrical bumps on the handle surface. He had round tops,
folded shoulders, tube-shaped spouts, thin waists, handles, and bag-shaped
feet. Some white pottery he were decorated with two circles of string
patterns on the belly and some were carved with triangle patterns on the
handle. White pottery dou had open mouths, thin waists, handles and bag-
shaped feet. Overall, white pottery at the time was characterized by hard,
fine body texture and relatively thin walls.12





Fig. 2.13 White pottery gui (鬶), Xia Dynasty,
height: 26 cm, in the Henan Museum

2.3.2 Special Features
White pottery of the early Shang Dynasty included jue in addition to gui (鬶),
he and jia. Jue often had open mouths, deep bellies, thin waists, flattened
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
handles, flat bottoms and three drill-shaped feet. The handle was often
carved with a herringbone pattern. Researchers have also found fragments
of white pottery basins stamped with rope patterns and additional stacking
patterns. White pottery of the mid-Shang Dynasty included dou, jars and
bowls besides gui (鬶), he, jia and jue. Most wares had plain polished
surfaces and only a small number were imprinted with rope patterns.13
White pottery of the late Shang included lei with small mouths, short necks,
round shoulders, deep bellies and flat bottoms, pots with small mouths, long
necks, swollen bellies and circular feet, zhi (drinking vessels) with small
mouths, long necks, swollen bellies and flat bottoms, you with small
mouths, swollen bellies and double knobs, and gui (簋) with open mouths,
swollen bellies and circular feet. These wares, fine in workmanship and
high in value, were enjoyed only by the aristocratic class, while the
common people could only use mass produced gray pottery.
    In summary, the late Shang was a peak time for ancient Chinese white
pottery. The white pottery of the period was pure white with a fine body
texture and exquisite patterns such as taotie, kuilong, and yunlei on the
surface. (Fig. 2.14) The shape and surface decoration of some white pottery
wares clearly indicate that they were imitating bronze ritual wares of the
time. The firing technique and skills reached a high point. Yet when it came
to the Western Zhou Dynasty, white pottery became rare, perhaps due to the
increased production of imprinted hard pottery and primitive porcelain.

2.4 Imprinted Hard Pottery of the Xia and Shang
Dynasties
2.4.1 Making and Firing
Imprinted pottery is imprinted with geometric patterns on the surface. It can
be classified into imprinted soft and hard pottery according to the body
texture and firing temperature. The former, due to a relatively low firing
temperature, had a soft texture and simple, crude, and uneven imprints, and
was an early form of imprinted pottery, while the latter, due to its high
firing temperature, had a hard texture and rich, varied and orderly arranged
imprints.
   The body of imprinted hard pottery was finer and harder than regular
clay pottery. Its firing temperature reached 1,100 degrees Celsius, higher
than that of regular pottery, almost reaching the level required for full
sintering. Some imprinted hard pottery had a certain luster like a thin layer
of glaze that resulted from high temperature firing and when struck would
give off a powerful and clear sound resembling that of primitive porcelain.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Imprinted hard pottery was fired at similar temperatures to primitive
porcelain and so the two were often fired in the same kiln. The body
material of the two was also similar, except that the imprinted hard pottery
had a higher iron content. Imprinted hard pottery and primitive porcelain of
the Shang and Zhou was often unearthed at the same sites and the two had
similar decorative patterns. So, it could be deduced that the two must be
related to each other.
   Imprinted hard pottery was fired from a type of iron-rich clay. They
were mostly formed by coiling, complemented by hand or model shaping.
Accessories like knobs and handles were hand-kneaded and then stuck onto
the ware bodies. The surface decorative patterns were pressed and stamped
onto the ware by one hand with molds carved with the patterns after coiling
was finished but before the greenware dried out. Meanwhile, the other hand
held a mushroom-shaped tool against the inner wall to avoid wall
deformation from the pressing and stamping on the outside. The pressing
and stamping not only imprinted patterns onto the ware, but also made the
coils of clay strips stick tighter together. Such methods of stamping patterns
onto pottery wares may be traced back to the early Neolithic, when rope
patterns, basket patterns, weave patterns and checks were imprinted, mainly
for the functional purpose of solidifying greenware. Later the practice
developed into a distinctive pottery decorative art. Because the patterns
were mostly regular geometric shapes, the wares were also called
“geometric imprinted pottery. (Fig. 2.15).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

Fig. 2.15 Imprinted pottery qing,
Shang Dynasty, top diam.: 19.5 cm, height: 27.4 cm, in the Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural
Heritage and Archaeology

2.4.2 Development
The existence of imprinted hard pottery in the central plains during the Xia
Dynasty has not been confirmed. Nevertheless, imprinted hard pottery
fragments with leaf vein patterns have been unearthed at sites in Jiangxi,
Hunan, Fujian, and elsewhere, which for the time being are dated as being
from the late Neolithic (some of the sites might be contemporaneous with
the Xia Dynasty on the central plains). Carbon-14 dating shows the
fragments are from about 4,000 years ago, which coincides with the Xia
Dynasty.14
   The Shang Dynasty was a period of development for imprinted hard
pottery, which has been found at Shang sites in the middle and lower
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
reaches of the Yellow and Yangtze rivers. Those along the Yangtze River
were larger in number, richer in variety and more diverse in decorative
pattern than those unearthed at contemporaneous sites along the Yellow
River. It can be seen that during the Shang Dynasty, imprinted hard pottery
was already fired and used in large numbers in the middle and lower
reaches of the Yangtze River.
   Imprinted hard pottery wares in the middle and lower reaches of the
Yellow River during the Shang Dynasty were mostly containers such as
urns, zun and jars. Their necks were left with string patterns from their
formation with the potter’s wheel and their bellies were mostly stamped
with leaf vein, yunlei and herringbone patterns. The body color was
dominated by purplish and yellowish-brown, along with some grayish
brown. Imprinted hard pottery from the Shang unearthed in the middle and
lower reaches of the Yangtze River was more numerous and appeared
earlier than those along the Yellow River. Apart from containers such as
urns, zun and jars, there were also cauldrons, bowls, cups and dou. In terms
of body color, apart from purplish and yellowish-brown, there were also a
certain number of red and reddish browns. Common patterns included
yunlei, leaf veins, checks, qiequ (an “S”-shaped band) and square spirals.
    Differences in the firing and making of imprinted hard pottery in
different regions are to some extent reflections of certain commonalities and
individualities of the materials and cultural lives in different regions during
the Shang. Moreover, cultural remains of imprinted pottery were
concentrated in regions south of the Yangtze River and along the southeast
coast. It is no coincidence that Yuyao in Zhejiang later became the origin of
porcelain—the firing of imprinted hard pottery expedited the birth of
primitive porcelain because it needed a high temperature and the two were
often fired in the same kilns. The constant rise in kiln temperature gave rise
to primitive porcelain and eventually to porcelain in the real sense.
Therefore, to a certain extent imprinted hard pottery marked an important
transition period from Chinas pottery to porcelain culture.

2.5 Primitive Porcelain of the Shang Dynasty
2.5.1 Significance of the Emergence of Primitive Porcelain
Apart from white pottery and imprinted hard pottery, another ceramic
invention of the Shang was primitive porcelain, which appeared no later
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
than the mid-Shang since it has been unearthed at mid-Shang sites and
tombs in Henan, Hebei, and Shanxi in the middle and lower reaches of the
Yellow River and in Hunan, Hubei, Jiangxi, and southern Jiangsu in the
middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River. Primitive porcelain made
up only a small portion of ceramic products at the time, accounting for only
0.5% in southern China, and a lower 0.001%, on the central plains.
    Primitive porcelain was an intermediate ceramic form between pottery
and porcelain, or a primary form of porcelain. Setting it apart from
contemporaneous pottery and giving it the name “primitive porcelainwere
the following three features. First, it required a higher firing temperature,
specifically, 1,100 to 1,200 degrees Celsius or higher, a level that no other
pottery, expect perhaps imprinted hard pottery of the same period could
reach. Second, it had glaze on its surface, a feature absent in other
contemporaneous pottery types, including imprinted pottery. Third, its
material contained porcelain clay. The material of white pottery also
contained porcelain clay, but the firing temperature of white pottery was not
as high and it did not carry glaze.
   The invention of high-fired glaze can be said to be a major contribution
of the Chinese people. The invention occurred much earlier than the first
appearance of low-fired glazes in west Asia. In contrast with the
flamboyant low-fired glazes that appeared later in west Asia and southern
Europe, high-fired glaze, dominated by olive green, green, bluish green,
blue, yellow and brown, was quiet, subtle, elegant and mellow, and it later
grew into a unique style of Chinese porcelain, a style that continued well
down through history until the gradual rise to the mainstream of
polychrome porcelain during the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties.
   The first appearance of primitive blue glaze on the primitive porcelain
of the Shang Dynasty was probably coincidental. One possibility was that
in well-sealed and high-temperature kilns, while the firing proceeded, wood
ash from the fuel fell onto the ware surface and was melted into the felspar
in the porcelain clay to form a thin layer of glaze on the surface of the
wares. This gave potters the idea of mixing burnt plant ash into diluted
porcelain clay mud, which was then applied to the surface of the
greenwares, which gave birth to the earliest gray glaze. Such glaze, which
contained plant ash and traces of iron, turned out to be yellow or brown
when fired in an oxidizing flame and blue or bluish green when fired in a
reducing flame.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Almost all primitive peoples in the world made pottery, but to invent
porcelain so early was not something any group could accomplish. First,
firing porcelain required a higher temperature, and to achieve that, kilns had
to be well designed with good heat-preserving conditions, and fuels with a
high firing capacity had to be used. Second, one had to be good at using
porcelain clay and master the formulation of high temperature glaze
material. The mechanisms behind all these factors do not appear to be that
complex, but China was the first to master the skills necessary for firing
porcelain. East Asia only gradually learnt the technique under the influence
of China, while Europe started making porcelain only after the eighteenth
century, also under the influence of China. Thus, China could be said to be
the birthplace and hometown of the world’s porcelain, and the invention of
porcelain was a major contribution to world culture.

2.5.2 Improvement and Development of Primitive Porcelain
Common varieties of primitive porcelain in the mid-Shang Dynasty
included zun, lei, bowls, urns, jars, dou and gui (簋). Their bodies were hard
and mostly grayish white or grayish brown. A small number had white
bodies with a tinge of yellow. The surface glaze color was dominated by
bluish green, complemented by pea green, deep green and yellowish green.
The formation technique was similar to that of imprinted hard pottery, that
is, they were firstly shaped by coiling and then stamped with molds
imprinted with various patterns, on the one hand to make the clay coils stick
more tightly together and on the other to decorate the ware surface. Then in
the end the ware had glaze applied and was sent for firing. In terms of
underglaze surface decoration, apart from plain surfaces, most wares were
stamped with checks, leaf vein patterns, serrations, string patterns, mat
patterns and “S” patterns. There were also circle patterns and rope
patterns.15 (Fig. 2.16).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 2.16 Primitive porcelain zun with bluish brown glaze,
Shang Dynasty, top diam.: 27 cm, height: 28 cm, in the Zhengzhou Museum, Henan

    Primitive porcelain exhibited strong potential for practical use right
after its invention because it is sturdy and durable, and because it is
resistant to stain and easy to clean, a feature brought about by the glaze.
Nevertheless, initially it did not enjoy rapid development. Only a small
number of primitive porcelain remains were discovered at some sites in the
middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, and most were unearthed in
the lower reaches of the Yangtze River and the southeastern coastal areas.
The development of primitive porcelain picked up speed during the late
Shang and became especially rapid towards the end of the Shang Dynasty.
Compared to the mid-Shang period, primitive porcelain wares by the end of
the Shang featured more varieties, wider production and usage, and better
quality. Common varieties included zun (Fig. 2.17), urns, lei, jars, basins,
bowls, dou, and lids. Primitive porcelain fragments of pots with tight
mouths, folded rims, short necks and raised shoulders, round-shouldered
zun with big open mouths, and circular footed gui (簋) have also been found.
The body color was still dominated by grayish white. There were also small
numbers of bluish yellow, light yellow and gray wares. The surface glaze
was mostly blue or pea green, complemented by caramel, light yellow, and
dark reddish purple. Geometric patterns stamped onto ware surfaces
included checks, serrations, leaf vein patterns, net patterns, dots, and string
patterns. Apart from inheriting these various geometric patterns from
previous periods, decoration also saw development and innovation with the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
appearance of carved and scratched patterns and additional stacking
patterns.





Fig. 2.17 Porcelain zun with blue glaze and string patterns,
Shang Dynasty, top diam.: 19.6 cm, height: 18 cm, in the Shanghai Museum

   Remains of Shang Dynasty primitive porcelain unearthed in regions
south of the Yangtze River were much more than those unearthed in the
middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River in terms of quantity, variety
and underglaze decoration, indicating that during the Shang Dynasty the
firing and use of primitive porcelain was still rare in the middle and lower
reaches of the Yellow River, and in contrast was relatively concentrated in
some places south of the Yangtze River. The foundation laid in this time
period must be associated with the fact that later in the Eastern Han
Dynasty it was in areas around present-day Zhejiang in southern China that
celadon in a real sense appeared.

2.6 Conclusion
2.6.1 Invention of Porcelain and Its Impact
The Xia and Shang dynasties represented an important period in the history
of Chinese ceramics. Though pottery was no longer the most significant or
valuable vessel in people’s lives, especially in the life of the aristocratic
class, who shifted much of their attention to the more exquisite
bronzewares, pottery wares were still indispensable daily utensils,
especially for the common people, to whom pottery was still rather
important and precious. During the Xia and Shang, gray pottery underwent
tremendous growth and was used in great quantities in daily life. The
production volume and number of varieties surpassed any previous period.
In fact, besides being used as daily utensils, gray pottery was for some time
a substitute for bronze ritual wares and burial objects. Later, due to the
development of white pottery and imprinted hard pottery, and with the
introduction of primitive porcelain, gray pottery began to decline. The
development of white pottery and imprinted pottery led to the birth of
primitive porcelain, a major milestone in the history of ceramics world-
wide. The birth of primitive porcelain eventually led to the invention of
porcelain in the real sense and made China the first country to step onto the
stage of porcelain art. When talking about ancient China’s contribution to
the world, we often mention papermaking, printing, gunpowder and the
compass, namely, the four great inventions. I believe porcelain is also a
great invention of ancient China. Moreover, it represented not only the
invention of a material or a technology; porcelain is also a cultural medium.
Embodied in porcelain making is the deep philosophical thought and unique
aesthetic aspirations of the Chinese people, and it all began with the
primitive pottery of the Shang Dynasty.

2.6.2 Shared Artistic Vocabulary of Ceramics and Bronze
The Shang Dynasty was the heyday of bronze culture and during that period
the most exquisite decorative patterns were used on bronzewares.
Decorations of everyday pottery wares were comparably simple, mostly
rope patterns, basket patterns, weave patterns, checks, serration, leaf vein
patterns, net patterns, and dots. Later, under the heavy influence of bronze
culture, geometric patterns originally applied on bronzewares, such as
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
yunlei, qiequ, and circular bands, also appeared on pottery wares. There
were also animal patterns, for instance taotie, kuilong, cicada, fish, and bird,
but in general these were only used on ritual objects imitating bronzewares.
Bronze ritual objects were mostly food and wine vessels, and these vessels
in turn generally inherited their shape designs from pottery wares.
Therefore, initially the shape designs of bronze and pottery wares originated
from the same source. It was only due to later differences in terms of
cultural connotations, functions and materials that bronzewares started
developing their own special discourse which then in turn influenced the
shape design and decoration of pottery wares.
  No art arises from a vacuum. The appearance and existence of all arts is
built on certain cultural backgrounds and historical bases. One example is
the taotie pattern commonly used on bronzewares and ritual pottery vessels.
Taotie is the collective name of zoomorphic patterns. Some were designed
based on animals such as tigers, goats and oxen. Only the face and feet of
these animals were depicted, yet in an exaggerated manner to form pointy
horns, huge eyes and sharp claws. The taotie most frequently seen was in
the image of one straight nose flanked by two kuilong in profile to form a
frontal taotie, also with curved pointed horns, round bulging eyes, fierce
toothy mouths and large sharp claws. The decoration of ritual objects with
beast face patterns appeared early on the painted pottery of the Banpo type
and is believed to symbolize some sort of divine power. The beast face
pattern, often half human, half animal, for instance a combination of human
and tiger, human and bird, or human and fish, was often painted on
calabash bottles used as ritual objects. The jade cong (a long hollow piece
of jade with rectangular sides) of the Liangzhu Culture, also a ritual object,
was also often carved with mask-like faces combing human and beast. The
faces mostly had large eyes, broad noses, and large open mouths showing
fangs. Human and beast were merged into one. The human was given the
strength and fierceness of the beast and the beast was granted the spirit and
soul of the human. The pattern gives a sense of awe and represented certain
meanings and connotations associated with strength, authority and mythical
power typical of the patriarchal era. The taotie designs on later bronze
vessels had similar meanings. Yet they represented the crown instead of
patriarchal power. They had to accommodate deterrence, dignity, terror and
awe in order to express the unquestionable authority of the slave owners
and thus help cement a strong slave regime. These beast face and taotie
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
patterns carved on bronze vessels created a kind of beauty, one that is
dignified, deterring and at times frightening. Such beauty was also
embodied in contemporaneous pottery, especially in ritual objects imitating
bronze vessels, which were mostly white pottery, imprinted hard pottery
and primitive porcelain.
    Naturally, pottery wares of the Shang Dynasty were still predominately
used as daily utensils. The use of common bronzeware animal patterns on
pottery was still infrequent, while geometric patterns commonly used as
background decoration for bronze vessels were often used on pottery wares.
The most representative of such geometric patterns was yunlei. The yunlei
pattern in fact first appeared on pottery. Initially, they were mostly round,
like two connected snails. Then it was first on the painted pottery of the
Machang Type that the round snails turned into ones with square corners.
When it came to the Xindian Culture, continuous square spirals appeared.
Thus the yunlei pattern could be said to have originated in pottery
decoration. As for its meaning, Shen Kuo of the Song Dynasty gave the
following explanation in his Mengxi bitan (“Brush Talks from Dream
Brook”): “     is the ancient script for 云 (cloud) and describes the shape of a
cloud; ⦾ is the ancient script for 雷 (thunder) and describes the echoing
sound of thunder. Decorations on bronze lei comprising    alternating with
⦾, describe clouds and thunder”. Mr. Fu Baoshi states in his Collection of
Fu Baoshi’s Articles on Fine Arts: “Yunlei patterns are various derivatives
based on swirling lines as the stem. Swirl patterns started to be used by
humans back in the Neolithic. And how were they related to the yunlei
patterns on Chinese bronzewares? Did the latter develop from the former or
was their similarity merely coincidental? This is a question worth looking
into. The appearance of the pottery drinking vessel “leialready marked the
birth of the yunlei pattern. In the early agricultural era, nothing concerned
people more than rain. Since clouds and thunder were the prelude to rain, it
was only natural that people carved them, natural phenomena that they
cared a lot about, on their everyday vessels”.16 Some other researchers
believe yunlei evolved from some sort of weave pattern and was only for
the purpose of decoration and had no deeper meaning. Yet I am still
inclined to the view that it embodied certain cultural meanings. It is my
belief that all patterns on ritual objects are symbolic. They are different
from the rope pattern, basket pattern and weave pattern randomly stamped
onto wares.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Geometric patterns similar to yunlei at that time also included qiequ,
circular bands, swirls, circles, zigzags, and scales. One common feature of
these patterns was the combination of ying and yang, namely, the
coexistence of black and blank sections. In addition, the patterns all feature
continuous, swirling and revolving lines, with the turning points at times
round, at times square, and at times both. Such patterns had connections
with the black and white patterns and revolving images suggestive of taiji
on painted pottery in terms of philosophical meanings and techniques of
expression.
    History develops along two lines, one vertical and one horizontal. The
vertical line reaches far back in time. Any moment in human history can be
reached step by step from the past. This is inheritance, the accumulation of
tradition. The horizontal line, in contrast, connects contemporaneous social
and cultural elements in one space. It also includes the mutual assimilation
of different arts. The two lines, one temporal and one spatial, form the
general characteristics of the culture and art of a given era, characteristics
that cover all art schools and forms, endowing them with commonalities of
their time despite their respective individualities. This also applies to the
development of pottery art during the Xia and Shang.
