Fig. 5.23 Big pottery horse figure,
Qin Dynasty, height: 150 cm, length: 200 cm, in Qin Shi Huang’s Mausoleum Museum

   The figures were originally painted with bright pigments, but much of
the color coating has flaked off or become greatly faded during their 2,000-
year burial in soil. While the unremitting efforts of cultural relic restoration
experts in Shaanxi means that the full range of broken arms and legs and
dirt-covered parts that were first unearthed have been restored to the
thousands of warriors and horses which are now neatly ranked in the pits,
they were still colorless and gray and were not restored to their
multicolored original because the preservation of the archaic condition is
desired in relic restoration.12 But we may imagine how colorful and
magnificent they must have looked when they were newly painted and
placed in the pits.
     It should be noted that previous studies on the terracotta warriors and
horses of the Qin Shi Huang Mausoleum all focused on the sculpture works
found in the burial pits. Though a few researchers did investigate the
production of the pottery sculptures, little research has been done on the
kilns. In 2003, researchers at the Shaanxi Provincial Institute of
Archaeology excavated two local pottery kilns and concluded that they
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
were probably kilns in the mausoleum park for firing building bricks or
daily utensils. People have not been able to locate the kilns responsible for
firing the terracotta army, nor the site where the waste pieces were stacked.
   Scholars believe that craftsmen manufactured the life-sized figures by
creating body parts separately and then assembling the pieces together. To
make a complete figure was presumably a challenging task at the time, and
the quality control of the warriors and horses must have been very strict
since they were made for the emperors mausoleum.13 So it is logical to
deduce that a large number of rejected waste products would inevitably be
produced in the process of making all the components of the sculptures, just
as there is always lots of discarded waste in any large project we may
undertake now. In addition to the over 8,000 terracotta warriors and horses
that have been discovered in the mausoleum, there might be many more in
the vicinity of the pits that have not yet been uncovered. Therefore, it could
be inferred that the number of terracotta figures made at the time must be
well in excess of 8,000. Besides, since specific parts were manufactured
first and then assembled after being fired, many spare parts must have been
made. Even more must have been fired to replace those that were damaged
during firing, those broken during transport and assembly, and those
rejected due to poor quality. It is conceivable that the time spent for
planning and manufacturing such large quantities of terracotta figures might
be far longer than one year, perhaps even three or five years. It is likely that
apart from the kiln site which is yet to be discovered, there is still another
huge cultural relic site buried somewhere in the Guanzhong Plain, i.e., the
site of abandoned pieces and kiln tools of the Terracotta Army. Though the
remains would mostly be discarded items, the quantities would be huge.14
  How is it, then, that we have found no trace of the discarded items when
there must be so many? Folk kilns usually discarded tools and waste pieces
at will, but obviously the waste pieces of the Terracotta Army were buried
in a certain spot, for otherwise such a large project would not have left no
trace. It was a common practice of ancient Chinese official kilns to bury
remaining substandard items after firing for the purpose of confidentiality,
and some scholars believe the waste pieces of the Terracotta Army would
have been buried for the same reason. In fact, the pottery kiln that fired the
Terracotta Army of the Qin Shi Huang Mausoleum could be regarded as an
official kiln, indeed, the first official kiln that can be confirmed in the
history of Chinese ceramics, though it was not a porcelain kiln but a pottery
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
kiln and that its site has yet to be discovered.15 So we can infer that perhaps
all the waste items of the kiln were buried because it is an official kiln
devoted to firing pottery for the emperor.
    Nevertheless, whether the Terracotta Army kiln was an official kiln
remains to be proven by further archaeological discovery. Traditionally
official kilns in a narrow sense are defined as those independent of folk
kilns and with a strict royal production system, while in a broad sense all
kilns that produce and supply porcelain for the royal family may be
regarded as official kilns. According to these definitions the earliest official
kilns in the narrow sense appeared in the Song Dynasty, while those in the
broad sense emerged back in the Tang and Five dynasties because at that
time some Yue kilns supplied porcelain to the royal family. It would be
significant if the Terracotta Army kiln is defined as an official kiln, in one
sense because that would push the appearance of official kilns in China
further back in history, and in another because that would set the first
precedent for a pottery kiln to be recognized as an official kiln since
previously all official kilns in China were porcelain kilns.

5.5.2 Pottery Sculptures of the Early and Middle Western Han
In the early Han Dynasty, though the ruling group hoped to follow the
grand and magnificent plastic arts tradition of the Qin Dynasty, the
economic strength and political situation were not comparable with those of
the strong and prosperous Qin period and did not permit such extravagance.
Besides, the lesson of the Qin Dynasty’s collapse caused by its harsh
treatment of the common people coupled with the desire for a more stable
society when the Han regime was first established led the Han ruling class
to practice a governance of inaction, to advocate thrift and recuperation, and
to strive for recovery and development of the social economy down to the
reign of Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing. Therefore, although the tombs of
early Han emperors contained burial warrior and horse figures of no less
numbers than those of Qin Shi Huang’s Mausoleum, the size of the figures
was obviously reduced. The Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang’s
Mausoleum is life-sized while the figurines in the Han tombs are only one-
third human size. Moreover, the artistic features of early Han Dynasty
figurines, on the one hand inheriting the Qin system and on the other hand
following the Chu style, had not fully developed a style which reflected
their own era. The pottery figurines of the early Han Dynasty can be
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
classified into two types. One followed faithfully the features of the Qin
figurines, that is to say the figurines had sculpted clothes, belts and shoes,
and were color painted. The other type, vastly different from the Qin style,
molded nude men and women who were then dressed in silk clothes. In any
case, since the Western Han Dynasty, large life-sized pottery figures never
appeared again, making the Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang’s
Mausoleum a unique historic instance. In the Han Dynasty, besides the
emperors, some famous generals were also honored by military formations
at their funerals and were buried with military figurines. For example, after
Huo Qubing died of illness, “the Son of Heaven mourned him and arrayed
armored soldiers from Chang’an (modern-day Xi’an, capital of the Han
Dynasty) to the Mao Mausoleum (the Mausoleum of Emperor Wu of Han,
located in modern-day Xingping in Xianyang)”. In 1956, 2,375 pottery
figurines, including 583 cavalryman figures, along with some wooden
chariot models were unearthed from the 11 pits discovered in Yangjiawan,
Xianyang.16 In 1980, long trenches full of burial pottery, painted warriors
and farmyard animal models were found around the top opening of the
wooden chamber of No. 11 tomb of the Mausoleum of Emperor Hui of Han
in Baimiao Village, Xianyang. In 1984, more than 2,300 pottery warriors
and horses were unearthed in Shizishan, Xuzhou, Jiangsu Province. They
were probably buried with a certain prince of the Chu state in the early
Western Han Dynasty. (Fig. 5.24).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

Fig. 5.24 Pottery warriors and horses,
Eastern Han Dynasty, height: 25 to 54 cm, in the Xuzhou Han Dynasty Terracotta Army Museum

    After the mid-Han Dynasty, pottery sculpture style underwent some
changes. On the one hand, the sculpting technique became bolder and freer,
evolving from the meticulous portrayal of human figures in the Qin and
early Han dynasties to a style focused more on the overall, concise and
general shape. On the other hand, the subject matter and themes became
broader and more varied with more emphasis on the depiction of secular
life and entertainment scenes. One example is the painted pottery and the
music, dance and acrobatic figurines unearthed in the Western Han tomb
discovered in the northern suburbs of Jinan in 1969.17 (Fig. 5.25) The
discovery comprised a group of pottery figurines, both performers and
spectators, placed on a 67 cm by 47.5 cm rectangular pottery tray, depicting
a complete performance scene. At the back is the band accompaniment
comprising two women playing the sheng (a reed pipe wind instrument),
and five men each playing a se (a twenty-five-stringed plucked instrument,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
similar to a zither), a small drum, bells, a chime stone, and a Jian drum (a
combination of a drum and a pillar that goes through the drum and fixes it
to the drum base). In the middle of the scene are dancers and acrobats,
specifically, two women singing and dancing and four men doing
handstands and somersaults. On the two sides stand seven spectators
dressed in long robes with wide sleeves who are cupping one hand in the
other and enjoying the performance attentively. All the characters, including
the band, the performers and the audience are arranged clearly and in order,
displaying the vivid and engrossing scene of an aristocratic banquet. The
sculptors have adopted an exaggerated and concise artistic approach that
focused on capturing and describing the motion and spirit of the characters
and did not take pains to depict the facial features and other details of the
characters. With such an approach the sculpted characters appear innocent
and lovely though somewhat clumsy. In addition, the change of burial
objects from the previously dominant household servants to themes of
music, dance and acrobatics during this period reflects the change of
people’s attitudes towards household life and merrymaking. The pottery
sculptures in this period were all shaped with molds, painted with white
powder as a backdrop and then painted with red, black, brown, green and
other colorings.

5.5.3 Pottery Sculptures of the Late Western Han and Eastern
Han
From the late Western Han Dynasty to the Eastern Han, pottery works
expressed more extensive themes and richer contents. In addition to
figurines of warriors (Fig. 5.26), officials, singers, dancers and acrobats
which had appeared previously, there also emerged among burial objects,
thanks to the development of the manor economy after the mid-Eastern
Han, pottery models simulating farmlands and buildings, mainly
warehouses, multi-storied pagodas, water pavilions (Fig. 5.27), and even
castles. The burial objects expressed people’s wish to bring the manor and
fields in their possession to their tombs. Even figurines of people working
on the manor were made and buried with the dead to more comprehensively
reproduce the everyday life scene of the manor. There are household
servants and cooks carrying pots or bottles, sweeping the floor or cutting
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
fish, and peasants holding winnowing pans, shovels, or plows. The peasant
figurines wear straw sandals and cloth gowns, and some carry long swords
at their waist. They give a true portrayal of peasants affiliated to powerful
clans in the feudal late Eastern Han and the special relationship between
them and their owners, namely, they were on the one hand laborers and on
the other hand armed forces. There are also figurines of peasants carrying
heavy loads, weeding or working in paddy fields. For instance, in the
pottery model of paddy fields and boats unearthed in Foshan, Guangdong,
the paddy fields are divided into six plots with ridges, each with one
peasant toiling. One is plowing with a hat on, one is bending down
transplanting rice seedlings, one is fertilizing with a shovel, one is reaping
with a sickle, one is sharpening a sickle on the field ridge, and one is
threshing. Even the rice seedlings, compost heaps and grain heaps in the
fields are minutely sculpted, reproducing a vivid scene of agricultural
labor.18 In addition, the set of green glazed pottery models of rural
architecture and courtyards of the Eastern Han Dynasty as shown in Figs.
5.28 and 5.29, collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S.,
paint a vivid picture of rural life in the Han Dynasty. A house with a yard, a
barn, a stove and a well, constitute the central part of the image, surrounded
by pigpens and other livestock sheds. There is also a multi-story
watchtower for protection, a pagoda circled by a moat, a storeroom with
strong walls, and a pavilion with a forecourt.

Other common themes of pottery sculpture at the time included horse-
drawn carriages and groups of male and female servants along with musical
and dancing figures. Among the music, dance and acrobatics figures of the
day, the most vivid was the topless “story-telling figurine” unearthed in
suburban Chengdu (Fig. 5.30). There were also various “dancing figurines”,
“instrument-playing figurines”, “seated figurines”, and “baby-carrying
figurines”, as well as the “knife-holding figurines”, “drumming figurines”
and “zither-playing figurines” unearthed in Chongqing. The group figurines
of “village dancers” (Fig. 5.31), plain yet vivid and full of the flavor of life,
truthfully and comprehensively depict the everyday customs of the Han
Dynasty. The “pottery tomb figurines of two gentlemen playing liubo with
game board and pieces” (Fig. 5.32) collected by the Metropolitan Museum
of Art vividly captures an exciting moment during the game. Liubo
(literally “six sticks”) is an ancient Chinese board game that was immensely
popular during the Han Dynasty. It was played by two players, each of
whom had six chess pieces, often chips, markers or sticks, that were moved
around the points of a square game board. The creation of such burial
figurines expressed the Han Dynasty people’s love of leisure and
recreational activities and the wish to continue such activities in their next
life.

Animal pottery sculptures of the Han Dynasty were also very
successful. Pottery horses and dogs unearthed in Mianyang, Sichuan, 1.5 m
tall pottery horses pulling a carriage unearthed in Yangzishan, Chengdu,
and the group of animal sculptures unearthed in Huixian, Henan19 describe
a range of postures and characters of various animals, and are regarded to
be among the finest animal pottery works of any dynasty.

5.6 Architectural Pottery of the Qin and Han
Dynasties
5.6.1 Picture Bricks of the Han Dynasty
Architectural pottery in the Qin and Han dynasties occupied a very
important position in the ceramics production of the time. Significant
expansion and progress had been made when compared to the Warring
States period in terms of variety, quality, production scale and firing
technology. The most representative and artistic architectural pottery at the
time were painted bricks and eave tiles.
   The painted bricks, famous for their bas-relief and intaglio, were mostly
used for building coffin pits and thus were also called tomb bricks. They
were used to build the door and top back wall of the coffin chamber, and
some were inlaid in the middle part of the two side walls of the tomb
tunnel. The bricks were made hollow to facilitate firing as well as to reduce
weight. Rectangular or double circular holes were left on both ends. Images
were imprinted onto their surface while they were half-dry to complete the
greenware. Then the greenware was fired in kilns, after which it was
colored and painted in more detail. Though the painted bricks we see today
are colorless like the Terracotta Army of the Qin Dynasty, we may infer
from the remaining colorings on some of the bricks that they must have
been brightly colored when they were first made. Time has robbed the
bricks of their colors, yet such loss of color to a certain degree granted them
some sort of new artistic charm, a charm that lies in their generality and
lack of detail.
   Ceramics production in the Qin and Han dynasties had developed a fine
division of labor, and the prevalence of elaborate funerals created a demand
for large numbers of painted bricks. These led to the birth of workshops and
management organizations specializing in the production of painted bricks
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
in the Han Dynasty. For example, royal kiln sites have been found in Xi’an
and folk kiln sites have been found in Sichuan and other places. The
remains of the sites indicate that they were ruins of painted brick and
figurine production. The “Eastern Garden Artisans” of the Eastern Han
Dynasty was specially set up to preside over the production and supply of
objects in the royal mausoleum. Based on this we may presume that the
painted pottery bricks must be a type of commodity that could be circulated.
Commodities need mass production, and the bricks could be mass-produced
because they were stamped with molds and then fired. This is evidenced by
the discovery of bricks with the same images in different tombs. The same
images did not occur on large quantities of bricks. Presumably bricks with
rich image varieties were produced in small batches to meet the different
needs of people. Different from the monotonous pure pattern images on
painted bricks of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, the pictures on Han bricks
tell more stories and have more interesting plots, and therefore are richer in
artistic expression.
   The emergence of any new art variety is not achieved overnight but is
based on traditional foundations and technical preparation. The making of
pottery molds for bronzewares since the Shang and Zhou dynasties served
as technical preparation for the appearance of Han painted bricks because
the most common techniques used in making these bricks, including incised
carving, relief carving, and background clearing, can all find origin in the
carving of pottery molds. The method of stamping with a mold was
invented in the Eastern Zhou Dynasty. If we go further back, the bone and
jade carving that appeared in the Neolithic were earlier technical and artistic
origins of the painted bricks of the Han Dynasty.
    Painted bricks of the Han Dynasty have been unearthed in many places
across the country, yet are the most concentrated in Sichuan Province,
including the following representative works: the “sowing picture” brick
unearthed in Deyang (Fig. 5.33), the “shooting and harvesting picture”
brick unearthed in Fenghuangshan, Chengdu (Fig. 5.34), the “picking lotus
picture” brick unearthed in Mianyang, the “wine-making picture” brick
unearthed in Zengjiabao, Chengdu, the “mansion picture” brick unearthed
in Qingyang, and the “courtyard picture” brick, the “banquet and dance
picture” brick and the “carriage and attendants picture” brick unearthed in
the suburbs of Chengdu.

     It can be seen that the brick paintings covered a wide range of themes
and contents. They were often drawn from the tomb owners’ life and
prevailing values and customs at the time. Therefore, as truthful portraits of
various aspects of the social life in the Han Dynasty, these pictures bear
significant value for historic, scientific and artistic study. The rich and
extensive themes of the paintings can be put into the following categories.
The first describes the manor life and economy before the tomb owner’s
death, or more likely, instead of a realistic portrayal of their life when alive,
a richer life that they fancied to lead in another world. Such manor life is
depicted with various agricultural and handicraft production and labor
scenes, including sowing, harvesting, brewing, salt wells, mulberry gardens,
lotus picking and prospecting. These are truthful portraits of the working
people’s lives at the time and constitute the most prominent part of Han
Dynasty painted bricks. The second category describes entertainment
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
activities at home. These are images depicting the home life of landlords
and the nobility, including those of kitchens and cuisine, banquets, games,
singing and dancing, acrobatics, buildings, and fairs (Fig. 5.35). They
expressed people’s desire for a good life at the time, a life featured by
having wine to drink and meat to eat, having singing, dancing and
acrobatics to enjoy, having huge houses to live in, having the attendance of
servants, and having the protection of retainers. The images offered a
glimpse into the social customs, architectural style, home furnishings,
market scenes, etc. of the time. The third category describes the impressive
and dignified manner of the tomb owner. The Han Dynasty was a time of
striving for career success and of great enterprising spirit. People believed
that “a real man should soar instead of lying low”. This spirit was reflected
on tomb brick paintings that showed a tomb owner’s majesty before death
as well as their glory after death. Typical images depicted the grand scene
of traveling with many carriages and horses accompanied by many officials
and staff members. They reproduced the spectacle of the bureaucratic and
aristocratic class traveling with riders and drummers leading the procession
as well as many carriages following. The pictures also enable us to learn
about the various vehicles used by the dignitaries and the rich in the Han
Dynasty since most of these vehicles failed to be handed down and the
brick pictures offered precious images of them for later generations to
appreciate the shape of these vehicles. The fourth category focuses on the
theme of immortality. People of the Han Dynasty attached great importance
to the continuation of life, hoping to stay alive forever whilst living, and
wanting to ascend to Heaven after death and to live another life in another
world. Such aspirations resulted in the many brick pictures depicting
fairyland mythologies. Common imageries found in these pictures were the
Queen Mother of the West, Nüwa, Fuxi, the three-legged crow, the ninetail
fox, double dragons, the White Tiger, the Vermilion Bird, the sun, the moon
and toads. These pictures reflected people’s spiritual world and values at the
time from different angles. (Figs. 5.36 and 5.37).

5.6.2 Eave Tiles of the Qin and Han Dynasties
Eave tiles of the Qin and Han dynasties were another type of highly artistic
architectural pottery equally famous with the painted bricks. They
originated in the Western Zhou Dynasty and developed greatly during the
Warring States period. After the unification of the Qin Dynasty, decorative
patterns on the tiles, mainly animals, plants and clouds, underwent
substantial changes. Those unearthed near Qin Shi Huang’s Mausoleum had
animal patterns such as running deer, phoenix birds, and dogs. (Fig. 5.38)
Eave tiles unearthed in the Xianyang Palace (royal palace of the state of Qin
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
before the Chinese unification and the palace of Qin Shi Huang when China
was unified) were decorated with various patterns in four symmetrical fan-
shaped sections and one inner circle. The inner circle was usually decorated
with checks, net patterns, dots, four-leaf patterns, tree leaf patterns, etc.,
while the surrounding fan-shaped sections were filled with lifelike and
vivid images of double deer, insects, etc. (Fig. 5.39) Also unearthed are
eave tiles with images of lotus petals, sunflowers, curly lines and rolling
clouds. Few eave tiles of the Qin state had words on them. After Qin Shi
Huang unified China, there emerged tiles with 12 characters such as “维天降灵延元万
年天下康宁”(“May the mandate of Heaven be obeyed, may the rule continue for
10,000 years, may all lands under Heaven be safe and prosper”) (Fig. 5.40)
or with four characters such as “羽阳千秋” or “羽阳千岁” (“May Yuyang last for 1,000
years;”Yuyang Palace was built by Emperor Xiao of Qin). The words,
adopting the literary style of an imperial edict since the beginning of the
Shang and Zhou dynasties, were concise and succinct with four characters
constituting one sentence. The type of writing was Xiaozhuan (“small seal”
script).

   The eave tile art reached a zenith in the Han Dynasty. In addition to
previous animal, plant and cloud patterns, there emerged large numbers of
tiles decorated with words, which can be roughly divided into four
categories according to content: palaces, offices, ancestral tombs and
auspicious sayings. Of the first three categories, some indicate the name of
the architecture on which the tiles were used. For instance, “长乐” refers to the
Changle Palace, “未央” refers to the Weiyang Palace, and “上林” refers to the
imperial palace for short stays in Shanglin Garden. Some of the text
indicates the function of the architecture. For instance, tiles with the
character “关” were used on buildings at passes and gateways, those with “卫”
were used on offices of the imperial guards, those with “庾” were used on the
granary of the Agricultural Minister, and those with “冢” were used on
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
mausoleum buildings. Common examples of the fourth category, auspicious
languages, included “长生无极” (Life everlasting), “延寿万年” (Long life), “与天长久”
(Longevity equaling Heaven), “吉月照灯” (Light of auspicious moon), and “涌泉混流”
(Springs and rivers). The eave tile with the words “汉并天下” (The Han rule
everything under Heaven) (Fig. 5.41) was unearthed at the old site of the
Yueyang Capital of the early Western Han and was probably made when
Liu Bang set to unify the country. The wording was probably borrowed
from an imperial edict of the Qin Dynasty “the Emperor rules everything
under Heaven”. Besides eave tiles with words, also popular during the reign
of Wang Mang were the four-symbol themed tiles with derivative images of
the Azure Dragon, the White Tiger, the Vermilion Bird and the Black Turtle
(Fig. 5.42). These four mythological creatures were popular not only on
eave tiles, but also as tomb decorations at the time. Their roles differed
when used in different places. As tomb decorations, their symbolic
meanings and functions could be summarized as “Azure Dragon on the left
and White Tiger on the right exorcise inauspicious forces, and Vermilion
Bird and Black Turtle make yin and yang right”. When used on the eave
tiles of houses, they represent directions and seasons. The Azure Dragon
was an imaginary creature associated with summoning wind and calling for
rain. The head of the four symbols, it represented the East, the left and the
spring. The Vermilion Bird was also an imaginary auspicious bird and
symbolized the South, the low and the summer. The White Tiger
symbolized the West, the right and the fall. The Black Turtle was an image
composed of a turtle and a snake and symbolized the North, the high and
the winter. These four-symbol themed tiles all have a bump in the center
that corresponds with the thick tile frame, which gives the tiles a solemn
structural beauty. The animal patterns are vivid and magnificent. (Figs. 5.43
and 5.44).

5.7 Conclusion
Achievements in the ceramics industry were made during the Qin and Han
dynasties in both technology and artistic expression.
    In terms of ceramic technology, the primary achievement was the
transformation from primitive porcelain to porcelain. Before the Eastern
Han Dynasty there was no real porcelain in China and pottery played the
leading role in the history of Chinese ceramics, until by the later years of
the Eastern Han, the successful firing of porcelain made China the first
country in the world to invent porcelain and since then porcelain has
occupied the center stage of China’s ceramics history. Another important
technological achievement was the successful firing of low-temperature
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
lead glaze, which not only enriched the ceramic art expression of the Qin
and Han dynasties, but also laid the groundwork for the emergence of other
colorful glaze types later.
   From the artistic point of view, ceramic plastic arts of the Qin and Han
dynasties experienced a transition from imitating bronzeware and
lacquerware to independent development. The transition was also part of
Chinese pottery’s gradual alienation from its long-assumed religious tasks.
Many practical pottery wares were free of their ritual functions. Ceramic
production was dominated by utensils emphasizing daily use and
practicality by the Eastern Han Dynasty when primitive porcelain ritual
objects such as bu, fang and ding disappeared while practical wares
represented by pots, jars and lei increased dramatically. There also emerged
new daily use utensils such as five-linked jars, incense burners, tiger-shaped
chamber pots, water pots and mortars. By the end of the Eastern Han
Dynasty, ritual ceramic wares were no longer produced at all. Emphasis on
practicality and convenience found expression in the design of ceramic
wares, resulting in larger and plumper sizes, simpler shapes and plainer
decoration. The time had passed of ceramic wares being an important
carrier of images describing people’s values, production activities and
religious beliefs. These functions were taken by painting, which gradually
became an art form in its own right, independent of wares. Artists devoted
to painting appeared in the court and many nongovernmental painters also
emerged. These paintings found their place on large numbers of royal
palace murals and temple murals, large numbers of picture stones and
picture bricks in tomb chambers, and the highly artistic silk paintings and
lacquerwares as burial objects.
   The most outstanding achievements of ceramic art in this period was
found not in daily use wares, but in the large numbers of funerary objects
and architectural pottery, the former including low-fired glazed pottery,
pottery with painting, and various pottery figurines and models, the latter
represented by the Han picture bricks, which were used for decorating
tombs or other purposes, and eave tiles, which were mainly used for
decorating the front of roof tiles.
   Of course, the most astonishing ceramic art of the Qin and Han
dynasties was the terracotta warriors and horses unearthed in Qin Shi
Huang’s Mausoleum. The magnificently imposing manner, the
spectacularly grand scale and the meticulously realistic style were not to be
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
seen again in later Chinese ceramic arts. The Terracotta Army was a
historical feat of the Chinese people rivalling the Great Wall.
   The Qin and Han dynasties were a great era of strength and rapid
development following the unification of China. The social background of
the entire country surging forward was reflected in the grand and
magnificent style of the period’s arts, a style that was expressed not only by
the Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang, but also by the pottery figurines and
sculptures of the Han Dynasty. Compared with the society before the Qin
Dynasty, the Han Dynasty featured a more pragmatic trend and plebeian
participation in governance. Such a pragmatic aesthetic pursuit can be seen
in the many burial objects. It can be said that pottery sculptures of this
period represented a zenith in the history of China’s ceramic sculpture art.
The figurines, with perfect artistic form and vivid lifelike expressions, told
of the physiological features, psychological characteristics and even the
inner spirit of people from different regions and different classes at the
time. The figurines were evidence of the long-standing realist tradition and
the bright, concise, profound and grand style of Chinese sculpture art. The
pottery sculptures made in large quantities as burial objects are the most
vivid and authentic material for us to understand the social life back in the
Qin and Han dynasties thanks to the richness and extensiveness of their
subject matter and the detailed description of the scenes and customs of
people’s lives at the time.
   People in the Han Dynasty believed that after death there would be a
fairy world ruled by the Queen Mother of the West. This was why on burial
objects, low-fired glazed pottery, pottery with painting and Han picture
bricks alike, there were many images of the Queen Mother of the West and
other mythical figures and animals. In these pictures exaggerated and
strange-looking deities, flying fairies and mythical beasts wandered to and
fro amid flowing clouds and towering immortal mountains, or roamed
freely upward and downward in a space–time filled with yin and yang
energies. The burial objects also described the tomb owner’s life before
death and their attachment to the human world. Thus, in these pictures, “the
living and the dead, immortals, ghosts and historical figures, and reality and
myth intermingled, and primitive totem, Confucian doctrine and witchcraft
superstition coexisted. Such images where myth and historical reality, and
immortal figures and animals shared one stage showed us a romantic world
with chaotic yet rich imaginations and passionate and bold feelings”.20 The
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
pictures also broke free of previously strict and orderly utilitarian
decorative patterns and took on a new approach that combined free romance
and realistic depiction.
    After the Eastern Han Dynasty, burial object pictures describing
fairyland scenes began to decrease while those describing human life began
to increase, which was related to the prevailing social trend at the time.
Land privatization accelerated and the manor economy developed rapidly,
quickly giving birth to a new landlord class, who not only sped up the
agricultural production of society, but also engaged in other industries
including rice wine brewing, salt well excavation, mulberry planting, and
iron ore smelting. The development of social productive forces brought an
affluent personal life and the demand for entertainment and pleasure. The
wealthy life of the landlord class was reflected in entities commonly found
on picture bricks at the time, such as horse-drawn carriages, hunting and
prey, board games, female singers and dancers, comedians, attendants,
kitchens and cooks, and pavilions. People hoped to bring such pleasures to
the underworld so that they might continue to enjoy them after death. While
some of the tomb picture bricks depicted people’s real lives, some were
fanciful lives that people were not able to lead when alive and hoped to
have after death. Such aspiration for an ideal life drove the creation of many
valuable artistic works for later generations to appreciate and laid a solid
foundation for the further development of ceramic arts.
   China’s development was never cut off from the outside world. Since
early times people of the central plains began economic and trade contacts
with various ethnic groups in surrounding areas. Emperor Wu of Han
expanded the northern and western frontiers and adopted conciliatory
policies towards ethnic minorities. In such a harmonious atmosphere, large
quantities of tributes and royal gifts flowed between the frontier and the
central plains. The royal gifts to the frontier included silks and ceramics, the
recipients of which then sold them to the Middle East and even to the
Roman Empire around the Mediterranean. Gradually, small cities grew out
of major junctions along the trade route connecting Chang’an (present-day
Xi’an), capital of the Han Dynasty, and Central Asia. These cities thrived,
benefitting from this “Silk Road”.21 This means as early as the Han
Dynasty, Chinese ceramics started to be exported to surrounding countries
and regions. Since then the foreign trade in ceramics has always been an
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
important part of China’s economic development and an important part of
China’s foreign cultural exchanges.

6. Ceramics of Wei, Jin and Southern and
Northern Dynasties

Lili Fang1
(1)  Chinese National Academy of Arts, Beijing, China



   Lili Fang
  Email: zhongzl@fltrp.com

6.1 Introduction
At the close of the Han Dynasty, internal fights for the throne and the power
struggle between relatives of the royal family and eunuchs led to the decline
of the Han regime. Successive droughts and floods caused great damage to
the agricultural economy of the Han Empire and peasant revolts rose one
after another, among which the Yellow Turbans Uprising and the movement
of the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice were widespread. Generals and
princesses in different regions revolted for their own protection, including
Cao Cao, who “controlled the emperor and commanded the nobles in his
name” and in the end virtually overthrew the unified rule of the Han
Dynasty, thus leading the country into the divided Three Kingdoms period,
which lasted from CE 220 to 280. The Jin Dynasty (the Western Jin) unified
China briefly from CE 280 to 316, but soon abandoned the defense of
northern China against the attack of northern ethnic groups such as the
Xiongnu, Xianbei, Jie, Di and Qiang, who crossed the Great Wall
southward. These northern groups established new regimes in northern
China and were increasingly assimilated by the Han people. For instance,
assimilated Xiongnu people established the Northern Han after occupying
Luoyang. From CE 304 to 384, these northern ethnic groups established in
succession 16 small regimes or states in northern China. At the same time,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the Jin Dynasty retreated to south of the Huaihe River and remained in
southern China until CE 420, a period which was called “the Eastern Jin
Dynasty”.
   With the southward migration of the Jin regime, the center of Confucian
culture also migrated southward. The six dynasties in southern China, all
regimes of the Han people that controlled only half of the country, namely,
Wu, the Eastern Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen (from CE 317 to 589), were
referred to as “the Six Dynasties”. Meanwhile, the small states in the north
were gradually swallowed up by the powerful Northern Wei. The ancestor
of the Northern Wei was the highly Sinicized Tuoba clan of the Xianbei.
Tuoba encouraged intermarriage with the Han, gave high regard to
Confucius, revered Confucianism and advocated the revitalization of the
rites and music. They adopted and further promoted the noble patriarchal
system of the Han—nobles of both ethnic minorities and the Han were
ranked into nine grades and appointed positions based on family reputation.
The construction of the capital city of the Northern Wei strictly followed the
Kao Gong Ji (Records of Examination of Craftsman). Such adoption of
Confucian theories and the exemplary bureaucratic system of the Han
Dynasty brought high administrative efficiency and contributed to the
increasing strength of the Northern Wei. In the latter half of the Northern
Wei Dynasty, it even moved its capital from Datong to southern Luoyang.
     It can be seen from the coexistence and intermingling of northern and
southern regimes that the Great Wall did not stop ethnic fusion. The
differentiation of “Hanand “non-Han” regimes only serves to look at issues
from different viewpoints and in different times, when in fact, cultural and
ethnic integration never ceased and the geographical boundary between
agricultural and husbandry economies was always blurred on the Asian
continent. The emergence of 16 states in the north also indicates that the
northern ethnic minorities, while constantly drawing upon the Confucian
culture, increasingly merged into the grand family of the Chinese nation.1
This period of history was collectively called the Wei, Jin and Southern &
Northern Dynasties.
    After the more than 400 years of unification of the Qin and Han
dynasties, China entered an era of division, yet also an era of great ethnic
and religious integration. The most prominent features of the era were the
fusion of new ethnic groups and the introduction of a new religion, both of
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
which were to exert an immense impact on the later development of
Chinese culture. This impact was also reflected in the ceramic art style.

6.1.1 Fusion of New Ethnic Groups
After the end of the Eastern Han Dynasty, the vigorous development of the
manor economy and land annexation strengthened the power of local
landlords, which led to conflicts among the ruling class and between
powerful landlords and the peasants who depended on them. The
intensification of these conflicts gave rise to the outbreak of the Yellow
Turbans Uprising in CE 184 in the Eastern Han. Failure of the uprising was
followed by fierce struggles for power and interest among despotic
landlords, and some nomadic minority ethnic groups also joined the
struggle.
   At the end of the Eastern Han Dynasty, there were Xiongnu in the north,
Xianbei in the northeast and Di and Qiang in the northwest. These peoples
were considered alien at the time, but in the historical records and legends
they were from the same ancestors as the people of the central plains.2
    Traditionally, Chinese people value culture more than blood. They place
emphasis on education and cultural levels and do not distinguish people or
their intelligence based on ethnicity or blood. The so-called “different
ethnic groups” in Chinese history refers to a group with a different lifestyle
and culture. (Fig. 6.1).





Fig. 6.1 Picture brick with Qiang girl,
Wei and Jin dynasties, unearthed from Tomb 7 in Xigou Village, Guoyuan, Jiuquan. The picture
depicts a young girl in long robes with her hair down walking towards a felt tent in the mountains
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and reflects the cohabitation of Han people and ethnic minority groups in the Helong area at the time

   While at this time China was divided into north and south, they all
belonged to the same system of Chinese traditional culture. The north at the
time must not be regarded as an alien culture of nomadic peoples that was
independent of the Chinese culture. Though lots of Chinese literati crossed
the Yangtze River to the south with the Jin royal family, most of them
remained in northern China. They were successors to and protectors of
Chinese traditional culture in the north. At that time, despotic lords in the
north enthroned non-Han monarchs, but it was Chinese literati that presided
over and implemented the politics. Though the nomads, stronger in military
force, rose in chaos and overthrew traditional regimes, they met and had to
compromise with the resistance of scholar-bureaucratic forces that remained
strong in various sectors of society and who could not be wiped out by mere
violence. This resulted in cooperation between the nomadic and Han
peoples in northern China.3 Chinese intellectuals in the north did their best
to educate and assimilate the nomadic peoples.4
   While intellectuals in the north were successors to and protectors of
traditional Chinese culture, those in the south took up the task of
publicizing and promoting traditional Chinese culture, since at that time
lands south of the Yangtze River were also inhabited by many descendants
of ancient non-Han races that were considered alien. Therefore, at this time
ethnic fusion and cultural dissemination were taking place in both the north
and the south, promoting traditional culture and assimilating new
ethnicities. History researchers often devote more attention to the political
significance of this process while overlooking the great importance of the
social and cultural transformation which it engendered. In fact, the Wei, Jin
and Southern & Northern Dynasties absorbed the social conditions
obtaining before the Spring and Autumn period and completed the second
great ethnic integration and national formation in the history of China. This
shows the strong vitality and tenacity of Chinese culture in the face of such
harsh tests. The entry and fusion of new ethnic cultures also injected new
style and appearance into ceramic art, a topic which will be discussed later.

6.1.2 Introduction of Buddhism
The historian Qian Mu has argued that Chinese traditional culture had
transcended religious needs before the Qin Dynasty, meaning that at that
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
time people already no longer relied on religious beliefs to realize the ideal
life. However, when it came to the second half of the Eastern Han Dynasty,
the general need for religion was resurrected, largely due to the wane of
Confucianism as the central philosophy of society and of individuals. The
most striking sign of such a decline was the corruption in the Eastern Han
royal family and the rise of the scholar-bureaucratic clans mentioned
above.5
   Before the collapse of the Eastern Han regime, Buddhism in China grew
only latently at the bottom of society, a situation that changed dramatically
once it came to the Three Kingdoms era. With the toppling of the traditional
royal family of the Western and Eastern Han that had lasted some 400
years, the society was thrown into turmoil, people lost faith in the Han
regime, and traditional culture was no longer respected and revered. It was
against such a backdrop that the Chinese people began converting to
Buddhism.
    In northern China at that time Buddhist temple building was luxurious
and Buddha statues such as the Yique and Yungang Grottoes were
extremely wasteful. Viewed from the standpoint of traditional political
theory and social order, the rise of Buddhism brought more harm than
benefit. The situation was exacerbated by several rounds of contention
between Taoism and Buddhism in northern China. In the end, by the time of
the Northern Zhou and early Sui and Tang dynasties, both had retreated to a
secondary position and real political leadership remained in the hands of the
scholar-bureaucrats, and traditional Confucianism was revived.
    In southern China, Buddhism became widely popular after the Eastern
Jin, but the prevailing customs differed from those in the north. In the north
Buddhism was often supported by the royal family, who seemed intent on
creating a theocracy albeit with no success, while in the south Buddhist
doctrines were studied freely by scholar-officials who approached
Buddhism from a purely philosophical perspective. The goal was to replace
Confucian thought with Buddhist philosophy to serve as a new compass for
seeking truth in life. These scholar-officials were followers of Buddhism
but not monks. To summarize, Buddhism in the north was more “political”
while that in the south was more “philosophical”.
   The practice of lecturing and teaching by commoners started from
Confucius and Mozi and lasted almost 1,000 years until the time of Ma
Rong and Zheng Xuan at the end of the Eastern Han Dynasty. The social
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
emphasis on learning only grew stronger over the millennium. Yet the
fashion of lecturing and learning experienced a sudden decline at the dawn
of the chaotic Three Kingdoms era, and Buddhist temples and monks, as a
substitution, rose to take over the task of edifying the common people. It is
obvious that Chinese Buddhism lays more emphasis on doctrinal study than
on belief, which reflected a kind of special spirit of Chinese culture.
Buddhist followers were driven by religious zeal, but more importantly,
they were inspired by a thirst and hunger for life’s truths. They believed in
Buddhism not merely for the comfort of the soul and the expression of
belief, but almost solely for the pursuit of knowledge, of the ultimate truth
in life. (Fig. 6.2).





Fig. 6.2 Instrument playing picture brick,
Wei and Jin dynasties, unearthed from Tomb 7 in Xigou Village, Guoyuan, Jiuquan. The picture
depicts two musicians sitting facing each other, one playing a zither and the other playing a Ruan
(plucked stringed instrument)

   The Wei, Jin and Southern & Northern Dynasties could be said to be a
period of decline in Chinese history. Yet in terms of academic
breakthroughs and innovative spirit, this period was not inferior to and even
more spectacular than the Western Han Dynasty. Eminent monks of the
period far surpassed the Confucian scholars in the Han Dynasty in terms of
personality, energy, vision and open-mindedness. From the standpoint of
cultural history, in the Wei, Jin and Southern & Northern Dynasties, the
evolution of Chinese culture was not declining but was in fact moving
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
forward vigorously. The entry of new ethnic elements only restructured
Chinas social order and the introduction of new religious beliefs only
expanded Chinas ideological horizons. In the history of Chinese culture,
there have only been “assimilation, integration and expansion”, and not
“division, conflict and elimination”.6
   Such “assimilation, integration and expansion” found reflection in the
ceramic production at the time. New religion and new ethnic cultures
brought new fashions to ceramic modeling and decoration in the Wei, Jin
and Southern & Northern dynasties. (Fig. 6.3).





Fig. 6.3 Yue kiln four-lugged jar decorated with Buddhas,
Western Jin Dynasty, height: 18.4 cm, top diam.: 14.5 cm, in the Cultural Relics Management
Committee of Shengxian County, Zhejiang

6.1.3 Development of a New Ceramics Industry
Above is a discussion on how cultural and ideological fields at the time
might influence ceramic art from the viewpoint of ethnic fusion and
religious development. In this part we will examine how economic
development promoted the production of ceramics.
   Over the 360 years from the beginning of the Three Kingdoms to the
end of the Southern & Northern dynasties, except for a short-term
unification during the Western Jin, Chinas north and south were long
trapped in disunion and hostility. Comparatively speaking there was less
war and more stability in the vast areas south of the Yangtze River. The
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
southward migration of large numbers of commoners, scholar-bureaucrats
and landlords from the central plains injected new vitality into the
previously sparsely populated vast south, where exchanges and integration
of northern and southern cultures took place. As the working population
increased, the economy of the south developed rapidly and important cities
emerged, such as Jiankang, Jingkou, Shanyin, Shouchun, Xiangyang,
Jiangling, Chengdu and Panyu. Economic growth, convenient
transportation, prosperous commerce and the appearance of cities created
conditions for the handicraft industry to develop. In such a favorable social
environment the porcelain industry that had newly emerged during the late
Eastern Han Dynasty enjoyed rapid development.
   The history of ceramics was almost entirely dominated by pottery until
the end of the Eastern Han Dynasty when the once primitive porcelain
began to assume a mature form, marked by the creative firing of celadon in
Zhejiang Province. (Fig. 6.4) Following that, porcelain took center stage in
the history of Chinese ceramics and Zhejiang, as the birthplace of celadon,
flourished for some 1,800 years. At the end of the Eastern Han Dynasty
porcelain started maturing but had not completely freed itself from the
shackles of primitive porcelain. It developed further after the Wei, Jin and
Southern & Northern Dynasties.





Fig. 6.4 Yue kiln basin,
Western Jin Dynasty, height: 10.5 cm, top diam.: 35.7 cm, in the Cultural Relics Management
Committee of Shaoxing, Zhejiang

6.1.3.1 Development of Porcelain Production
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
From the Three Kingdoms to the Southern & Northern Dynasties was a
period of disunion and turmoil in China’s history, but in terms of ideology it
was a period of integration of the Yellow River and Yangtze River cultures.
Particularly magnificent was the culture and art of the southern Six
Dynasties, which, as the link succeeding the Qin and Han dynasties and
preceding the Sui and Tang dynasties, made great contributions to Chinese
culture and art. The porcelain-making craft of this period was an example,
and a precious intangible cultural heritage.
   During the Six Dynasties, the porcelain industry developed rapidly,
blooming almost universally with widely distributed kilns. Production bases
wide in scope, large in scale, with numerous kilns and high skill levels
ranged from Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Fujian in the lower reaches of the
Yangtze River and along the southeast coast to Jiangxi, Hubei, Hunan and
Sichuan in the middle and upper reaches of the Yangtze River, each with
their own unique system. Some of them were built based on earlier
porcelain kilns, but most were newly established during the Six Dynasties.7
   The celadon of the Six Dynasties, with clear green or tea green glaze,
exquisite and diverse shapes, and rich and colorful decoration, gradually
replaced the gaudy and fragile pottery, expensive and time-consuming
bronze and lacquer ware, and became popular and indispensable daily
necessities as well as burial objects. What is most striking about celadon in
the Six Dynasties was its plastic arts, which could be said to have reached
the marvelous and ingenious level of “harmony of Heaven and man”. It not
only embodied the Confucian doctrine of the mean and benevolence, but
also reflected the peaceful compatibility of yin and yang held by Taoism,
along with Buddhisms compassion for the world and the individual.
   The shape design of early Chinese porcelain following the Shang
Dynasty emphasized practicality and often imitated the shape of pottery or
bronzewares, while both practical and ornamental purposes were taken into
consideration in the shape design of the celadon in the Six Dynasties, which
was a major advance in the history of arts and crafts. Drawing upon animal
images in shape design was a major artistic feature of celadon in the Six
Dynasties. Sometimes imitating an animal as a whole and sometimes in
part, the approach invariably resulted in vivid, unique and interesting
effects.8
   Looking back into the materials for making daily utensils in previous
periods in China, we can see that during the Neolithic it was mainly the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
production of pottery. Over the more than 1,000 years from Shang to Zhou
and the Spring and Autumn and Warring States, the development of bronze
craft occupied an important position, and from the Warring States period to
the Han Dynasty, bronze craft in effect came to an end and in its place rose
lacquerware. But lacquerware could not entirely replace bronzeware and
gradually declined after hundreds of years because of high manufacturing
costs and more importantly, poor practicability.
    Porcelain was highly practical because it was strong, durable, clean,
acid-resistant, easy to wash, non-reactive and thus had no taste of its own,
and at the same time it was perfectly aligned with people’s aesthetic
pursuits at the time because it was delicate, smooth and translucent with a
jade-like color and mellowness. Therefore, it was only natural that
porcelain would become the most popular and commonly used utensil in
people’s lives at the time as it further developed in the Six Dynasties after
maturing in the Eastern Han from the primitive porcelain of the Shang
Dynasty. Thanks to increasing demand, porcelain production flourished
everywhere south of the Yangtze River. Porcelain kiln sites from the period
have been found in today’s Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian, Jiangsu, Hunan and
elsewhere.
   At the end of the fourth century, as the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei
unified the Yellow River basin and established the Northern Wei regime, the
economy of the central plains enjoyed some recovery and development. In
the context of economic and cultural communication between the north and
south, and under the impact of the southern ceramics industry, northern
ceramic craftsmen successfully produced celadon with local characteristics,
and then succeeded in firing black porcelain and white porcelain.
   The main achievement of ceramics production in Wei, Jin and the
Southern & Northern Dynasties lay in the production of porcelain, among
which celadon was the most successful, followed by black porcelain and
white porcelain. During this period pottery continued to be made, but on a
smaller scale. Daily use pottery was mainly gray with a poor firing
temperature, rough quality, small volume and limited variety. Yet
outstanding achievements were made in the production of burial objects and
architectural pottery. Low-fired glazed pottery saw new development based
on the Han Dynasty’s advances. The preliminary firing of tricolor glazed
pottery laid the foundation for the prosperity of the tricolor pottery of the
Tang Dynasty.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
As porcelain was produced as a commodity, namely, daily necessities
for sale, kilns had to consider the issue of transportation from the place of
origin to the outside world. Water routes were favored as they were the
most stable means of transportation with great capacity and low cost.
Therefore, most kilns were built near rivers, streams, lakes or seaports. For
instance, the Yue kilns were distributed on both sides of the Cao’e River
and near Hangzhou Bay, the Ou kilns were in the lower reaches of the
Oujiang River and the eastern coast in Wenzhou, the Wuzhou kilns were
concentrated in the vicinity of the Dongyang River, the Nanshan kilns were
by Taihu Lake in the east, the Luohu kilns in Jiangxi Province were by
Poyang Lake in the north and near the junction of the Ganjiang and Jinjiang
rivers, the Xiangyin kilns in Hunan Province lay to the east of the
Xiangjiang River, the Qingyanggong kilns in Sichuan Province were
located at the confluence of the Modi and Huanhuaxi rivers, the Huai’an
kilns in Fujian Province were in the lower reaches of the Minjiang River
and the eastern coast, and the Cizao kilns were located by the Jinjiang River
and on the southeastern coast. The highly developed shipbuilding industry
in the Six Dynasties made shipment of porcelain products possible.9

6.2 Celadon of Wei, Jin and Southern and
Northern Dynasties
6.2.1 Celadon Production in the South
Primitive porcelain matured into porcelain proper at the end of the Eastern
Han Dynasty and porcelain production further developed over the period
from the Three Kingdoms to the Southern Dynasties. The development of
porcelain production was particularly rapid in lands south of the Yangtze
River, which were relatively stable compared with the central plains.
During the two Jin dynasties, four kiln systems with different
characteristics, namely, the Yue, Ou, Wuzhou and Deqing kilns, took shape
in Zhejiang Province. By the late Southern Dynasties, the porcelain-making
industry had spread to vast areas of modern-day Jiangsu, Sichuan, Hunan,
Jiangxi, Guangdong, Guangxi and Fujian. Yet it was still Zhejiang that
produced porcelain on the largest scale. Kiln sites from the Wei, Jin and
Southern & Northern Dynasties have been found in many places in
Zhejiang, including Shangyu, Xiaoshan, Lishui, Jinhua, Linhai, Yongjia and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Shaoxing. The most important porcelain type at the time was celadon,
which was developed from primitive porcelain. Celadon was produced in
almost every site of porcelain production. (Fig. 6.5).





Fig. 6.5 Celadon sheep,
Western Jin Dynasty, length: 15 cm, width: 11 cm, height: 13.5 cm, in the Palace Museum

     Still, the center of celadon production remained in Zhejiang, the
birthplace of celadon. Among the kilns of Zhejiang, the Yue kilns led
celadon development due to their rapid growth, large volume, wide
distribution, high product quality and immense influence on surrounding
areas. The name “Yue kilns” came from the Tang Dynasty. In the Tang
Dynasty, kilns were usually called by their place of location, and “Yue kilns
“was a shortened form of “Yuezhou kilns”. The Yuezhou kilns were mainly
located in Yuyao and Shangyu under the jurisdiction of Yuezhou. Although
the name “Yue kilns” originated during the Tang Dynasty, the kilns
themselves could be traced back to the Han Dynasty. Following the first
successful firing of mature celadon in places including Shangyu in the late
Eastern Han Dynasty, the porcelain industry in this area flourished down
through history without interruption. Although over time the style of the
products underwent change, the inheritance and succession relationship
between different periods was very clear. Thus, academia regards porcelain
kilns in Shaoxing, Shangyu and other old places of Yuezhou as belonging to
the same system as the Yue kilns in the Tang and Song dynasties and refers
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
to them collectively as the Yue kilns. The Yue kilns before the Tang
Dynasty are often referred to as “early Yue kilns”, or “ancient Yue kilns” as
termed by Japanese academia. The history and name origin of the Ou and
Wuzhou kilns in Zhejiang Province are similar in general. (Figs. 6.6 and
6.7).





Fig. 6.6 Celadon double-lugged jar,
Western Jin Dynasty, height: 26.6 cm, top diam.: 14.9 cm, base diam.: 11.2 cm, in the Palace
Museum
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.7 Celadon double-lugged you (wine container),
Western Jin Dynasty, height: 23.7 cm, top diam.: 11.7 × 10.6 cm, base diam.: 16.4 cm, in the Palace

  Among the four kiln systems in Zhejiang, the Yue, Ou and Wuzhou
kilns mainly produced celadon and only the Deqing kilns fired black
porcelain as well as celadon.
   The Yue kilns covered a wide range of areas, mainly in modern-day
eastern Zhejiang, with Shangyu, Shaoxing, Cixi and Yuyao as centers. The
celadon was fired in dragon kilns at a high temperature, all over 1,200
degrees Celsius with a maximum of 1,300 degrees. Celadon fired in Yue
kilns during the Three Kingdoms period had the same body and glaze color
as that of the Eastern Han Dynasty. That is, the body was fine in texture,
grayish white in color, fully sintered and hard, and nonabsorbent. The body
had an even layer of celadon glaze applied. Wares were glazed on different
parts according to their uses. Bowls, small cups and basins were glazed
fully on the inside and to the bottom on the outside, while pots, jars and
other containers were often glazed on the mouth rim and outer surface but
not on the inside. The color of the body served as a base color of the glaze.
Thus, the glaze of Yue kiln celadon during the Three Kingdoms looked
bluish green because the body color was lighter, while the thick and even
glaze of Western Jin celadon, which had a relatively thicker and darker
body, generally appeared greenish gray. In the early Eastern Jin, the celadon
of the Yue kilns maintained the style of the Western Jin and not much
change can be seen. After the mid-Eastern Jin, the Deqing kilns rose and the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Ou kilns along with the Wuzhou kilns experienced accelerated
development, forming rivalries with the Yue kilns. At the same time, the
porcelain industry in Jiangxi, Hunan, Sichuan and other areas also
developed, and new kilns were set up to produce celadon to meet local
needs. As a result, the Yue kilns in Shangyu and Shaoxing decreased in
number. The number of porcelain kiln sites from this period discovered in
Shangyu number less than 30.10 Kilns were also more scattered. Small
numbers of new kilns were built in modern-day Shangdong in Xiaoshan,
Shigai Village11, Xiaobaishi in Yinxian12, and Shanglin Lake in Yuyao.
During the Southern Dynasties, porcelain kilns and ware varieties
decreased. As Buddhism became prevalent, carved lotus petals became the
main decorative pattern of porcelain. (Fig. 6.8).





Fig. 6.8 Celadon lotus pattern bowl with holder,
Southern Dynasty, height: 10.9 cm, top diam.: 15.5 cm, in the Jiangsu Museum

   The Ou kilns were located in Wenzhou in southern Zhejiang with the
sea to the east, Fujian to the south, and the Kuocang Mountains to the
northwest. The Oujiang and Feiyun rivers flow eastward to the sea. The
area was one of the ancient trading ports in China and was advanced in
multiple industries including porcelain making, shipbuilding and
embroidery. Moreover, the geographical location and natural resources
offered favorable conditions for porcelain making in the area. The
mountains produced wood as fuel and porcelain raw materials and the rivers
offered convenient water transportation. Most of the kilns were located on
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
both banks of the Oujiang, Feiyun and Nanxi rivers so that products could
be shipped to cities like Wenzhou by boat or raft. To date, more than 200
Ou kiln sites have been found and they are widely distributed in modern-
day Yongjia, Yueqing, Rui’an, Wencheng and Taishun counties as well as
Wenzhou City. It was one of many large-scale porcelain kiln systems in
China. Yongjia on the north bank of the Oujiang River started producing
primitive porcelain as early as the Han Dynasty and succeeded in firing
celadon by the end of the Eastern Han. The body of Ou kiln porcelain was
white with a tinge of gray and the glaze was light blue with a high
transparency. Scholars believe this kind of glaze color was probably the
light blue porcelain mentioned by the Jin Dynasty poet Pan Yue in his “Ode
to Sheng”. Thus, Ou kiln celadon was also known as “light-blue porcelain”.
Zhu Yan of the Qin Dynasty said in his On Ceramics that “Pan’s ‘Ode’
mentioned light blue porcelain, indicating that light blue was favored at the
time, setting the precedent for mountain green and sky blue that became
popular later”. It can be seen that the light blue color was quite the fashion
in society at that time. Lu Yu of the Tang Dynasty quotes “Ode to Late
Tea“in his Book of Tea, mentioning “selected ceramic vessels from east
Ou”. Later, Zhu Yan further highlighted the fame of the Ou kilns in his On
Ceramics, saying, “Ou was part of Yuezhou and was already well-known
before the Yuezhou kilns rose to fame”. Records of Jingdezhen Ceramics
also states: “Ou, now Wenzhou of Zhejiang, started ceramic production in
the Jin Dynasty and was well known at that time”. It can be seen that the Ou
kilns were accorded high regard in ceramic circles, although the volume
and production scale of the Ou kilns that have been discovered are smaller
than the Yue kilns. The craftsmanship and decoration of Ou porcelain is
also not as meticulous or exquisite as those of Yue ware. Porcelain
unearthed across the country indicates that the supply of Ou kiln products
was not as wide as that of Yue kiln products, and that most porcelain used
by the nobles and officials at the time were produced by the Yue kilns. It
could be inferred that the Yue kilns had a greater social impact than the Ou
kilns. Ou porcelain is believed to have developed from the primitive
porcelain industry of the Han Dynasty because the sites and ware shapes of
the two are similar. (Fig. 6.9).
