   The Wuzhou kilns were located in the central areas of modern-day
Zhejiang. The main production sites were in Jinhua, Wuyi, Dongyang and
Yiwu. There were also some kilns in modern-day Yongkang, Lanxi,
Pujiang, Longyou, Jiangshan and Changshan counties. The distribution of
the kilns was very wide. Archaeological investigations have found more
than 600 ancient kiln sites ranging from the Han Dynasty to the Ming. The
large number of kiln sites and the long production period are rare in China’s
porcelain kiln systems, giving the Wuzhou kilns a special position in the
history of ceramics. People used to believe that the Wuzhou kilns started in
the Tang Dynasty because of the record in Lu Yu’s Book of Tea that “for
bowls, Yuezhou products are the best, followed by Dingzhou and
Wuzhou…” But kiln site location and information found in ancient tombs
indicate that the Wuzhou kilns originated in the Eastern Han Dynasty. They
developed from the Han Dynasty ceramic kilns in Hengluzhu Village in
Shangweitou Township, Longyou County. The Six Dynasties was a period
of development for the Wuzhou kilns, during which they expanded
production capacity and improved technology. The period from the Tang
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Dynasty to the Northern Song was the zenith of the Wuzhou kilns, and so
far most kiln sites discovered were from this period. The body of Wuzhou
kiln celadon in the Three Kingdoms period was mostly light gray. The clay
was not finely processed, so the fracture surface was coarse. The body was
not fully sintered, and the degree of vitrification was poor. The glaze was
uneven in thickness and there were condensed lumps in the shape of sesame
seeds. Most glaze was light blue while some was bluish gray or yellowish
blue. Dense crackles covered the glaze. There were often cream-colored
crystals precipitating at places where the glaze was not firmly stuck on the
body and where the glaze surface cracked. Such crystallization was a
phenomenon inherent in Wuzhou kiln celadon. By the late Western Jin
Dynasty, because the porcelain clay deposits in the area were scattered in
small, thin beds and thus difficult to exploit, the potters of the Wuzhou kilns
started using red clay as body material since it was ubiquitous in the area,
easy to exploit and crush, and had good plasticity. Nevertheless, a high iron
oxide and titanium oxide content in the red clay13 led to a deep purple body
color after firing, which affected the color expression of the celadon glaze.
Thus, a layer of fine textured white engobe was first applied to the surface
of the body to cover its purple color. Thanks to the white engobe, the glaze
layer turned out to be mellow and soft. The color was bluish gray or bluish
yellow with a tinge of brown. But the cracking and crystallization of the
glaze surface were more serious than those of celadon made from porcelain
clay. In general, Wuzhou kiln porcelain from the Southern Dynasties mostly
had a bluish yellow glaze that was poorly bonded to the body and thus
prone to peeling off.
   The Deqing kilns were located in the northern part of Zhejiang
Province. Although celadon was among their products, they mainly fired
black porcelain. (Fig. 6.10).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.10 Deqing kiln black glazed spittoon,
Eastern Jin Dynasty, height: 10 cm, top diam.: 9.4 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Apart from those in Zhejiang Province, celadon kilns from the time
have also been found in the middle and upper reaches of the Yangtze River,
including in modern-day Jiangxi, Sichuan, Hunan and Hubei. But these
areas started firing celadon later than Jiangsu and Zhejiang in the lower
reaches of the Yangtze River. The kilns here were probably not built until
the Jin Dynasty.
   The site of the Nanshan kilns lies at the northern foot of Nanshan
Mountain near Tangdu Village in Dingshu Town in southeastern Yixing,
Jiangsu Province. As early as the Eastern Han Dynasty, dragon kilns
appeared in Yixing to fire pottery and primitive porcelain. In the late Wu
and early Jin dynasties, the kilns absorbed the advanced technology of the
Yue kilns in adjacent Wuxing and Shangyu and developed into a base for
celadon firing. Products of the Nanshan kilns were often of the same style
as those of the Yue kilns, but the quality was generally inferior to Yue kiln
products. Nanshan kiln porcelain had a grayish white body and bluish
yellow or bluish gray glaze, mostly with ice crackles. Bonding between
glaze and body was weak and peeling off was common. However, as
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
technology advanced and craftsmanship improved, more exquisite products
appeared from the Nanshan kilns, such as the sculptured celadon jars
displayed in the Yixing Ceramic Exhibition Hall of Dingshu Town, some of
which were meticulously made with bright and clear glaze.14
   The Jingchu area (modern-day Hubei) started producing high quality
primitive porcelain and a small amount of celadon back in the Wu Kingdom
of the Three Kingdoms period. The products had a purplish red or light gray
body which had yellowish-brown or celadon glaze applied. The glaze was
uneven in thickness and often broke away from the body. Strictly speaking
the products had not reached the standard of porcelain proper. By the
Western Jin Dynasty, porcelain clay started to be used to shape the body,
resulting in a fine texture and bluish gray or grayish white color. The body
then had yellowish green glaze applied. The color of the glaze varied from
yellow to green. Some were yellow with green hues and some were brown.
Crazing was common. The bonding between glaze and body was not good
and peeling was common. For some wares all the glaze peeled off. By the
Eastern Jin Dynasty production quality improved, but glaze crazing and
shivering were still prevalent due to a mismatch between the expansion
coefficient of the glaze and the body.
   The Xiangyin kilns also produced celadon, and their sites were densely
located, mainly in Chengguan Town on the east bank of the Xiangjiang
River in Xiangyin, Hunan Province. Among the Xiangyin kilns, the
Qingzhu Temple Kiln, Macaopo Kiln, Fengshuzui Kiln, Zhuyuanli Kiln,
Hulushan Kiln, Changdipo Kiln, and Wujiadu Kiln came into being in the
Eastern Han Dynasty, while the Shexingshan Kiln and Mawangkan Kiln
originated in the two Jin dynasties. Porcelain made in the Xiangyin kilns
had a light gray (grayish white) body and their early glaze was green with a
yellow shade. It was a type of celadon with a high calcium gray glaze and
high silica body. By the Western Jin Dynasty and following, glaze colors
became more varied to include bean green, shrimp blue and bluish brown.
The glaze became lustrous and smooth with no shivering, basically reaching
the level of Yue kiln celadon. Early decorative patterns were the same as
those of the Han Dynasty, namely, linen patterns, ripple patterns, string
patterns, rope patterns, etc. In the later stages brown dots were painted on
ware rims as decoration. In the early period of the Six Dynasties, the
porcelain making of the Xiangyin and Yue kilns mutually influenced each
other. For instance, porcelain from the two during the Three Kingdoms and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the two Jin dynasties were basically the same in terms of decoration and
shape. Yet by the late period of the Six Dynasties, porcelain made by the
Xiangyin kilns showed more resemblance and mutual influence with
contemporaneous porcelain produced in modern-day Jiangxi and Fujian.15
Most of these products were daily use wares and burial objects were rare.
   Celadon has also been widely found in Southern & Northern Dynasties
tombs in Zhaohua, Guangyuan, Mianyang, Deyang, Chengdu and other
places in Sichuan Province. Porcelain kilns have also been found in
Chengdu. Celadon in this area has a finer body texture. The body was light
gray. The glaze, mostly yellowish blue or yellow, was relatively even in
thickness albeit also highly prone to crazing and shivering.
   During the Six Dynasties the porcelain industry also rose successively
in many places in the middle and upper reaches of the Yangtze River.
Varying quantities of porcelain have been unearthed in tombs discovered in
Wuchang, Changsha and Liuyang in today’s Hunan and Hubei provinces.
The Luohu kilns, widely distributed in the hilly area on the west bank of the
Ganjiang River in the northeast of Fengcheng, Jiangxi Province, started
firing porcelain during the Southern Dynasties. The Luohu kilns are also
known as the Hongzhou kilns because Fengcheng was under the
jurisdiction of Hongzhou in the Tang Dynasty. The glaze color of Luohu
kiln porcelain was mainly yellowish-brown and caramel brown. There was
also bluish green glaze.16
    Jiangxi was one of the primitive porcelain producing areas in China,
affording it an excellent foundation for making porcelain. Burial objects
found in local tombs indicate celadon might have begun to be fired here in
the Three Kingdoms period and mass production started in the Western Jin
Dynasty. The body of celadon produced in Jiangxi in the Western Jin
Dynasty, made from washed clay, has a fine texture and bluish gray or
grayish white color. The wares had bluish green, beige or green glaze
applied which did not cover the outer wall to the bottom. There seemed to
be no good interfacial layer formed between glaze and body so that the
glaze was prone to shivering and crazing. Celadon workshops from the
Southern Dynasties have been found in Luohu in Fengcheng, Jiangxi
Province. Kiln sites in the area had a wide distribution and were large in
scale. Some deposits of waste pieces are up to five or six meters thick,
which shows that the porcelain industry there was very developed in ancient
times. Fengcheng belonged to Hongzhou in the Tang Dynasty. Its products
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
were transported by boats through the Ganjiang River and could reach the
seat of the Hongzhou state government, that is, modern-day Nanchang, in
one day. It thus enjoyed convenient conditions for production and
marketing. Some scholars therefore believe that the Tang dynasty porcelain
kilns in Fengcheng were the “Hongzhou kilns” as recorded in ancient
literature and that the Southern Dynasties kilns were their predecessor.
   Besides the Yangtze River valley, celadon was also produced in
Guangdong and Fujian. Though no kiln site of the Six Dynasties period has
been found in Guangdong so far, porcelain unearthed from local tombs
suggests that there were probably porcelain kilns in production back in the
two Jin dynasties. The porcelain body was grayish white with an external
blue glaze. Mostly bluish yellow or bluish green, the glaze had crackles and
was prone to peeling. The influence of the Yue and Ou kilns can be seen in
the decorative techniques, which suggests maritime traffic was already
developed at that time, allowing cultural and economic exchanges and
reciprocal influences between different coastal areas. Porcelain making in
Fujian started relatively late, around the Eastern Jin Dynasty. Major kilns
included the Huai’an and Cizao kilns. The former, located in the southwest
of the Tianshan and Maling mountains in Huai’an Village, Jianxin
Township in the western suburbs of Fuzhou, Fujian Province, started firing
porcelain in the late Jin Dynasty and the early Southern Dynasties, and the
latter, located in the Xikou Mountain area in Cizao Town in Jinjiang,
Quanzhou, started firing porcelain in the Southern Dynasties. Huai’an kiln
products had a gray, dark body and blue glaze. The craftsmanship was
rough. The products of the Cizao kilns had a relatively loose body texture.
The body was grayish white and the glaze was bluish gray with a tinge of
yellow and iron spots. The shape design of both Huai’an and Cizao wares
resembled the celadon produced in Jiangxi in the same period and differed
from the porcelain made in Jiangsu and Zhejiang. The shape design of some
vessels had strong local features.17 Porcelain kilns from the Southern
Dynasties have been found in Huai’an Village. The celadon produced was
dominated by daily use wares, and the craftsmanship and shape design
displayed influence from the Yue kilns.

6.2.2 Celadon Production in the North
The widespread production of celadon in the south would inevitably lead to
the development of celadon making in the north. The interaction between
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the north and south would also take celadon production technologies of the
south to the north. But till now no definitive evidence has been found to
explain when celadon production in the north began. The majority of
northern celadon kilns discovered are confined to the Zhaili kilns in Zibo,
Shandong Province. From products of the Zhaili kilns we can see the
difference between northern and southern celadon in terms of body material
and glaze. Southern celadon (mainly from Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces)
was made from high-iron clay. Thus, the color of the body was deeper,
especially Wuzhou kiln products, whose body turned out to be dark purple
after firing and therefore affected the look of the celadon glaze. Northern
celadon, however, was made from clay with relatively lower iron content
and higher aluminum content. The resultant body color was lighter, creating
conditions for the production of white porcelain. The celadon glazing of
both the north and south at the time belonged to ash glazes, that is, glazes
made with a recipe using limestone and plant ash mixed with porcelain
clay. The plant ash in the south was mostly burnt from straw and ferns in
the mountains while that in the north was mostly burnt from shrubs. This
difference in recipe resulted in differences in glaze color.
    Generally, the production of celadon at the time was mainly
concentrated in the south, which betokened the ceramic production map of
“southern celadon and northern white” later in the Tang Dynasty.

6.2.3 Shape Design and Decoration of Celadon
The types, shapes and appearance of celadon during the Eastern Han
Dynasty were basically the same as pottery of the same period and the only
difference was in texture, indicating that in the early stage of porcelain-
making, traditional pottery designs were adopted without change since there
had not developed new and better designs suited to the new art form. By the
Six Dynasties the varieties and shapes of celadon had abandoned the
influence of pottery. New shape designs that better highlighted the thin
walls and bright glaze of porcelain were created and innovations were made
in terms of decorative techniques. The most distinctive varieties in terms of
shape design were pots with rooster head spouts, spittoons, frog-shaped
water pots, lotus flower zun and tiger-shaped chamber pots (Fig. 6.11), as
well as granary urns (soul jars) that were used purely as burial objects (Fig.
6.12). Celadon was also used to make daily use vessels previously made of
bronze or lacquerware, the former including incense burners and washers,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and the latter including plates and eared cups. Porcelain had now entered all
aspects of people’s lives as food containers, wine vessels, stationery, lamps
and lanterns, washing vessels, etc. Varieties were many and designs were
fresh and practical.





Fig. 6.11 Celadon tiger-shaped chamber pot,
height: 20.9 cm, length: 26.6 cm, in the Shanghai Museum
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.12 Celadon granary urn,
Wu Dynasty, height: 46.4 cm, base diam.: 15.3 cm, in the Palace Museum

   To adapt to people’s new lifestyles and aesthetic preferences, celadon
design during this period, while endeavoring to go beyond the customary
design traditions of pottery, created many new models, drawing upon
animal images. Some wares used animal images as the outline, such as zun
in the shape of a crouching goat, water pots in the shape of a floating frog,
porcelain oil lamps carried by squatting bears, and lion-shaped
candleholders. (Fig. 6.13) Those using animal sculptures as partial
decoration were more flexible and varied. Commonly used animals
included birds, goats, bears, and rabbits. A representative work was the
bird-shaped cup unearthed in 1974 in a Western Jin tomb found in Baiguan
Town in Shangyu, Zhejiang Province. A flying bird with spread wings was
sculpted on the front of the cup and a tail was sculpted on the back. The cup
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
served as the body of the bird and the bird had its head turned to look back
at its tail, creating a strong sense of motion. (Fig. 6.14).

text:
With the development of new materials, celadon in the Six Dynasties
adopted new decorative techniques in addition to innovating shape design.
Carving and sculpturing grew to be popular decorative skills during the
period due to their positive effect of highlighting the special quality of
celadon glazing. Decorative motifs were plain and simple, mostly
composed of checks, linked beads, rhombuses, clouds and strings. There
were also stuck sculptures of Red Phoenixes, winged immortals and
mythological creatures. In the Eastern Jin Dynasty the decorative patterns
became even simpler to further highlight the beauty of the glittering glaze.
In the Southern Dynasties, the prevalence of Buddhism was reflected in the
rise of lotus patterns in celadon decoration. Bowls and cups were often
decorated with upward-facing lotus petals on the outer wall and plates were
often ornamented with lotus petals radiating from the center of the well,
making the entire ware look like a blooming lotus flower. Representative
wares were the downward-facing lotus green-glazed jar with six lugs
unearthed in Chengdu, Sichuan, the large lotus celadon zun unearthed in the
Liang dynasty tomb in Linshan, Nanjing, the celadon saucer with lotus petal
pattern unearthed in Ji’an, Jiangxi, and the celadon lotus zun unearthed in
the Feng family tomb cluster in Jingxian, Hebei. (Fig. 6.15).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.15 Celadon lotus zun,
Northern Qi Dynasty, height: 67 cm, top diam.: 19 cm, base diam.: 20 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Another popular decorative technique at the time was the ornamentation
of the celadon glaze with caramel-brown glaze spots. Such caramel-brown
glaze in fact also used iron as the coloring agent like celadon glaze, except
that its iron content was higher. If the iron content was higher still, black
glaze would be produced. The discovery of this decorative technique was
probably accidental, that is, high-iron glaze dots inadvertently got mixed
with celadon glaze and formed caramel-brown spots strewn on celadon
glaze after firing, creating a rather beautiful effect and therefore became a
desired attribute that was deliberately produced.
  A major feature of Yue kiln porcelain during the Western Jin Dynasty
was the diversity of decorative techniques. Often multiple decorative
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
patterns and techniques were used on the same ware. Sometimes on one
vessel there were carved strings, pressed grids, poked bead patterns, and
molded rings with beast-head bases, Buddha statuettes, tiger heads and
other ornaments. For some vessels, linked bead patterns were imprinted
above and below grid patterns, and molded ornaments such as rings with
beast-head bases were stuck below the mouth rims or on the shoulders. Jars
with piled sculptures were the epitome of the simultaneous adoption of
multiple decorative means such as carving, scratching, stamping, poking,
molding, kneading and sculpting. Flying birds, walking beasts and
swimming fish could all be decorative motifs and one motif could be used
in multiple ways. For instance, bears could be squatting at the four corners
of a building wall on jars with piled sculptures and could also be the feet of
incense burners and inkstones. The tiger could also be used in a variety of
ways. The hoop handle of chamber pots was sometimes shaped like a
running tiger. The feet of zun and washers were sometimes in the shape of a
tiger. And tiger images were sometimes used together with dragons,
phoenixes and other mythological creatures to form pattern bands to
decorate the shoulder and belly of washers, bowls and jars, which added
dignity, elegance and beauty to the vessels. The use of a variety of
decorative techniques and patterns on the same ware endowed both depth
and shallowness as well as both static and dynamic beauty to it, achieving a
remarkable artistic performance. It is worth mentioning that patterns and
ornaments were not created in isolation or applied blindly. Rather, their
creation and application closely followed the requirements of production
technologies. The decoration and the technology complemented and added
radiance to each other. Products of Yue kilns in the Western Jin Dynasty
combined practical value and decorative purpose in design. Being both
practical vessels and ornaments with aesthetic appeal, these artifacts
represented a new achievement in ceramic art.18
   The evolution of the commonly used patterns included the following:
rhombus checks originated in the Wu Yong’an Third Year (CE 260) of the
Three Kingdoms period; molded Buddha images were first seen in the Wu
Yong’an Sixth Year (CE 263); wing (carved) patterns rose in the Wu Ganlu
First Year (CE 265) and disappeared after the Xiankang era of the Eastern
Jin Dynasty; linked bead patterns appeared in the late Wu Dynasty and
early Western Jin Dynasty; brown spots as a decoration first appeared in the
Wu Jianheng Second Year (CE 270) and became popular in the Eastern Jin
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Dynasty; and the lotus pattern, popular during the Southern Dynasties, first
originated in the Qi Yongming First Year (CE 483).19
    In summary, the shape and decoration of celadon in the Wei, Jin and
Southern & Northern Dynasties presented a new vista for carrying forward
the past and opening up the future and laid a solid foundation for later
developments in porcelain art.

6.2.4 Achievements and Features of Celadon
The development of the porcelain industry in the Six Dynasties was
manifest not only in its extensive production scale covering vast areas south
of the Yangtze River and its large product volume, but also in the
remarkable achievements made in production technologies. The porcelain
craftsmen’s innovation in and superior mastery of raw material selection,
molding techniques, engobe use, glaze preparation, decorative pattern
adoption, kiln structure improvement and firing technologies in the period
made celadon production a new industry.

6.2.4.1 Selection of Materials and Use of Engobe
Different areas selected locally rich raw materials to improve product
quality and to enhance their competitive advantage over other localities.
During the Western Jin Dynasty, Yue kiln potters purposely chose porcelain
clay with high iron and titanium contents as material for the body, or added
small amounts of “zijin“(reddish purple) clay to the material, so that the
content of iron oxide in the body material increased from less than 2%
(generally between 1.5 and 1.75%) in the Eastern Han Dynasty and the
Three Kingdoms period to 2.5–3% and the content of titanium from less
than 1% (generally 0.82–0.97%) to over 1%. Such body materials were
suitable for reducing flame firing. The resultant body color was gray, a
perfect foil to the glaze layer, which would look grayish blue with a quieter
tone. In comparison, porcelain clay used by Ou kilns contained more
alumina oxide and less iron oxide and titanium oxide, thus bringing about
different styles of the two kiln systems in terms of body texture and glaze
color.
   The creative use of engobe (porcelain clay with very low iron oxide) by
the Wuzhou kilns was an outstanding achievement. It made rough body
surfaces smooth and tidy and covered the dark color of the body, which in
one way created conditions for the use of relatively poor body materials and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
in another gave richer and softer shades to the glaze color, thus raising the
overall quality of the product. This innovative technology was subsequently
adopted in the celadon production of some Yue and Deqing kilns, and later
in the Southern Dynasties was successively adopted by some kilns of the
upper and middle reaches of the Yangtze River.

6.2.4.2 Constant Improvement and Innovation of Production
Technologies
Rapid development of the porcelain industry brought higher requirements to
the forming of wares. Porcelain craftsmen improved the wheel and adopted
many forming methods including jiggering, patching, kneading, openwork,
sticking and molding to make highly artistic works with complex shapes
and huge size differences between mouth, neck, and belly, such as jar with
piled sculptures, goat-shaped candleholder, eagle-shaped jar and lotus
zun.20
   Brown spots and brown painting were also innovative achievements in
this period. The use of brown spots added beauty to the monotonous glaze
of celadon and was one important decorative technique of the day.
Researchers used to believe that the technique was first invented and used
in the Yue kiln system in the late Western Jin and early Eastern Jin
dynasties, but new archaeological evidence shows that it had come into
being as early as the early Three Kingdoms. For example, a celadon bowl
unearthed in No. 6 Cliff Tomb of late Shu Han, one of the Three Kingdoms,
on Womadang Mountain in Tujing, Zhongxian County, Sichuan was
decorated with several sets of brown spots along the mouth rim, the
caramel-yellow glazed porcelain dish unearthed in the Maqiao Tomb in
Nanling County, Anhui had three groups of brown spots on the mouth rim,
and the small porcelain jar with bluish yellow glaze unearthed in the tomb
dated to Wu Tian’ce First Year (CE 275) in Lingjiao Mountain in
Shangfang, Jiangning, Jiangsu Province was decorated with a circle of
brown spots around the shoulder and the belly. Another example was the
lidded pot with plate-shaped mouth found in 1983 in the No. 5 Tomb from
the end of the Wu Kingdom to the beginning of the Western Jin Dynasty in
Changgang Village, Yuhuatai, Nanjing. With slightly grayish white body
and bluish yellow glaze, the pot was shaped elegantly like the pots with
plate-shaped mouths produced by the Wuzhou kilns. It was painted with
brown images all over. The lid, neck, shoulder and belly were respectively
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
painted with persimmon calyx, a human-headed bird-bodied creature (the
so-called “wansui”, literally “ten thousand years”), a magic herb, exotic
animals, and strange-looking deities as well as clouds, arcs, lotus petals and
other patterns in between. The shoulder was also stuck with Buddha
statuettes, rings with a beast-head base, conjoined twin birds and other
decorations. The patterns were full of mystery and were important
specimens for studying the early painting art of the Six Dynasties. The
brown coloring was painted on the grayish white body before the ware was
glazed. This pot was not only one of the earliest painted porcelain works in
China, but also an underglaze painted porcelain ware. It pushed the
commencement of underglaze painted porcelain production in China from
the previously held Tang Dynasty (porcelain of the Tongguan kilns in
Changsha) to the Three Kingdoms period or the early Jin Dynasty.

6.2.4.3 Improvements in Kilns, Kiln Tools and Laying and Firing
Technology
Dragon kilns had a long history in areas south of the Yangtze River. They
were used to fire pottery imprinted with geometric patterns, primitive
porcelain, etc. as early as the Shang and Zhou dynasties and started to be
used to fire porcelain in the Eastern Han Dynasty. But by the Three
Kingdoms period the structure of dragon kilns was still imperfect or
unsatisfactory. At that time, limited by the length of the fuel flame, the
utilization rate of waste heat was low and so many products were
insufficiently fired. Yet the problem was eventually solved by kiln workers
by perfecting the slope of the kiln, by adding firewood feeding holes at the
vault of the kiln to allow sectional firing, and by improving kiln tool design
and how greenware was laid in the kiln. Thanks to such improvements in
kiln design and firing skills, the reducing atmosphere was perfectly
controlled, producing sufficiently sintered porcelain that had a fine, hard
body, transparent glaze layer, and the lowest possible water absorption and
porosity rates.21

6.3 Black and White Porcelain of Wei, Jin and the
Southern and Northern Dynasties
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Though the Six Dynasties was dominated by blue glazed porcelain, black
glazed porcelain was also produced. The production of black glazed
porcelain can be traced back to the Han Dynasty. It was often fired in the
same kiln as blue glazed porcelain. As mentioned above, the coloring agent
of both black glazed and blue glazed porcelain was iron, the content of
which determined the depth of the glaze color. Once craftsmen grasped the
relationship between iron content and glaze color, they were able to prepare
glaze of different shades. That is why many celadon kilns also produced
black glazed porcelain. Yue kilns have long been famous for their celadon
products, yet Eastern Han kilns in modern-day Shangyu and Ningbo were
found to be firing black glazed porcelain at the same time. Black glazed
porcelain has also been unearthed in Han tombs in Hubei, Jiangsu and
Anhui. Those unearthed in the “Jianning Third Year”(CE 170) tombs in
Boxian County, Anhui Province proved black glazed porcelain commenced
firing in the middle and late Eastern Han Dynasty.
    Representative kilns producing black glazed porcelain among southern
kilns during the Six Dynasties were the Deqing kilns. Located in modern-
day northern Zhejiang, Deqing County is adjacent to Yuhang in the south
and Wuxing in the north with the Tianmu Mountains passing through. The
Dongming River flows through the county town from south to north and
then into Taihu Lake, offering convenient transportation. The Deqing
porcelain kiln system, never mentioned in ancient literature, was discovered
only after the 1950s and they are the earliest kilns found to produce black
porcelain. Ancient kiln sites found up to now are in four locations, Jiaoshan
in the eastern suburbs of the county town and Daijiashan, Chenshan and
Dingshan in the southwestern suburbs. The relics are rich and cover a wide
range.22 Two more porcelain kiln sites were found near Dalu Orchard of
Yuhang County in 1974. The varieties, style and age of the products are the
same as those of kiln sites around Deqing county town. The location of
Dalu Orchard is very close to the site of the famous Liangzhu Culture in the
late primitive society of China, which indicates that the area has a long
history of ceramic production.
   Deqing kilns produced both celadon and black porcelain, mainly blue
glazed porcelain decorated with brown spots and black glazed porcelain. In
1983, during a cultural ruins survey, the Deqing County Museum found kiln
sites from the Eastern Han Dynasty, the Three Kingdoms period, the Jin
Dynasty and the Sui and Tang dynasties in Qingshanwu of Erdu Township,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Huangjiaoshan, Shiliutou in Luoshe Township, Xiaomashan in the county
town, and elsewhere. The discovery of these kiln sites pushed the history of
the Deqing kilns further back to the Han Dynasty.
   The body of black porcelain produced by Deqing kilns was mostly brick
red, purple or light brown. The chemical composition of the body was very
similar to that of the purple porcelain body produced by Wuzhou kilns in
the Eastern Jin Dynasty. The body color might be the result of using red
clay as material or adding suitable amounts of zijin clay to the porcelain
clay. The main glaze coloring agent was iron oxide, the content of which
reached 8%, resulting in thin-walled black porcelain which was dark and
bright like lacquer.
  A group of black glazed porcelain wares, including rooster-head pots,
incense burners, spittoons, lamps, cases, small jars and eared cups with tray,
were unearthed from the Xingning Second Year (CE 364) tomb from the
Eastern Jin Dynasty in Laohe Mountain, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province in
1960. These were all typical black porcelain varieties at that time. (Fig.
6.16).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.16 Deqing kiln black glazed pot,
Eastern Jin Dynasty, height: 18 cm, top diam.: 8 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Deqing kiln products were dignified, simple and practical. For instance,
cases, jars and pots all had lids that tightly fitted the mouth of the wares,
making them more suitable for storing food. Teacups were coupled with
plate-shaped holders to form a new type of tea set that was elegant and
practical, setting a precedent for the popularity of cup holders in the Tang
and Song dynasties. The celadon boshan incense burner unearthed in the
outskirts of Zhenjiang City has a cover in the shape of three layers of peaks,
each layer composed of five well-arranged peaks which were clouded with
incense smoke when the burner was used. The design of the entire ware
ingeniously combined aesthetic value and practical requirement, making it
one of the finest celadon products of the Deqing kilns with a high artistic
level.23
    Just when black porcelain originated in northern China is not yet clear,
but it is credible that relatively mature black porcelain had appeared in the
Northern Qi Dynasty. The characteristics of northern black porcelain of the
period were epitomized by a black glazed four-lugged vat unearthed in Cui
Ang’s tomb of the Northern Qi Dynasty in Pingshan, Hebei Province. Its
shape was significantly different from that of Deqing kiln products. Shaped
like an inverted pear, the vat has a big mouth, no neck, a wide shoulder,
deep belly and flat bottom. The diameter is the greatest at the shoulder,
which has four lugs connecting to the mouth rim. From the lugs downward
the ware narrows in the shape of a reverse arc. The height is 14 cm and the
diameter of both the mouth and the bottom is 9.4 cm. The ware was fully
covered with a thick layer of black glaze on the outside. The upper part
where the glaze was thicker was dark brown and the glaze on the lower part
was lighter, appearing tea-brown. Strictly speaking it was not pure black.24
Nevertheless, the hard body texture and uniform, bright glaze color indicate
that the four-lugged vat had reached a fairly high technological level and
suggests that its appearance was preceded by and was the result of a period
of growth.
   While both celadon and black porcelain originated in the south, white
porcelain first appeared in the north and was a great achievement of
northern ceramic production and development. The emergence of white
porcelain was also a major event in the history of Chinese ceramics because
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
it provided conditions and a basis for the development of painted porcelain
during the later Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties.
   China’s early porcelains all belonged to the blue glaze system and white
glazed porcelains appeared several hundred years later. Academia is split on
this issue. One section argues that the creation of white porcelain had no
association with celadon and that the two were independent systems
developing in isolation from each other. The other argues that white
porcelain was invented based on celadon when craftsmen controlled the
iron content in body and glaze materials and overcame iron’s interference in
coloring. I believe both views make sense but neither of them is complete.
It is not beyond the realm of possibility that white porcelain and celadon
were two independently developing systems since the earliest white
porcelain we have discovered was in Fan Cui’s tomb dated to the Wuping
Sixth Year (CE 575) of the Northern Qi Dynasty in Anyang, Henan
Province. Areas of modern-day Henan were major production areas of
white pottery as early as the Xia and Shang dynasties. The chemical
composition of white pottery at that time was already close to that of
kaolinite with a low iron content and high aluminum content, the perfect
clay for firing white porcelain. Thus, there are historical causes and
geographical conditions that argue for white porcelain having originated not
in the south but in the north. Nevertheless, it is also incorrect to say that its
creation had nothing to do with celadon, for it would have been impossible
to successfully fire white porcelain without firstly mastering mature celadon
technologies.
   White porcelain in northern China in the Northern Dynasties was
characterized by carefully washed clay that was fine and white. No engobe
was used. The glaze layer was thin and bright. Glaze color was milky white
but still mostly with a tinge of blue, and thickly glazed parts looked
positively blue. One possible reason was that craftsmen at the time had not
mastered iron removal technology so that the porcelain clay they used still
contained some, albeit very little, iron, leading to the blue tone of the white
porcelain after firing. Another possible reason was that while craftsmen had
mastered iron removal technology, their kills were not advanced, resulting
in a less than perfect white glaze color. Unearthed white porcelain varieties
from the time were mostly daily use utensils, such as bowls, cups, three-
lugged vats, four-lugged vats and long-necked bottles (Fig. 6.17). The shape
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
design was basically the same as the celadon of the Northern Dynasties and
the decorative patterns were mainly lotus petals. (Fig. 6.18).





Fig. 6.17 White porcelain long-necked bottle with green coloring,
Wuping Sixth Year of the Northern Qi Dynasty, height: 22.5 cm, top diam.: 7 cm, in the Henan
Museum
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.18 White porcelain lotus pattern jar,
Wuping Sixth Year of the Northern Qi Dynasty, height: 19 cm, top diam.: 7.5 cm, in the Henan
Museum

    Successful firing of white porcelain in the Northern Dynasties prepared
the ground for the emergence of polychrome porcelains later, pioneered the
Xing kilns in the Tang Dynasty and Ding kilns in the Song Dynasty, and
betokened the Tang and Song ceramic production map of “southern celadon
and northern white”.

6.4 Pottery Vessels, Burial Pottery, and
Architectural Pottery of Wei, Jin and Southern
and Northern Dynasties
6.4.1 Pottery Vessels
Gray pottery was still the main type of pottery in this period, though in fact
almost all daily use vessels had been replaced by porcelain. Gray pottery
during this period was low fired and of poor quality. But there were new
changes in shape design. For instance, new varieties such as plate-mouthed
pots, double-eared vats, four-lugged vats and fruit boxes were all created
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
thanks to the influence of the southern celadon design. Imprinted hard
pottery also declined due to the mass production of blue glazed porcelain.
  A relatively more successful pottery type in this period was still the
low-fired lead-glazed pottery which once flourished in the Han Dynasty and
then hit a low point in the Three Kingdoms and two Jin dynasties. After the
founding of the Northern Wei regime, ceramics production in northern
China entered a period of revival and low-fired lead-glazed pottery rose
again and was used in court buildings. An improvement based on the Han
Dynasty’s tradition, it was used in increasingly wider areas and took on a
new appearance as varieties, designs, and colors increased and glaze
became brighter. Glazing became more colorful. Some vessels had green
coloring applied on a yellow backdrop and some used red, yellow and
brown together, evolving from the single-color glaze of the Han Dynasty to
a multicolor glaze and laying the foundation for the transition to the tricolor
pottery of the Tang Dynasty.

6.4.2 Burial Pottery
Although daily use pottery vessels were gradually replaced by the
increasingly popular porcelain, pottery remained important and made some
achievements as burial objects, figurines and architectural material. As the
funerary customs of the time basically inherited the tradition of the Han
Dynasty, burial objects were still mainly various utensils, sculptures and
models. Utensils decreased in number and common varieties included jars,
plates, bowls, vats and eared cups. Sculptures and models found in tombs of
the Wu Kingdom and the Western Jin Dynasty were dominated by grain
processing tools, daily life utensils and various poultry and livestock. These
models mostly had a red body covered by an extremely thin layer of
brownish yellow glaze. After the Eastern Jin Dynasty, these burial models
were gradually replaced by others, chiefly horses and chariots.
   The most common burial objects in tombs of the Wu Kingdom and the
Western Jin Dynasty included mortars, pestles, mills, winnowing pans,
sieves, brooms, wells, stoves (Fig. 6.19), barrels, and vats, as well as dogs,
horses, sheep, pigs, cattle, chickens and ducks. Areas south of the Yangtze
River also yielded pottery jars with piled sculptures of human figures and
pavilions, whose style was basically the same as the celadon granary urns.
On the jars there are two-story pavilions, around the foot of which are
molded statues and on the roof of which are groups of birds and sparrows.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Some of these jars are also decorated with turtles, fish, snakes, dogs and
other land and water animals on the belly. Pottery jars and porcelain bottles
of a form known as “soul jars” were popular among common folks for a
long time and remained prevalent till the Yuan Dynasty. For instance, Fig.
6.20 shows a green glazed soul jar from the Western Jin Dynasty which I
viewed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S. The jar’s style was
from areas south of the Yangtze River, mainly in northern Zhejiang and
southern Jiangsu. The style was popular from CE 250 to 300. The green
glazed porcelain ware was a perfect example of the rich themes of
sculptured models and the imagery of multi-story buildings which was
commonly used on such jars. Particularly interesting was the row of
Buddhas meditating on lion seats and lotus petals, which was the earliest
known Buddhist images on pottery in China.





Fig. 6.19 Blue glazed stove,
Western Jin Dynasty, length: 23.2 cm, base width: 14 cm, height: 12 cm, in the Palace Museum
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.20 Green glazed soul jar,
Western Jin Dynasty, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

    Pottery figurines as burial objects in this period were not as developed
as those in the Han Dynasty, especially in the south. As the popular custom
in the south was to bury blue glazed porcelain with the dead, pottery
figurine production did not occupy an important position. Nevertheless,
there were pottery figurines of warriors, people carrying various objects,
people kneeling, people horse-riding, sitting figures and writing figures in
this period. But most of these figurines were stiff and lacking in expression.
They were hand-made or molded, with few fine works of high
craftsmanship. The Wei, Jin and Southern & Northern Dynasties was a
period of ethnic integration in China and the cohabitation of different
ethnicities was reflected in the different characteristics of the dress and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
adornment of pottery figurines unearthed from the period. For example, the
female servant figurines of the Southern & Northern Dynasties unearthed in
Nanjing in 1957 wore a fan-shaped headscarf, a half-moon-shaped hair
dress on the forehead, a round collar undergarment, and a long sleeve outer
garment. Such costumes and adornment were totally different from those of
female servant figurines of the Northern Dynasties. Warrior figurines of the
two Jin dynasties unearthed in tombs in Luoyang and Zhengzhou do not
resemble the appearance of Han people with deep eye sockets and high
noses. Their prototypes were probably minority ethnicities which the ruling
class hired from the northwest as armed force subordinates at the time. (Fig.
6.21) The production level of pottery figurines in northern China was also
low during this period.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 6.21 Painted figurine of horse-riding warrior sounding trumpet,
Northern Wei Dynasty, height: 39 cm, in the Shaanxi History Museum

    After the Northern Dynasties, as Buddhism was introduced into the
central plains, Buddhist grotto statue building prevailed in the north, which
led to continued progress of the pottery sculpture art. Pottery sculptures at
that time, human figures and animals alike, jettisoned the previous clumsy
and rigid style and absorbed the features of Buddhist art on the basis of
inheriting the tradition of the Han Dynasty. For human figurines, attention
was given to the depiction of facial expressions and the manners were more
varied and vivid than before. There were civil officials wearing hats, long
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
robes and belts, standing with two hands folded in front, drooping down, or
pressing their swords. There were also Xianbei servant figurines with deep
eye sockets and high noses, wearing round hats and wide sleeved overalls,
and with hands folded in front of their chests. Meanwhile, the most
characteristic were the warrior figurines which were armored all over and
stood with the left hand against the sword and the right hand carrying
another weapon. With eyes staring and chests protruding, they struck quite a
fierce image. Such warriors are quite common in tombs from the Northern
Wei to the Northern Qi, indicating that they were popular burial objects at
the time. Their design and costumes were mostly the same. During this
period there also appeared armored cavalryman figurines. The cavalrymen
and horses, both covered in armor, are ranked in gallant formations. Not
seen previously in the Han Dynasty or earlier, the cavalryman figurines
symbolized the powerful cavalries of ethnic minorities such as the Xianbei,
who were newly developed yet the primary military forces of the Northern
Dynasties and also among the strongest forces at the time. Thus, wealthy
and influential nobles often buried such figurines in tombs to show their
prestige and power. In addition, there were also large numbers of figurines
depicting slaves and servants, including male servants, female servants,
musicians and dancers, and honor guards displaying all sorts of postures,
carrying tools, squatting, sitting, kneeling, playing music, leading horses, or
standing respectfully with hands drooping. The figurines vividly reflected
the social lives of the different classes of the day.
   Besides human figurines, animal figurines at this time also had
distinctive characteristics. Animal figurines that did not exist or were
previously rare appeared, notably camels, which became popular during this
period. As camels were from outside the Great Wall and were not
commonly seen in the central plains, the appearance of these figurines in
tombs proved there were extensive cultural exchanges among different
ethnicities at the time. (Fig. 6.22) Pottery figurines of tomb-guarding beasts
were also popular, but the design differed from north to south. Beasts of the
Northern Dynasties were like dogs but also resembled oxen, with three tufts
of horn-shaped manes standing on the neck. These “mythical dogs” were
supposed to be able to expel evil spirits (Fig. 6.23). The tomb-guarding
beasts popular in the Southern Dynasties, called “Qiongqi”, looked more
like rhinoceros with a single horn on the head and four standing bunches of
horn-shaped bristles on the back. These beasts had their heads turned to the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
tomb gate as if guarding. The Qiongqi unearthed in the Southern-dynasties
tomb in Shashishan, Nanjing in 1955 was just like this.25 Pottery horses
(Fig. 6.24) and pottery cattle were also very characteristic animal figurines
of the time. Their common features were strong legs, tight muscles and lean
athletic bodies. Especially so were the pottery oxen, whose two forward-
pointing horns were exaggerated and full of power. These oxen figures had
gorgeous decorations on the body and head and were brightly painted.
Vividly depicting the look and spirit of the animals, the figurines were of
high artistic value. In addition, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the
United States displays a pair of seated eagle tamer figurines, which
demonstrates the ecological relationship between humans and animals at the
time. The apparently northern ethnic style dress of the eagle tamer reflects
the multiethnic cohabitation of the day. (Figs. 6.25, 6.26).
