   Some pottery figurines during this period were gray pottery with color
painting and some were low-fired pottery covered by green or yellow lead
glaze. Few were single-colored. Nevertheless, as color paint often fell off
with the passage of time, for some of these figurines only the colorless body
remains with no trace of the original painting at all. The thin, bony and
plain characteristics of this period’s sculpture was also reflected in pottery
figurines.

6.4.3 Architectural Pottery
The development of the pottery industry during the Six Dynasties occurred
not only in daily use and burial pottery, but also in architectural pottery. As
the economy grew, the architectural pottery industry developed rapidly,
with output expanded and quality improved.
   Bricks and tiles reduced in size. The large hollow bricks which
prevailed during the Han Dynasty were in gradual decline while regular
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
rectangular bricks, mostly 35 cm long, 17 cm wide and five cm thick,
became common. These bricks were often imprinted with line patterns on
the front surface and sloping line patterns, rhombus patterns and
inscriptions indicating the year of manufacture on the long side surface.
Bricks from the Southern Dynasties were imprinted on the front surface
with images of female servants, warriors, honeysuckle and lotus flowers, or
characters such as “千秋” (1,000 Autumns) and “万岁” (10,000 Years). The short
side surfaces of a number of bricks were also imprinted so that together
they formed patterns of honeysuckle and lotus flowers or a myriad pictures
of flying fairies, phoenixes, the Azure Dragon, the White Tiger, the Black
Turtle, flying horses, lions, the Four Recluse Scholars of Shangshan
Mountain, noble women traveling, music bands, oxen plowing, Buddha
statues, traveling carriages and horses, and winged immortals sporting with
tigers. The relief-murals on the bricks of the great Southern-dynasties tombs
discovered in Nanjing and Danyang, titled “Seven Sages of the Bamboo
Grove and Rong Qiqi” are composed of hundreds of bricks. The portraits
were magnificent with extraordinary momentum. Some had title
inscriptions on the corner. Tomb bricks of the Western Jin Dynasty
unearthed in Guangzhou were inscribed with verse describing the social
landscape of the late Western Jin, that is, wars in the central plains and
relative peace and stability in the south. Such verse is valuable material for
historical studies. Another type of architectural pottery of the period was
eave tiles, which were mostly round, about 15 cm in diameter and hard in
texture. Before the Southern Dynasties, decorations on these tiles were
dominated by cloud patterns, a custom left by the Han Dynasty, and by the
Southern Dynasties lotus patterns became widely popular as a result of the
extensive and profound influence of Buddhism. The beast face pattern was
also a major feature of eave tiles in this period.26

6.5 Appearance of Porcelain Burial Objects
During the Six Dynasties, besides pottery, there also appeared various kinds
of porcelain sculptures of animals and persons as funerary objects. The
porcelain plastic art of the Six Dynasties was developed based on the
prosperity of the pottery sculpture of the Qin and Han dynasties. Porcelain
craftsmen used porcelain clay instead of common clay as the raw material
and molded it into certain human or animal shapes using various techniques
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
such as sculpting, kneading, open-work, carving, scratching and stacking.
Then the sculptures were glazed and placed into kilns for firing.
Archaeological excavations since the founding of New China have found
the largest number of celadon sculptures from the Western Jin Dynasty.27
   As the economy developed and porcelain firing technology improved,
the use of porcelain gradually penetrated all aspects of people’s daily lives.
The increasing demand for porcelain year on year can be seen from the
continuous expansion of kilns in various places. In addition, porcelain
products accounted for a large proportion of burial objects unearthed from
tombs of this period around the country. For example, from the three large
tombs of the Fu family of the Western Jin on Shizi Mountain, Wuxian
County, as many as 46 celadon wares were unearthed even though one of
the tombs had been robbed and one had been seriously damaged. These
wares included funerary granary urns, flat pots, baskets, incense burners, ge
(compartmentalized boxes for assorted fruits/desserts), water pots, washers,
spittoons, urns, and tiger-shaped chamber pots. They were all Yue kiln
products. Most of the Six Dynasties celadon unearthed in Jiangsu was from
tombs. Incomplete statistics show that since the founding of New China
more than 1,000 tombs from the Six Dynasties have been excavated and the
number of celadon items unearthed is in the tens of thousands.28
    Porcelain burial objects were popular from the late Eastern Han
Dynasty to the Western Jin Dynasty. They were mainly five-linked jars,
stoves, and wells in the late Eastern Han Dynasty, and jars with piled
sculptures, stoves and wells in the early Wu Kingdom of the Three
Kingdoms. After the Fenghuang First Year of the Wu Kingdom (CE 272)
chicken cages and pigsties began to appear. After the Taikang Ninth Year
(CE 288) there were dogs, sheep, goose pens, mills and buckets, and by the
Yongning Second Year (CE 302) there emerged human and animal
figurines. Then by the Eastern Jin Dynasty, objects specially made for
burial purposes disappeared.
    Jars with piled sculptures were a typical example of the evolution of
burial objects. Initially in the form of five-tube bottles in the Eastern Han,
they evolved into five-linked jars by the Xiping Fourth Year (CE 175), and
then into jars with piled sculptures by the Taiping Second Year of the Wu
Kingdom (CE 257). By the Western Jin, the five tubes on these jars had
been replaced by buildings, towers, and pavilions and the bellies were
decorated with sculptures of human figures, flying beasts and Buddha
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
statues. Inscriptions started appearing on the jars in the Yong’an Third Year
of the Wu Kingdom (CE 260) and became widely popular in the Western
Jin.29 After the Yongjia Seventh Year of the Western Jin (CE 313) these jars
with piled sculptures disappeared.
   These jars with piled sculptures, also known as funerary granary urns or
“soul jars”, namely, vessels or habitats for the soul of the deceased, were a
kind of burial object that was very characteristic of the time and one that
represented the Chinese view of the universe and of life and death. Popular
from the late Wu Kingdom of the Three Kingdoms to the Western Jin
Dynasty, they were found mainly in Zhejiang and Jiangsu provinces in the
lower reaches of the Yangtze River, and were also occasionally unearthed in
tombs from that time in Anhui and Jiangxi provinces. They were mostly
celadon. They evolved from the five-linked jars of the Han Dynasty. “Five-
linked jars are so called because of the additional four pot-shaped jars
attached to the mouth and shoulder of the larger jar. The four additional jars
were relatively small and were not connected to the belly of the main jar.
The shoulder and upper belly of the vessel were stacked with sculptures of
monkeys and insects. Such five-linked jars developed into funerary granary
urns during the Eastern Wu and Western Jin dynasties30.
   The design of the five-linked jars of the Han Dynasty and the celadon
funerary granary urns of the Wu Kingdom and Jin Dynasty exhibited
obvious influences of the philosophy of yin and yang and the Five
Elements. Craftsmen modeled a new world dedicated to the habitation of
the dead, one that is different from the real world, by organically combining
the five-linked jars with the five elements of Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and
Water. The entire vessel was a harmonious whole. Not only is the shape of
the four small jars very similar to that of the main jar, even the upper and
lower parts of the vessel are quite similar. The peculiar design of five linked
jars containing each other implies the simple natural philosophy of “the Tao
begets the One, the One begets two, two begets three, and three begets the
myriad things”. It seems to imply that all things in the world were born
from these storage jars. These five-linked jars or granary urns seem to
encompass the huge and dazzling world, including all the lands, all four
seasons and all five elements, into one inconspicuous vessel.
   Compared to the five-linked jars of the Han Dynasty, the celadon
granary urns of the Wu Kingdom and Jin Dynasty were much taller and
larger, mostly over 40 cm tall with some reaching 60 cm. The large vessels
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
with layer upon layer of decorations are suggestive of steps that sorcerers
take to reach the top to communicate with Heaven and Earth. In the
prehistoric primitive culture of China, sorcerers sought communication
between Heaven, Earth, man and deities with the help of mountains, divine
trees, birds, jade, etc. For example, the tall bronze divine trees and deity
statues unearthed from the Sanxingdui Culture sacrificial pit in Guanghan,
Sichuan undoubtedly have sorcery connotations. Similarly, the celadon
granary urns, purposely made to be buried with the dead, embodied
primitive witchcraft ideas about and desire for communicating with Heaven
and Earth, were closely associated with people’s views on life, death and
the soul at the time, and could not be separated from the influence of
witchcraft traditions in their place of origin, that is, the Wu Yue area. Of the
“nine strategies to conquer the Wu State” suggested to King Goujian of the
Yue State by his advisor Wen Zhong, the first was “respecting Heaven and
Earth, sacrificing to ghosts and gods”. Such a practice of regarding
witchcraft activities as fundamental to the founding of a regime indicates
there were deep-rooted and indelible primitive witchcraft traditions in Wu
Yue folk culture.31
     It was not random that the celadon granary urns of the Wu Kingdom
and Jin Dynasty took the shape of a jar. It was an intentional choice of the
craftsmen. Jars were the most commonly used vessels for storing grains,
seeds, wine, water, and other daily necessities in ancient China and played
an immeasurable role in the ancient agricultural economy. Jars could be
regarded as a symbol of a granary for all grains32, and the granary
represented having ample food and clothing.
   Important decorative themes of these funerary granary urns included
traditional auspicious imageries such as the qilin (also known as the
Chinese unicorn, a mythical beast that symbolizes good luck and
prosperity), the lingzhi mushroom, and the divine ding, celestial phenomena
such the sun, moon, stars, and clouds, as well as the four mythological
creatures symbolizing constellations in four directions, that is, the Azure
Dragon, the White Tiger, the Vermilion Bird, and the Black Turtle. In
addition, the architectures sculpted on the urns, including double eave
pavilions, entrance buildings, corridors and watchtowers, were drawn from
the manors or castles of powerful landlords. Figurines of northern ethnic
minority performers dancing and playing music and of groups of honor
guards described the pleasure-seeking life of manor owners. The blue-
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
glazed funerary granary urn with piled sculptures collected by the Cixi
Museum of Zhejiang Province in 1979 was decorated with the image of a
hunter running with a spear, a typical scene of the manor economy known
for its fishing and hunting. Some urns were decorated with sculptures of
relatives and children of the deceased in mourning dress keeping vigil
beside the coffin to promote the Confucian concepts of loyalty and filial
piety. Some were decorated with images of Buddhas and monks, immortals
riding dragons and phoenixes, deities with human heads and bird bodies,
etc., which depicted a fairyland different from the real world, though it is
difficult to attribute these images to a specific myth. Buddha statues were
particularly common. In the minds of people at the time, Buddhas were
mythological entities as miraculous as Taoist immortals. The colorful birds
and qilin, and the Vermilion Bird and the Azure Dragon obviously
symbolized celestial phenomena and expressed the wish for the soul of the
deceased to ascend to Heaven. Clear traces of the common subject matter of
murals and picture bricks of the Han Dynasty can be found in the decorative
imageries of the celadon granary urns of the Wu Kingdom and Jin Dynasty;
it is only that the form of artistic expression of the two was different.
   The murals and picture bricks in tomb chambers of the Han Dynasty
used painting and carving, both two-dimensional artistic techniques, to
describe the brilliant life of the deceased and the wish for them to have a
good afterlife, while the celadon funerary granary urns of the Wu Kingdom
and Jin Dynasty used advanced porcelain technology in southern China and
the artistic approach of three-dimensional sculpting to meet the needs of
elaborate funerals that had been widely popular since the Han Dynasty. As
described by the Chinese characters often inscribed on tortoise-mounted
stelae on these urns, the wish was for an elaborate funeral to benefit future
generations of the family.
    In a word, the granary urns of the Wu Kingdom and Jin Dynasty were
typical funerary art works and indicated the continuation and development
of the Han Dynasty’s elaborate funeral custom in the Wu and Jin periods.
Creatively applying the advanced ceramic technologies at that time,
southern ceramics craftsmen portrayed burial themes previously painted
and carved on murals and picture bricks on tomb walls in the Han Dynasty
in a three-dimensional manner by molding similar artistic images onto
granary jars with special shapes and meanings. Such ingenuity in terms of
artistic creation also adapted to the environmental condition that it was
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
difficult to decorate tombs in southern China with murals due to the
abundant groundwater there. Thus, it is easy to understand why celadon
granary urns during the Wu and Jin periods were popular only in Jiangsu
and Zhejiang in the south.33

6.6 Export Porcelain Following the Han and Jin
Dynasties
China was never a closed country developing in isolation from the outside
world. In fact, her contacts with overseas regions started very early in
ancient times. Although the term “globalization” did not appear until
modern times, globalization started earlier than commonly believed. It is
only that in ancient times the process was slow and did not attract much
attention. If we look closely at history, we will find that the area of present-
day Ningbo on the southeastern coast of China had developed a maritime
transport capacity a long time ago. The six oars, pottery boats and the bones
of some giant whales and sharks unearthed at the Hemudu site in Yuyao
from 7,000 years ago indicate that ancestors living there in the Neolithic
could already manufacture boats and use them for fishing and other
production activities at sea. We may therefore speculate that contacts
between Ningbo and overseas areas may have started very early, which is
also supported by the obvious similarities of the imprinted pottery and
stepped adzes across different areas along the southeastern coast in the pre-
Qin period. The stepped adze is especially strong evidence. Research shows
that it was a widely distributed canoe making tool, having been found in
Taiwan Province, the Philippines, North Borneo, Sulawesi Island in
Indonesia, the Polynesian Islands in the Pacific Ocean and other places.
“This implies a trade relationship between canoeing ancestors of the Wu
Yue area and distant islands”.34
   China’s social development history must be studied and examined in the
context of globalization and against a larger picture where frequent cultural
exchanges and interactions take place. The study of China’s ceramics
history is especially so, for ceramics was not only an industry, but also a
cultural and economic exchange activity. China was the first country to
invent porcelain in the world. The celadon of the Yue kilns matured in the
Eastern Han Dynasty and became important daily life utensils in the Wei,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Jin and Southern & Northern Dynasties. It is therefore plausible that its use
might not have been confined to China and must have also drawn the
attention of faraway overseas markets.
   China established a Maritime Ceramics Road to export goods, mainly
ceramics, back in the Han Dynasty. According to the Treatise on
Geography in the Book of Han, “About five months of sea travel takes
people to the Kingdom of Duyuan (northeastern Sumatra or the southern
Malay Peninsula). After another four months’ travel one arrives at the
Kingdom of Yilumo (near Pegu, Myanmar). Another 20 days’ sea travel
takes you to the Kingdom of Shenli (by the Irrawaddy River, Myanmar).
Then after traveling on foot for over 10 days, one arrives at the Kingdom of
Fugandulu (near modern-day Prome in the middle reaches of the Irrawaddy
River, Myanmar). Two months’ sea travel from the Kingdom of Fugandulu
takes people to the Kingdom of Huangzhi (near Conjevaram in southwest
Madras, India) … South of the Kingdom of Huangzhi there is the Kingdom
of Yichengbu (Sri Lanka)”. This record shows that the official maritime
transport and trade of the Western Han Dynasty reached modern-day south
India and Sri Lanka. In fact, the West Asia style silver box unearthed from
the tomb of Zhao Mo, Emperor Wendi of Southern Yue, in Guangzhou
indicates that this overseas transportation route was opened up long before
Emperor Wu of Han conquered the Southern Yue (111 BCE) and had
already reached the coastal countries of West Asia. By the Eastern Han
Dynasty this route had reached the Eastern Roman Empire (Daqin).35 The
most important two ports of the Maritime Ceramics Road at that time were
respectively near modern-day Ningbo in Zhejiang Province and along the
coast of modern-day Guangdong Province.
   During the Han and Jin dynasties, as society progressed and
productivity grew, the shipbuilding industry in the Ningbo area became
more developed, the navigation ability improved, and activities at sea
became more frequent. Archaeological excavations in today’s Ningbo area
have found that during the Han and Jin dynasties there were already many
overseas commodities as well as traces of foreigner activity in Ningbo,
indicating that Maritime Silk Road activities and non-governmental
exchanges of commercial goods in Ningbo had already started at that
time.36 Though there is yet no precise data to prove the overseas sales sites
of Yue kiln celadon at that time, signs of foreign cultural exchange can be
seen on the celadon unearthed. One example is that some celadon incense
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
burners locally produced in today’s Ningshao area used incense from
overseas, such as the Yue celadon incense burners unearthed from the Han
Xiping Fourth Year (CE 175) tomb found in Baidu Village, Fenghua in
1978, from the Western Jin Yongjia Seventh Year tomb found in Fenghuang
Mountain in Shangjiang Village, Shaoxing, and from Jin dynasty tombs in
Yuyao, Cixi, and others. Literature of the Han Dynasty also mentioned
foreign fragrances like storax. Figurines of Western people dancing,
juggling or playing music are often seen on Yue kiln celadon five-linked
jars and jars with piled sculptures of the Han Dynasty, the Three Kingdoms
period or the Western Jin Dynasty unearthed in today’s Ningbo City and
nearby Yinxian, Fenghua, Yuyao, Cixi and other places.37 Modern day
Yuyao and Cixi were the earliest porcelain producing sites in China and
were adjacent to Ningbo, making it convenient for them to communicate
with overseas countries.
   Apart from Ningbo, Guangdong, situated on the South China Sea, has
also been a major transportation hub connecting China to the outside world
since ancient times. The route that begins at the Pearl River estuary leading
westward to reach Southeast Asia and South Asia was the oldest South
China Sea route. It was opened back in the pre-Qin period. The late Han
Dynasty or the Three Kingdoms period to the Southern & Northern
Dynasties saw initial development of the Maritime Silk Road on the South
China Sea. Due to war and turbulence in the central plains at the time, the
land Silk Road to the northwest was blocked, while the relative stability in
areas south of the Five Ridges (roughly present-day Guangdong and
Guangxi) added prominence to the important position of Guangzhou as the
central base of the Silk Road on the South China Sea and a port for foreign
trade.38 The main commodities for foreign trade at that time were silk and
ceramics. The production of ceramics for export was closely related to, and
mutually promoted the development of overseas transport and trade.
   Before the Qin unified areas south of the Five Ridges, the area roughly
corresponding to modern-day Guangdong was called Nanyue. The Jin
Dynasty scholar Zhang Hua states in his Bowuzhi (“Records of Diverse
Matters”): “The country of Nanyue is adjacent to the Chu State and
extended from the Five Ridges to the South Sea”. It was Nanyue that first
developed maritime traffic on the South China Sea. During the reign of
Emperor Wu of Han, envoys were sent from Panyu to Xuwen, and then
from Xuwen they travelled through some countries in Southeast Asia to
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
reach southern India and returned from there. The exploration and gradual
development of this route promoted the earliest cultural exchange and
export of ceramics. In the Han Dynasty glazed pottery and primitive
celadon were produced on a large scale in Guangdong and became funerary
objects that were commonly buried in tombs around the country. More and
more glazed pottery from the Han Dynasty has been found in Southeast
Asia today, as recorded by Han Huaizhun in his Chinese Export Porcelain
Left in Southeast Asia. In the Eastern Jin Dynasty people had grasped the
law of the trade winds and were able to use the winds in navigation to cross
oceans. During the Southern Dynasties, sea routes along the eastern coast of
Hainan Island and along the Xisha Islands were opened, which has been
proven by the blue glazed pottery jars and celadon cups from the Southern
Dynasties discovered by archaeologists.39 Archaeological data and ceramics
unearthed from tombs show that large quantities of celadon were fired in
Guangdong from the Jin Dynasty to the Tang Dynasty. In 1960
archaeologists from the Guangdong Museum unearthed an Eastern Jin
celadon rooster-head pot from Tomb No. 1 at Piyunlou in Gaoyao County,
Guangdong Province. The pot was produced by a Guangdong kiln. It has a
plate-shaped mouth, long neck, lightly flat round belly, flat bottom, a pair of
symmetrical bridge-shaped ears on the shoulder, a rooster-head-shaped
spout at the front, and a round holder at the back. It had bright, clear glaze
fully applied that was blue with a tinge of yellow. The glaze, with glass-like
texture and fine crackles, was akin to the Jin dynasty celadon produced in
Zhejiang.40
   Not much information has been uncovered to date of the export of
ceramics to Southeast Asia in this period and only a few discoveries have
been made. It is the same with ceramics exports to the neighboring Japan in
the east—the only known ware from this period unearthed in Japan so far
was the Eastern Jin Celadon Rooster Pot held by the Tokyo National
Museum. But the number of Six Dynasties celadon wares unearthed in
South Korea is quite considerable. An exhibition of Chinese ceramics
unearthed in South Korea staged by the Daegu National Museum in 2004
displayed the following Chinese celadon from the Six Dynasties: tiger-
shaped chamber pots, rooster pots, goat-shaped zun, plate-mouthed pots,
inkstones, four-eared pots, six-eared pots, lotus pattern bowls, bowls, small
cups and bottles. Also exhibited were black-glazed porcelain rooster pots,
jars, four-eared bottles, and more from the same period. Discovery sites as
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
shown on the exhibition signs included Cheongju, Gaeseong, Wonju,
Cheonan, Pocheon, Gongju (Tomb of King Muryeong), Busan, Iksan, and
Gyeongju (the Royal Tombs Complex). Thus, South Korea is so far known
to be the country where the largest number of Six Dynasties porcelain has
been unearthed abroad and in the largest number of sites. The celadon
exhibited had clear, pure and lustrous glaze that was bluish gray and
subdued in color, making them quite similar to Yue kiln products, while the
black glazed porcelain exhibited were probably products of Deqing kilns.41
These products might have been transported to South Korea via the
Maritime Ceramics Road at the time.
   Besides sea routes, land transportation was also quite developed from
the Han Dynasty to the Wei, Jin and Southern & Northern Dynasties. After
Zhang Qian’s two missions to the Western Regions in the second century
BCE, Chinese silk started to be continuously exported via the overland road
connecting China and the West. The 7,000-km-long Silk Road comprised
two routes. The southern route started from Chang’an, passed through
Dunhuang, Loulan, Yutian, Shache, etc., transversed the Pamirs to reach the
Great Yuezhi (in present-day Afghanistan) and Anxi (present-day Iran), and
then led further westward to reach Tiaozhi (present-day Iraq or Arabia) and
Daqin (the Roman Empire). The northern route started from Chang’an,
passed through Dunhuang, capital of the Cheshiqian Kingdom (present-day
Turpan), Qiuci (present-day Kuqa), Shule (present-day Kashgar), etc., then
travelled over the Pamirs to reach Dayuan (present-day Fergana) and
Kangju (present-day Samarqand), and thence further southwest to pass
through Anxi and reach Daqin.42
   The Silk Road did not only transport and sell silk. Ceramics were also
among its major export products. Some Yue kiln products and many
products of other kilns were exported via this overland road.
   As the most advanced daily utensil material at the time, porcelain
immediately won the favor of domestic and foreign markets upon its
maturity. For the subsequent two thousand years, China has always been the
most important country exporting ceramic products and technologies to the
world.
   Through an examination of the history of ceramics we can see that the
globalization of China began from economic exchanges and trade, and
ceramics were a most important component of ancient China’s foreign
economic exchange and trade. Studying the export and sale of Chinese
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
ceramics can help understand the formation of Chinese culture, which is not
only the result of the integration of multiple ethnicities within China as one
national state, but also the fruit of interactions with diverse world cultures.

6.7 Conclusion
Over the 369 years from the Three Kingdoms in the late Han Dynasty to the
end of the Southern & Northern Dynasties, the aesthetic style of Chinese
ceramics took a major turn. The change was in one way due to the
maturation of porcelain-making technologies. In other words, new materials
and new techniques called for new modeling and decorative skills. In
another sense the change was caused by the change in the aesthetic trends
of the time, which was in turn brought about by the change in philosophical
ideas and the introduction of foreign nationalities and religions.
   At the end of the Eastern Han Dynasty, China had, for all practical
purposes, lost control over its unification and the country was thrown into
division. Long-term war made people’s lives miserable. Suffering real pain,
people had no choice but to place hope in the next life, which offered great
potential for the newly introduced Buddhism to take root in common
people’s lives. The misery of real life also inspired much philosophical
questioning by scholars of the future of the world and an ultimate concern
for life. Such questioning shook the fundamental position of Confucianism
as the orthodox ideology. As Confucian doctrines such as centralized
unification and strict hierarchy of monarchs and subjects began to be
questioned, Taoist beliefs gained more ground. During the Wei and Jin
dynasties, the Laozi, Zhuangzi, and Zhouyi were collectively known as the
“Three Abstruse (Texts)”(the three Xuan), and literati and scholars studying
them were called metaphysicians (Xuan scholars). These metaphysicians
were also interested in Buddhism, and gradually, by combining the best
parts of Taoist philosophy and Buddhism, gave birth to the Chan sect of
Chinese Buddhism.
   These explorations and discussions made this period an era of
philosophical emancipation, active thinking, question raising and fruitful
outcomes. It was the second climax of ideological and cultural collision and
exchange in Chinese history after the pre-Qin period. Though it was no
match for the pre-Qin period in terms of duration, breadth, scale and
number of schools in the discussions, the purity and depth of the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
philosophical thinking at the time was unprecedented. It was such thought-
centered, rational, and “pure” philosophy that gave birth to a kind of “pure”
literature and art whose sole purpose was to express feelings. Such “pure”
philosophy and “pure” art brought about a leap in the history of Chinese
aesthetic thought and had a major impact on the Chinese philosophy, poetry
and painting that followed. This impact can also be seen on the
development of ceramic art, especially porcelain.
   At this time there emerged many spiritual gatherings for discussion and
exchange. At such gatherings, what people deemed fashionable was not
wine, but tea, for tea not only quenched the thirst and refreshed the mind,
but also, compared with wine, was a type of drink that was less worldly and
offered more subtle flavors for the palate. Compared with the flamboyant
gold, silver or lacquer wares, porcelain, with its jade-like clarity, elegance
and gentility, made much better vessels for tea. Therefore, with the
prevalence of tea drinking, tea sets made of porcelain also became popular.
    Literati and scholars at the time often aspired to reach a realm of
ultimate emptiness and silence. To do this, they had to clean themselves of
all impurities, get rid of all worldly ideas and enter a state of
unconsciousness and extreme oblivion. This seemingly unconscious and
emotionless state was in fact the clearest, the most thorough and the most
encompassing consciousness. This mental state was also a pure aesthetic
state. In this state of mind and aesthetics Buddhist monks and Taoist literati
meditated, burned incense, tasted tea and held casual chats. On these
occasions the tea sets, flower arrangement vessels and other ornaments they
used naturally had to be in harmony with the particular atmosphere, and
celadon, with its quiet color and jade-like warmth, mellowness and
translucence, met this aesthetic requirement perfectly. Such an aesthetic
demand was also why porcelain production at the time was dominated by
celadon even though black and white porcelain was also fired. As blue and
green were cold colors considered to be quiet, mysterious, and profound,
celadon won the favor of the literati and became important objects of
handling, appreciation and use by upper class scholars and nobles. As a
result, porcelain became the daily necessities of not only ordinary people
but also nobles and scholars. Porcelain art no longer pursued gorgeous and
complicated decorations because what people sought was the beauty of the
glaze color and texture itself instead of the beauty of surface paintings or
images. This pursuit was the pursuit of nature over appearance, a pursuit
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
that was closer to the aesthetic aspiration of Taoism and Chan Buddhism.
This pursuit continued to the Song Dynasty and exalted the texture and
glaze beauty of Chinese porcelain to an unparalleled height.
   While pursuing the monochrome beauty of single-glazed porcelain,
people also tried decorating celadon with brown spots. In fact, this
decorative approach utilizing two different glaze colors had already been
tried with the low-fired lead glaze in the Eastern Han Dynasty, that is,
applying yellowish-brown glaze to a green glaze background or applying
green glaze to a yellowish-brown glaze backdrop. By the Wei, Jin and
Southern & Northern Dynasties this tradition became more prominent and
was also applied to the decoration of porcelain. Though a simple means of
adornment, it was the pioneer of China’s underglaze decoration.
   The opening of maritime and overland transport routes and the
development of overseas trade also brought foreign culture, the impact of
which was obvious on ceramics, especially the impact of Buddhist arts
introduced from India. Lotus, a sacred and auspicious flower in Buddhism,
was widely used in the decoration of porcelain. Various bowls, small cups,
zun, pots, jars, and incense burners decorated with lotus petal patterns or
structured like lotus flowers came into vogue. In addition, the style of many
pottery sculptures was deeply influenced by Buddhist grotto art and
demonstrated masterly expressive techniques.
   Buddhist art as a kind of foreign religious art, exerted an influence on
ceramic decoration, and similarly, the influence of secular arts of different
foreign nationalities can also be seen in the ceramic art of the time. For
example, figurines of dancing, music playing, and juggling Westerners can
often be seen on the Yue kiln celadon five-linked jars and jars with piled
sculptures of the Han Dynasty, the Three Kingdoms period and the Western
Jin Dynasty unearthed in Ningbo City, Yinxian, Fenghua, Yuyao and Cixi.
Under the influence of foreign religions and alien cultures of different
nationalities, the ceramic art of the Wei, Jin and Southern & Northern
Dynasties developed its own style, which, coupled with the special aesthetic
pursuits of the entire society at the time, resulted in a type of artistic beauty
featuring simplicity and leanness.

7. Ceramics of the Sui, Tang and Five
Dynasties

Lili Fang1
(1)  Chinese National Academy of Arts, Beijing, China



   Lili Fang
  Email: zhongzl@fltrp.com

7.1 Introduction
7.1.1 Creation of a Strong Country and Open Society
After a period of decline in the Wei, Jin and Southern & Northern
Dynasties, Chinese history arrived at another period of prosperity, that is,
the Sui and Tang dynasties. From the perspective of dynastic progression
and political evolution, the ancient Chinese cultural system could be said to
have been established in the Qin and Han dynasties and matured in the Sui
and Tang dynasties. In fact, the course of development of these two periods
of history was very similar in a certain sense. In other words, they both
comprised a short-lived dynasty with drastic changes and a strong dynasty
with moderate reforms. Fan Wenlan points out: “Qin Shi Huang created the
Qin system which was inherited by all dynasties since the Han Dynasty, as
Emperor Wen of Sui created the Sui system which was followed by all
dynasties since the Tang Dynasty. The Qin and Sui dynasties both made
great contributions and their role in history should not be neglected because
of their short durations.”1
    In CE 581, Yang Jian forced Emperor Jing of the Northern Zhou to
abdicate the throne, established himself as emperor and founded the Sui
Dynasty. Known as Emperor Wen of Sui, he unified the north and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
subsequently conquered the Chen Kingdom in the south and the Shu
Kingdom in the west, thus ending the division of China from the end of the
Jin Dynasty. The rule of the Sui Dynasty, that is, from CE 581 to 618,
experienced the reign of two emperors, both of whom were historically
extraordinary in terms of political and military achievements. Emperor
Yang of Sui went to great efforts to stabilize the frontier and expand Sui’s
territory. He repeatedly dispatched armed forced to suppress Tuyuhun,
Tujue, Koryo and Northern Vietnam, and reopened the Silk Road. In
addition, the two emperors completed huge infrastructure projects including
the 300-km-long Guangtong Canal, which connected Tongguan with the
capital Daxing (Xi’an), and the 2800-km-long Grand Canal which
connected Hangzhou, Luoyang and Zhuojun (Beijing). The construction of
these two canals utilized 3.6 million peasant workers, which was one tenth
of the country’s population. In addition to these two major projects, the
construction of the Great Wall and the new capital Daxing also seriously
impacted the agricultural economy which had been slowly recovering its
vitality. These huge projects caused extensive peasant revolts and cut short
the reign of the Sui Dynasty, but benefited future dynasties, especially the
immediate successor of the Sui, the Tang Dynasty.2
   Li Yuan, the founding emperor of the Tang Dynasty, was born of the
powerful Guanlong group of Xianbei descent. His grandfather was one of
the eight great generals of the Northern Zhou Dynasty and was awarded the
honorary title State Duke of Tang after his death. In the Sui Dynasty, Li
Yuan was chief of the Taiyuan guard units. After Emperor Yang of Sui was
killed, he established the Tang Dynasty (CE 618 to 907) and made himself
emperor. With the political and military achievements of the emperors of
the Tang Dynasty, China was politically united and its national strength was
strong. At the time of the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras (the reign of Emperor
Xuanzong), the Tang’s territory reached Andong (Korea) in the east, Anxi
(Central Asia) in the west, Rinan (Vietnam) in the South and the Chanyu
Protectorate in the north.
   Following the Sui Dynasty, the Tang Dynasty built official granaries
and state-run schools in important cities, promoted laws and codes, and
elevated the traditional rites and music system to a new peak. Through the
rites and music system, the social status of people with different identities
was defined. The Zhenguan Rites, Xianqing Rites and Kaiyuan Rites
prescribed by the Tang Dynasty covered far more than the rites system of
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties. In the Tang Dynasty, all individuals
from the emperor to the people had to learn about and dutifully conduct the
rites, which changed the earlier condition of “rites do not extend to the
common people.”A “governance by riteslandscape in the real sense was
thus formed, in which the legitimacy of rule was affirmed from the
perspective of the relationship between Heaven and man, between the
monarch and subjects, between government officials themselves and
between China and the surrounding countries. A government school system
and an Imperial-Examinations-based official selection system were
established based on the official edition of the Five Classics and their
explanations compiled by two great Confucian scholars, Kong Yingda and
Yan Shigu (Definitive Edition of the Five Classics and Correct Meaning of
the Five Classics). The influence of the school system and official selection
system on Confucianism was even greater than that of Emperor Wu of
Han’s decision to dismiss all other schools and exclusively promote
Confucianism. During the Tang Dynasty, Confucianism and its code of
conduct became the mainstream of society, and the Imperial Examinations
broke the nobility’s monopoly on administrative careers. Nevertheless, the
advocacy of Confucianism in the Tang Dynasty did not lead to rejection of
Buddhism or Taoism. In fact, Buddhism and Taoism received strong
support from the emperor from time to time, and on many occasions the
imperial court encouraged and subsidized eminent monks to go abroad to
seek Buddhist sutras. As a result, during the Tang Dynasty, Buddhism and
Taoism entered a heyday and Buddhism developed four major schools in
China (including the locally developed Chan sect), which shows the
inclusiveness of Confucianism. Western scholars believe that, for East Asia,
the Tang Dynasty was the turning point from the Middle Ages to modern
society and that the Tang regime was the political and cultural center of
East Asia that was imitated by neighboring regions and nations including
Japan, Silla, Nanzhao (a local regime in ancient China), Tubo (the Tibetan
regime in ancient China) and Vietnam. The Tang civilization even spread to
the Mediterranean coast through the Silk Road.
   With the expansion of Tang’s territory and its tolerant foreign policy, its
Confucian governance pattern was held in high esteem and imitated by
surrounding countries. Japan’s Taika Reforms (Zhenguan 19th Year, i.e. CE
645) were based on the Tang Dynasty system and have been the cornerstone
of the Japanese civilization up to the present day. Since the Tang royal
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
family had nomadic ethnic origins, it became a unique characteristic of the
period to appoint non-Han ethnic minority personnel in the civil service and
military systems. Ethnic minority officials could be found not only in
border institutions such as the protectorates, but also in the imperial court.
To summarize, the Tang Dynasty was tolerant to both foreign cultures
outside and ethnic minority cultures within, making itself a model of East
Asian society: an open society that was inclusive externally and internally.
   The economic civilization of the Sui and Tang dynasties was even
grander than that of the Qin and Han dynasties. When the Tang Dynasty
was at its peak, its territory covered the desert in the north and An’nan
(Vietnam) in the south. Though the northeast was a bit narrower compared
with the Han Dynasty, the western frontier was much wider. At that time,
Emperor Taizong of Tang was respectfully titled the “Great Khan” by all
surrounding ethnic minorities. In the event of a deceased general in any
nearby nomadic regime, it fell to the Tang Dynasty to issue an imperial
edict to appoint an heir. This was like a world federation with the Tang as
the mother country.3
    In terms of commerce, the Han Dynasty implemented restraining
policies against businessmen while the Tang Dynasty adopted more of a
laissez-faire approach. During the reign of Emperor Wu of Han, salt and
iron were monopolized by the government and were not allowed to be sold
by merchants. Yet in the early Tang Dynasty businesses were allowed and
no tax was levied. It can be said that the economic policies of the Han
Dynasty, especially during the period of Emperor Wu of Han, often focused
on suppressing the high-level economy and concurrently neglected the low-
level economy, while the economic policies of the Tang Dynasty, especially
in the early Tang Dynasty such as during the reign of Emperor Taizong,
purposely cultivated the low-level economy and at the same time granted
more leniency and freedom towards the high-level economy. As a result,
society during the Tang Dynasty was richer and more developed than
during the Han Dynasty.

7.1.2 New Urban Layout and Development of the Crafts
Industry
The second revival of Confucianism exerted an obvious influence on the
structure of Chinese cities. The Chinese urbanization that slowly took shape
following the Han Dynasty was consolidated throughout the Tang.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
1.
  The layout of urban spaces accommodated rites and music principles
   such as order, rank and unity.
2.
  A north–south central axis, often in the form of a city’s main road, ran
   through the whole city, embodying the rites and music principles of
   impartiality and regularity.
3.
  The palace (imperial court and royal residence) formed a special area in
   the central north of the city separated from its other parts, which
   symbolized the supremacy of imperial power.
4.
   Since the imperial palace was located in the north, the “city” was
  moved to the residential areas in the south, transposing the traditional
   arrangement of “court in the front and city at the back”.
5.
  The ancestral temple and the earth altar, two important Confucian rites
   and music structures, were still located in the imperial city according to
   the tradition of “temple on the left and altar on the right”, and this made
   relevant ritual activities visible to the public.4
   Such a layout widened the distance between the court and the citizenry.
Following the tradition of restraining commerce that had been practiced
from the Zhou to the Han Dynasty, the Li-Fang system (sectioning the city
area into walled wards for residence or commerce) was established, which
further confined the activities of citizens. Houses were not allowed to open
doors on ward walls except for those of officials with a top three ranking.
Commercial activities in cities were also strictly controlled by the
government and were only allowed to be conducted in the “marketplace”,
which only prefectures and counties with a population of more than 3,000
households were allowed to set up. The rapid development of trade and
handicraft industries led to the concentration of similar kinds of goods in a
certain zone of the market and accordingly merchants vending similar
goods clustered to form guilds. Records show 220 industries in the Tang
Dynasty. The heads of the industries were responsible for inspecting
commodity quality and supervising the execution of sales contracts. They
also assisted the head of the marketplace to regularly grade and price
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
commodities based on their quality. In the late Tang Dynasty, night markets
also appeared in some big cities.
   Some cities in the Tang Dynasty specially set up markets for foreign
businessmen, demonstrating the Tang Dynasty’s encouragement of foreign
trade and its inclusive urban culture.5 The stress on neatness and hierarchy
in the layout of Chang’an city was even stronger than that in the Han, Wei
and Southern & Northern Dynasties. Chang’an was the first capital city of a
unified China to perfectly follow the system of the Xia, Shang and Zhou
dynasties and thus became a model of mature Confucian urban civilization
and city structure. CE 724 to 781 was the peak period for the import of
Tang civilization into Japan. In addition to codes and laws, science and
technology, and literature and language, the design of the new Japanese
capital city was also modeled after the Tang style. Even the names of some
major palaces (Taiji Palace) and streets (Vermilion Bird Street) were the
same as those in Chang’an.6 (Fig. 7.1).





Fig. 7.1 Map of the royal palace and imperial city of Chang’an
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Chang’an, covering 87 square kilometers, was the largest city in the
world at the time; it was also a pre-planned and walled city. The population
living within the city walls reached one million and a further million or so
lived on the outskirts of the city. Compared with later medieval cities in
Europe, Chang’an was a freer and more open city, where various ethnicities,
cultures, religions and commodities were tolerated and treated with
courtesy. Nevertheless, Chang’an’s Li-Fang system indicates that it was still
a strictly managed city. Unlike the West, Chinese Confucian tradition holds
that one should repair to the wilderness rather than to the bustling city for
individual freedom.7
   During this period Chang’an as the capital city was not only
magnificent and grand, but also exquisitely laid out. Basically square-
shaped, it consisted of three parts: the imperial palace, the imperial city and
the outer city. The imperial palace lay in the middle of the northern part of
the city to symbolize the status of the emperor who commanded the whole
country from central north. The imperial city contained ancestral temples,
sacrificial altars, and central government offices, where all civil and
military officials handled administrative affairs. The Chengtian Gate of the
imperial palace and the Vermilion Bird Street of the imperial city formed a
north–south axis dividing the city into an eastern and western part. Fourteen
east-west streets and 11 north–south streets divided the city into 108 neatly
laid out wards, which served as residential or commercial areas for citizens.
The city featured two large marketplaces, one in the east and one in the
west, each covering one square kilometer. Each marketplace was divided
into nine square units for businessmen from all walks of life to buy and sell.
Chang’an city had 81 Buddhist monasteries, 28 Buddhist nunneries, 30
Taoist abbeys, six Taoist nunneries, two Persian temples, four Zoroastrian
temples and several theaters, gardens and Musical Houses (courts for
imperial musicians). Locust trees and elegant weeping willows in neat lines
added radiance to the green tiles, red walls and gold and silver shop signs.
The outer wall enclosing the city was about 12 m thick with three doors on
each of the four sides. The city was truly a spectacle.8
   The building of the capital city and the development of commerce
inevitably led to advancement in the handicraft industry. Literature records
that during the Tang Dynasty many artisans were recruited to work in shifts
in manufacturing various articles, and dedicated government positions were
established to take charge of the construction of palaces, ancestral temples,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
mausoleums and other pieces of architecture, the manufacturing of royal
handicrafts including gold, jade, textile and embroidery, the management of
royal clothes, treasures, precious cuisine, etc., and the operation of the royal
kitchens as well as weaving and dyeing houses. Meanwhile private
handicraft workshops manufacturing paper, wine, dye works, blankets, etc.
emerged like mushrooms after spring rain and flourished. Guild
organizations also came into being to look after the group interests of the
private handicraft industry. Various famous handicrafts, such as porcelain,
lacquerware, embroidery, dyeing and weaving, smelting and casting, and
gold and silver processing, were further improved, innovated and
developed.9 The origin of secret-color porcelain in the Tang Dynasty must
be attributed to the government’s emphasis on handicraft development at
that time.
   Another major contributor to the progress of the ceramics industry
during the period was the perfection of kilns. During the Wei, Jin and
Southern & Northern Dynasties, sectional firing was invented and used by
dragon kilns in the south. The technique made it possible to fully fire
greenware placed in any part of the dragon kilns and made it possible to
extend the kiln body, which led to rapid popularization of celadon
technology in southeastern China. Kiln yards emerged in all areas south of
the Yangtze River, which promoted the improvement and development of
other porcelain-making techniques. The expansion of porcelain production
and application forced wooden, lacquer and bronzewares to abandon their
traditional tableware market and seek other directions for development.
Another technological innovation was the invention of the sagger, which
was popularized in the Sui and Tang dynasties and enabled better protection
and more efficient arrangement of greenware in kilns during firing. The use
of saggers allowed the building of higher dragon kilns and made it possible
to open kiln doors. This reduced the labor intensity of kiln workers because
now they could operate in spacious kiln chambers without having to bend
down and enter and exit through a door on the side of the kiln. These
technological advancements were also conducive to the establishment of
mass production systems and led to the wider popularization of ceramic
manufacturing.10

7.1.3 Civil Service Examination System and the Life of Scholar
Elites
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
An important advancement of the Tang Dynasty was the creation of the
Imperial Examination System, which offered people at the bottom of
society an opportunity to be selected to high administrative office through
study. Most of the examination candidates came from the countryside since
the environment there was more conducive to cultivating personnel with
both knowledge and virtue. Urban society, bustling with industry and
commerce, was certainly not a good place to incubate such talents. It was
by relying on the Imperial Examination System that throughout the feudal
period of China the seeds of traditional culture were retained in the
countryside nationwide, with roots growing ever deeper and stems reaching
ever higher. All villages in the land had aspiring men who studied hard, and
as a result now almost every locality in China has its own famous historical
figures and historic sites. The countryside became the incubation ground for
Chinese culture. This is why Qian Mu believes that the two backbones of
Chinas cultural history were the Han Dynasty’s various plans for politics
and society and the Tang Dynasty’s diverse interest in literature and art, and
that China in later generations was supported by these two backbones. The
establishment of political and social systems stabilized the common aspects
of people’s lives. The refinement of literature and art fulfilled a unique yen
in life at the time.11 The significance of the Imperial Examination System to
ceramics was amplified by the fact that before the Ming Dynasty, when
ceramics production became a specialized urban profession, potters were
also farmers and their lives involved both ceramic production and farming.
So the abovementioned rural-incubated culture was bound to influence the
artistic creation of potters at the time, which was beneficial to the
development of the ceramics industry because ceramics were not only
practical commodities but also handicraft works that embodied the thoughts
and philosophies of the Chinese literati. The advancement of the handicraft
industry and commerce promoted the production and circulation of ceramic
products while progress in literature and the arts elevated their artistic taste.
   Behind the promotion of any technology there must be the support of
culture and lifestyle factors. The popularity of metaphysical studies in the
literary life of the Wei, Jin and Southern & Northern Dynasties contributed
to the origin of the Chan Buddhist sect in China, which became prevalent in
China by the reign of Wu Zetian in the Tang Dynasty. The essence of Chan
was the pursuit of plainness and tranquility amid the reality of daily life.
Such a pursuit represented spiritual freedom and a break from worldly
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
bondage. In fact, the lively, natural, spiritual and unrestrained style typical
of Chinese literature and art since the Tang Dynasty has always been
profoundly associated with the Chan spirit. Therefore, the Chan sect of the
Tang Dynasty could be regarded as a “religious revolution” or
“Renaissance” in Chinese history.
   The rise of the Chan sect represented a new wave and a new trend rising
out of the flood of Southern Chinese blood and life into the mainstream of
old traditional Chinese culture which had previously been dominated by the
Yellow River basin in the north, because eight or nine out of every 10 Chan
sect founders in the Tang Dynasty were born and raised in areas south of the
Yangtze River. Similarly, celadon, which originated in the south like the
Chan, also began to appear in the north. The south brought not only Chan
and celadon (Fig. 7.2), but also tea culture. Throughout the history of
China, the rise and fall of ceramics was often closely related to tea culture.
Tea was initially used as medicine and drinking tea as a beverage was first
practiced by southern Chinese. Later, along with the northward
dissemination of the Chan sect, tea drinking also spread to the north and
gradually grew from a religious custom to a social fashion.

7.1.4 Tea Culture and Porcelain
Most tea vessels at the time were made of porcelain. Lu Yu of the mid-Tang
Dynasty was respected as the Sage of Tea and was renowned for his work
Book of Tea, in which he commented on the porcelain of the day, based on
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
its suitability as a tea vessel: “to make bowls, porcelain of the Yuezhou (越州)
kilns is the best and that of Dingzhou and Wuzhou is inferior, and that of
the Yuezhou (岳州) kilns is the best while that of Shouzhou and Hongzhou is
inferior. Some believe that Xingzhou porcelain is better than that of
Yuezhou (越州). I do not agree—for the following three advantages of Yue
ware. First, Xing ware is like silver while Yue ware is like jade; second,
Xing ware is like snow while Yue ware is like ice; third, Xing ware is white
and tea contained in it looks red, while Yue ware is blue and the tea looks
green.”(Fig. 7.3).





Fig. 7.3 Yue kiln large crabapple flower bowl,
Tang Dynasty, height: 10.8 cm, diam.: 32.2 cm, in the Shanghai Museum

   The relationship between porcelain and tea at the time can also be found
in the works of poets of the Tang Dynasty. Lu Guimeng, Meng Jiao and Shi
Jianwu all mentioned or described southern Yue celadon from the
perspective of tea drinking and appreciation in their poems. It can be seen
that the popularity of tea drinking in the Tang Dynasty promoted the
development of tea sets, of porcelain-making technology and of porcelain
utensil quality.

text:
During the archaeological excavations conducted at the Tang poet Bai
Juyis former residence in Lvdaofang in Luoyang by the Institute of
Archaeology of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences from 1992 to
1993, more than 800 pieces of porcelain were unearthed from the Tang
dynasty stratum at the site, which can be divided into 13 categories, namely
pots, jars, basins, filters, bowls, plates, yu, cups, teacup saucers, small
teacups, tea grinders, boxes and inkstones. According to historical records
and the remains unearthed from Tang dynasty sites including tombs and
kilns across the country, porcelain production was dominated by daily use
items, and especially bowls of different sizes. For instance, of the bowls
unearthed from the Changsha kilns in Hunan Province, 81% are tight-
mouthed items with the inscription “茶土宛” or “荼土宛” (“tea bowl”), and 17% are
open-mouthed items with the inscription” 岳麓寺茶土宛” (“Yuelu Temple Tea
Bowl”).12 Tea sets account for a considerable proportion of the porcelain
unearthed from the period, indicating that the rise of the tea culture in a
certain sense promoted the development of the ceramics industry at the
time.

7.1.5 Cultural Communication Brought by Foreign Population
The Tang Dynasty was a powerful world empire in its day. Its highly
developed economy and culture shone all over the world and its open door
policy attracted all nationalities and countries. Foreigners from surrounding
countries laboriously covered thousands of miles to arrive in the Tang
Empire where they did business or studied the classics. Some even got
married, had children, and settled in Chang’an for the rest of their lives. The
Six Statutes of the Tang Dynasty records that the Tang Empire maintained
friendly exchanges with more than 300 countries and regions. With the
renewed flourishing of the Silk Road, Chang’an, capital of the Tang
Dynasty, became a gathering place for foreign businessmen and a center of
world commodities. In the city there were institutions dedicated to the
reception of foreign guests and ethnic minority envoys, such as the Bureau
of State Ceremonies, the Customs and Guests Department, and the Official
Etiquette House. Among the Tang dynasty pottery figurines unearthed we
can see many foreigners living in China at the time. Figure 7.4 shows
figurines of three foreign men carrying shovels and hoes, looking like
Europeans in appearance and dress. Figures 7.5 and 7.6 respectively show a
man and a woman on horseback, who from their dress are probably Arabs.

   Westerners’ exceptional talent for singing and dancing greatly impacted
the dance and music of the Tang Dynasty. The Tang Dynasty poet Wang
Jian mentioned that “foreign music is played in every household in
Luoyang” in his poem A Visit to Liangzhou. Six of the 10 pieces of music in
the Tang Dynasty were from the Western Regions and were named after
their local country, indicating that the Tang Dynasty had great achievements
in absorbing foreign cultures and promoting the renewal of national dance
and music. The Tang Empire was an oriental paradise with enchanting
charm in the minds of ethnic minorities and its capital Chang’an was a
place they yearned to visit. According to the Old Book of Tang, more than
4,000 foreigners lived in Chang’an for as long as 40 years during the reign
of Emperor Dezong of Tang. These Westerners with different customs and
ethnic affiliations came to the Tang Empire from distant foreign lands
accompanied by tinkling camel bells and marvelous dance steps, bringing
with them colorful cultures of different nationalities, which greatly enriched
the culture of the Tang Dynasty. Amid such organic cultural fusion, foreign
songs and dances swept the imperial court, foreign dress and styles came
into vogue, and foreign music and food became highly fashionable. The
Treatise of Five Elements of the New Book of Tang records: “In the early
Tianbao era, nobles and commoners liked foreign dresses and hats”. In An
Lushan Stories by Yao Runeng, it is also mentioned that “in the early
Tianbao era… sleeves of clothes tended to be narrow”. Yuan Zhen wrote in
his Taoist music piece that “women preferred marrying Westerners and
adopted the Western dress style, and musicians preferred learning and
performing Western music,”and that “Western dress and costumes were
constantly introduced over five decades”. The Treatise of Carriages and
Clothes from the Old Book of Tang records that “in the early Kaiyuan era…
riders from the palace all wore foreign hats…”and that “in the late Kaiyuan
era… women all eagerly dressed themselves in foreign clothes”. Such
scenes can be seen in many pottery figurines from the time, like the vivid
foreign dancer shown in Fig. 7.9.

   Many pottery figurines used as burial objects were in the form of
tricolor wares. Their unique exotic features enriched the artistic style of the
tricolor glazed earthenware of the Tang Dynasty. At the same time, the
introduction of foreign cultures and the changes made to meet the needs of
different markets at home and abroad led to the emergence of many new
ceramic types in the Tang Dynasty. For example, the underglaze decorated
porcelain of the Changsha Tongguan kilns and the Tang blue and white
porcelain of the Gongxian kilns were produced mainly to meet the needs of
overseas markets.

7.2 Celadon of the Sui and Tang Dynasties
7.2.1 Celadon of the Sui Dynasty
The Sui Dynasty unified China on the basis of the Northern Dynasties, so
it’s cultural landscape largely inherited that of the Northern Dynasties. As
Daxing (now southeast of Xi’an, Shaanxi Province) was made capital of the
Sui Dynasty, the political center of the Sui was in the north and more
southern goods and technologies spread northward, including porcelain
making. As a result, the porcelain industry in the north developed rapidly
and entered a new era.
   The porcelain industry of the Sui Dynasty inherited the framework of
the previous period, namely, celadon was still the mainstream and was
divided into two systems, the south and the north. The Yue kilns in modern-
day eastern Zhejiang Province successfully fired primitive celadon as early
as the Shang and Zhou dynasties, and eventually became the first place to
fire celadon in a real sense in the Eastern Han Dynasty after thousands of
years of development and improvement. The south as the base of celadon
production continued into the Sui Dynasty, during which kilns in modern-
day Zhejiang and Jiangsu further increased and celadon production in
present-day Anhui, Hunan and Sichuan gradually grew in scale and
matured. Representative kilns in the south during the Sui Dynasty were the
Yue kilns in Zhejiang, the Xiangyin kilns in Hunan, the Huainan kilns in
Anhui, the Fengcheng kilns in Jiangxi and the Chengdu kilns in Sichuan.
Northern celadon in the Sui Dynasty developed rapidly based on Northern
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Qi celadon. The central production areas lay in modern-day Hebei and
Henan, followed by Shandong. The main kilns were the Jiabi kilns in
Cixian County, Hebei, the Anyang kilns in Henan, and the Zhaili,
Zhongchenhao and Zhuchen kilns in Shandong.
   The color of celadon in the Sui Dynasty differed slightly from north to
south. The porcelain body of southern celadon generally had a denser
texture, thinner walls and a bluish gray color. These features were firstly
due to the quality of the porcelain clay used in the south, which was mostly
native kaolin, namely, locally weathered clay characterized by less foreign
substances and a high purity. The second contributor to the features of
southern celadon was the special structure of the southern kilns, mainly
dragon kilns built on slopes (the length of the dragon kilns was generally
between 30 to 80 m and the inclination was 10 to 20 degrees). The structure
enabled quick rises and falls in temperature and was suitable for producing
reducing flame. However, because the firing temperature could only reach
about 1,200 degrees Celsius, the resultant bodycolor was generally bluish
gray. Yet there were also special cases like the purplish red body color of
celadon produced by the Qionglai and Qingyanggong kilns in Sichuan.
   Northern celadon generally had a relatively loose body texture, thicker
body walls, and blue or yellowish blue glaze. The differences with southern
celadon were mainly due to the different firing atmosphere and glaze
composition. Northern porcelain kilns were mostly shaped like steamed
bun, which allowed full burning of the fuel and were conducive to the
formation of oxidizing flame. The firing temperature could reach about
1,300 degrees Celsius, giving a yellow or green tinge to northern celadon.
In addition, the high content of titanium dioxide (TiO2) in the body was also
a major cause of the poor color of northern celadon. The kaolin used for
northern celadon was usually deposited kaolin (secondary kaolin), that is,
the deposits of weathered clay and sediments having been carried by water.
The characteristic of this kaolin was its high content of impurities. Rich
organic matter offered the clay high viscosity. In addition, the amount of
alumina oxide (Al2O3) in porcelain clay is also a deciding factor in the
density of the body texture after firing. Because of the low content of
alumina oxide in southern clay and the comparatively high content in
northern clay, when both were fired to a temperature range of 1,200 to
1,270 degrees Celsius, southern celadon resulted in a higher density,
reaching full sintering, while northern celadon barely reached high density
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
or full sintering. During the Sui Dynasty the use of engobe became common
in both southern and northern porcelain kilns, such as the Qionglai kilns in
Sichuan, the Hongzhou kilns in Jiangxi, and the Xing kilns in Hebei. This
was another feature of Sui dynasty porcelain making.
    In terms of shape design, the porcelain of the Sui Dynasty inherited a lot
of the basic characteristics of the Southern & Northern Dynasties and many
varieties of the Southern & Northern Dynasties could still be found among
Sui dynasty porcelain. Yet on careful observation we can see that Sui
porcelain had its own distinct features in terms of shape design. Compared
with previous periods, Sui porcelain wares were generally taller, and most
pots and bottles had oval bellies, making them look more elegant. Vessels
like bottles, pots, zun and spittoons were mostly topped with a mouth in the
shape of a tall plate or shallow cup, and their thin necks and plump bellies
were mostly decorated with raised string patterns, which added a sense of
dignity and solemnity to the slender vessel body. Pots can be classified into
ones with spouts and ones without, the former rooster-head pots and the
latter plate-mouthed pots. Rooster-head pots were more slender than those
of the Southern Dynasties with taller plate mouths and thinner necks. The
mid-section was often decorated with string patterns and the rooster head
was more realistic. The handle preserved the dragon form of the Southern
Dynasties while the lug pair on the shoulder took on new features. The foot
extended slightly outward. (Figs. 7.10 and 7.11) Plate-mouthed pots were
characterized by taller plate mouths, longer necks, oval bellies, and mostly
strip-shaped lugs that were attached to the shoulder. (Fig. 7.12) While
southern celadon was slender, northern vessels were comparatively stout, a
point that is manifest in the two types of jars that were popular in the south
and north respectively. Southern celadon jars generally had six or eight
lugs, often one strip-shaped and one bridge-shaped in between. The belly
was oval with the lower part gradually narrowing. The mouth was straight
and generous. The shoulder and belly were often carved with decorative
patterns. (Fig. 7.13) Northern celadon jars, in contrast, mostly had four lugs
on the shoulder, all strip-shaped. The belly was round with a raised string in
the middle dividing the vessel into two hemispheres. Northern jars also had
a straight mouth and were neckless. Rooster-head pots and plate-mouthed
bottles were prevalent mainly in the south and were rarely unearthed in
northern kiln sites. Southern celadon glaze often had decorative patterns
while northern celadon was mostly plain.

   Although northern and southern celadon differed in terms of shape
design, body texture and glaze character, they inevitably exerted an impact
on each other because they existed in society as commodities, especially
with the favorable conditions for north–south trade and exchange brought
about by the opening of the Grand Canal. Craftsmen also experienced more
exchanges in ceramic firing technology. The confluence of northern and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
southern styles gave birth to many varieties that could often be seen in both
the north and the south, like long stem plates, lugged jars, bowl-shaped
vessels and straight bellied bowls, which were mass produced by both
southern and northern kilns in the Sui Dynasty. Another example was the
white porcelain rooster-head pot unearthed in the tomb of Li Jingxun in
Shaanxi Province, a masterpiece of northern craftsmen (Fig. 7.14), though
rooster-head pots were once prevalent mainly in the south. Common
varieties included daily use vessels such as bowls, plates, bottles, pots,
basins, cups, cases, stoves, lamps, vats, candlesticks and spittoons (Figs.
7.15 and 7.16), as well as study articles such as chessboards, inkstones and
water pots. There were also burial objects such as figurines of the 12
Chinese zodiac animals, tomb guarding beasts, warriors (Fig. 7.17),
officials, houses, wells, and cabinets. Many varieties close to people’s daily
lives gradually turned from burial objects in the Southern & Northern
Dynasties into practical ones.

   Commonly used decorative techniques included engraving, scratching,
printing, sticking, stamping and comb scratching. Engraving refers to the
technique of carving patterns in relief on greenware with iron, bamboo or
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
bone blades, and then applying glaze and dispatching for firing. Scratching
refers to applying needle-like tools to the greenware to scratch out lines in
intaglio before glazing and firing. Printing refers to pressing decorative
images onto semi-dried greenware with a pattern-bearing molding tool.
Sticking refers to attaching ready-made sculptures onto the greenware body,
which creates a three-dimensional effect like a shallow relief.
    In terms of decorative patterns, Sui porcelain not only inherited some
plant patterns prevalent in the Southern & Northern Dynasties, but also
cleverly interpolated and replaced certain themes in image layout to create
new patterns. The shoulders and bellies of bottles and jars were usually
decorated with ribbons made of blossoms and rolled leaves. Plates and
bowls were often decorated in the center with a circular pattern composed
of individual blossoms or rolled leaves. The circular pattern might contain
one, three, five or seven layers based on the size of the ware. Main patterns
included flowers such as lotus petals, individual blossoms, honeysuckle,
blades of grass, and plum blossoms, and geometric patterns included
strings, ropes, waves, triangles, linked beads, double circles, mat patterns
and vertical lines. These flower and geometric patterns often formed
ribbons that decorated the neck, belly and outer side of the mouth rim of the
vessels or constituted circular decorations of one, three or five layers that
decorated the well of bowls or plates according to the shape design of the
vessels. Animal imageries included dragons, phoenixes, rooster heads, lion
heads, elephant heads, and monkeys. There were also human images. These
decorations were mostly first molded and then attached to the surface of the
vessels. In general, compared with those of the Wei, Jin, and Southern &
Northern Dynasties, the decorative porcelain patterns of the Sui Dynasty
featured less animal themes and more plant imageries. (Fig. 7.18).
