7.3.2 Non-Xing Kilns
7.3.2.1 Gongxian Kilns in Henan
The Gongxian kilns were discovered in 1956 with sites located in
Xiaohuangye Village, Tiejianglu Village and Baihe Township in today’s
Gongxian County. The main products were white porcelain and some three-
color pottery. Gongxian kilns were the first white porcelain kilns found in
Henan Province. Xiaohuangye Village fired mainly white porcelain and
some tricolor pottery; Tiejianglu Village mainly fired white porcelain; the
products of Baihe Township were basically the same as those of
Xiaohuangye Village. White porcelain was the longest fired porcelain of the
Gongxian kilns in the Tang Dynasty. A comparison of the white porcelain
unearthed from Tang tombs with that unearthed from the kiln sites showed
that white porcelain produced by the Gongxian kilns was already widely
spread across the country in the early Tang Dynasty, specifically, from the
late Wuzhou era of Wu Zetian’s reign to the Kaiyuan era of Xuanzong’s
reign. The decline of white porcelain began following the Tianbao era.
   Records of Henan mass producing white porcelain and paying tribute to
the capital Chang’an can be found in the Guo Shi Bu, Yuanhe County Atlas,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and Treatise on Geography of the New Book of Tang. These records were
confirmed by the discovery of Gongxian kiln white porcelain among finds
from the Tang Chang’an City West Market Site and the Tang Daming
Palace Site, as well as by the discovery by Feng Xianming and others in
July 1957 during an investigation in the Gongxian area of white glazed
porcelain shards in Xiaohuangye Village, Tiejianglu Village and Baihe
Township which were the same as those collected at the Tang Daming
Palace Site in 1957. In addition, in 1976 the cultural relics department of
Henan Province collected a white porcelain egg ball in Gongxian County,
which was as thin as eggshell, almost transparent and bright white. It was
among the finest white porcelain work.20 This finding also proved that the
Gongxian area was probably the source of the white porcelain tributes in
the Kaiyuan era. Additionally, in the Tang Dynasty, Gongxian County, less
than two kilometers away from the Luohe River, was connected to
Chang’an via very convenient transportation routes. Porcelain could be
transported to Luoyang by boat, and then enter the Weihe River from the
Yellow River to reach Chang’an.
   The varieties produced by the Gongxian kilns were rich. Both the Tang
Yu Lin and the Guo Shi Bu record that potters in Gongxian made porcelain
figurines that they named “Lu Hongjian” (another name for Lu Yu), which
they would offer for free to customers who bought more than 10 vessels as
a means of boosting sales. As a matter of fact, one such porcelain figurine
was discovered among the finds from the kiln sites. Another example was
that up until the Song Dynasty, poets were still writing in praise of the
celadon pillows of the Gongxian kilns, such as Zhang Lei’s description in
one of his poems of the beautiful celadon pillow that he received as a gift
from a friend that kept his mind cool.
   The white porcelain of the Gongxian kilns had a fine, hard texture, and
a white or grayish white body. The glaze tones of the wares were diverse
with some white, some white with a tinge of yellow and some white with a
tinge of blue. The glaze surface displayed fine crackles. The distinction
between coarse and fine white porcelain ware can be seen from the tools
and shards unearthed from the kiln sites. Fine white porcelain was mostly
contained in saggers for firing. The glaze was pure and the walls were
relatively thin.
   The Gongxian kilns used wood as a fuel and their firing temperature
was 1,300 to 1,350 ℃. Most wares were only semi-glazed. Some were fully
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
glazed but not on the foot. In contrast, products of the Xing and Ding kilns
were mostly fully or semi-glazed both inside and out, and fine white wares
were glazed down to the outside of the foot and even the inner bottom was
often glazed.
   Besides white porcelain, the Gongxian kilns also fired black glazed
vessels, which often had a thicker body. They usually had black glaze
applied on the outside, white glaze on the inside and no glaze on the mouth
rim, a feature most common in bowls and plates. Such a glazing practice
has also been found on the plates and bowls unearthed from the Tang
dynasty Hunyuan kiln site in Shanxi Province, but has rarely been seen in
other Tang dynasty kiln sites.
   White porcelain products of the Gongxian kilns included bowls, plates,
jars, pots, bottles and pillows, but mainly bowls and plates. Bowls
represented the greatest quantity and richest designs, of which there were
up to a dozen. They can roughly be classified into shallow and deep bowls.
Shallow bowls had an open, flared or petal mouth. Those with an open
mouth had thick lips, heavy walls, and a bi shaped foot. Those with flared
mouths had thin lips, gradually thickened downwards, and the foot was
either bi shaped or thick and circular. Bowls with a petal mouth also had
thin walls like the flared mouth bowls, but the rim was in the shape of four
flower petals. Four protruding lines extended down from between the petals
on the inside of the bowl. The foot was either in the shape of a bi or was
thick and circular. Deep bowls, on the other hand, had straight mouths and
flat bottoms. Some special design bowls, mostly with spherical bellies and
flat bottoms, had double ears or short spouts. Plates had four-petal shaped
mouths, four protruding lines on the inside, and thin circular feet, and their
center was glazed. Jars were dominated by double-lugged items and the
molded lugs were a prominent characteristic. There was another type of jar
featuring flared mouths, short necks, broad shoulders and flat bottoms. Pots,
all with handles, came in diverse designs, with high or low bellies and long
or short spouts. Bottles and yu (wide-mouthed jars/pots) had plate mouths,
thin necks and spherical bellies. Other varieties apart from daily use utensils
were architectural ceramics, burial objects and children’s toys, all of
exquisite design and unique characteristics. The general style was grace,
grandeur, and an emphasis on both practicality and beauty. Gongxian kiln
white porcelain, along with products of the Xing and Ding kilns in Hebei
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Province, embodied the characteristics of the Tang Dynasty and were
models of white porcelain from that time. (Fig. 7.42).





Fig. 7.42 Gongxian kiln white-glazed flower-mouth spittoon,
Tang Dynasty, height: 9.8 cm, top diam.: 13.7 cm, base diam.: 7.8 cm, in the Palace Museum

7.3.2.2 Ding Kilns in Hebei
The Ding kilns were located in modern-day Quyang in Hebei Province and
are thus also referred to as the “Quyang kilns “in some works. Kiln sites
from the Tang Dynasty discovered so far are mostly in the north and east of
Jianci Village. Some white porcelain from the Tang Dynasty found at the
sites is no less attractive than the fine ware of the Xing kilns. There are
even near-transparent white wares, which were produced later in the Song
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and Jin dynasties. White porcelain of the late Tang and Five Dynasties is
mostly bowls, plates, pots, basins, stoves and small toys. The body, with a
relatively crude texture, is thick and grayish or yellowish white in color.
The glaze, appearing whiter thanks to the use of engobe, is rarely applied
down to the base, and looks bluish green at the lowest point where drops
gather. Thick vessels have coarser glaze and a small number of fine
crackles, while those with a finer body and glaze exhibit a pure, bright and
lustrous glaze color. (Fig. 7.43).





Fig. 7.43 Ding kiln white-glazed rolled-rim bowl,
Tang Dynasty, height: 3.4 cm, top diam.: 14.5 cm, base diam.: 7.7 cm, in the Palace Museum

   The body of Tang dynasty white porcelain from the Ding kilns had a
high alumina content, with the Al2O3 content reaching 29.95% to 34.53%,
and a relatively low silicon content, with SiO2 accounting for 59.79 to
59.82%. The body of most vessels contained less than 1% iron (Fe2O3) and
titanium (TiO2), while a limited number contained more than 1%.
Nevertheless, thanks to a high firing temperature of about 1,300 ℃, the
body of most products was fully and compactly sintered with porosity lower
than 1% and water absorption rate also low. Since products of the Tang and
Five Dynasties were fired in a reducing flame fed by wood, the glaze color
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
was white with green shades, completely different from the yellowish white
glaze fired with coal in later periods. However, owing to the high Fe2O3
content and low TiO2 content in the glaze, if fired in an oxidizing
atmosphere, the glaze color would inevitably turn yellowish white. This
was a feature shared by Tang dynasty white porcelain of both the Xing and
Gongxian kilns. (Fig. 7.44).





Fig. 7.44 Ding kiln white-glazed case,
Tang Dynasty, height: 6.9 cm, top diam.: 9.8 cm, base diam.: 5.4 cm, in the Palace Museum

    In the early Tang Dynasty, the quality of white porcelain produced by
Ding kilns was very poor. The iron content of the body of some vessels
reached an unusually high 2.58%. The fracture surface of the body was
brownish yellow, and the density was also poor, requiring a layer of engobe
between the body and the glaze to improve the whiteness of the glaze. After
the late Tang Dynasty, quality improved remarkably. Engobe started to be
discarded and clay materials with less iron content and higher purity in the
first place were selected to be made into greenware. Though product quality
was higher than before, in some cases the body still contained small
bubbles, which was due to insufficient clay kneading and molding by hand.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
7.3.2.3 Cizhou Kilns in Hebei
The Cizhou kilns, located in modern-day Cixian County, Hebei Province,
are so named because the area belonged to Cizhou in ancient times. The
Cizhou kilns rose to fame in the Song and Jin dynasties and were in
production for more than a thousand years. Products from the Northern Qi
and Sui Dynasties have been successively unearthed. In the spring of 2002,
the cultural relics departments of prefectural and district levels in Handan
jointly conducted preliminary excavations of the Linshui Town ancient
porcelain kiln sites located in the Fengfeng mining area where they
discovered workshops, material pools, water wells and kiln furniture from
the Tang, Song, Jin and Yuan Dynasties, and found over 300,000 pieces of
porcelain shards of multiple types, namely, celadon, black porcelain, white
porcelain, black and white porcelain, red and green porcelain, engraved
porcelain, printed porcelain and Jun glazed porcelain. The excavations
made up for the lack of material evidence for research on Cizhou kilns.
After decades of investigations and excavations, archaeologists discovered
the sites of Cizhou kilns from many historical periods including the
Northern Dynasties, the Song Dynasty, the Jin Dynasty, the Yuan Dynasty,
the Ming Dynasty and the Qing Dynasty, yet had long been baffled by the
whereabouts of the sites from the Tang Dynasty. Now this question has
finally been answered with a milestone discovery. Under the Song and Jin
cultural layer of the ancient kiln site in Linshui Town, remains of a small
kiln were discovered, where two gray pottery jars were excavated, 12 bluish
green material pools were found, 11 “Kaiyuan Tongbao” copper coins of
the Tang Dynasty were collected, and several pieces of white porcelain and
403 shards of black-glazed porcelain jars and unglazed flat-bottom bluish
yellow vessels were unearthed. The finds indicate that this was the site of a
Tang dynasty kiln, thus filling the aforementioned “gap” in the
archaeological record about the Cizhou kilns21.

7.3.2.4 Mixian Kilns in Henan
The Mixian kilns were in production from the Tang Dynasty to the early
Song. The kiln site was discovered in 1961 in the Xiguan area of Mixian
(now Xinmi City). Compared with the products of the Gongxian and Ding
kilns, the white porcelain body of the Mixian kilns had a slightly rougher
texture and was thicker and heavier, yet extensive use of engobe granted
Mixian white porcelain a delicate appearance and a clear white color. The
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
pot and jar shards found at the site were decorated with green that dripped
naturally downward to form simple vertical stripe patterns. This natural
decorative method broke the dull uniformity of white porcelain and opened
up a new avenue for white porcelain decoration in later periods.

7.3.2.5 Hunyuan Kilns in Shanxi
The Hunyuan kilns were an important ancient porcelain kiln cluster in
Shanxi Province. In addition to black porcelain and white porcelain, the
Hunyuan kilns also fired a kind of ware with tea-leaf color glaze, mostly
with engraved decorative patterns, but the glaze lacked gloss. Hunyuan kiln
products bore distinct regional characteristics, for both their shape design
and decorative patterns were different from those of vessels produced in
Hebei and Henan, except for perhaps the jade bi shaped bottom that was a
common style across almost all kilns of the time. Although in the Tang
Dynasty the main varieties fired by the Hunyuan kilns were also daily life
utensils such as bowls, plates and jars, the rolled rim bowl that was the
common style of the Xing and Ding kilns was replaced by mat pattern
shallow bowls of diverse design by the Hunyuan kilns. Bowls and jars with
mat patterns were mostly thick and heavy with a pale grayish white body
and lustrous glaze. Although they have lasted for over a thousand years,
some remain as new. Especially exquisite is the white glaze, which is pure
and thick with the whiteness reaching 61.8 degrees. Though the white
glazed vessels are not as famous as those of the Xing and Ding kilns of the
same time, they are still rare and valuable works. In recent years more white
porcelain kiln sites from the Tang Dynasty have been found in Shanxi,
among which the Pingding, Hejin, and Xiangning kilns are important. The
discovery of these kilns is helpful to the comprehensive exploration of the
development of northern white porcelain in the Tang Dynasty.
   From the last section we can see that apart from the Yaozhou kilns, most
celadon kilns in the Sui and Tang dynasties were in the south, and from this
section it can be seen that kilns producing white porcelain were mostly in
northern China. Therefore, the ceramic production landscape in the Sui and
Tang Dynasties can be summarized as “southern celadon and northern
white”.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
7.4 Underglaze Decorated Porcelain and Other
Porcelains of the Tang and Five Dynasties
“Southern celadon and northern white porcelain” was only a description of
the ceramic production landscape of the Tang Dynasty in general. Besides
celadon and white porcelain, new varieties such as “underglaze decorated
porcelain” and “colorful porcelain” were also produced in the Tang
Dynasty. Still another important achievement of porcelain-making
technology of the Tang Dynasty was “tricolor pottery.”

7.4.1 Underglaze Decorated Porcelain
It was in the Tang Dynasty that underglaze decorated earthenware was
created and experienced initial development. It is my firm belief that no
ceramic variety came into being in isolation from the others. In fact, the
appearance of underglaze decorated ware in the Tang Dynasty was closely
related to the development of the tricolor ware and fambe flower ware of
the same period, and the development of tricolor ware and underglaze
decorated ware in turn promoted the development of the blue and white
porcelain of the Tang Dynasty. The most famous producers of underglaze
decorated ware in the Tang Dynasty were the Changsha kilns in Hunan
(Fig. 7.45), Qiong kilns in Sichuan, and Huai’an kilns in Fujian.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 7.45 Changsha kiln yellow-glazed brown-painting bird pattern pot,
Tang Dynasty, height: 19.2 cm, top diam.: 10.4 cm, in the Hunan Tongguan Ceramics Corporation
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
7.4.1.1 Changsha Kilns in Hunan
The Changsha kilns, located in Tongguan Town in Changsha, Hunan, were
also called the Tongguan kilns in the past. The sites were discovered in
1956. In 1964 the Changsha Cultural Bureau conducted focused
excavations based on previous investigations. The excavations retrieved
about 2,000 pieces of porcelain work, cleared two dragon kilns and
discovered a large number of kiln tools, providing tangible materials for the
study of the history, technology, and product variety and features of the
Changsha kilns. More comprehensive excavations were carried out in 1983
that offered a further insight into all aspects of the Changsha kilns’ ceramic
production during the Tang Dynasty.
   The Changsha kilns mainly fired celadon in its early stages, started
firing celadon with brown painting in the mid-Tang Dynasty, and then
progressed to produce celadon with brown and green painting, white glazed
ware with green painting, and white glazed ware with brown and green
painting. Production of these wares continued for 140 years into the late
Tang and Five Dynasties. A major contribution of the Changsha kilns
during the Tang Dynasty was the maturity of the underglaze decoration
technique.
   The beauty and diversity of Changsha kiln ware was rare in Tang kilns.
Products included daily use utensils, stationery, sculptures and toys. Early
Changsha kilns mainly produced bowls, plates, pots, jars and yu, which
were of uniform design. Then more daily use objects appeared, including
washers, pillows, lamps, holders and boxes, on top of which there also
emerged stationery including paperweights, inkstone water holders, writing-
brush basins, writing-brush holders, and ink slabs, as well as various
sculptured toys including figurines, birds, dogs, pigs, elephants, goats,
lions, frogs, roosters, geese, horses, oxen, camels and tigers. Also produced
were vivid and lifelike sculptures of people riding lions, horses or
elephants, figurines holding fruit, figurines with balls in their arms, and
figurines drumming.
  Common decoration techniques of Chang kiln products were decals,
molding, carving, openwork, imprinting, etc. Decals were often fixed under
the spout or lugs of pots or on the bellies of washers. The decals often had a
layer of brown glaze patches applied to highlight their decorative effect.
Molded patterns included human figures, lions, grapes, lingzhi mushrooms,
Cyathea, date palm patterns, female dancers, and Buddhist warriors. The
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
exotic themes were obviously introduced during interaction with foreign
cultures and were presumably related to the mass export of Changsha kiln
products at the time. Carved patterns were often used on bottles, yi (gourd-
shaped ladles), pots and other vessels. Through-carved holes were used to
decorate candle holders, incense burners, vessel lids and vessel bases.
Imprinted patterns were used on the wells of plates and bowls and on the
ears and handles of pots and jars. Relief patterns of lotus flowers, lotus
roots and birds were stamped onto vessels with molds carved with the
images. (Fig. 7.46).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 7.46 Changsha kiln pot with underglaze flower and bird pattern,
Tang Dynasty, height: 22.7 cm, top diam.: 11 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Underglaze color painting as a means of decoration developed from a
single brown color to brown and green, and the themes developed from
brown and green spots to more complex images. (Fig. 7.47) The brown
coloring, with iron vitriol as the chromogenic reagent, was quite stable.
Painting with it offered stable color and smooth strokes just like painting on
paper with ink. Green coloring, on the other hand, with copper oxide as the
chromogenic reagent, was not stable at high temperature. Therefore, in most
cases brown coloring was used to draw lines while green coloring was used
to fill the color. Sometimes green color patches were painted as leaves and
petals while brown color was used to draw the stems and stamens. The
effect was also remarkable. Although only brown and green were used for
the underglaze painting, the two colors could create diverse effects through
alternate or repeated use.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 7.47 Changsha kiln jar with brown and green cloud pattern,
Tang Dynasty, height: 29.4 cm, top diam.: 16.2 cm, in the Yangzhou Museum

    Initially underglaze painting was used on decals or simply used to apply
brown spots on vessel surfaces, when in fact a substantial portion of
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Changsha kiln wares had plain surfaces. Later as the single brown color
developed into brown and green colors, the patterns depicted became more
complex and evolved from realism to freehand brushwork. The composition
was concise, and the images vivid. A unique feature of Changsha kiln
porcelains was the deep or shallow, thick or light tones formed by the
infiltration of copper green glaze into the ceramic body at high temperature.
The decoration was mostly used on both sides of a pot’s spout and handle,
on a pillow’s surface or at the center of a bowl’s well.
   The themes of the underglaze paintings of Changsha kiln celadon
included plants, animals and human figures. The lines were simple but
vivid, and the artistic conception was fresh and far-reaching. Some images
were made up entirely of brown and green colors without initial line-art.
Though they might contain only a few sketches, they gave wonderful play
to the beauty of impressionism and set a model for the ceramic decoration
of later times. Another major feature of the underglaze painting of
Changsha kiln celadon in the Tang Dynasty was the use of poetry and
calligraphy as decoration. Of the vessels found during the kiln site
excavations in 1983, some 248 articles carried inscriptions and over 60
poems were found among the inscriptions. The poems were usually written
right under the spouts of pots, or on the surface of pillows and on the inner
walls of bowls and dishes. Each vessel was inscribed with a poem, or with
ballads, proverbs, mottoes, maxims, other well-known sayings and
sometimes general idioms. Most inscriptions were written in Xingshu
(semi-cursive or running script) and small numbers of Caoshu (cursive or
sloppy script) were also employed. Though text as ceramic decoration had
already appeared in some cases prior to the period, the rich and diverse use
of text by Changsha kiln ware was unprecedented. Subsequently, the
inscription by the Changsha of poetry on ceramics became an important
style in Chinese ceramic decoration. (Fig. 7.48).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 7.48 Changsha kiln blue-glazed pot with brown poetry inscription,
Tang Dynasty, height: 19 cm, top diam.: 11 cm, Cultural Relics Work Team of Changsha, Hunan
Province

   The poems on Changsha wares were rich in content, concise in
language, profound in meaning, and easy to pronounce and understand.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Some described scenery, some taught people to do good and to be grateful
to parents, some expressed the homesickness of young men traveling, some
expressed the melancholy of parting, some depicted military life at frontier
fortresses, some reflected the darkness and misery of society, and still
others urged people to study hard and make progress. The large number of
simple poems show us that the Tang Dynasty was truly a world of poetry, a
time when poems were not only created and appreciated by the elite literati,
but also had deep roots in the common people and reached the bottom of
society as well.
   The Tang Dynasty was an era of openness. Accordingly, Changsha kiln
products were not only for the domestic market but were also exported to
more and more overseas markets with the continuous expansion of foreign
trade at the time. While spreading to foreign lands, Changsha kiln products
were also enriched by foreign cultures and such foreign influence helped
them better meet the needs of export. Specifically, the vessels used West
Asian and Persian style decals as decoration, such as images of dancing
foreigners, lion dances, coconut groves, grapes, and exotic birds and
magpies. Although export of Changsha ware began later than that of Xing
and Yue ware, Changsha ware later surpassed them and rose to the top in
early overseas Chinese porcelain sales, because the shape and decoration of
Changsha kiln products better suited the preferences and needs of overseas
markets.

7.4.1.2 Qiong Kilns in Sichuan
Other than celadon, the Qiong kilns also produced underglaze decorated
porcelain. Like the Changsha kilns, the Qiong kilns also used clay with a
high iron content to make the body, which was first covered with a layer of
white engobe and then fired at a high temperature. Decorative patterns were
also similar to the Changsha kilns, including linked beads, joint circles,
grass blades, and brown and green patches and stripes, except that the
decorative images of Changsha kiln products were even richer and more
colorful, especially the poem inscriptions, painted landscapes and human
figures. In the Tang Dynasty green opaque glaze was the main glaze used
by both the Qiong and Changsha kilns. It is only that the Qiong kilns started
using green opaque glaze in the late Southern Dynasties or the beginning of
the Sui Dynasty, about two centuries earlier than the Changsha kilns. A
joint contribution of the two kiln groups was that “the potters of the Qiong
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and Changsha kilns first discovered red copper glaze, took the initiative to
experiment with it, and passed it on to later generations. Thus, the
origination of red copper glaze should be attributed to them”. A prominent
difference between the products of the two kiln groups was in terms of
decoration. The Changsha kilns were good at attaching molded patterns of
individual human figures or animals onto conspicuous parts of handled pots
or jars, while the Qiong kilns mainly used brown or yellow patches as
decoration. Such yellow patch decoration has not been found on Changsha
kiln products to date.22
   Other commonalities between the Qiong and Changsha kilns included
the general style of blue glaze decorated with brown and green spots, and
the same throwing method. In fact, the products of the two kiln groups were
basically the same. These similarities must not be coincidental and suggest
close relations between the two. That is also why some scholars believe that
the Changsha kilns inherited and developed the advanced technology of the
Qiong kilns.23

7.4.1.3 Huai’an Kilns in Fujian
The earliest underglaze decorated porcelain produced in Fujian that has
been found to date was made by the Huai’an kilns and dates back to the
period from the Liang Dynasty of the Southern Dynasties to the Zhenyuan
era of the Tang Dynasty. Still, analysis of Huai’an kiln products unearthed
in Japan suggest there were other kilns producing such ware that have not
been discovered in areas near Huai’an. These undiscovered kilns must be
from the late eighth century to the end of the tenth century.24
   Huai’an kilns underglaze decorated ware during the Tang and Five
Dynasties was relatively lacking in style, with only blue glazed vessels
decorated with brown or caramel colors. Decorative techniques were
monotonous as well—only brown spots or patches were applied on a few
varieties, namely, plate-mouthed pots, handled pots, jars and bowls, mostly
on the mouth, shoulder, belly or on the area below the handles, lugs and
spout. The Shanghai Institute of Ceramics of the Chinese Academy of
Sciences tested the products and described them as “looking like cream and
jade with no cracking, very few glaze bubbles, solid texture, and smooth
fracture surfaces; in general superior to later porcelains in quality”. This
shows that the Huai’an kilns had mastered relatively advanced porcelain-
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
making technologies and had acquired exceptional temperature control
ability.25

7.4.2 Other Porcelains of the Tang Dynasty
As mentioned above, porcelains of the Tang Dynasty were not limited to
“southern celadon and northern white”. There were also underglaze
decorated ware, “colorful porcelain,”multi-clay ware, black porcelain, etc.,
the first of which has just been introduced. This section will be devoted to
the latter three.

7.4.2.1 “Colorful Porcelain”
The appearance of “colorful porcelain” was another major achievement of
the Tang Dynasty’s ceramic technology. The so-called “colorful porcelain”
referred to a kind of ware with a black or brown backdrop glaze on which
there was milky white glaze with blue, gray or purple spots (Fig. 7.49),
creating an effect similar to the naturally formed “fambe glaze” (when in
fact it was an artificial decoration). The decorations were natural, vivid and
unrestrained, some like a cloud, some like a leaf, some like a wave, and
some like a splash of ink. The main varieties were pots, jars and hand
drums. Most of the existing colorful porcelain vessels were unearthed
before the 1950s by non-official means. After the 1950s, some were
unearthed in the Tang tombs in Zhengzhou, Biyang, and Jiaxian in Henan
Province. Some articles had appeared in the antique market and were called
“Tang Jun.”According to the Records of the Jie Drums by Nan Zhuo of the
Tang Dynasty, colorful porcelain waist drums were produced in Lushan,
Henan Province. In 1977, the Palace Museum for a third time sent
researchers to Lushan to determine the production kilns of colorful
porcelain. The investigators finally found a number of fragments of black-
glazed spotted waist drums at the Duandian kiln site in Lushan, which were
exactly the same as the waist drum collected by the Palace Museum, and
therefore confirmed the record in Nan Zhuo’s Records of the Jie Drums.
They also learnt that apart from the Huangdao kilns in Jiaxian and the
Duandian kilns in Lushan, the Shangbaiyu kilns in Yuxian (modern-day
Yuzhou) also fired “colorful porcelain,”because similar shards of waist
drums were also found at that site. The fact that Yuzhou was the hometown
of the Jun kilns in the Song Dynasty suggested that the appearance of the
Jun kilns in the Song Dynasty was closely related to “colorful porcelain.”I
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
once saw an extremely exquisite lidded jar with black backdrop glaze and
milky white glaze in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S. (Fig.
7.50).





Fig. 7.49 Lushan kiln black-glazed pot with blue spots,
Tang Dynasty, height: 21.2 cm, top diam.: 7.9 cm, base diam.: 9.1 cm
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 7.50 Lushan kiln black-glazed lidded jar with colorful spots,
Tang Dynasty, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

  Among the collections of the Palace Museum is an extremely rare
colorful glaze hand drum, the largest and most intact artifact of its kind
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
known so far. (Fig. 7.51) Other such artifacts collected elsewhere are
smaller in size and mostly restored from fragments. In the 1980s, fragments
of colorful glaze ware were also found at the Yaozhou kiln site. The
fragments mostly had black, blue or tea-leaf colored glaze dotted with
white, blue and yellow spots. Apart from colorful spots, Yaozhou kiln
colorful porcelain featured more complex decorative patterns such as
blossoms and twigs of flowers. Varieties included plates, handled pots, yu,
and hand drums. Among the fragments unearthed, many were of hand
drums, which were of three types, namely, black glaze with white color,
blue glaze with milky yellow color, and tea-leaf glaze with yellow color,
with the first type accounting for the majority.

7.4.2.2 Multi-clay Ware
Multi-clay and multi-glaze ware was a type of porcelain that appeared in
northern China, notably in Henan and Hebei, in the Tang Dynasty, and so
far has not been found before this period. The ware was made from mixing
two different materials together to produce special patterns. In the industry
it is customary to refer to those made from two different body materials as
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
“multi-clay ware” and those made from two different glazes “multi-glaze
ware.”The special pattern of multi-clay ware resided in the body while that
of multi-glaze ware, in most cases simpler, was only on the surface of the
objects. The patterns, some like rolling clouds and flowing water, some
resembling the texture of marble, and some similar to the texture of feathers
or wood, are of great natural interest. Creating such ware required a high
technological level since the expansion coefficient and shrinkage ratio of
the materials of different colors must be the same, otherwise the object
would crack or deform when being fired in the kiln. (Fig. 7.52).





Fig. 7.52 Multi-clay pillow,
Tang Dynasty, height: 8 cm, base: 12.5 × 8.8 cm

   Tang dynasty multi-clay porcelain shards have been found in Lushan
and Gongxian in Henan and at the Yaozhou kiln site in Shaanxi. Multi-clay
shards from the Song Dynasty have subsequently been found at the sites of
the Dangyangyu kilns in Henan, the Yuci kilns in Shanxi and the Zibo kilns
in Shandong. Those from the Tang Dynasty used yellow and brown clay
with yellow as the main color, while those from the Song Dynasty used
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
white to set the tone and black or brown as the accompanying color. Song
dynasty multi-clay ware was of an especially high standard of
craftsmanship with more developed decorative patterns, some of which
resembled mat patterns and some arranged like feathers. (Fig. 7.53).





Fig. 7.53 Multi-clay pillow,
Tang Dynasty, height: 8.2 cm, length: 14.5 cm, width: 10.6 cm, in the Shanghai Museum

    Multi-clay porcelain was only found in the Tang and Song dynasties.
Although later during the reigns of Yongzheng and Qianlong of the Qing
Dynasty there appeared similar products, their patterns were painted with
color glazes to imitate the multi-clay effect rather than made from the
mixture of two types of clay. Products imitating and following the
technique of multi-clay ware have even been found in the modern history of
both Japanese and Western porcelains, which demonstrates the far-reaching
influence of Tang and Song Dynasty multi-clay ware.

7.4.2.3 Black Porcelain
Apart from celadon and white porcelain, there was yet another type of once-
glazed porcelain in the Tang Dynasty, namely, black porcelain, which was
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
fired in a wide range of places by almost all kilns that produced white
porcelain and celadon. That was because its composition differed from
celadon and white porcelain only in iron content and the firing atmosphere
differed only in using oxidizing or reducing flame. That black porcelain was
widely fired is an evidence-based observation since remains of black ware
were found in almost every ancient kiln site in both the south and north that
have been excavated over the years. Large numbers of black glazed shards
have been unearthed from the Tang dynasty strata of the sites of many
famous northern kilns, such as the Ding kilns in Quyang and the Xing kilns
in Neiqiu (Hebei), the Hunyuan kilns (Shanxi), the Tiejianglu kilns in
Gongxian, the Xiguan kilns in Mixian and the Hebiji kilns in Tangyin
(Henan), and the Yaozhou kilns in Tongchuan (Shaanxi). Black porcelain
production was undertaken in both southern and northern China, but the
output was not high due to limited market demand. (Fig. 7.54).

7.5 Tricolor Pottery of the Tang Dynasty
7.5.1 Firing Techniques and Kiln Locations
The large-scale production of porcelain during the Tang Dynasty to a large
extent pushed pottery out of people’s daily lives, but pottery still firmly
dominated burial object production and even saw new development, namely
the invention of tricolor pottery. Tang tricolor pottery differed from
ordinary low-temperature glazed pottery. Its body was made of white clay
(kaolinite) and it had low-temperature glaze containing lead applied. The
glaze used multiple metals including iron, copper, manganese and cobalt as
colorants. Different metals had different coloring effects. For instance, after
firing copper oxide was green, iron oxide was yellowish-brown, and cobalt
oxide was blue. Lead was used as a glaze solvent to take advantage of its
fluidity in the firing process to bring out a rich variety of colors including
yellow, ochre, jade green, dark green, sky blue, brownish red, and eggplant
purple. The gorgeous mixture of bright colors fill people’s imagination with
the splendor of the epic Tang Dynasty. The vessels were fired twice. First
plain greenware was fired at about 1,100 ℃, then glaze was applied, and
finally it was fired at a lower temperature of about 900 ℃. The technology
was developed based on the lead-glazed pottery of the Han Dynasty. The
so-called “tricolor”, a literal translation of its Chinese name, actually meant
colorful or multicolor. In fact, the colors were in no way limited to three.
Green, yellow, ochre, brown, red, white, blue, black and many other colors
could all be seen, sometimes only one for one ware but in most cases
several in a mixture.
   The origin of the tricolor pottery of the Tang Dynasty can be found in
the lead-glazed pottery of the Han Dynasty. Back in the Han Dynasty
Chinese potters succeeded in making monochrome glazed pottery with a
glossy and brightly colored appearance. Later in the Southern & Northern
Dynasties, lead-glazed pottery in the north witnessed new developments,
taking a step further from the monochrome glaze of the Han Dynasty to the
firing of ware with a white background and green coloring, ware with a
yellow background and green coloring, and triple-color ware of yellow,
brown and green. (Fig. 7.55).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 7.55 Tricolor plate,
Tang Dynasty, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the U.S

   Thus it is safe to say that the emergence of the Tang tricolor ware was
an inevitable result of the development of the glazed pottery of the Han and
Wei dynasties, yet the magnificence, splendor and unusual effervescence of
Tang Dynasty tricolor pottery was far from something that the Han dynasty
glazed pottery or any other painted pottery could compare with.
   Tang tricolor pottery was first fired during Emperor Gaozong’s reign
and became prevalent as burial objects in Tang tombs by the reign of
Emperor Xuanzong. As for the production site, it was generally believed
that there must be large-scale workshops in the vicinity of Chang’an, the
capital of the Tang Dynasty, and Luoyang, the eastern capital. This belief
has been proven true by investigations. Luoyang was the main distribution
center of Tang tricolor pottery at the time, and Gongxian, the nearest county
to Luoyang, was the main production area. In 1976, Henan Museum and the
Gongxian Cultural Relics Management Committee discovered kiln groups
that produced Tang tricolor pottery in Dahuangye, Xiaohuangye,
Longwangmiao, and other places in Gongxian County, and unearthed a rich
variety of specimens, including triple-color (yellow, green and white)
double-lugged bowls, white glazed bowls with blue coloring, blue glazed
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
vases, and decal pottery molds. Gongxian County was not the only place
that produced tricolor pottery in the Tang Dynasty. Other production sites in
Henan included the Duandian kilns in Lushan, the Liujiamen and
Yangjiagou kilns in Yuzhou, and the Quhe kilns in Dengfeng.
   The second tricolor pottery kiln site in the Tang Dynasty discovered in
China after Gongxian County was the Yaozhou kilns. During excavations of
the Huangbao site in Tongchuan, archaeologists found a group of
workshops and three kilns devoted to the production of Tang tricolor
pottery. Discovered in the workshops were Tang Dynasty glazed tiles,
including green, yellow, yellowish green, yellowish-brown and brown, as
well as triple-color tiles and triple-color lotus-pattern eave tiles. The glazed
tiles seem to have been made for palaces in the capital Chang’an since
green and yellow glazed tiles were once also unearthed at the Chang’an
Daming Palace Site. In May 1999, another kiln site for the production of
Tang tricolor pottery was found near Xi’an Airport, which, compared to the
Yaozhou kilns in the remote Tongchuan, enjoyed much more convenient
transportation to supply tricolor pottery to the capital city of Chang’an back
in the Tang Dynasty. Products unearthed there included bowl-shaped
remnants with blue or green coloring, a style that was different from the
tricolor ware of the Yaozhou kilns, but similar to the tricolor products of the
Gongxian kilns.26
   The Yaozhou kilns in Shaanxi and the Gongxian and Lushan kilns in
Henan were by no means the only production sites of Tang tricolor pottery.
In fact, shards of Tang tricolor pottery have also been found in the Xing
kilns in Neiqiu and the Ding kilns in Quyang, both in Hebei Province, and
workshops of Tang tricolor pottery have been found in Sichuan. Ye Zhemin
argues that not all production sites of Tang tricolor pottery have been found
because the demand for tricolor pottery in the Tang Dynasty was huge, yet
the scale of the kiln sites found so far has been limited, and the remnants
unearthed in the sites do not exactly tally with the tricolor artifacts found in
Tang tombs in terms of shape and color. This suggests there are still a
considerable number of production sites yet to be discovered in modern-day
Shaanxi, Henan, Hebei, Shanxi, Hunan, Sichuan, and elsewhere.27

7.5.2 Functions and Decorative Techniques
Because of their high lead content, Tang tricolor wares were seldom used in
daily life and were mostly burial objects. They can be roughly divided into
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
three categories, vessels, figurines and models. There were over 10 varieties
of vessel, including bottles, pots, jars, bowls, cups, plates, yu, candlesticks,
and pillows (Figs. 7.56, 7.57, and 7.58), and each variety had many styles.
For bottles alone there were double-dragon-eared bottles, double-lugged flat
bottles, flowery mouthed bottles, washer-style-mouthed bottles, and thin-
necked melon-belly bottles. Figurines were of both human and animal, the
former including ladies, female and male servants, horse-leading men, civil
officials, warriors, foreigners, and guardians of Buddhism, (Fig. 7.59) and
the latter including horses, donkeys, camels, pigs, cattle, sheep, dogs,
chickens, and ducks. The third category was models of various architectures
and household utilities, covering almost everything that the dead may have
enjoyed when alive, with the most common being buildings, towers,
gardens with rockery and waterside pavilions, and all kinds of houses,
warehouses, toilets, carriages, and cabinets. Tricolor figurines came into
existence later than tricolor vessels and appeared in large numbers in tombs
only after the reign of Wu Zetian.

text:
Tang tricolor pottery, overcoming the limitation of previous
monochrome glazes, used a variety of glaze colors for decoration and
achieved an extraordinarily exquisite artistic effect. Although the surface
decoration techniques of Tang tricolor ware were traditional, like printing,
decals, engraving, and sculpting, it had its own unique prominence. Potters
used a brush that had been dipped in glaze to draw reticulate patterns,
speckles and colorful ribbons on the vessels, or, imitating the batik process
of Tang Dynasty silk, put wax on certain areas of the vessel surface and
then applied glaze so that the waxed areas were not colored by glaze and
retained the original white body, which set off and added radiance to the
colorful and brilliant patterns. Another common decorative technique of
tricolor pottery was the application of bright colorful glazes on sculptured
or imprinted patterns to create an effect similar to that of relief. The
development of tricolor decorative art in the Tang Dynasty was influenced
not only by ceramic art itself, but also, directly or indirectly, by
contemporaneous sister art forms such as painting, gold and silver ware,
sculpture, lacquerware, and shell embedding technology.
   The clay used by Tang tricolor pottery had excellent plasticity and
therefore allowed rich molding methods, among which the most commonly
used were clay slice bonding, the potter’s wheel and fashioning with
models. Objects fashioned by clay slice bonding were mostly square or
rectangular, such as pillows and couches, while bottles, jars, plates, bowls
and dishes were shaped with the wheel.
   The Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras in the Tang Dynasty (CE 713 to 756)
were the peak period for tricolor pottery production. Tricolor pottery during
this period was produced in large quantities and with good quality, and was
of varied colors and diverse shapes. After the Tianbao era the volume of
tricolor pottery gradually decreased and after the middle and late Tang
Dynasty it was scarcely found in tombs and was gradually replaced by
porcelain. However, its influence was far-reaching, having close relations
with later ceramic categories such as the tricolor ware of the Liao Dynasty,
the tricolor ware of the Song Dynasty, the Liuli and Fahua ware of the Yuan
and Ming dynasties, and the plain tricolor ware and wucai ware of the Ming
and Qing dynasties.
   Another contribution of Tang tricolor pottery was the use of cobalt
(CoO). Cobalt oxide is blue and its pioneering use in ceramics
foreshadowed the emergence of blue and white porcelain later. In fact, in
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
1975, a fragment of a Tang blue and white porcelain pillow was found at
the Yangzhou Tang city site. Then in 1983 more shards of Tang blue and
white porcelain were found in Yangzhou. Tests on the body and glaze of the
shards found that the coloring used on them, low manganese (MnO) cobalt
ore, was the same as the blue coloring of Tang tricolor pottery. Laser
microscopic analysis also showed that the coloring had a low manganese
content and contained a small amount of copper (CuO). Its MnO/CoO ratio
and CoO/CuO ratio was similar to those of the blue glaze of Henan Tang
tricolor ware.28 However, due to the limited amount of evidence found, the
origin and development history of the blue coloring is still to be further
investigated and discussed.

7.5.3 Tricolor Pottery Statues
Burying pottery statues with the dead had long been popular before the
Tang Dynasty, notably the terracotta warriors and horses of the Qin Dynasty
and the various human and animal figurines of the Han Dynasty. Such a
funerary custom continued into the Tang Dynasty and as a result Tang
tricolor pottery as burial objects experienced rapid development, especially
pottery statues, which, with their rich varieties and wide range, can serve as
a key for us to learn about and understand the culture of the Tang Dynasty.
   One example was upper class female figurines, which made up a
considerable proportion of the tricolor pottery of the Tang Dynasty. Mostly
unearthed from the tombs of high officials and dignitaries, the figurines
represented the image of noble women in the Tang Dynasty, with some the
symbols of the tomb owner. Under the influence of the imperial court’s
pursuit of luxury, the clothes of noble women in the Tang Dynasty were
gorgeously colored and meticulously collocated. The dresses of the tricolor
pottery figurines unearthed in Tang tombs in Shaanxi and Henan are breath-
taking. They are accurate reproductions of women’s clothes at the time. The
prosperity of the economy and culture in the Tang Dynasty brought about
women’s liberation. A large amount of materials unearthed from the tombs
of the Tang Dynasty showed that women at that time could follow their own
interests in dress, and were also allowed to go on excursions or go hunting
on horseback, play polo, and participate in other sports activities like men.
The large number of horse-riding women figurines unearthed from tombs of
the Tang Dynasty were a true portrayal of the social fashion.29
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Horse statues make up a large proportion of the cultural relics unearthed
from the Tang Dynasty, and among them tricolor pottery horses are an
especially prominent part of the Tang Dynasty’s funerary culture. Tang
tricolor horses had a strong style unique to the time with small heads, long
necks, and plump bodies. They are of two sizes, large between 69 and
81 cm and small about 30 cm. The horses came in multiple colors,
including blue, yellow, white, black and green, with neatly trimmed bristles
and saddles. The saddles had green mud barriers, and some were decorated
with green tassels. Some horses had decorative accessories on their bodies
and heads, such as apricot leaf shaped patterns on the headstall and the
same pattern or blossoms on the leather straps. Statues of horse dancing,
horse-leading figurines and horse-training figurines were also common.
Some of the horse-leading figurines portrayed Westerners and some Han
people, based on their facial features. Figure 7.60 shows such a tricolor
figurine.

   Elephant statues were also very characteristic and exotic. One such
figurine depicts a tame elephant standing on a rectangular floor with a
circular felt blanket on its back. The blanket has tassels and sitting on it are
two Westerner figurines that wear pointed felt caps and high felt boots.30
   Oxcart statues are a new form of burial object that appeared in the Tang
Dynasty. The green glazed pottery oxcart in the collection of the Shaanxi
Museum, 15 cm high, is a model of a cart pulled by an ox on a rectangular
base. The ox appears quite strong with short, thick legs and upright horns
and has a very vivid look. It is fastened between thills that pull the carriage.
The front of the rectangular carriage is sheltered with curtains, the top is
covered with an arch-shaped roof and above the roof is a semi-circular
canopy. The large wheels of the carriage each have eight spokes. The Tang
tricolor oxcart unearthed at the Yaozhou kiln site in Tongchuan, Shaanxi
Province in 1984 is 18 cm tall. It consists of a carriage, shafts, a crosspiece
and wheels. The square carriage opens on the right side of the rear end and
has a canopy that curls up at the front and back ends. Each wheel of the cart
has six spokes.31
   Camel statues were another kind of animal figurine that constituted a
considerable proportion of burial objects and tricolor pottery products of the
Tang Dynasty. There are many highly exquisite camel statues from the
time. Tang people loved camels like they loved horses. Long known as the
“boats of the desert”, camels were an important as well as the most
commonly used means of transportation in the desert and on the ancient
Silk Road at the time. The large number of camel statues excavated reflects
the busyness of the Silk Road and the frequent cultural exchanges between
China and foreign countries in the Tang Dynasty. (Fig. 7.61).

    In addition, figurines of civil officials, military officers, guardians of
Buddhism, and tomb-guarding beasts also frequently appeared in the tombs
of the Tang dynasty nobility, and occupied an important position in the
funerary culture of the Tang Dynasty. Figurines of civil officials had kind
expressions, neat clothes, and standard postures, in general a sage-like,
gentle, respectful and modest demeanor. Figurines of military officers, on
the contrary, were daunting in both facial expression and clothing. They
were symbols of force and majesty, the nemesis of demons and ghosts, and
defenders of the underworld.32 (Fig. 7.62) The guardians of Buddhism,
according to legend, could not only protect Buddhist altars from demons,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

but also protect tombs from evil. With the rising popularity of Buddhism,
production of such figurines became prevalent in the Tang Dynasty and the
figurines were very popular in large and medium-sized tombs of the Tang
Dynasty. Figurines of tomb-guarding beasts, mostly squatting, with human
or animal faces, large curved horns and big ears on their heads, and wings
and flames on their shoulders and backs. They were ferocious and believed
to drive away vile forces, repel epidemic diseases, and keep the soul of the
tomb owner at peace.33

7.6 Blue and White Porcelain of the Tang Dynasty
Before the 1970s academic circles paid attention only to the Yuan Dynasty
when it came to the creation of blue and white porcelain because
researchers did not know much about the blue and white porcelain of the
Tang Dynasty, a circumstance that began to change upon the first discovery
of Tang blue and white porcelain in Yangzhou in 1975. In the four decades
since then, nearly 100 pieces of Tang blue and white porcelain wares with
different shapes have been unearthed in Yangzhou during archaeological
excavations and urban reconstruction. In addition, a number of white glazed
boxes with blue coloring, white glazed vessels with yellow and blue
colorings, etc. have also been unearthed in the city site. So far, the blue and
white porcelain shards found in Yangzhou are of bowls, plates, pillows,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
boxes, bottles (pots) and so on. Bowls and plates make up the most and
some of them could be restored.34

7.6.1 Market of Tang Blue and White Porcelain
The blue and white porcelain of the Yuan Dynasty was produced mainly to
meet the needs of Islamic countries, yet the destinations of the Tang blue
and white porcelain market, domestic or overseas, remains a topic to be
explored. Presumably the development of the porcelain industry in the Tang
Dynasty was not only to meet the needs of the domestic market, but also to
expand foreign trade. With the progress of China’s shipbuilding industry
and the continuous improvement in navigation technology, the Maritime
Silk Road developed rapidly, and water transportation facilitated the export
of ceramics, which by this time had become the main commodity in China’s
maritime foreign trade. One famous foreign trade port of the Tang Dynasty
was Yangzhou, which, located on the Yangtze River at a major juncture of
water and land transportation, attracted with its advantageous geographical
conditions many foreign businessmen who engaged in various commercial
activities and even lived there permanently. It became a famous commercial
metropolis in the Tang Dynasty. The large volume of Persian pottery
unearthed in the city suggests there were many Persian businessmen living
in Yangzhou at the time, and among them were many porcelain dealers who
transported ceramics from different parts of China to Yangzhou and then
transported them from Yangzhou to overseas markets through the Maritime
Silk Road.35 The theory that the blue and white porcelain of the Tang
Dynasty was produced primarily for export would be a good explanation for
the fact that very few remains of Tang blue and white porcelain have been
found in China. Even if it was not made for the domestic market at all,
which overseas markets it mainly targeted is still a question worth
exploring.
   The distribution of porcelain shards unearthed in archaeological
excavations suggested that porcelain shops in Yangzhou in the Tang
Dynasty were concentrated in the busy districts on the east and west banks
of the Guanhe River, which, also called the “City River,”was a major
transportation route extending from the north to the south through
Yangzhou in the Tang Dynasty and a distribution center for commodities
from local and other areas. On the east bank of the river was the famous
“Ten-kilometer Street” of the Tang Dynasty, which was the most
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
prosperous commercial district in Yangzhou at the time. In the middle and
late Tang Dynasty strata of this area, rich accumulations of ceramic shards
from various kilns have been found. The large quantity, rich variety, high
quality and fine decoration of these findings are rarely seen in other ancient
city sites in China. It was in the middle and late Tang strata of this area that
the blue and white porcelain of the Tang Dynasty was unearthed (Fig. 7.65).
Unearthed along with the blue and white porcelain from the same strata
were also a large quantity of white porcelain, polychrome porcelain and
Changsha kiln celadon, among which Changsha kiln celadon was the most
common. Many of the shards bear no signs of use or wear, indicating that
they were probably relics of commodities for export, which might have
been defective and so were left in the transportation center instead of being
transshipped.36 Is it true that these blue and white wares were not for use
but for export? Was blue and white porcelain of the Tang Dynasty, like that
of the Yuan Dynasty, produced also first for the Islamic market, and then
spread to other overseas markets? Another piece of supporting evidence for
this conjecture was the many West Asian style decorative patterns on the
Tang blue and white porcelain, such as geometric linked beads, clouds, vine
rhombuses, palms and grapes which were all popular decorative patterns in
the West Asian market. But still, so far it is only conjecture that Tang blue
and white porcelain was for export and the true story will require more
archaeological discoveries to substantiate.
