Song Dynasty, height: 27.5 cm, top diam.: 4.9 cm, base diam.: 7 cm, old collection of the Qing
palace

    In the Song Dynasty, Jun kilns used copper oxide as a colorant and for
the first time successfully fired copper red glaze in a reducing atmosphere, a
breakthrough in ceramic technology and a tremendous achievement at the
time. This also laid the foundation for the successful firing of high-
temperature red glaze later. The coloring of copper red glaze was extremely
sensitive to the addition of coloring agent, to the chemical composition of
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the glaze material, as well as to temperature, atmosphere and other factors.
Any deviation in these conditions would be sufficient to disrupt the
achievement of the normal red color. Such technical difficulties also
produced extremely varied glaze coloration during firing. Some became
rose purple, some crabapple flower red, some pale blue, some sky blue, and
some sky blue strewn with purplish red, like a sunset glow (Fig. 8.27).
There is a saying in China’s ceramic world: “there’s no identical Jun kiln
wares.” No two porcelain wares of the Jun kilns, even fired in the same
kiln, were completely the same, because their glaze color was naturally
formed and could not be artificially controlled. This was also in line with
the highest aesthetic ideal pursued at the time.





Fig. 8.27 Jun kiln blue-glazed bowl with purple patches,
Song Dynasty, height: 8.5 cm, top diam.: 9.5 cm, base diam.: 3.5 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Another feature of Jun ware was the “earthworm trail pattern,” which
refers to marks on the glaze surface which looked like the trail left by an
earthworm moving through mud. This was actually a defect that occurred
during the firing of Song Jun ware. The glaze layer of Jun ware was very
thick and thus was prone to cracking when the temperature was still low as
the kiln heated up. When the temperature moved higher, part of the glaze
with lower viscosity would flow into the cracks to fill them, thus creating
the earthworm trail pattern, which, like crackled glaze, was a defect formed
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
unintentionally in the firing process but which achieved a distinctive
decorative effect. Jun ware relied on unique glaze colors for decoration and
was therefore in no need of any engraved, carved or stuck ornamentation
(Fig. 8.28).





Fig. 8.28 Jun kiln rose-purple glaze rectangular flowerpot,
Song Dynasty, in the Palace Museum

   The flowerpots, zun and washers produced by the Jun kilns, mostly
imitating ancient bronze ritual objects, had archaic, simple and elegant
shapes and exquisite workmanship, and shared common characteristics with
Guan and Ru kiln ware of the same period. Hence, they must have been
fired for the needs of the court. The flower decoration that was popular with
porcelain in this period was also embodied in Jun ware. Yet it did not use
flower patterns. Rather, many varieties were designed in the shapes of
flowers, the common ones being crabapple-style mirror cases, crabapple-
style flowerpots, crabapple-style flower bowls, crabapple-style washers,
lotus-style flowerpots, lotus-style pot trays, and sunflower-style pot trays
(Fig. 8.29). The main varieties produced by official kilns were flowerpots,
mirror cases, washers, cuspidors, zun, bowls, plates, etc. Folk kilns fired
richer varieties thanks to their longer period of production. Apart from the
usual bowls and plates, there were also flagons, saucers, incense burners,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
jars, pillows, bottles and other wares, all of which were renowned for their
exquisite shapes and unique glaze colors.





Fig. 8.29 Jun kiln rose-purple glaze sunflower-style flowerpot,
Song Dynasty, height: 15.8 cm, top diam.: 22.8 cm, base diam.: 11.5 cm, in the Palace Museum

   The glaze texture of Jun porcelain was thick and moist in the first
instance and turned brighter and more crystal-like after firing due to the
fambe effect. Kiln workers carefully controlled the firing process based on
the metal oxides contained in the glaze to achieve brilliant and colorful
artistic effects on the glaze surface. The main shades were sky blue, pale
blue and rose purple, which blended and added radiance to each other.
Some wares were blue as the sky, some were pale blue like the moon or
jade, some were deep red like ripe crabapple fruit, and some were more
brilliant and wonderful with a mingling of red, purple, azure, and blue. As
described by the ancient Chinese, “one color when put into the kiln, and one
thousand colors when taken out” is a perfect illustration of the miraculous
transformation and brilliant artistic effects of Jun wares, which added a
most colorful chapter to China’s ceramic technology and aesthetics (Fig.
8.30).
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Fig. 8.30 Jun kiln blue-glazed jar,
Northern Song Dynasty, the Victoria & Albert Museum in the UK

   The Jun kiln system took shape later than the Yaozhou, Ding and
Cizhou kilns, but lasted longer than the Yaozhou and Ding kilns. The
system had its center in the Jun kilns in Yuzhou, Henan Province, but its
influence reached far beyond that. Archaeological investigations have found
sites of kilns firing Jun ware in 27 counties and prefectures in four
provinces and autonomous regions in northern China. In Henan, apart from
Yuzhou, there are also 17 counties and prefectures, including Ruzhou,
Jiaxian, Xuchang, Hebi, Anyang, Dengfeng, Baofeng, Lushan, Neixiang,
Yiyang, Xin’an, Jiaozuo, Qixian, Huixian, and Linzhou. Outside Henan
there are Cixian in Hebei, Hunyuan County in Shanxi, and Hohhot in Inner
Mongolia. The Juntai kilns in Yuzhou were official in nature and their Jun
ware products were all used as ornamental objects in the imperial palace
and were of exquisite workmanship and excellent quality. Shenhou in
Yuzhou was home to a concentrated number of Jun kilns in the Northern
Song Dynasty as the area boasted rich local resources such as porcelain clay
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and fuel, and more importantly, abundant malachite, a copper ore, in nearby
mountainous areas, which could bring out the ideal copper red color if
ground into powder, added to plant ash, mixed into the glaze material, and
fired in a reducing flame at high temperature. This new technique became
popular once successful and the technology of firing Jun ware thus
gradually spread.34

8.2.5 The Ru Kilns
The Ru kilns were a famous kiln system in the Song Dynasty, one that is
frequently mentioned in the notes of Southern Song scholars. However,
previous understanding of the Ru kilns was only from their products that
were handed down through generations, while the exact production site of
the Ru kilns was never found, a situation that changed only in 1986 when
archaeologists discovered a kiln site for firing palace-use porcelain at
Qingliang Temple in Baofeng, Henan. Several excavations in recent years
have answered many outstanding questions about the Ru kilns. Now it is
clear that the site of the Ru kilns is Qingliang Temple Village, Hanzhuang
Village and Baishipo Village in Daying Town, Baofeng, Henan, and the
total protected area of the site is some 1,332,000 m2. The site was listed in
the Top Ten New Archaeological Discoveries in China in 2000 and was
included among the 100 Major Protected Sites in China project in 2005.
Excavation of the site is still in progress (Figs. 8.31, 8.32, and 8.33).

    In the early and middle Northern Song Dynasty, the Yue kilns, after
almost one thousand years of glory, experienced a rapid decline due to a
fuel shortage, rising artisan salaries and heavy kiln industry taxes in the
Ningshao area of Zhejiang Province, transiting from large-scale commercial
production to small-scale production for local sales only. The craftsmanship
also became rough and crude in order to reduce costs and product quality
was far from the refined product that defined the peak of the Yue kilns. As
the Yue kilns declined, a brand-new celadon type rose and developed
rapidly in Henan, and that was Ru kiln celadon. The Ru kilns were deeply
influenced by the Yue and Yaozhou kilns in many respects. Some shape
designs were directly inherited from the Yue and Yaozhou kilns, such as the
outwardly extending circular foot of bowls and plates, which corresponded
exactly with that of Yue kiln ware. Some other shape designs were based on
those of Yue and Yaozhou kiln products but exhibited some changes. In
terms of decoration, the engraved, carved and sgraffito lotus petal patterns
popular in the Yue and Yaozhou kilns were also commonly seen on Ru kiln
porcelain. In terms of firing technology, the small sesame nails, a type of
kiln tool often used by Ru kilns, came from the Yaozhou kilns.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Soon after its emergence, Ru ware won the favor of the government and
became the first-choice porcelain of the court thanks to its exquisite
craftsmanship and the Song court’s preference for celadon. Lu You of the
Southern Song Dynasty recorded in his Notes in Old Scholar Hut: “In times
of the former capital (Northern Song), Ding porcelain was not allowed into
the imperial palace, and only Ru porcelain was used.”35
   Baofeng came under the jurisdiction of Ruzhou in the Sui Dynasty and
remained so until the Song Dynasty. Thus, it was natural that kilns in
Baofeng in the Song Dynasty were called Ru kilns. The discovery and
excavation of the sites of Ru official kilns in Qingliang Temple in Baofeng
confirmed the record that “Ru ware came from Ruzhou,” located the kilns
that fired the Ru ware handed down through dynasties and answered some
other historical problems concerning Ru ware that had been puzzling
researchers. The specimens unearthed had common characteristics with Jun
ware except for Ru official porcelain.
   The belief that the Ru kilns in the Song Dynasty used agate to make
glaze for tributary ware was corroborated by evidence of rich agate deposits
in the local area. Du Wan of the Song Dynasty recorded in his Stone
Catalogue of Cloudy Forest: “Agate stones could be found in sand or water
in Ruzhou. They were greenish white, pink and transparent, with some silk-
like patterns.” Zhou Hui wrote in his Qing Bo Za Zhi: in the Zhenghe
Fourth Year the Capital Transport Department reported receiving 25,000 jin
(12,500 kg) of agate produced in Ruzhou, with each stone weighing 21.5
jin. The two records showed that Ruzhou produced agate with a high yield
and good quality. History of Song, Records of Food and Goods, Mining and
Smelting further recorded: “In the beginning of the Zhenghe years…
Qingling Town in Ruzhou produced agate.” Qingling Town in Ruzhou is
present-day Daying Town in Baofeng, indicating that the Ru kilns had easy
access to local agate to make glaze.36
   The Ru kilns fired porcelain for the court for only two decades and were
folk kilns for the rest of their history. And even during the 20 years they
were official kilns, they were folk kilns at the same time and actually fired
more folk ware than court ware. That is why Ru official ware is rare and
precious, and it is because of such rarity that people in the Ming and Qing
dynasties often put Ru kilns in first place when talking about famous kilns
in the Song Dynasty. The glaze colors of Ru ware included sky blue, pale
blue, azure, pea green, greenish blue and egg-white. The Ru celadon
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
collected by the Palace Museum, Shanghai Museum, and Tianjin Art
Museum had a light azure glaze color, some slightly deeper, some slightly
paler, but all within the basic tone of light azure. The glaze color was on the
one hand due to the rulers’ aesthetic pursuit regarding official kiln
porcelain, and on the other hand attributable to the raw materials and firing
technology of porcelain making at the time. Studies show that the opacity of
celadon glaze was associated with the crystallization of anorthite, which in
turn was associated with the chemical composition and firing temperature
of the glaze. Anorthite crystallization reaches a maximum at 1125 ℃, yet
gradually dissolves with any further rise in temperature, and little would
remain if the firing temperature exceeded 1250 ℃.37 When firing celadon,
Ru official kilns on the one hand first used an oxidizing flame and then a
reducing flame, while on the other hand controlled the temperature at a
relatively low level (1125–1225 ℃) and allowed a period of time for slow
cooling, which all served to catalyze crystallization so that a large number
of short acicular crystals of anorthite would form, which actually made up
more than half of the volume of the glaze, and at the same time a large
number of small bubble groups appeared.38 It was thanks to such good
crystallization during firing that the glaze of Ru celadon not only had a light
azure color but also took on its wonderful jade-like opacity (Fig. 8.34).





Fig. 8.34 Ru kiln tripod plate,
Song Dynasty, height: 3.6 cm, top diam.: 18.3 cm, distance between feet: 16.7 cm, in the Palace
Museum

text:
The Ru ware that survives today is mostly plates and dishes, which can
be large or small, deep or shallow. Most have circular feet and some have
dented bottoms. There are also round or oval washers, some with three feet,
and oval four-legged washers which were unique to the Ru kilns of the
Song Dynasty. Bowls are rare. There are three types of bottles, namely
yuhuchun (pear-shaped vases), gallbladder bottles and paper-mallet-shaped
bottles, but only a small number have survived. There are also tripod zun
and chuji zun (flanged zun) which were inspired by bronze models, but the
numbers of such wares that have been handed down are extremely small,
numbering only one or two. Ru ware was mostly small, with the height
generally around 20 cm, and never exceeding 30 cm. The top diameter of
plates, washers, dishes and other round utensils is generally 10–16 cm, with
only a few rare items exceeding 20 cm.
   The body of Ru ware was thin and had an incense ash color. All round
vessels like plates and bowls were fully glazed with no body exposure on
the inside or outside or on the rim or foot. Propping tools, mainly nails,
were used to support the wares when they were being fired (Fig. 8.35),
leaving several marks on the bottom of the vessels, three at least and five at
most. The marks were very small and have been described by the ancients
as “small sesame-like needle marks on the bottom.” The glaze of Ru ware
mostly had crack patterns. Generally speaking, the crack pattern of
porcelain made by the Ge kilns was the densest and deepest. The cracks
were of different depths, the deeper ones appearing black and the shallower
ones pale yellow. Cracks with the two colors intertwined were called
“golden threads and iron lines.” The cracks of Guan kiln porcelain were
sparser and shallower, yet more obvious than that of Ru ware. Cracks of Ru
ware were even shallower and thinner. Barely visible, they looked like
transparent cracks on ice (Figs. 8.36 and 8.37).

   Described above are the characteristics of Ru official ware. Ru folk
kilns, which featured a longer manufacturing period and wider production
scale, might not have been as meticulous as Ru official kilns in terms of
glaze color or shape design. They fired more varieties, including bowls,
plates, zun, bottles, narcissus basins, yu (wide-mouthed jars/pots), saucers,
lamp holders and pillows. Their decorative techniques were also more
diverse than the Ru official kilns. In the early Northern Song Dynasty Ru
folk kilns did not attach much importance to decorative patterns, and
decorative techniques were simple. In the mid-Northern Song Dynasty, Ru
folk ware was mostly carved with simple lotus petals on the outer surface
and straight lines which formed a radiating pattern on the inner surface.
Bowls were mostly printed with chrysanthemum patterns on the inner
center and carved with algae patterns on the inner side of the wall. By the
late Northern Song Dynasty, the decorative techniques of Ru folk ware
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
grew to be extremely rich and there appeared a large number of vessels with
printed patterns.

8.2.6 Northern Song Guan Kilns
Official kilns in the strict sense came into existence only in the Northern
Song Dynasty in China. Before the Northern Song Dynasty there were no
official kilns, only tributary kilns, which referred to outstanding folk kilns
that were selected by the royal family to fire imperial use articles. The
nature of official kilns was fundamentally different to that of tributary kilns.
Firstly, official kiln ware, fired exclusively for the royal family, followed
the design norms of the palace in terms of shape, decoration and glaze color
and displayed a strong court style. Secondly, the reason why official kilns
devoted to making imperial porcelain were established in the Northern
Dynasty was probably related to the ritual utensils used in royal sacrificial
ceremonies.
    Traditional Chinese ritualistic activities featured great variety. Court
sacrificial rites came in three types in terms of scale, namely, great
sacrifices, middle sacrifices, and inferior sacrifices. Great sacrifices
included ceremonies that sacrificed to Heaven and Earth, to the supreme
god, to the imperial ancestral temple, and to the gods of land and grain
(together called She Ji, often used to refer to the country itself). Middle
sacrifices included ceremonies that offered sacrifices to the sun, the moon,
the agricultural ancestor (Xian Nong), the silkworm goddess (Xian Can),
previous emperors, and the Grand Duke Jupiter (Tai Sui). Inferior sacrifices
were ceremonies that sacrificed to all temples and ancestral shrines. Court
rites also included weddings and funerals in the imperial palace. During
such sacrificial rites and ceremonies commemorating major life events,
many ritual objects, previously mostly metal ones, were used. During the
Yuanfeng reign of the Song Dynasty a change took place, that is, ceramic
wares started to be used for royal sacrifices to Heaven and Earth. It was
recorded in The History of Song that in the Yuanfeng First Year the court
issued ritual rules requiring the use of ceramics as containers for sacrifices
to Heaven and Earth.
   This means that in the first year of the Yuanfeng reign (1078) the Song
court was already producing ceramic sacrificial utensils to be used in ritual
activities. In the Daguan Fourth Year the Ritual and Ceremony Bureau
emphasized that sacrifices to Heaven and Earth were different from those to
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
ancestral temples and that ceramic wares should be used in sacrifices to
Heaven and Earth. This was approved by Emperor Huizong. Yet the pursuit
of simplicity and the use of ceramic wares (which were simpler than gold or
bronzewares and deemed to represent “quality and sincerity” as upheld by
ancient rites) as sacrificial utensils must have already started during the
reign of Emperor Shenzong. The emphasis placed on the “quality and
sincerity” of ceramics appears to be a reflection of the Xifeng Reforms in
rites and etiquette.39
     It can be seen that the official kilns were established in the Song
Dynasty to make ceremonial utensils for ritual activities, mainly for
offering sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, She Ji and so on. Therefore, these
vessels were not daily utensils, but sacred articles, which should conform to
special requirements not only in form but also in color. Porcelain was
chosen as ceremonial ware not only because of its simplicity, but also
because of its jade-like texture. There had always been a tradition of jade
worship in China. The ritual objects used back in the Liangzhu Culture
were jade. Besides, the azure color of jade resembled “the celestial color,”
making jade-like azure porcelain the ideal carrier of “upholding quality and
sincerity.” The sacredness of ceremonial vessels required that they needed
to be “pure and uniform” and natural in color. That is why official kiln
products in the Northern Song Dynasty mostly had plain surfaces and thin
walls, and had one layer of glaze applied. Such a simple yet charming and
elegant style was very much in line with the profound and archaic interest
advocated by the upper class of the Song Dynasty.40 In this way, this
aesthetic taste dominated by the official kilns virtually became the
mainstream style of Song porcelain.
    Official kiln products were for the exclusive use of the imperial palace,
and ordinary officials were allowed to use them only after conferment by
the emperor. They were non-commercial and strictly forbidden for civilian
use. To prevent the dispersal of the products among the common people,
once they were fired, those deemed not good enough for use were all
smashed and buried. The meticulous production division, the absence of a
budget limit, the skillful and exquisite workmanship, the non-commercial
nature, and the special user group of official kilns determined that the shape
designs, technological characteristics and aesthetic pursuit of their products
were vastly different from folk kiln products.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Song official kilns included Northern Song Guan kilns and Southern
Song Guan kilns, the former located in Bianjing and the latter established in
Hangzhou by the Song royal family after they moved south. To facilitate
production management and product transportation, the royal family built
official kilns near the capital. Bianjing was located in modern-day Kaifeng,
but due to multiple flooding events of the Yellow River, the site of the
capital Bianjing of the Northern Song Dynasty has long been buried by
sand. Exploration has shown that the site is six meters underneath today’s
Kaifeng. Inspection of the Bianjing Guan kiln site is made more difficult by
the high groundwater level resulting from the fact that the riverbed of the
Yellow River is elevated above the ground level.
   Yet historical records and surviving vessels indicate that Northern Song
official kilns did exist. It is believed by some that the Bianjing Guan kilns
were actually Ru kilns based on the statement “the more superior Bianjing
Guan ware was similar to Ru ware” in the Ge Gu Yao Lun, a Ming dynasty
manual on ceramics by Cao Zhao. Yet a comparison of surviving Guan and
Ru ware would show that the products of the two kilns were distinctly
different in both shape and glaze color. Therefore, the Bianjing Guan kilns
and Ru kilns should be two separate kiln clusters rather than the same. Still,
some doubt the existence of “Bianjing Guan wares” on the grounds that
Ming and Qing books on ceramics only mention “Guan kilns” and never
mention “Bianjing Guan kilns.” In fact, Gu Wenjian of the Southern Song
Dynasty explicitly mentions Bianjing Guan ware in his Fu Xuan Za Lu
(Miscellaneous Records from Where the Sun is Warming My Back), and Ye
Zhi, also of the Southern Song Dynasty, states in his Notes in Tan Study that
the building of the Xiuneisi Guan kiln was “inherited from the former
capital,” meaning that the Guan kilns of the Southern Song Dynasty were
built following the system and practice of the Guan kilns in Bianjing, the
capital of the Northern Song. If we look at the issue by comparing physical
specimens, the two kinds of washers in the collection of the Palace Museum
can serve as good evidence. One kind has almost vertical walls that slightly
extend outwards to the mouth. Some have flat bottoms, (Fig. 8.38) and
some have shallow and wide circular feet. The washers are fully glazed
both inside and out and marks of prop nails can be seen on their bottoms.
The glazing and propping methods are roughly the same as the Ru kilns,
which indicates that the Bianjing Guan kilns were influenced by the Ru
kilns. In fact, it was probably that the craftsmen of the Bianjing Guan kilns
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
came from the Ru kilns. The other kind of round washers had shallow, wide
circular feet that exposed their iron-black bodies. The wide circular feet
were used as props during firing and there were no nail marks on the
bottoms. The treatment of the ware bottoms and the propping method were
completely different from those of the Bianjing Guan kilns. Many such
washers were unearthed at the Jiaotan site on Tortoise Mountain in
Hangzhou, which seems to prove that they were products of the Tortoise
Mountain Guan kiln in the Southern Song Dynasty.





Fig. 8.38 Guan kiln round washer,
Song Dynasty, height: 6.4 cm, top diam.: 22.6 cm, base diam.: 19 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Surviving Guan wares of the Northern Song Dynasty are rare and
include mainly bowls, bottles, and washers. Created to serve as the state’s
ceremonial ware, Northern Song Guan wares mostly imitated the shape
design of bronzewares. They were modeled on the designs from the Xuanhe
Bogu Tu (“Illustrations on a wide ranges of antiques from the Xuanhe era”)
compiled by the edict of Emperor Huizong of Song, who himself was an art
enthusiast. Based on these “famous ancient wares,” the porcelain pieces all
carried cultural allusions and profound meanings. Northern Song Guan
wares can be put into two categories, the first being ritual objects mainly for
the use of the court, represented by bottles, zun, ding, stoves, gu, and plates,
and the second being stationeries, which were closely related to Emperor
Huizong’s personal preferences and also mainly for his personal use. The
stationeries, represented by the “four treasures of the study,” had a thick,
black body and light blue glaze that was bright, mellow and graceful, and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
especially known for its large cracks. The wares were also characterized by
“purple rims and iron feet,” which set them apart from the products of the
Southern Song Guan, Ru and Longquan kilns.
   The Northern Song Guan kilns expended much effort in the pursuit of
perfect glaze colors. The products had no decoration on the body and
pursued artistic supremacy mainly by their generous glaze layer, attractive
glaze color and ingenious crack patterns. Common glaze colors were azure,
greenish blue, pale blue, fried rice yellow, etc. with greenish blue
considered the finest. Ming dynasty commentator Gao Lian writes in his
Appreciation Notes in Leisure Time, On Guan and Ge Ware: “The character
of Guan ware was basically the same as that of Ge ware. The best color is
greenish blue, followed by pale white; and oil gray is the worst of the
colors.” In the “Guan ware” column of the second volume of the
encyclopedic Ci Yuan (“Origin of Words”), whose compilation began in the
34th year of Emperor Guangxu’s reign in the Qing Dynasty, the Guan kilns
are described as: “…one of the five famous kilns in the Song Dynasty.
During the Daguan years of the Northern Song Dynasty the capital
established kilns to fire porcelain. The porcelain body could be white, gray
or red. The clay was collected from Biandong and Yangdi and was
extremely refined. Glaze colors included azure, emerald, greenish blue, pale
blue and green, with greenish blue the top color followed by pale blue.”
   The cracking of Northern Song Guan ware glaze was of especially high
artistic value due to its strong sense of rhythm and smoothness like water
ripples. The cracking benefited from its unique technology. What is
especially marvelous was that small wares could also have big cracks the
size of tortoiseshell patterns with “eel blood” lines, which produced
amazing beauty. Such a special effect came from special technology. The
cracking of glaze surfaces was initially a defect arising out of poor bonding
between the body and the glaze, yet Northern Song Guan kilns took
advantage of this defect to create the renowned crackled glaze, and in
addition, with a unique body and glaze formula, unique glazing method and
unique firing technology, they created special decorative effects such as
“golden threads and iron lines” and “purple rim and iron feet.” Strictly
speaking, these effects that could not be entirely artificially controlled or
designed should not be regarded as decorative techniques. Rather, they
represented beauty which arose out of the material itself, a kind of essential
beauty. Some scholars also believe the “eel blood” pattern ware of the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Northern Song Guan kilns to be of the highest quality, as expressed by Gao
Lian in his Appreciation Notes in Leisure Time: “Of Guan ware patterns, ice
cracks and eel blood are the top, followed by plum blossom cracks and ink
patterns, while small cracks are the most inferior of the patterns.”
   The “purple rim and iron feet” feature of Northern Song Guan ware
should be attributed to Emperor Huizong’s favor for and assimilation of the
porcelain-making craft of kilns around Kaifeng, which were rising at the
time. These kilns used clay with an exceedingly high iron content to make
the body, resulting in a body texture that was markedly different from that
of Ru ware which had a low iron content. Such a body with an extremely
high iron content took on a blackish purple color after firing at high
temperature in a reducing flame, giving rise to the “purple rim” feature
when the glaze applied at the mouth of the vessel dripped down slightly and
slimly exposed the body at the rim. The “iron feet” effect emerged via the
same mechanism, that is, unglazed parts at the bottom of the feet turned
blackish red due to the reducing atmosphere (Fig. 8.39).





Fig. 8.39 Guan kiln sunflower petal mouthed washer,
Song Dynasty, height: 4.4 cm, top diam.: 16.8 cm, base diam.: 12 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Guan ware belonged to celadon, like Ru and Ge ware. Yet its glaze
colors were not uniform. While Ru ware was mostly azure and incense ash
color, Guan and Ge ware shared similar tones, including light greenish blue,
pale blue, putty color and bluish yellow. The different glaze tones were to
an extent realized through different body colors, including blackish gray,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
dark gray, light gray, and earthen yellow, which imparted different shades of
blue to the glaze. It was the deep body color that gave Song Guan ware its
calm, deep and somewhat mysterious glaze color, a color and feeling that
was pursued by the literati of the day.

8.3 Porcelain Kilns in the South
8.3.1 The Jingdezhen Kilns
The Jingdezhen kilns started production in the Five Dynasties and
developed a mature porcelain-making technology by the Song Dynasty. In
the Five Dynasties when the Jingdezhen kilns arose, there emerged the
prosperous scene of every village hosting a kiln and every family molding
pottery. Large numbers of Song dynasty ceramics deposits have been found
in ancient kiln sites at many places in the suburbs of Jingdezhen, such as
Liujiawan, Nanshijie, Zhuxi, Sitian, Jiantian, Yangmeiting, Hutian,
Shihuwan, and Huangnitou. This shows that during the Song Dynasty folk
kilns in the area were gradually concentrating around what is now urban
Jingdezhen and that the porcelain-making technology had been greatly
improved. In fact, the name “Jingdezhen” itself came into existence only
during this period. Before the Song Dynasty the place was named Xinping
or “Changnan,” and was renamed Jingdezhen (“Jingde Town”) during the
Jingde era of Emperor Zhenzong’s reign in the Northern Song Dynasty. The
Comprehensive History of Jiangxi records: “During the Jingde years of
Song the town was established, and officials were ordered to make
porcelain for the capital to be used by the government. Potters were ordered
to write ‘Jingde’ on the wares.” Meanwhile, Lan Pu in the fifth volume
“Examinations of Kilns of Past Dynasties” of his Accounts of Ceramics at
Jingdezhen notes that: “all called it Jingdezhen ware and ‘Changnan’ as a
diminutive name.”
   From Emperor Zhenzong’s reign to the end of the dynasty the Song
court established and maintained tax administrators in Jingdezhen called
“Town Supervisors” and appointed officials to preside over the production
of the folk kilns. Thus, the porcelain industry of Jingdezhen in the Song
Dynasty was a private handicraft industry and its development also
reflected the development of commodity production as a whole in the Song
Dynasty.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Regarding the characteristics of Jingdezhen’s porcelain in the Song
Dynasty, it is recorded in the fifth volume “Examinations of Kilns of Past
Dynasties” of Accounts of Ceramics at Jingdezhen that: “(Jingdezhen)
selected white clay to mold the body, the texture is thin and fine, the color is
mellow and lustrous… the ware is exceedingly bright and attractive. It
became popular and was held as an example in the country.” In Records of
Porcelain Making Jiang Qi recalls Jingdezhen ware in the Northern Song
Dynasty as being: “all praised to be like ‘beautiful jade’.”
   Jingdezhen’s main porcelain products at the time were qingbai wares
with a thin body, clear glaze and jade-like color. They were renowned as the
champion of all kilns for their pure texture and fine workmanship and
became a precious product that represented the top porcelain-making level
of the Song Dynasty. Under their influence, many kilns at the time in
today’s Fujian, Guangdong, Sichuan, Zhejiang, Anhui, Hubei, Yunnan,
Guangxi and other provinces and prefectures all started imitating
Jingdezhen in firing qingbai porcelain. The impact of the Jingdezhen kilns
was so far-reaching that a “qingbai porcelain kiln system” was formed and
became an important chapter in the history of China’s ceramics. Within the
Jiangxi kilns imitating qingbai porcelain were the Jizhou and Baishe kilns
in Nanfeng, the Qilizhen kilns in Ganzhou, as well as the Ningdu, Leping,
and Jing’an kilns.
    In the Five Dynasties, what Jingdezhen produced was celadon and white
porcelain. Qingbai porcelain had not appeared at that time. The general
development trend of China’s porcelain kilns was to inherit and innovate on
the basis of the traditional types of the previous period, yet Jingdezhen was
an exception. By the Song Dynasty, the celadon and white porcelain that
were popular in Jingdezhen back in the Five Dynasties disappeared and
were replaced by qingbai porcelain. The reason behind this, as posited by
Feng Xianming, was probably that craftsmen in Jingdezhen intentionally
fired qingbai porcelain with a jade-like texture by ingeniously utilizing
excellent local materials to meet consumer needs because jade had always
been a rare commodity monopolized by the ruling class and bluish white
jade, while desirable, was even more rare and hard to come by. It was
because this porcelain type was created to imitate the color feature of bluish
white jade that its glaze color was between blue and white. Hence, “qingbai
(bluish white) porcelain” was used to refer to whitish blue ware or bluish
white ware. It was called “ying (影) qing (shadow blue)” by the folks, and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
sometimes “ying (映) qing (reflected blue),” “yin (隐) qing (subtle blue),” and
“zhao qing (covered blue).” The qingbai porcelain produced by Jingdezhen
in the Song Dynasty had a fine, white, delicate body, a bluish white glaze
color resembling ice and jade, a color so bright and clear that it was able to
show reflections. Mellow and crystalline, elegant and refined, such
porcelain really deserved the praise “like beautiful jade” as recorded in
literature (Fig. 8.40).





Fig. 8.40 Qingbai glaze engraved large bowl,
Song Dynasty, height: 6.7 cm, top diam.: 20.8 cm, base diam.: 6 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Almost all of Jingdezhen’s qingbai porcelain kilns in the Song Dynasty
were distributed in the Donghe and Nanhe river basins, with the majority
concentrated in the Nanhe river basin where porcelain stones were
produced. Representative kiln sites from the early Song Dynasty were
located in Xianghu, Huangnitou, Shihuwan and Hutian, those from the
middle Song Dynasty in Hutian, Nanshijie, Liujiawan and Xiaowuli, and
those from the late Song Dynasty in Hutian, which was close to modern-day
urban Jingdezhen.
    Representative kilns in the early Song Dynasty were in Huangnitou,
Xianghu, Shihuwan, Hutian, and elsewhere. Qingbai porcelain of this
period featured a relatively thick body and obvious signs of being “shaped
from wet clay.” Pots and similar varieties at the time were shaped by
throwing and processed while the clay was wet. The forming of bowls and
plates involved three procedures, namely throwing, internal mold casting
and foot embellishing. As to the method of loading wares in the kiln, the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Five Dynasties practice of pile firing was abandoned. Wares were instead
protected by saggers and multiple cushion pads, and fired face up, a method
that was called “face-upward firing.” Owing to insufficient mastery of the
reducing flame, the glaze color of products of the period lacked green notes
and was more gray or light beige yellow. The shape designs were similar to
those of the Five Dynasties. Most bowls and small cups maintained the
rolled rim or sunflower rim of the Five Dynasties and featured a high
circular foot and slanting belly wall, or short circular foot and funnel shape
(Fig. 8.41). Pots were melon-shaped and still had signs of imitating metal
ware. Pots unearthed from early tombs all had a lid topped with a lion
figurine. Almost no ware had a decorative pattern on its surface. Bowls,
small cups, etc. were mostly fired using the “face-upward firing” method.
In general, qingbai wares from this period had monotonous shapes and had
not developed the characteristics of yingqing (shadow blue) glaze. Yet,
compared with the regular celadon and daily use porcelain of the time, they
show a fairly high level of craftsmanship.





Fig. 8.41 Qingbai glaze engraved bowl,
Song Dynasty, height: 5.1 cm, top diam.: 14.5 cm, base diam.: 3.3 cm, in the Palace Museum

   By the mid-Song Dynasty (i.e. from the end of the Northern Song
Dynasty to the beginning of the Southern Song), obvious equidistant
spinning patterns appeared on vessels, indicating that the wares were
preliminarily shaped by throwing and then, after becoming leather hard,
trimmed with an iron blade while being spun. The resultant utensils were
thus much thinner, finer and neater than those from the Five Dynasties or
early Song Dynasty (Fig. 8.42). Due to the special feature (poor plasticity)
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
of the raw material used by Jingdezhen porcelain, trimming, also called
turning, was widely used to form the wares. By the middle of the Song
Dynasty, a forming approach where turning played the major role, while
throwing was supplementary, emerged in Jingdezhen, setting it apart from
northern kilns. Nevertheless, the most outstanding achievement of
Jingdezhen potters in this period was the skillful mastery of the strong
reducing flame which not only realized a mellow jade-like bluish white
color, but also improved the density and transparency of the ware body. The
glaze color of most wares turned from the grayish blue or fired rice yellow
of the early Song Dynasty to bluish green. Thus, the glaze layer of this
period began to display the characteristics of typical yingqing glazed
porcelain. Manufactured in the greatest numbers were bowls and plates,
which were of many varieties. There were also vases, incense burners,
porcelain pillows, decorative sculptures and other artworks, which were
elegantly shaped, thin walled, and decorated with carving and painting. The
decorative patterns had graceful lines and strong artistry with such themes
as water ripples, grass, peony, lotus, fish, and phoenix bird. Of the kilns
producing yingqing porcelain in different places, Hutian and Xianghu
achieved the highest technological level. Their products had a fine body
texture, thin wall and attractive shape design, and both their transparency
and hardness reached the standard of modern hard porcelain (Figs. 8.43,
8.44 and 8.45).

    In the late Song Dynasty (the Southern Song), Jingdezhen began to use
the kiln tools combined with cushion pads which had been invented by the
Ding kilns to hold bowls and plates with an unglazed rim for firing.
Compared with multi-layer cushion bowls, such kiln tools did not require
saggers and were able to accommodate multiple greenware of the same
specifications. Compared with face-upward firing saggers, they could
increase the vertical holding capacity of the kiln space by four to six times
and thus save 75% of the fuel, and in the meantime could prevent product
deformation. Yet using this tool would leave an unglazed rim on the wares,
thus affecting their practical value. In addition, the fact that the tool was
made of greenware and could only be used once meant that during firing its
usage increased moisture in the kiln space which was not easy to eliminate.
This in turn slowed down the temperature rise in the kiln and easily led to
defects such as damp yellowness of the glaze. Due to the popularity of
inverted firing, engraved or carved patterns on round wares were reduced
and gradually replaced by printed decoration featuring complicated and
overelaborate patterns, which were rigid compared to engraved patterns but
which facilitated production. Popular pots and bottles in later periods were
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
also mostly imprinted with external molds, resulting in simple shapes and a
rigid appearance. Daily use bowls and small cups mostly had unglazed rims
and the shape design changed from the previous style featuring lighter tops
and heavier bottoms to the present one featuring thicker mouths and rims
and thinner middle and lower parts (Fig. 8.46). The circular foot became
shorter than the early and middle periods. Some wares only had a trace of
the circular foot left. The structure of bowl walls was also designed to suit
the requirements of inverted firing, that is, to increase the stacking density
in the kiln chamber.41 The adoption of inverted firing to make yingqing
porcelain in the Southern Song Dynasty was on the one hand influenced by
the Ding kilns in pursuit of better profits and reduced costs, and on the other
hand due to a change in raw materials. Liu Xinyuan believed that only one
kind of raw material was used for making porcelain in the Song Dynasty,
namely, porcelain stone, which could be classified into upper layer
porcelain stone and lower layer, the former being more suited for firing at
high temperature. When the upper layer porcelain stone, which was easier
to mine yet of limited reserves, was exhausted in the Northern Song
Dynasty, potters of the Southern Song Dynasty started using middle and
lower layer porcelain stone, a material that was prone to deformation. To
counter possible deformation, potters placed bowls made of middle and
lower layer stone upside down on cushion rings so that the bowls were
dome-shaped and less prone to deformation during firing. Yet as a result of
this practice almost all yingqing wares of the Southern Song Dynasty ended
up with an unglazed rim.42

text:
The Wuyuan Museum cleared the tomb of Wang Geng, governor of
Tingzhou in the Southern Song Dynasty, and his wife in 1979 and cleared
the tomb of Wang Lu, magistrate of Leping County of the Northern Song
Dynasty, and his wife in 1981. Although the two tombs had been
desecrated, the ceramics buried with the deceased were well preserved, of
which there were many precious yingqing wares that served as invaluable
materials for the study of Jingdezhen yingqing porcelain in the Northern
and Southern Song dynasties.
   The yingqing wares in the tomb of the Wang Geng couple has been
confirmed to be the products of the Jingdezhen kilns, but the producing kiln
of those in the tomb of the Wang Lu couple is yet to be determined.
Nevertheless, since both Wang Lu’s hometown, Wuyuan, and where he took
office, Leping, were very close to Jingdezhen, the yingqing wares in his
tomb would probably have come from the vicinity of Jingdezhen even if
they were not from the Jingdezhen kilns per se and could therefore still
offer information about the yingqing porcelain production of Jingdezhen at
that time.43
   The two tombs (hereinafter referred to as the Northern Song tomb and
the Southern Song tomb) were more than 90 years apart in time. The
Jingdezhen yingqing wares unearthed from them can tell us about the
differences between the Northern and Southern Song in terms of local
porcelain production and the production development conditions at the
time. For example, most of the yingqing wares unearthed from the Northern
Song tomb were fired face up, and only a few adopted inverted firing or the
prop nail pile firing of the Five Dynasties, while almost all yingqing wares
unearthed from the Southern Song tomb were fired face down with an
unglazed yet silver-edged rim and the face-upward firing method was
scarcely inherited. Since Wang Geng was a court official, the porcelains he
used were naturally quite exquisite. Though all the wares unearthed from
his tomb had an unglazed rim, the rim was edged with silver. Such wares
could in no way be used by the common people.
   The porcelains unearthed in the Southern Song tomb were identical to
the products of “Zhen kilns” mentioned in the Records of Porcelain Making
by Jiang Qi of the Southern Song Dynasty. They can offer a glimpse into
the porcelain-making level of the mid-Southern Song Dynasty. After
Emperor Xiaozong’s reign in the Southern Song, society was relatively
stable, and the economy enjoyed a temporary recovery (evidenced by
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Lin’an’s prosperous market as described in Meng Liang Lu by Wu Zimu of
the Southern Song Dynasty). In addition, as the population south of the
Yangtze River increased and the handicraft industry developed, Jingdezhen
yingqing porcelain, which was already favored by the then emperor, was
naturally required to be continuously manufactured as tribute to the court.
As a result, a large number of skilled craftsmen from folk kilns were
required to gather together at any given time to produce high-grade
porcelain.
   Compared with the Northern Song Dynasty the porcelain manufacturing
of the Southern Song deteriorated, the reasons for which, apart from the raw
material issue mentioned above, also included social unrest and the harsh
tax system, which dealt a heavy blow to the porcelain industry in
Jingdezhen. Despite this setback, to provide high-quality porcelain for the
imperial palace and the nobles, Jingdezhen retained the firing technologies
and craftsmanship that had been skillfully mastered during the Northern
Song Dynasty. Most decorations were engraved or carved and pursued the
effect of being “exceedingly bright and beautiful,” which offered later
generations a glimpse into the high craft level of Jingdezhen folk kilns in
the middle of the Southern Song Dynasty. In fact, by the latter part of the
Southern Song Dynasty, Jingdezhen had almost become the largest kiln
cluster in China in terms of technology, production scale and commodity
circulation. Following the mid-Song Dynasty, the Jingdezhen folk kilns
experienced a development process from the primary to the advanced, that
is, they gradually broke free from a reliance on agriculture to become an
independent handicraft industry with a complex division of labor and
cooperation. Their large production scale, wide sales coverage, and high
technological and artistic achievements won the Jingdezhen kilns a well-
deserved fame equal to the Ding and Longquan kilns following the
celebrated “Ru, Guan, Ge and Jun” kilns.44 The excellent raw material of
Jingdezhen resulted in the high whiteness and transparency of the qingbai
porcelain body which was close to the whiteness and transparency of
modern fine porcelain. Jingdezhen qingbai ware from the Song Dynasty
was the first in China to develop porcelain from transparent glaze to semi-
transparent body, which was the third leap in the development of China’s
porcelain.45 This leap laid the foundation for the development of the
porcelain industry in the Yuan Dynasty (Fig. 8.47).

8.3.2 The Guan Kilns in the Southern Song Dynasty
The Guan kilns of the Southern Song Dynasty were newly set up in
Hangzhou after the Northern Song ended and Emperor Gaozong fled to the
south. At that time Lin’an (now Hangzhou) was the center of politics,
culture and the economy as well as the largest consumer city. There were
also Mingzhou (now Ningbo), Yuezhou (now Shaoxing), Wenzhou,
Wuzhou (now Jinhua), and Chuzhou (now Lishui). These cities and towns,
with long histories and an advanced porcelain industry, were both
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
production centers and markets and distribution centers of porcelain. Yue
ware, Wuzhou kiln ware and Longquan celadon had a long-established
fame for their unique features. The Jingkang Incident marked the end of the
Northern Song regime and amidst the war, the most famous kilns on the
central plains were destroyed. The Song royal family, led by Zhao Gou, fled
southeast, made Lin’an his capital and set up the Southern Song Dynasty.
The Southern Song court established the Xiuneisi Guan kiln on Phoenix
Mountain, Hangzhou, and a new Guan kiln near Jiaotan in the Bagua Cave,
Tortoise Mountain. In the Xiuneisi kiln and the new Guan kiln the best
craftsmen from the north and south gathered to fire celadon required by the
court and dignitaries. These kilns were a continuation of the Bianjing Guan
kilns of the Northern Song Dynasty and were historically called the Guan
kilns of the Southern Song. The earliest record of the Guan kilns of the
Southern Song is found in the Notes in Tan Study by Ye Zhi of the Southern
Song: “During the Zhenghe years the capital established its own kilns to
fire porcelain, called the Guan kilns. After the royal family crossed the
Yangtze River, Shao Chengzhang proposed establishing the Shao Bureau. A
kiln was set up in Xiuneisi to make celadon, called the Nei kiln, inheriting
the legacy of the former capital. Clay was finely washed to be made into
models. The products, extremely exquisite with clear glaze, were favored
by the people. Later a new kiln was set up in Jiaotan, which was quite
different from the old kiln. The others, such as the Wuni, Yuhang, and Xu
kilns, could not be compared with the Guan kilns. As for the old Yue kilns,
they no longer existed.” This description is the earliest written record
discovered to date of the history of Southern Song’s Guan kilns and has
been used as textual research materials by subsequent researchers.
According to the text, the Guan kilns were set up back in the Northern Song
Dynasty and the Guan kilns of the Southern Song Dynasty inherited their
technology and production methods. The text classified Southern Song’s
Guan kilns into “Xiuneisi” and “Jiaotan,” the former “called the Nei kiln”
and the latter “the new kiln,” and explicitly pointed out that the new kiln
“was quite different from the old kiln.” It is mentioned that the Xiuneisi kiln
was also named the “Nei kiln,” that it used finely washed clay to make
models, and produced extremely standard products that were cherished by
the people for their clear and transparent glaze. According to the Ge Gu Yao
Lun, an early Ming manual on ceramics by Cao Zhao, “Products fired by
the Song Dynasty’s Xiuneisi (Guan kiln) were made from fine clay, had a
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
blue color with a pinkness of differing shades, and featured a crab claw
pattern, purple rim and iron feet. The wares of fine color were similar to Ru
ware. Those made from black clay were called Wuni wares. Fake ones were
fired by the Longquan kilns and had no pattern.” Here the characteristics of
the porcelain fired by the Xiuneisi kiln were described in detail. As for the
location of the kiln, Gao Lian of the Ming Dynasty wrote in his book Zun
Sheng Ba Jian that “the Guan kiln was at the foot of Phoenix Mountain,”
yet for many years people only found a lot of scattered porcelain shards and
fragments of kiln furniture in the area and had not really discovered the
exact location of the kiln site.
    In September 1996, the Tiger Cave kiln site near the Southern Song
imperial city site on Phoenix Mountain was discovered by chance when
flooding exposed large numbers of celadon shards and kiln furniture. In
November that year, the Hangzhou Institute of Cultural Relics and
Archaeology conducted a one-month-long archaeological survey of the site
and named it the Tiger Cave kiln site following the place’s name as used by
the local people. The geographical location of the kiln site is very special
because it coincides perfectly with the location of the Southern Song
Xiuneisi Guan kiln as recorded. From then until 2001, archaeological
departments comprehensively inspected the celadon kiln site which spanned
the Southern Song and Yuan dynasties with three excavation and
investigation works. The large number of site remains and physical
materials excavated from the Southern Song Dynasty strata showed
conclusively that the site was once an important part of the Guan kilns of
the Southern Song Dynasty.46 (Fig. 8.48).

   During excavation, the Hangzhou Institute of Cultural Relics and
Archaeology unearthed a large number of Guan kiln porcelain shards and
kiln tools. The main varieties were bowls, plates, cups, jars, saucers, pots,
washers, lamps, chopstick shelves and other daily utensils, as well as
decorative wares such as gu (goblets with broad lips, long narrow stems,
and flared bases), cong-style bottles, incense burners, pedestals, and
flowerpots. Body color might be incense ash color, dark gray, purple, or
black. Purple rims and iron feet were common. Thick bodies and thick
glaze layers dominated while thin bodies or thin glaze layers were rare.
Glaze color was mainly greenish blue and beige yellow, as well as emerald
green, grayish blue, light purple, and yellow. Most glazes had ice cracks
(Fig. 8.49). Some of the porcelain shards were found to have the words
“Xiuneisi” and “Guan kiln” written in brown under the glaze.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

Fig. 8.49 Guan kiln vase with string pattern,
Song Dynasty, height: 33.6 cm, top diam.: 9.9 cm, base diam.: 14.2 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Following the Xiuneisi Guan kiln, the Southern Song Dynasty built a
second Guan kiln called the Jiaotan Guan kiln, whose site is located in the
area of Tortoise Mountain in the southern suburbs of today’s Hangzhou.
The site was discovered at the beginning of the twentieth century and
porcelain shards had subsequently constantly flowed into the antique
markets of Hangzhou and Shanghai and thus attracted the attention of
ceramics researchers at home and abroad. In the 1950s the Zhejiang
Provincial Cultural Relics Management Committee carried out a small-
scale trial excavation of the site, cleaned up a dragon kiln, and excavated
some of the shard accumulations beside the kiln. Then a Lin’an
archaeological team officially excavated the site in 1985 and conducted
supplementary excavations in 1988 to support the building of the Southern
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Song Guan Kiln Museum. These excavations offered a clear understanding
of the Southern Song Jiaotan Guan kiln. Of the unearthed porcelain shards,
23 varieties of wares were complete or restored. In addition to daily utensils
which were unearthed in the largest number such as bowls, plates, bottles,
jars, pots, and basins, there were also a number of decorative objects such
as gu, cong-style bottles, incense burners, pedestals, and flowerpots. The
decorative objects were mostly for ceremonial use and imitations of bronze
and jade wares of the Shang, Zhou, Qin and Han dynasties (Fig. 8.50).
Wares can be classified into thick and thin based on body thickness, and
glaze color was mainly greenish blue and beige yellow, though shades of
yellowish-brown and earthy yellow were also common.47 Daily use utensils
accounted for the largest number of the wares unearthed, yet among the
Song Guan wares collected by the Palace Museum and the Taipei Palace
Museum, daily use utensils are fewer while display ceramics account for
the majority, which is probably because the former suffered a high rate of
damage while the latter enjoyed better preservation. This also shows the
important position of display ceramics as ceremonial wares in the
production of the Southern Song Guan kilns.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

Fig. 8.50 Guan kiln flat vase with double pierced handles,
Song Dynasty, height: 23 cm, top diam.: 9.4 × 6.4 cm, base diam.: 6.3 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Southern Song Guan celadon excelled mainly through its jade-like
mellow glaze color, its archaic, simple and dignified shape design, along
with its crack pattern, and therefore it did not require any rich decorative
themes. Besides common plant and animal patterns, there were also various
string patterns, Eight Trigrams patterns, yunlei patterns, square spirals,
double circles, and bump patterns. Commonly used decorative techniques
were engraving, molding, stacking, kneading, hollowing out and openwork;
engraving was mostly used on daily use utensils such as bowls and plates,
molding was used on a wide range of varieties, stacking was mostly used on
wares imitating ancient vessels such as bottles, pots, stoves and gu, and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
openwork was mostly used on lids, pedestals and stoves. The rich
decorative techniques, the improvement in firing technology and the
diversity of kiln tools for loading and firing on the one hand reflected the
attention the Southern Song Guan kilns were receiving in terms of
production technology and on the other hand explained the reasons behind
the excellent quality of their products.48
   Guan kiln craftsmen who migrated south in the Southern Song Dynasty
brought technology to Hangzhou. The conditions in the south for porcelain
firing were relatively superior to those in the north. At that time the south
already had a solid foundation with the Yue kilns, secret-color ware and the
Longquan kilns and it would have been easy and quick for the south to
learn to fire Guan wares. In the early years of the Southern Song Dynasty
the products still demonstrated a heavy influence from the Northern Song
Guan kilns, mainly in their thin body, thin glaze layer and the use of prop
nails for firing. For instance, the samples unearthed at the Jiaotan kiln site
had a thin, fine body which could be light gray, gray or deep gray. The outer
surface had a thin layer of greenish blue, bluish gray or beige yellow glaze
applied. The commonality of beige yellow glaze indicates that the porcelain
firing technology of potters in this period was still in the exploratory stage.
The circular feet of bowls, plates and washers were high and flared. Nails
were used to prop the wares during firing, leaving needle-like marks on the
glaze of the outer bottom.
   As the Southern Song regime consolidated its power, the imperial court
required higher quality porcelain. Consequently, the technology of the Guan
kilns was constantly improved. The technique of multiple firing and
multiple glazing was adopted to achieve an improved jade texture of
celadon, and the mouth and belly wall of wares, especially of small wares
such as bowls, plates, washers and saucers, was thinned down to make the
wares more lightweight and graceful. The greatly thickened glaze layer also
prompted kiln workers to reform kiln tools, such as replacing prop nails
with cushion pads to avoid the nails getting stuck to the thick glaze during
firing and rendering the products defective. The adoption of cushion pads
allowed the circular foot of wares to take on the function of bearing the
weight of the ware, prompting previous flared circular feet to be gradually
replaced by straight ones.49
   The Southern Song Guan ware not only inherited the simple yet
dignified shape design and thick glaze texture of famous northern wares
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
such as the Northern Song Bianjing Guan and Ru wares, but also
assimilated the thin body combined with thick glaze, bright, clear glaze
surface and exquisite shapes of famous southern wares such as Yue and
Longquan wares. Cao Zhao of the Ming Dynasty described Southern Song
Guan ware in his Ge Gu Yao Lun as: “Products fired by Song Dynasty’s
Xiuneisi (Guan kiln) were made from fine clay, had blue color with
pinkness of different shades, and featured crab claw patterns, purple rims
and iron feet.”
   The characteristics of Southern Song Guan ware could be summarized
as “purple rim and iron feet,” “greenish blue glaze,” “ice crack patterns”
and “thin body and thick glaze.” Of the seven major glaze colors of Guan
ware, namely, beeswax yellow, pale blue, greenish blue, light greenish blue,
deep greenish blue, crab color and putty color, greenish blue was the finest.
Repeated polishing and firing of the greenware achieved an extremely thin
body while the glaze thickness was more than three times that of ordinary
ceramic glaze. It can be seen that the attraction of the Southern Song Guan
celadon lay not in its decoration, but mainly in its jade-like, dignified,
elegant and mysterious natural beauty.

8.3.3 The Ge Kilns
The inclusion of the Ge kilns among the celebrated kilns of the Song
Dynasty was first seen in the Ming Xuande period publication Manual of
Xuande Ritual Vessels (Xuande ding yi pu), which noted: “the Chai, Ru,
Guan, Ge, Jun and Ding wares [were] collected by the imperial storage.”
That Ge ware was ranked after Ru and Guan and before Jun and Ding
indicates that the Ge kilns were regarded as famous kilns of the Song
Dynasty and their products were important items for collection. Most Ge
wares handed down from the Southern Song Dynasty have been collected
by the Palace Museum, Shanghai Museum and the Taipei Palace Museum,
except for some that were scattered abroad. Varieties included various
bottles, burners, washers, plates, and jars. The body might be thick or thin,
the body texture fine porcelain or sandy, the body color blackish gray, deep
gray, light gray, earthy yellow, etc., and the glaze color greenish blue, pale
blue, putty color, bluish yellow, etc. The glaze surface had ice crackles, fine
crackles, Hundredfold crackles or a fish-roe pattern (Fig. 8.51). The crack
patches were large (ice) or small (fish-roe) and the crevices could be thick
(iron wire) or thin (silk). The crevices were often filled with black, gold or
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
red colorings, so the patterns were called “golden threads and iron lines.”
(Fig. 8.52).

   There is little archaeological data available to corroborate the Ge wares
which survive today because the Ge kilns have not been found in literature
from the Song Dynasty and their site has not been located. This has given
rise to a number of different views about the Ge kilns. Some believe “they
were one of the official kiln clusters in the Song Dynasty”50 on the grounds
that common Ge ware varieties such as tripod burners, fish eared burners,
double-eared nipple-footed burners, zhi-style bottles, gallbladder bottles and
folded-waist plates mostly imitated ancient bronze ceremonial ware, were
all of the style of court use porcelain, and shared common designs with Ru
and Guan ware while being quite different from folk porcelain (Figs. 8.53
and 8.54).

   Also supporting this view is the record in Zun Sheng Ba Jian that “the
character of Guan ware is roughly the same as that of Ge ware,” that “the
kiln is under the Phoenix Mountain in Hangzhou,” and that “Ge kilns were
managed by the private sector and sourced all the clay used locally.”
Records of Jingdezhen Ceramics quotes the similar view of Tang Bingjun in
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
his Wen Fang Si Kao Tu Shuo that “(Ge kilns)…called Gege kilns (“elder
brother kilns”), also used clay from Hangzhou.” From these records some
deduce that the Ge kilns were the “Gege kilns” near Hangzhou and were
probably the “Guan kilns” run by Xiuneisi or civilian kilns supervised by
the government and under the charge of Xiuneisi.51
   The earliest record concerning the Ge (elder brother) and Di (younger
brother) kilns is found in the Comprehensive History of Zhejiang compiled
during the Jiajing era of the Ming Dynasty. The book records the legend of
two brothers, Zhang Shengyi and Zhang Shenger, who came to Liutian at
the foot of Liuhua Mountain in Chuzhou, where most of the inhabitants
took pottery as their occupation, to make the best greenware of the time
each with his own kiln. But the book also states, “the time of the two
brothers is unknown.” The Sequel to Qi Xiu Lei Gao published in the
Jiajing 45th Year further states: “Both the Ge kilns and Longquan kilns
were in Longquan County in Chuzhou. In the Southern Song two brothers,
Zhang Shengyi and Zhang Shenger, each fired one kiln, and those made by
Shengyi were Ge ware…those made by Shenger were Longquan ware,
named after the place. The color was blue of different shades and the feet
were an iron color also of different shades. Previously there was said to be
purple feet, which are rare nowadays. Wares made from fine clay with pure
glaze color are the most precious. Ge ware has more fragmented cracks,
called Hundredfold crackles…” Published five years later than A
Comprehensive History of Zhejiang, the Sequel to Qi Xiu Lei Gao states
that the two brothers were from the Southern Song Dynasty and also points
out that they made porcelain in Longquan County in Chuzhou. This is the
earliest literature known so far indicating that the two brothers were from
the Southern Song, and later literature on the Ge and Di kilns after the
Jiajing years of the Ming Dynasty mostly relies on this.
   However, tests on Ge ware specimens show that the chemical
composition of their body and glaze, the color of the cracks and the
polishing method of the feet are all different from those of the Longquan
black-body celadon unearthed, and are instead similar to the crackled glaze
wares produced in Jiangxi that imitated Guan ware. So some people think
that Ge wares were imitations of Guan wares (Fig. 8.55).

   The Shanghai Institute of Ceramics of the Chinese Academy of
Sciences tested the Song Dynasty Longquan black-body celadon samples
and came to the following conclusion: “the view of some that they were
imitations of Guan ware is well based since their body composition is very
close to that of northern kiln products but quite different from that of
general Longquan ware.”52
    Still some believe that the Ge wares passed down to the present are
imitations of Guan wares but were not fired by Longquan kilns, and that the
place of production was somewhere near Jingdezhen in Jiangxi. Besides,
Ge Gu Yao Lun makes reference to a crackled glaze ware kiln that was in
Yonghe Town in Ji’an. Since crackled glaze ware was similar to Ge ware
with cracks, it is likely that the two were related.53
     If a summary is to be made, accounts differ, and opinions vary about
many issues surrounding Ge ware and to find the truth requires further
exploration by cultural relic archaeologists.

8.3.4 The Longquan Kilns
The Longquan kilns were located in the southwestern part of Zhejiang
Province. Neighboring counties such as Qingyuan, Yunhe, Lishui, Wuyi
and Jiangshan, as well as Pucheng and Songxi counties of Fujian Province
were all important celadon producers, yet Longquan was the most thriving.
Specimens unearthed from the kiln site indicate that the Longquan kilns
started production in the early Northern Song Dynasty, reached their zenith
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
in the late Southern Song, developed further in the Yuan Dynasty, and
declined after the mid-Ming Dynasty as craftsmen gradually dispersed to
other places. From beginning to end the Longquan kilns’ porcelain
production lasted for six or seven hundred years.
   The rise of the Longquan kilns in the Song Dynasty was directly related
to the decline of the Yue kilns. In the early and middle Northern Song
Dynasty, the Yue kilns, after almost one thousand years of glory,
experienced a decline due to fuel shortage, rising artisan salaries and heavy
kiln industry taxes in the Ningshao area, transiting from large-scale
commercial production to small-scale production only for local sales.
Craftsmanship also became rough and crude, probably in order to reduce
costs. Of the Yue wares unearthed in various Asian and African countries,
those of the mid-Northern Song Dynasty were of the latest period, which
indicates that as the Yue kilns declined their products were no longer
exported.
   The decline of the Yue kilns broke the supply and demand balance of
celadon, providing a perfect opportunity for the rise of the Longquan kilns.
The huge profits domestic and foreign markets had to offer were a natural
driving force for folk kilns devoted to commodity production. Moreover,
the decline of the Yue kilns drove some craftsmen to other places, one of
which was the mountainous Longquan kiln area, to make a living, and this
added to the technical strength of the Longquan kilns, contributed to their
rapid rise in the late Northern Song Dynasty, and enabled them to almost
completely inherit the traditions of Yue kiln porcelain making. It is worth
noting that in this early period of the Longquan kilns, their products were
sold not only in nearby areas, but were also found in trade ports and foreign
countries. This shows that porcelain for export started occupying an
important position in the Longquan kilns’ production from their early
period.54
   The decline of the Yue kilns after the mid-Northern Song Dynasty led
celadon technology to shift to other places suitable for its development.
Historical records state: “celadon originated from Liutian (刘田).” 刘田 was later
written as 琉田 (also pronounced Liutian), and this was the central production
area of the Longquan kilns. The production capacity of the Longquan kilns
was small in the late Northern Song and reached a larger scale only in the
late years of the Northern Song after a period of development.55
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Early products of the Longquan kilns were mainly plates, bowls and
pots, and a small number of jars. The main decorative technique was
engraved patterns, supplemented by comb points or comb-carved waves,
banana leaves, clouds and lotus petals. These early products of the
Longquan kilns bore similarities with Yue, Ou and Wuzhou wares in terms
of shape, decoration and glaze color, suggesting associations between the
Longquan kilns and the other kilns and reflecting the common local and
temporal characteristics of celadon in Zhejiang. After the mid-Northern
Song Dynasty, as the Yue and Ou kilns fell into decline, the Longquan kilns
gradually formed their own style. Varieties increased to include stoves,
bottles, plates, cuspidors and sculptures, each with diverse designs.
Decoration was still dominated by the engraved pattern (Fig. 8.56). Comb
patterns decreased and auspicious words such as 金玉满堂 (“Gold and jade fill
the hall”) and 河滨遗范 (“Good example set by predecessors at riverside”)
appeared on the wells of bowls. Decorative patterns included waves, clouds,
banana leaves, peonies, elaborate blossoms, and children at play. The shape
design and decorative patterns of a kind of shallow flat-based saucer were
quite similar to those of similar saucers produced by the Yaozhou kilns in
Shaanxi of the same period, both often with a swimming fish or a lotus
flower carved at their centers. This provided evidence for the judgement
that in the same period, porcelain kilns in different places often shared a
common style in terms of shape and decoration. In the late Northern Song
Dynasty lotus relief patterns became popular. They were often used to
decorate the outer surface of bowls. The petal tips were rounded, and the
petals were all carved with lines (Fig. 8.57).





Fig. 8.56 Longquan kiln engraved plate,
Song Dynasty, height: 3.2 cm, top diam.: 15.5 cm, base diam.: 5 cm, in the Palace Museum

   Longquan kiln products from the Northern Song Dynasty used local
porcelain stone with a high silicon and iron content, resulting in a thick,
heavy and steady-looking body. The body was mostly gray or light gray and
the glaze was relatively thin with a yellowish blue color (Fig. 8.58). The use
of lime glaze led to an excellent glaze surface luster because lime glaze has
a relatively low viscosity and good fluidity at high temperature. Glaze was
commonly troubled by yellow shades because kiln workers at the time had
not well mastered the skills of controlling reducing atmosphere.





Fig. 8.58 Longquan kiln double-fish washer,
Song Dynasty, height: 6 cm, top diam.: 13.5 cm, base diam.: 13 cm, in the Palace Museum

   By the Southern Song Dynasty, Hangzhou became the new political
center and the rise of the Guan kilns there also led to rapid development in
the Longquan kilns. Around the middle and late Southern Song Dynasty the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
quality of Longquan celadon improved quickly and significantly. In
addition to the kilns located within modern-day Longquan County that fired
celadon, many kilns in nearby areas, such as in Qingyuan, Suichang and
Yunhe and also in Jiangxi and Fujian also fired celadon following the
Longquan kiln style.56 In this period, Longquan kiln products were well-
made and sophisticated, and the varieties also increased. In addition to daily
utensils such as bowls, plates, pots and jars, new varieties of display objects
and sacrificial vessels emerged, many of which imitated ancient copper,
jade and lacquerware. The incense burner shown in Fig. 8.59 was a
Longquan celadon ware that imitated bronze incense burners back in the
Shang and Zhou dynasties. The ware shown in Fig. 8.60, called a “mallet
bottle”, also known as “kinuta” in Japan, usually employed in pairs as
burial objects or household sacrifices, took its shape design also from
similar bronzewares with large mouths and double fish ears. These celadon
wares imitating antique bronze vessels became the aesthetic fashion of
scholar-bureaucrats in the Southern Song Dynasty and this fashion in turn
promoted the development of Longquan celadon. Besides ancient bronzes,
Longquan ware also imitated Guan kiln ware and produced two different
types of Guan-style products, namely Dayao ware and Wayaoyang ware.
Dayao ware was white-bodied celadon with a thick body and glaze. Glaze
colors included greenish blue, plum green and pea green. Surface
decoration that were popular previously, such as engraved or printed
patterns, decreased because thickened glaze would conceal them and
compromise the effect. Instead more effort was spent on shape design.
Decorations included relief, bulging veins and decals, which appeared
simple, elegant and dignified against the backdrop of thick glaze.
Wayaoyang ware was back-bodied celadon with a thin body and thick glaze
and bore a remarkable resemblance to the thin-bodied thick-glaze products
of the Southern Song Guan kilns, not only in appearance, but also in
production technologies from body and glaze formula to firing method. The
Southern Song imperial family’s preference for celadon had a significant
impact on the trends of the upper class at the time, but the products of the
Guan kilns were strictly forbidden to be used by the common people.
