   As to where these Buddhist statues were produced, scholars have
different theories. Some believe that they were made by the Longquanwu
kilns in modern-day Mentougou, Beijing on the grounds that the tricolor
Bodhisattva statues found at the Longquanwu kiln site, which were
determined to be fired in the Liao Dynasty, were quite similar to the Yixian
tricolor Arhats in terms of material, body texture and glaze color. Yet some
researchers posit that this alone does not suffice to lead to the conclusion
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
that the Yixian porcelain Arhat statues were made in the Longquanwu kilns
because since Yixian County was not far from the Yanbei area of Shanxi
Province and Shanxi had a long Buddhist art tradition, there was a good
chance that the tricolor Arhat statues were produced near Yixian in Shanxi
or by Shanxi craftsmen.78 Another argument for this second theory was that
it would be difficult to transport such life-size porcelain statues across
hundreds of kilometers of bumpy roads from Longquanwu to Yixian either
by water or by land. Moreover, at that time there were countless ceramic
kilns under the jurisdiction of the Liao Dynasty, and it was not difficult to
construct new kilns. A simple kiln could be completed in only one or two
days. Thus, it was quite possible that there were ceramic kilns in or near
Yixian at the time and it is only that the kiln site has yet to be discovered.79
   Although few tricolor wares from the Liao Dynasty have survived, these
tricolor Arhats alone are enough to illustrate the height of tricolor porcelain
art and to demonstrate the achievements of Chinese ceramic sculptors,
especially of Buddha statues, at that time.

8.4.8 Contribution of Liao Dynasty’s Porcelain Industry
A summary of the historical contribution of the Liao Dynasty’s porcelain
industry is much called for as the previous narrative on the history of
ceramics was centered on the Han ethnicity and tended to overlook the
contribution of minority ethnic groups when discussing the achievements of
ceramics industry development.

8.4.8.1 Appearance of Vermilion Painting and Gilding on White
Porcelain
From the tomb of the Liao Emperor’s Son-in-law, the Prince of Weiguo,
there were unearthed two white porcelain plate-mouthed bottles with
vermilion and gold dragon patterns. Vermilion painting combined with
golden gilt was a new porcelain technique that appeared in the Liao
Dynasty, a technique that laid the foundation for the later appearance of gilt
colored porcelain of the Song Dynasty, the red and green porcelain of the
Yuan Dynasty, and the red and green wucai porcelain, gold painted
porcelain and wucai ware of the Ming and Qing dynasties.80

8.4.8.2 Adoption of Boron Glaze
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
The adoption of boron glaze was a major breakthrough in porcelain-making
technology that occurred in the Liao Dynasty. The Shanghai Institute of
Ceramics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences tested four green-glazed
specimen shards of the Liao Dynasty unearthed at the Baipu Temple kiln
site in Mentougou, Beijing, and found that some of the green glaze was
boron glaze, a finding that confirmed that Chinese craftsmen started making
and using boron glaze as early as the Liao Dynasty. The low-temperature
glaze of Chinese ceramics down through the dynasties mostly used lead
oxides as a solubilizer. These lead oxides greatly lowered the temperature
required to fire the glaze and enabled glass phase to grow in the glaze at a
relatively low temperature. Yet lead was harmful to the human body and
could be poisonous if used long-term. Boron, on the other hand, is harmless
to humans even in long-term use, and boron oxides can perform the same
solubilizing role and reduce the firing temperature of glaze as can lead,
making boron oxides a most ideal solubilizer. In fact boron glaze is still
widely used in ceramic production to this day. The pioneering use of boron
by craftsmen in the Liao Dynasty was a great contribution to the
development of Chinese ceramic technology.81

8.4.8.3 Adoption of Unglazed-Ring Stacked Firing
Previously, academic circles had long believed that unglazed-ring stacked
firing was conceived by the Ding kilns in Quyang, Hebei in the Jin
Dynasty, but this was in fact a misunderstanding. The so called “unglazed-
ring stacked firing” refers to the practice of scraping off a ring of glaze on
the shoulder or inner base of a ware to expose the body so that when
another ware is stacked on top of it to be sent together for firing, the two
wares will not get stuck to each other. A black-glazed bottle with raised
lines unearthed from the Xiao Shenwei Ancestor No. 4 Tomb from the Liao
Dynasty in Qinghemen, Yixian, Liaoning in 1950 indicated that the practice
had already been tried by craftsmen in the Liao Dynasty rather than being
conceived in the Jin Dynasty, because the bottle had a ring of glaze scraped
off on the shoulder to avoid sticking with the ware stacked on it during
firing.82

8.4.8.4 Geographical Expansion of China’s Ceramic Kilns
Before the establishment of the Khitan regime, most porcelain kilns in
China were on the central plains and southern areas such as Jiangsu and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Zhejiang while there had not been any porcelain kiln in northeast China
except for the Bohai Kingdom which produced some architectural ceramics,
a situation that changed during the Liao Dynasty as it successively set up
dozens of kilns large and small in all of its five circuits. The establishment
of these kilns, especially those on the northern prairie, not only expanded
the porcelain-making industry to areas north of the Great Wall, but also
facilitated the development of the industry in the north. This is a major
contribution of the Liao Dynasty’s ceramic culture in the history of Chinese
ceramics.

8.4.8.5 First to Use Dragon Kilns in Northern China
Archeological findings show that in southern China the dragon kiln started
to be used to fire pottery imprinted with geometric patterns and primitive
celadon before the Qin and Han dynasties and started to be used to produce
celadon wares in the Eastern Han Dynasty, while in northern China steamed
bun kilns continued to be used to fire porcelain up until the Tang and Song
dynasties. The Chifeng Gangwa kilns in the Liao Dynasty became the first
to introduce the dragon kiln to northern China, and especially to the
northern prairie by using it to fire coarse and large porcelain vessels such as
chicken-leg shaped crocks.83
    In addition to the contributions mentioned above, Liao ware had many
unique and original features in terms of shape design, body and glaze,
decorative technique, and pattern themes, which had a far-reaching impact
on the northern ceramic development of the Jin, Yuan and later dynasties,
and also had some influence on the development of the ceramics industry in
the south.

8.5 Porcelain of the Jin Dynasty
The Jin Dynasty (1115 to 1234) was a regime established by the ethnic
minority known as the Nuzhen (the Jurchens) in northeastern China. It was
founded by Wanyan Aguda and established its first capital in Huining
Prefecture (present-day Acheng District, Harbin, Heilongjiang Province). It
conquered the Liao in 1125, overthrew the Northern Song a short time later,
moved its capital to Zhongdu and then to Bianjing (present-day Kaifeng,
Henan Province), and started a prolonged confrontation with the Southern
Song Dynasty.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Like the Liao Dynasty, one important aspect of the Jin Dynasty’s
significance in Chinese history was that it strengthened and highlighted
ethnic minority regimes as a part of Chinese history proper. Unlike the
Liao, which ruled over only northern China, the Jin, after replacing the
Liao, occupied and established its center in the central plains area which
had traditionally been ruled by Han regimes and at the same time ruled over
the entire area east of the Liao River (roughly present-day Liaoning
Province) and part of the southern Gobi desert. Since the only Han regime
which conformed to the traditional concept of “China” at that time—the
Southern Song—had given up the central plains of China and ruled over
only areas south of the Qinling Mountains and the Huaihe River, a “China”
at that time with only the Southern Song and without the Jin regime could
not be said to have been complete. Therefore, the history of the Jin Dynasty
was an important link in China’s history and without it, China’s history
would not be complete and the Chinese civilization would not be as great.
In addition, the Jin Dynasty drew northeast China into the mainstream of
Chinese history and gave it an important position on the Chinese stage,
which was to have a significant impact on modern Chinese and indeed
global geopolitics.
   From the perspective of the history of ceramics, the territory of the Jin
Dynasty extended deep into the central plains to cover today’s Hebei,
Henan, Shandong, Shanxi, Shaanxi and Gansu, so that the famous kilns of
the Northern Song Dynasty such as the Ru, Ding, Yaozhou, Cizhou and Jun
were now all within Jin’s jurisdiction. However, previously Jin has not been
placed in an important position in the study of ceramic history, and some
researchers even omitted this historical period altogether when writing
ceramic history. This oversight was on the one hand due to the lack of
research materials and unearthed objects on the topic in the past, and on the
other hand, a lack of attention paid to ceramic production under the rule of
ethnic minority regimes owing to the influence of Han centrism. In recent
years, with an increasing quantity of cultural relics being unearthed from
the period, many scholars have begun to study the ceramics industry of the
Jin and have come to realize its important status in the history of ceramics.
   The development of Jin dynasty porcelains can be divided into two parts
according to geographical location. One part was originally the map of the
Liao Dynasty and then of the Jin before it advanced southward, that is,
mainly in present-day northeast China and Inner Mongolia. The main kilns
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
were the Chifeng Gangwa, Fushun Daguantun, Liaoyang Gangguantun,
Mentougou Longquanwu, Fangshan Cijiawu, Miyun Xiaoshuiyu, Longhua
Xiawazi, the Hunyuan Daciyao Village kilns, and the Qingciyao Village
kilns. Most of these kilns inherited the tradition of the Liao Dynasty and
mainly produced daily-use coarse wares. Whatever the glaze color, black,
white, caramel, chayemo (tea-dust) or white with black pattern, all the
wares had a turbid glaze surface, coarse, thick body, and a low degree of
sintering. The modeling process was rough, resulting in highly irregular
shapes. The main varieties were bowls, saucers, plates, jars, pots, etc.,
among which pots and jars mostly had two, three or four lugs. The other
batch of kilns were those originally in the Northern Song Dynasty, damaged
by the war and subsequently restored by the Jin regime after it occupied the
vast northern China plain. They were the Jun, Yaozhou, Ding, and Cizhou
kilns, etc.84 Of these the most distinctive were the Ding kilns. Ding ware
produced in the Jin Dynasty had a fine white texture, lustrous glaze color,
neat and delicate construction and gorgeous decoration.
  We will skip the ceramic production conditions in areas traditionally
ruled by the Jin Dynasty and only introduce representative kilns in the
central plains under the Jin’s rule in the following sections.

8.5.1 The Ding Kilns
In the study of Ding kilns, it is often emphasized that the peak period of
Ding kiln production was the late Northern Song Dynasty, especially the
time of Emperor Huizong. This view is so deeply rooted in people’s minds
that they often overlook the conditions of the Ding kilns in other periods
and often deem many exquisite Ding wares with engraved or printed
patterns to be made in the late Northern Song Dynasty.
   The traditional view also holds that since the Jin Dynasty, after bringing
the Liao Dynasty to an end, attacked the Song Dynasty, the central plains
suffered serious damage due to warfare. The Ding kilns in the Jin Dynasty,
also assumed to be damaged by the war, were often neglected in research.
The ruling center of the Northern Song, that is, central and western Henan
and the region north of the Huaihe River with Xuzhou at its center, indeed
suffered serious damage in the war between the Jin and the Song, yet how
much were the Ding kilns affected by the war? Archaeological data found
to date indicate that Ding kiln production continued from the late Northern
Song Dynasty well into the early Jin Dynasty and the view in the past that
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
there had been several decades of interruption was simply not the case.85 In
recent years, with the discovery of Ding wares in tombs of the Jin Dynasty
and the Southern Song Dynasty as well as at other sites with specific year
records, the production of Ding ware in the Jin Dynasty has attracted more
and more attention.
   So far researchers have found 16 tombs with year records from which
Ding ware of the Jin Dynasty (including of the Southern Song Dynasty) has
been unearthed. In addition, the discovery of Jin dynasty printing molds
with year inscriptions at the Ding kiln site in Quyang, Hebei provided
definitive age information for the study of Jin dynasty Ding porcelain. The
special historical background of the Song, Liao and Jin dynasties resulted in
the unique phenomenon of porcelains being stored in cellars. Many Ding
wares have been unearthed from some of these cellars, which were mainly
those in the north in the late Jin Dynasty, the most important ones being
Nong’an cellar in Jilin and Linzi cellar in Shandong. The original
excavators of Linzi cellar presumed it was from the late Northern Song
Dynasty based on the investigation and trial excavation data of the Quyang
Ding kiln site, yet in recent years some scholars have put forward the new
view that the products in the cellar must have been made in the Jin Dynasty,
based on their decorative style.86 Apart from northern China, cellars with
Ding wares have also been found in Sichuan in the south.
     It has also been found that some tombs previously deemed to be from
the Liao Dynasty now seem to have a greater chance of actually belonging
to the Jin Dynasty. One example is the batch of Ding white porcelain
unearthed from a stone coffin tomb in Qiaonan in the then Fengtai Town of
Beijing, which in the past had been taken by many scholars to be important
specimens of Ding ware from the mid-Northern Song Dynasty. But in
recent years researchers have consistently advanced new views on the age
of this tomb, positing that such stone coffin tombs composed of six large
stone slabs was a typical Jin dynasty tomb form.87 Japanese scholars have
conjectured that the white porcelain water jet in the tomb was produced in
the mid-eleventh century,88 yet pictures show that it is similar to the white
porcelain water jet unearthed from the mural tomb dated Zhenglong Fourth
Year of the Jin Dynasty (1159) in the southern suburbs of Datong, Shanxi
Province in terms of shape and style.89 Besides, the Ding kiln engraved
white porcelain unearthed from the stone coffin tomb was of a style
common to wares from the Jin Dynasty. Thus, both the style of the tomb
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and the style of the porcelain unearthed in it suggest that the tomb must be
from the Jin Dynasty.90
    In 2009 a joint archaeological team composed of the Cultural Relics
Institute of Hebei Province and Peking University made an important
discovery at the Ding kiln site in Jianci Village, Quyang, Hebei Province.
They excavated two kiln furnace sites and one workshop site and unearthed
a large number of porcelain shards from the early Northern Song Dynasty to
the Jin Dynasty, including items featuring dragon patterns and inscriptions
such as “Medicine Bureau.” The shards offered rich first-hand data for the
comprehensive study of the Ding kilns. Jin dynasty culture strata and
various ruins were found in every square unit in the Jianci, Beizhen District
as well as in the Yanchuan District. The thick culture strata and abundant
unearthed materials indicate that the Jin Dynasty was the largest production
period in terms of scale in the history of the Ding kilns. Unearthed at the
site was a batch of important relics that could shed light on the conditions
of Ding ware as imperial tribute in different periods. Such relics included
wares inscribed with the Chinese character guan (“official”) from the Five
Dynasties and the early Song strata, wares inscribed with “Food Bureau,”
“Medicine Bureau” or “Qiao Wei,” wares decorated with the dragon
pattern, wares imitating ancient bronze ritual vessels and exquisite
porcelain sculptures in the Northern Song stratum, and bowls and plates
inscribed with “Food Bureau” or “East Palace” in the Jin dynasty stratum,
all of which provided physical evidence for the study of the characteristics
and history of tributary wares of the Ding kilns. The above findings show
that the production of the Ding kilns retained its prosperity and developed
further on the basis of its status in the late Northern Song Dynasty as it
continued into the Jin Dynasty. From the unearthed objects we can see that
the shape design and engraved patterns of Ding ware demonstrated
historical continuity. Folded belly plates, funnel-shaped bowls and flat
bottom plates were all typical varieties after the late Northern Song
Dynasty, and carved daylily patterns, double fish patterns and single lotus
patterns were also popular decorations after the late Northern Song
Dynasty. Throughout the Jin Dynasty, wares fired upside down were the
most common and popular. In the early Jin Dynasty, engraved and carved
decorations were still prevalent, but in general they were not as neat and
meticulous as those of the late Northern Song Dynasty and instead, tended
to be quite random. By the middle and late Jin Dynasty, printed decorations
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
appeared in large numbers and became popular, gradually replacing carved
decorations. Ding ware was dominated by bowls, plates, washers and
saucers, with the quantities of bowls and plates increasing further in the
later period of the Jin Dynasty, which indicated that Jin porcelain was
mainly for folk use and had a broad domestic market.
   The nature of the Ding kilns as folk and commercial kilns should not be
negated by the fact that many research materials suggest the Ding kilns
produced a certain amount of tributary porcelain for the court of the
Northern Song Dynasty, and that they might have also been producing
tributary wares for the rulers of the Jin Dynasty (which can be inferred from
the bowls and plates inscribed with “Food Bureau” or “East Palace” found
in the Jin dynasty stratum at the Quyang Ding kiln site in 2009).
    After the Jin Dynasty occupied the central plains, the Nuzhen rulers
adopted a series of Sinicizing measures and the economy of the central
plains was rapidly restored and developed. As Jin’s territory expanded to
cover the central plains, the location of the Ding kilns, Zhongshan
Prefecture (Dingzhou), became the center of the Jin regime, which helped
the Ding kilns capture the vast northern market. From a wealth of
archaeological materials we can see that in many Song and Liao tombs,
regardless of the rank and social estate of the tomb owner, southern
porcelain in different quantities have been unearthed, with qingbai
porcelain being especially common. Yet in tombs and ruins from the Jin
Dynasty, though qingbai porcelain or Longquan celadon was occasionally
also seen, they were quite rare, which suggested that by the Jin Dynasty, the
Ding kilns had occupied the northern market given its comparative
advantage. The rare unearthing of southern produced porcelain in areas
ruled by the Jin Dynasty indicate that the absence of competition from
southern porcelain guaranteed an excellent market for the production and
sales of the porcelain kilns in northern China, including the Ding and
Cizhou kilns.91
   Ding ware was sold in the north as well as to the south. The political
and military confrontation between the Jin Dynasty in the north and the
Southern Song Dynasty in the south did not sever the economic ties
between them. After the Treaty of Shaoxing was reached, trade between the
two regimes became even more frequent. The trade was mainly carried out
in frontier trade zones called “que markets,” and in the meantime there was
a lot of tributary trade between the imperial courts, as well as smuggling. It
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
was through these various channels that Ding ware of the Jin Dynasty was
sold in large quantities to the south, and has been unearthed in border areas
between Song and Jin, namely, present-day Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Sichuan,
near the center of Southern Song Dynasty rule, and in economically
developed cities of the Southern Song Dynasty. Sizhou was a very
important frontier trade zone during the confrontation between the Song
and Jin dynasties, and Zhou Hui of the Southern Song recorded in his Qing
Bo Za Zhi that there was once Sizhou porcelain imitating Ding ware fired in
the area, which was a typical case of imitation occasioned by the large-scale
sales of Ding ware. In the trade, the Jin Dynasty had to import large
amounts of tea and other materials from the Southern Song Dynasty, yet the
Jin believed that “trading silk for tea” was “trading useful things for useless
things.” Thus, later it started trading salt and sundries for tea, and one
important commodity among these “sundries” would have been porcelain.
Besides, porcelain, and especially Ding ware, undoubtedly played an
important role in Song and Jin’s struggle for copper coins in the trade
between them, which could be another reason behind the prosperity of the
Ding kilns in the Jin Dynasty.92 In southern tombs, Ding ware is often
unearthed together with exquisite and precious silver objects, which has led
some researchers to believe that at the time, Ding ware was used as a
supplement to silver vessels.93
   During the Song and Jin dynasties, the white porcelain of the Ding kilns
was imitated by many other kiln yards due to its high quality and good
sales. The imitative products of these other kilns all had their own
characteristics, and some exhibited a passing resemblance to their models.
The following are the main northern kilns which imitated Ding ware:
   The site of the Jingxing kilns is in present-day Tianchang Town,
Jingxing, Hebei Province. White porcelain produced by the Jingxing kilns
during the Song and Jin dynasties was of good quality and exhibited
characteristics similar to those of Ding ware. The printed decoration in
particular resembled and was almost identical to that of Ding ware. It is
now certain that some of the products previously regarded as Ding ware
must have been fired by the Jingxing kilns.
   The site of the Shanxia kilns was located in Shanxia Village south of
Lincheng City in Hebei Province and is one of the Xing kiln sites in a broad
sense. The white porcelain of the Shanxia kilns were rough compared to the
products of the Ding kilns. Its engraved and imprinted decorations were not
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
as exquisite as similar products from the Ding kilns, its patterns were not as
clear, the body and glaze had an obvious bluish gray color, and the body
had a strong stone texture. Despite the inferior quality, the decorative
techniques and firing methods of Shanxia ware were obviously influenced
by the Ding kilns, especially the firing methods, which developed almost
concurrently with the Ding kilns.
   The Longquanwu kilns, with their site in Mentougou, Beijing, operated
in the Liao and Jin dynasties. Their products were mainly white porcelain
featuring a pure white body and yellowish white glaze similar to those of
Ding ware. The hardness of the body was higher than Ding ware with a
stronger stone texture. Some wares had a grayish white body. The engraved
and carved patterns were not as skillfully cut as those of Ding ware and
some patterns were crude. The glaze had a high brightness.
   The site of the Jiexiu kilns is in Hongshan Town, Jiexiu, Shanxi
Province. The most common varieties of Jiexiu white porcelain are bowls
and plates. Products in the early Song Dynasty had a thicker body. Later
under the influence of Ding ware, the Jiexiu kilns started making printed
white porcelain whose body and glaze were all finer. Typical decorative
patterns include children and peonies and children rowing boats.
   Another kiln yard producing porcelain like Ding ware was the Huo kiln,
named after the surname of the kiln owner but also called the Peng kiln,
named after the locality. The kiln started production in the Jin Dynasty and
reached its zenith in the Yuan Dynasty. Its site was found in Chencun
Village, Huoxian County, Shanxi Province. The products had a fine, white,
thin body and white glaze, some with plain surfaces and some with printed
decorations. The body texture was quite crisp and highly fragile. Some were
fired stacked with an unglazed ring to avoid sticking between vessels,
which was the same method used by the Ding kilns, while some were fired
stacked with support pins, a method not seen in Ding ware. The support
pins were very thin and left marks on the inner bottoms of most bowls and
plates. In most cases four to six pins were used and five was the most
common.
   Besides the many kilns in the north, some southern kilns such as the
Fanchang kilns in Anhui and the Jingdezhen kilns in Jiangxi also imitated
Ding ware. The large number of kilns imitating the products of the Ding
kilns in the Jin Dynasty show that Ding ware had a huge market demand
that could not be met by the Ding kilns’ own production alone. This also
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
shows that the Jin Dynasty was not a period of decline for the Ding kilns
but was rather a thriving period in their production process. Of course, the
exact production status of the Ding kilns in the Jin Dynasty still requires
more archaeological discoveries to shed light on the reality. In addition, the
prosperity of the Ding kilns in the Jin Dynasty might be partly due to the
preference of the northern ethnic minorities of the Jin Dynasty for the color
white. The preference of the ruler usually plays an important role in such
choices.

8.5.2 The Jun Kilns
After the Song Dynasty moved southward, the “official Jun kilns” in
Yuzhou, Henan Province were abandoned. Then, with the gradual
strengthening of the Jin regime, the production of the Jun kilns was
restored. Jin Dynasty Jun ware broke the “exclusive for imperial use law”
of the Jun official kilns of the Song Dynasty, that is, the wares stepped
down from the pedestal as objects for sacrificing to Heaven, vessels for
imperial use only, and symbols of the royal family, of power and dignity, to
disseminate among the common people, which blazed a trail for the
diversified development of Jun ware. In the meantime, Jun porcelain started
learning the excellent styles of Ding, Ru and Yaozhou ware and adopted
such decorative techniques as printing, carving and relief. With its rich
cultural connotations, while moving towards the common people, Jun ware
also aroused the enthusiasm of vast numbers of kiln workers, thus
expanding the scope of its own development so that by the Yuan Dynasty a
huge Jun kiln system had formed. To summarize, the development of the
Jun kilns in the Jin Dynasty was a continuation of Jun ware after the Jin
Dynasty started ruling the Yangdi area (present-day Yuzhou), and this
development enabled Jun ware, once defined as court culture, to return to
the common people, amongst whom it became regarded as a royal treasure
that was once lost and now recovered. This fact has been corroborated later
by the history of the porcelain industry in the Yuan, Ming and Qing
dynasties.
   As the products of the Jun kilns in the Jin Dynasty were mostly for the
practical use of the people, the most common varieties at the time were
basins, bowls, saucers, jars, bottles, cases and other daily necessities, while
ceremonial and display porcelain that purely emphasized aesthetic appeal
such as incense burners, ding and zun were fewer. This marked the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
transformation of Jun ware’s function and role from luxury good made by
official kilns to plain goods for folk use. The production of folk use
products also required more attention paid to costs, and as a result the
products were in many respects not as exquisite as the previous Northern
Song Dynasty Jun ware. The first aspect was body texture. Song Dynasty
Jun ware had a fine, dense body that was grayish brown in color, had low
water absorption, and boasted a high degree of ceramization. When struck it
gave off a clanging and melodious sound. An examination of the fracture
surface showed that the body was pure without impurities, devoid of
crevices and rarely troubled by glaze peeling. Jin Dynasty Jun ware, on the
other hand, except for a few high-quality products, were mostly impaired by
loose body texture and a body color that was not sufficiently gray and
tended to be yellowish or reddish. When struck, the sound it made was
numb, similar to the sound of pottery, which was mainly due to low firing
temperature and poor material selection.
   The second aspect was glaze color. The glaze color of Song Jun folk
kiln products was mostly azure, or pale blue, sky blue and verdant, and
official kiln ware was famous for its attractive fambe glaze realized by
using copper oxides as a colorant. Though compared to official ware, the
body and glaze of folk ware was slightly thinner, both folk and official ware
were fully glazed to an appropriate thickness, had brown (commonly known
as sesame butter color) protection glaze applied to the bottom, and were
rarely troubled by glaze flow or bottom sticking. The fambe glaze of
Northern Song Jun ware, realized by the coloring of various metal elements
in a high temperature reducing atmosphere, was highly colorful, changeable
and natural, while the glaze color of Jin Jun ware was relatively
monotonous. It was either sky blue, pale blue, or grayish blue, occasionally
decorated by purple spots, which nevertheless covered only small areas and
had traces of artificiality. Most Jun kiln works from the Jin Dynasty had a
shallow, dull, and monotonous glaze color, nothing near as artistically
appealing as the colorful and bright glaze of Song Jun ware. In addition,
yuanqi (wares in open forms) such as plates and bowls of the Song Dynasty
were mostly imperfectly glazed on the bottom, exposing some of the body,
and the circular foot was mostly caramel colored and unglazed.
   The third aspect was shaping and firing technique. Whether produced
by folk kilns or official kilns, the Jun ware of the Song Dynasty was neat
and meticulous. Drum nail washers, flowerpots, pot trays and plates were
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
propped with support pins when fired and other wares were supported with
bedders. In contrast, Jun ware of the Jin Dynasty was rarely propped during
firing except for the use of support plates. Vessels formed with the wheel
were irregular in shape. The circular feet of all basins, bowls, saucers and
jars were straight and cut out with one stroke, resulting in uneven surfaces
and varying depths. Blade and finger marks were left on the ware in
different places and were not modified or remedied in any way whatsoever.
  A comparison of all the above aspects shows that Jin Dynasty Jun ware
was far inferior to Northern Song Jun ware. The primary reason was that
they were made for different purposes and to serve different groups. Song
Jun ware was produced for imperial use so that perfection was striven for
regardless of time or cost in order to meet the high standards and strict
requirements of the court, while Jin Jun ware was produced for the market
and for common people’s daily use, which determined that production time
and cost was the priority because it was related to the price that buyers
would accept. Another possible reason for the debased quality of Jin
Dynasty Jun ware was that a portion of the skilled craftsmen in the north
migrated southward with the Song royal house and the remaining artists
lacked the necessary technical means or had only limited skills. Yet I do not
believe this to be a deciding factor because as long as there was demand,
corresponding technologies could arise to respond to that demand. A more
important fact here is that demand by the common people sustained the
development of Jun ware in the Jin Dynasty and helped it become more
popular and diversified.
     Still, there are some fine works among Jin Dynasty Jun kiln products.
The wine bowl as shown in Fig. 8.91 has a very unique shape design, with
one side of the mouth rim in the shape of a leaf, under which there is a ring
handle. The design might have been borrowed from gold and silver wares,
whose body was formed by hammering and whose extended rim on one
side of the mouth was first formed with a thin metal sheet and then welded
onto the bowl. This style was very popular in northern China at the time and
probably came from the Persian Sassanid Dynasty. Such wine bowls with
folded rim and ring handle appeared almost simultaneously among Yaozhou
ware, Ding ware and Jun ware in northern China, and similar wares have
also been excavated at the Longquan kiln site in southern China. This
shows that Jun ware in the Jin Dynasty was deeply influenced by the plastic
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
arts of foreign nationalities and other kilns, and that the arts of different
cultures and in different materials were interactive and interlinked.

8.5.3 The Yaozhou Kilns
The historical periodization of Yaozhou kilns in the early Jin Dynasty was
more complicated than that of other kilns because Yaozhou, where the
Huangbao kiln yard was located, was passed between the Song and Jin
several times after the Jingkang Incident. Correspondingly, the
periodization of the Yaozhou kilns during this era should also include the
Southern Song, making it difficult for later generations to date Yaozhou
wares. The traditional view was that the Yaozhou kilns started declining
after the Jin Dynasty. Yet in recent years, with the discovery of multiple
Yaozhou ware cellars from the Jin Dynasty, and with the revelation of
inscriptions about tributary porcelain on Jin dynasty tablets on Yaowang
Mountain, academic circles have developed a new understanding of the
historical status of the Yaozhou kilns in the Jin Dynasty: the Jin Dynasty
should not be simply regarded as a period of decline for the Yaozhou kilns,
and the achievements of the Yaozhou kilns in the Jin Dynasty should be
objectively recognized, that is, in the Jin Dynasty the Yaozhou kilns fired
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
no less products than in the Northern Song Dynasty and even made
innovations in terms of its pale blue glaze.94
   There are two ways to understand the porcelain production of the
Yaozhou kilns in the Jin Dynasty. One is to review relevant literature and
the other is to compare and verify physical objects that have been
discovered. Of the limited amount of research on this subject available so
far, this author has come across two articles by Du Wen, and the following
are some of his research results.
   The fifth volume of Qing Bo Za Zhi by Zhou Hui of the Southern Song
Dynasty has the following note: “I once heard a visitor from the north
saying that Huangpu (黄浦) Town in Yaozhou fires porcelain called Yao ware,
of which white items are considered the finest and are used in Heshuo for
tea.” Du Wen concludes that from the “once heard a visitor from the north
saying” it may be understood that Zhou Hui had not been to Huangbao (黄堡)
Town himself (in Guanzhong dialect “堡” (bao) is pronounced “pu,” the
same as the pronunciation of the Chinese character “浦” as recorded by Zhou
Hui). The most valuable information about Jin dynasty Yao ware mentioned
in the piece above is that “white ones are considered the finest and are used
in Heshuo for tea.” In ancient times Heshuo was used to refer to areas north
of the Yellow River. The record from Qing Bo Za Zhi indicates the wide
popularity of Yao ware in areas north of the Yellow River in the Jin
Dynasty, especially the popularity of “white” (pale blue) porcelain.95
    In addition, in the second volume of his Notes in Old Scholar Hut, Lu
You writes: “Yaozhou produces celadon ware, called Yue ware, which
seems to be because it is similar to the secret-color ware of Yuyao County.
Yet the quality is extremely coarse, simple and poor. Only restaurants use it
a lot for its durability.” Lu You was born in October 1125 in the late
Northern Song, but grew up in the Southern Song, and he wrote Notes in
Old Scholar Hut in his later years. From 1170 he took office successively in
Kuizhou (modern-day Fengjie, Sichuan), Hanzhong, Chengdu, Shuzhou,
Jiazhou and Rongzhou, until 1178 when he left Sichuan. Thus, Lu You
served in Sichuan for nearly 10 years. He mentioned that Yao ware was also
called “Yue ware”, “yet the quality is extremely coarse, simple and poor,”
which was quite strange since the celadon fired by the Huangbao kiln yard
(which belonged to the Yaozhou kilns, with inscriptions indicating their
time from the early Jin Dynasty) that have been found so far are generally
of good quality. “Only restaurants use it a lot for its durability” indicates
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
that the quantity of such ware imported into Sichuan was substantial. Du
Wen suggests that if Lu You saw large numbers of Yaozhou Jin style
celadon bowls and plates sold and used locally in Sichuan, it was very
likely that these Yaozhou type vessels included a large proportion of poor-
quality celadon products fired by local kilns in Sichuan such as the Tushan
kilns in imitation of Yaozhou ware.96
   Volume 72 of The History of Jin, Biography of Gou Ying (originally
named Ta Lan), records in detail the battle between Song and Jin in
Yaozhou during the Tianhui era and how Gou Ying led the army to ambush
and conquer Yaozhou. Then The History of Song records that in the fourth
month of Shaoxing First Year (1131), “Zhao Bin, commander of Jingyuan
of the Jin Dynasty, attacked Yaozhou, and was struck off by defend
commander Zhao Cheng” (Volume 26 of The History of Song, Gaozong
III), which indicates that it was less than half a year after Yaozhou came
under the suzerainty of the Jin regime that it was again occupied by the
army of the Southern Song. In 1140, the Jin army again occupied Shaanxi
and other places that were deemed to be under the jurisdiction of the
Southern Song Dynasty in the agreement reached by the two regimes
earlier. In the eighth month of 1142, the borderline across Shaanxi between
Jin and Song was drawn, and the two sides agreed that the Dasan Pass
should be the boundary, and it was only at this time that Yaozhou fell to the
rule of the Jin Dynasty. Yaozhou was located in the southernmost part of
northern Shaanxi. It was likely that during the war, Yaozhou kiln workers
retreated to Sichuan and southern Shaanxi with the army and civilians of
northern Shaanxi. This would also explain why in the Southern Song
Dynasty, kilns in the Ba-Shu (two ancient states in modern Sichuan) area
such as the Tushan kilns in Chongqing, Ciwanpu kilns in Dazhou, and
Zitong kilns imitated the printed blue and yellow glaze wares of the
Yaozhou kiln style, and that many kilns in Sichuan used steamed bun kilns
using coal as the fuel instead of the wood-burning dragon kiln which was
common in southern China. Sichuan and Shaanxi are adjacent to each other
and closely connected by the Jialing and Danjiang rivers, and the kiln
industry in the two provinces had exchanges in ancient times. One piece of
evidence is the Ciwanpu kiln that has been recently excavated in the
Tongchuan District of Dazhou. The kiln rose in the early Southern Song
Dynasty and was abandoned in the early Yuan Dynasty. Most of its
products were printed celadon in the Yaozhou kiln style, some of which
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
were decorated with the rare pattern of a Gyrfalcon clutching a swan.
Similar patterns were also found on wares produced in the late Jin and early
Yuan Dynasty by the Shangdian kiln yard, which belonged to the Yaozhou
kilns.97
    In addition, Song and Jin Yaozhou ware has been unearthed many times
along the route from Guanzhong to southern Shaanxi and Sichuan. For
instance, a Jin and Yuan porcelain cellar was discovered in Nanzhai,
Chengguan Town, Lantian County in 1959, and from it were unearthed a
pale blue glazed square stove, a three-legged stove with attached kuilong
pattern, etc. which were produced by the Yaozhou kilns. The Danfeng
Museum has in its display a picture of a Northern Song Yaozhou celadon
handled ewer with a carved pattern and a Ming white glazed long-foot
bowl. Some of the celadon unearthed in Shuangshipu in Fengxian County
and Fengzhou along the Baoji-Chengdu Railway can be judged to be
Yaozhou kiln porcelain from the Song and Jin dynasties from their
decoration and shape. Among the wares unearthed from the Song porcelain
cellar in Lveyang County, Shaanxi Province, three three-legged burners
were dated in black writing as the “seventh month of Jiatai Fourth Year
(1204)” in the Southern Song Dynasty. In 1984, 145 pieces of cellar
porcelain were unearthed in Rongchang County, Sichuan Province, among
which 66 pieces were produced by the Yaozhou kilns and have been
basically dated to be from the Jin Dynasty. The excavation of Song and Jin
Yaozhou ware along the route connecting Sichuan and Shaanxi proves that
there was a channel for importing Song and Jin Yaozhou ware into Sichuan,
that the Jin and the Southern Song maintained commercial trade, and that
Yaozhou ware could be shipped to southern Shaanxi along the Danjiang
River and then transported to Chengdu by way of Guangyuan or transported
to Sichuan and then to Chongqing via the Jialing River. The relics preserved
to today in different museums, wares unearthed in archeological
excavations and the record in Notes in Old Scholar Hut all suggest that
conditions were right and that Lu You indeed saw Yaozhou celadon in
Sichuan (or southern Shaanxi). Wares described by Lu You as favored by
folk restaurants because of its “durability,” “yet the quality is extremely
coarse, simple and poor” should refer to roughly made daily use celadon
plates and bowls of the Yaozhou kiln type in the Jin Dynasty.98 It can be
seen that in the Jin Dynasty the Yaozhou kilns not only continued their
production but also introduced their technologies to Sichuan. There is a
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
large number of extant Yaozhou ware from the Jin Dynasty and some of
these have obvious year marks. The Yuhua Temple, rebuilt from the Yuhua
Palace in the Tang Dynasty, was where master monk Xuanzang translated
Buddhist sutras and passed away. The temple was worshipped by visitors
throughout the Tang, Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. Its site is in Xunyi
and in 1999 the remnant of a three-legged round celadon burner from the
Jin Dynasty was unearthed at the temple site. Along the rim of the burner
the words “presented to Yuhua Temple by kiln owner Li Shiqing in
Huangbao Town” were inscribed, which indicates that the Yaozhou kilns
under the management of the Jin Dynasty had relatively stable kiln owners.
A Jin Dynasty Dading 10th Year cup mold was unearthed at the site of the
Huangbao kilns. An internal mold for making porcelain cups, it was round
and hollow with a curved slanting belly. It had a circular bottom edge on
which the cursive script “Dading 10th Year” was cut in intaglio. Pale
yellow, unglazed and fired from porcelain clay, it was 4.9 cm in height,
8.8 cm in bottom diameter, and 0.8–2.5 cm in wall thickness. In addition to
the above pieces of Jin dynasty Yaozhou kiln porcelain with year
inscriptions, shards engraved with “Da’an Second Year” of the Jin Dynasty
have been unearthed at the Huangbao kiln site.99
    In addition, Jin dynasty specimens mentioned in the Tongchuan
archeological report by the Shaanxi Provincial Institute of Archaeology also
include the remains of a blue glazed bowl engraved with the seventh month
of Zhenyuan Second Year (1154), remains of a blue glazed bowl engraved
with Mingchang Fifth Year (1194), and a blue glazed pillow inscribed with
Taihe Seventh Year (1207). The book Song, Liao and Jin Porcelain with
Year Marks also describes the Dading Second Year blue glazed warm bowl
with black inscription and carved water and flower pattern (the book refers
to it as a bowl, but its shape, size and unglazed ring indicate that it should
be classed as a Jin dynasty warm bowl, a bowl that could hold hot water to
keep food warm). Its top diameter is up to 20.3 cm. These Jin dynasty
celadon items with year marks had obvious characteristics of their time in
terms of glaze color, shape, bottom, and feet. They, and wares unearthed
from Jin dynasty tombs, could validate each other.100
   Though remains of Northern Song Yaozhou kiln porcelain have been
unearthed in Ningbo, Yangzhou and other places, fewer relics of Song and
Jin Yaozhou porcelain have been unearthed in Hangzhou, indicating that the
peak period of Yaozhou ware being transported to the south was the middle
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and late Northern Song Dynasty, and that by the time of the Southern Song
Dynasty, as the porcelain industry in Southern Song enjoyed unprecedented
development and as tax surged due to the confrontation between Song and
Jin, Yaozhou ware in the Jin Dynasty (including celadon of the Yaozhou
kiln system in Henan) lost the ability to be transported over long distances
into the south and still make a profit. An article in one issue of the Xi’an
Evening News in 2007 mentions the pale blue porcelain of the Yaozhou
kilns and posits that pale blue porcelain actually originated in the late
Northern Song and matured in the Jin Dynasty. Yet according to existing
archeological excavation results, pale blue porcelain was only fired in the
Huangbao Town central kiln yard, which represented the highest
workmanship of the Yaozhou kilns, and has not been found to be fired in
other kiln yards of the Yaozhou system such as the Yuhua kilns in Yijun
County, Shaanxi, Anren kilns in Xunyi County, Shaanxi, and those in
Henan, Guangxi, Guangdong, Ningxia and other provinces.
   The pale blue glaze initially fired by the Huangbao kiln yard in the late
Northern Song was whitish blue, quite different from the traditional olive or
pea green glaze produced by the kiln. At that time the inner wall or well of
plates and bowls were often printed with decoration. By the Jin Dynasty,
the blue shade of this type of glaze was greatly weakened and the whiteness
enhanced. Superior products of the type were white with subtle bluish
shades, while regular ones were grayish white or pale blue. The body
texture of such ware was uniform and dense, with characteristics similar to
those of celadon produced by the kiln in the same period, but the color of
the body was slightly white.
    Testing using modern technical means shows that a prominent
characteristic of the pale blue glaze in the Jin Dynasty was a high silicon
and low calcium content. The glaze material contained less fluxing agent
and the firing temperature was lower in comparison with that of the
Northern Song celadon produced by the kiln. Simulated firing tests show
that for pale blue porcelain with a low fluxing agent to achieve a bright
glaze, it could be successfully fired without adding opacifier but only by
increasing the fineness and density of the glaze material and prolonging the
heat preservation time during firing.101
   The above review and analysis of relevant data leads to the conclusion
that in the Jin Dynasty the Yaozhou kilns continued their production with
good quality and considerable output. Products were mainly of two types.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
The first was traditional celadon, which featured a dense, hard, relatively
thin and grayish white body, and a bright yet mellow glaze that was light
blue rather than ginger yellow as featured by Northern Song celadon. The
main varieties were bowls, plates, yuhuchun (pear-shaped vases), olive-
shaped handled ewers, lotus-leaf-shaped lidded jars, horizontal-legged
plates, and single-handle earcups and lamps. Decoration patterns were
mostly printed and dominated by flowers and children at play. There were
also new patterns such as rhinoceros contemplating the moon, falling
flowers and running water, the Eight Trigrams, deer, cranes, and immortals
riding the wind. Blank areas were often filled with a rolled leaf pattern so
that the decoration appeared extremely full. Another type of product was
the pale blue glazed ware that had newly emerged and featured an
extremely fine and mellow glaze surface, mostly plain without patterns.

8.5.4 The Cizhou Kilns
8.5.4.1 Overview
Of all the central plains kilns in the Jin Dynasty, the Cizhou kilns had the
largest output and widest influence, impacting profoundly the Liao ware
during the Northern Song Dynasty and the Jin ware in northeast China.
Many porcelain types such as black and white ware, green glazed carved
ware, tricolor glaze, and white porcelain imitating Ding ware were all
influenced by the Cizhou kilns. The more notable of the Cizhou kilns’
achievements in the Jin Dynasty was the development of polychrome
porcelains, notably black and white ware and red and green decoration,
which foreshadowed and prepared the way for the appearance of blue and
white porcelain in the Yuan Dynasty and of the red and green porcelain,
blue and white doucai porcelain, blue and white wucai porcelain and other
wucai ware in the Ming Dynasty. Therefore, the Jin dynasty Cizhou kilns
occupy an important position in the study of ceramics history.
   The Cizhou kilns included kiln yards in Guantai, Yezi, Aikou, and
Pengcheng, as well as similar kilns firing white ceramics with engobe, such
as the Hebiji, Xiuwu, Mixian, Pacun, Baofeng and Lushan kilns in Henan,
the Jiexiu, Yulin and Pingding kilns in Shanxi, the Zibo kilns in Shandong,
the Yaozhou kilns in Shaanxi and the Xiaoxian kilns in Anhui, which with
similar products constituted the huge Cizhou kiln system.
    In fact, a change of dynasty would not normally bring immediate
change to the variety, technique and decoration of a handicraft in any given
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
locality. Thus, it is sometimes not easy to distinguish between Cizhou ware
from the Jin Dynasty and that from the Northern Song Dynasty. For
example, the Japanese scholar Hasebe Gakuji writes the following in his
article “On Cizhou Ware in the Jin Dynasty”: The first investigation into the
Jin dynasty Cizhou kilns was the excavation of the Guantai kiln site carried
out in 1958. Seven strata were found five meters below the ditch, of which
the first and second strata were left from the Yuan Dynasty and the third
was from the Jin. The clue that enabled us to date the third stratum was the
Jin dynasty Zhenglong coins unearthed there and the craft style was much
more attractive than that of relics unearthed from the Yuan dynasty strata.
White ground sgraffito porcelain that used iron coloring was also popular in
the Jin Dynasty, yet there is a lack of solid evidence. One outstanding and
excellent feature of Cizhou ware in the Jin Dynasty was black patterns
painted on white ground with a brush. The technique for such black and
white porcelain originated in the late Northern Song Dynasty and reached
ultimate popularity in the Jin and Yuan dynasties. There were already many
black and white porcelain products in the early Jin Dynasty, but there is still
a lack of clues to help us distinguish between the black and white wares of
the late Northern Song Dynasty and those of the early Jin.102
   The article goes on to say that of the black and white wares made in the
twelfth century there is one that could constitute an important reference, a
tiger-shaped pillow in the collection of the Shanghai Museum. From the
“26th day of the sixth month in Dading Second Year” written in ink on the
bottom of the pillow it may be presumed that the pillow was made before
1162. The ink writing on the pillow may seem a little unreliable at first, but
a few years ago this author had the chance to view similar pillows in the
United States, and their bold and magnificent style suggested that they were
indeed made in or after the twelfth century, especially the skillfully and
concisely drawn waterfowl on the pillow surface that elegantly depicts a
scene of leisurely waterfront interest. Bird patterns often appear in pillow
paintings of the Jin Dynasty. Even though there might be slight differences,
they must all be from the same era. The pattern of birds standing on
branches painted on the tiger-shaped pillow in the US had a relatively rough
style, and bird patterns of the same painting style also appeared on a
porcelain pillow with the inscription “pillow of Zhang.” So presumably the
other pillows inscribed with “pillow of Zhang” or “made by Zhang” must
all be works of the late twelfth century or early thirteenth century.103
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Among the collection of the China Cizhou Kiln Museum in Cixian there
are many works of the Jin Dynasty Cizhou kilns such as wares with green
ground and white patterns, black ground and white patterns, and white
ground and black patterns. The works indicate that Cizhou kiln products in
the Jin Dynasty were quite different from those in the Northern Song; that
is, they were much richer in both variety and decorative style. There is an
especially salient difference in the paintings of black and white wares, with
works of the Jin Dynasty boasting much more skilled and superb techniques
than those of the Northern Song Dynasty.
  Ma Zhongli is a scholar from the front line of Cizhou kiln archaeology
and has participated in many excavations of Cizhou kilns. Thus, the
research data he has provided regarding the Cizhou kilns in the Jin Dynasty
should be largely accurate. In the work Cizhou Kilns of China edited by Ye
Zhemin and published in 2009, Ma Zhongli wrote the section “The
Modeling and Decoration Art of Cizhou Ware and Their Archaeological
Periodization.” He writes: three archeological excavations of Guantai kilns
show that the first stage of the Guantai kilns was from the end of the Five
Dynasties to the early Northern Song, the second stage was from the mid-
Northern Song Dynasty to the beginning of the Jin, during which time
wares of the first stage were still fired and in addition to those, there
emerged many new shapes, jars, lamps and bowls which took on richer
designs, and there also appeared small numbers of wares imitating products
of the Jian and Yonghe kilns in the south and the Ding kilns in the north.
The third stage was from the Tiande First Year of the Jin Dynasty to the
Xingding Third Year of Emperor Xuanzong’s reign in the late Jin Dynasty
when the Yuan army occupied Zhangde Prefecture, during which the shapes
and decorations of Guantai ware developed to their peak and more varieties
and designs than any other stage appeared in addition to bowls, plates,
pillows and bottles.104
  New archeological discoveries have been made of the Cizhou kilns,
with 10 kiln yards newly found in three clusters, namely, the Nanlianhua,
Pengcheng and Changfanzhuang kilns. Analysis of the strata excavated in
1987 indicates that the Guantai kiln area was not destroyed by the
southward advance of the Jin army. In fact, in the early Jin Dynasty, after
the Jin regime secured its rule over the central plains until the Dading era of
Emperor Shizong’s reign, the economy of the present-day Hebei area
recovered and grew as the north and south repaired relations. Against this
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
background, the Cizhou kilns developed rapidly, a phenomenon which was
also driven by the fact that the Cizhou kilns fulfilled the market demand
brought on by the destruction of the Linshui, Ding and Xing kilns.

8.5.4.2 Features of Jin Dynasty Cizhou Porcelain
Cizhou kiln porcelain of the Jin Dynasty had a rough body texture. The
glaze carried yellow tones and fine items had a bright and smooth glaze.
The most common decoration type was white glaze with black painting.
There were also white glaze with carved pattern, white glaze with black
sgraffito, white glaze with brownish yellow sgraffito, white ground with
black pattern, Jin tricolor ware, Jin red and green ware, white glazed ware,
black glazed ware, low temperature green glazed ware, and yellow glazed
ware. The main decorations were flowers, grass and insects, lotus petals,
fish and ducks, tigers and deer, flowers and birds, children at play, and
character stories. The pictures, mostly drawn with only a few strokes, were
free and vivid. The main varieties were jars, vases, basins, pillows, bowls,
plates, saucers, handle-less wine cups, and three-legged burners.
  A rare type of Cizhou ware in the Jin Dynasty was black glazed plum
vases and garden-stool-shaped bottles with brown flower patterns. The
glaze was bright black and the decorative pattern was dotted onto the
ware.105
   According to archaeological discoveries, the number of new varieties
unearthed in the Jin dynasty strata increased greatly. At the same time,
many products imitating Ding ware appeared, such as long-stem support-
pin bowls, spittoons, large cases, small cases, small bottles, small jars,
bowls, and incense burners. In addition, the traditional product structure of
the Cizhou kilns also underwent lots of changes in the Jin Dynasty.
Specifically, white glazed and blue glazed ware with pearl ground that was
popular in the Northern Song Dynasty decreased greatly, while white glazed
sgraffito ware increased significantly with representative varieties being
white-glazed lotus-mouthed large sgraffito vases, white-glazed low-belly
sgraffito vases, white-glazed three-legged sgraffito stoves, bowls, pillows,
incense burners and so on. Also very popular was white glazed ware with
black sgraffito, which among the Cizhou kilns’ decorative types involved
the most complex technology and required the highest level of
craftmanship. Even so, many fine products have survived to this day. Also
popular were many other decorative types, such as white glazed ware with
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
brownish yellow sgraffito, white glazed ware with sgraffito filled with
black coloring, and ware with black pattern against a white ground. In
addition, black glazed ware, low temperature green glazed ware, yellow
glazed ware and tricolor ware all saw an increase compared with the
Northern Song Dynasty.
   This author’s estimation is that among the decorative types of Cizhou
ware in the Jin Dynasty the most characteristic, the most vigorous and the
most abundant in terms of expressive themes is the black and white ware.
The Jin Dynasty was the peak period for Cizhou kiln black and white ware,
which inherited the tradition of the Northern Song Dynasty and took on
more shape varieties and richer decorative techniques. Black painting under
white glaze became the main feature of the Cizhou kiln system. The
decorations of Guantai ware were mostly flowers, butterflies, flying
phoenixes and rolled branches and leaves. Dong’aikou kiln products were
primarily porcelain pillows which came in three shapes, ruyi head, oval,
and octagonal. Ruyi-head-shaped items were decorated with rolled branches
and honeysuckle patterns on the sides and human figures, flowers, herons,
geese, waves, etc. on the top surface. Another feature of Cizhou kiln
underglaze black decoration in the Jin Dynasty was the combination of
painting and poetry, both of which were mostly based on the everyday life
scenes of people at the time and were full of artistic interest and humor.
   Writing popular poems and proverbs on porcelain as decoration began
with Changsha kiln ware in the Tang Dynasty. The underglaze black
painting ware of the Cizhou kilns inherited this tradition and brought it into
full play by the Jin Dynasty. In the Jin Dynasty shape varieties and the
images drawn were much richer than before, and the artisans’ painting
ability and decoration skills were also more sophisticated and refined. To
paint on greenware with engobe fully applied and not yet dry, painters had
to possess highly skilled brush painting techniques. They needed a clear
mental picture of the patterns to be painted and finish the painting at a rapid
pace in a single swoop so as to create a smooth brushwork effect and a
vivid artistic image. Although the Cizhou kilns already produced black and
white ware back in the Northern Song Dynasty, it was in the Jin Dynasty
that ceramic paintings with such charm and artistic acumen came into
being. In addition, the decorative approach was basically the same as that of
the folk blue and white porcelain that later appeared in Jingdezhen in the
Yuan and Ming dynasties, which also used the brush to paint, also on
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
porcelain greenware, and in the same rapid freehand manner. Also, the
“single lotus bundle” pattern on octagonal pillows in the Jin Dynasty was a
common image found on blue and white porcelain in the Yuan and Ming
dynasties. So it could be said that the decorative approach of Jingdezhen
blue and white ware followed the same line as Cizhou kiln black and white
ware and that the underglaze paintings of the latter in the Jin Dynasty
prepared and laid the foundation directly for the emergence of the former in
the Yuan Dynasty.

8.5.4.3 Porcelain Pillows and Text Decoration
The porcelain pillows of the Jin Dynasty were particularly suited to
paintings thanks to their large, flat surfaces, and so they became the most
typical and richest carrier of Jin dynasty underglaze engraving and painting.
The tradition of decorating porcelain with poems and paintings that started
in the Changsha kilns of the Tang Dynasty was inherited by the Cizhou
kilns in the Northern Song Dynasty and enjoyed further development to
become a major characteristic of the Cizhou kilns by the Jin Dynasty.
   Objects unearthed from the Jin dynasty stratum at the Guantai kiln site
in 1987 included porcelain pillows in many shapes, such as oval, bean
shaped, octagonal, ruyi head shaped, fan shaped and rectangle. The pillows
fully embodied a wide range of decorative techniques, among which black
and white decoration was the most representative and was adopted by more
porcelain pillows than any other. Common themes of the paintings were
birds such as geese, cranes or herons in reeds, various flowers such as
peony and lotus, and character stories against landscape or architectural
backgrounds, such as “Military Coup at Chenqiao,” “Visiting friend
carrying a zither,” and “Children angling for fish.” The shape design of the
pillows featured little difference from that of the Northern Song Dynasty
except that some were slightly larger. The bottom was usually stamped with
the words “Made by Zhang,” which are circled with double rectangles
topped with lotus leaves and supported by an upward-facing lotus flower
(Fig. 8.92). Tiger-shaped pillows were a new variety created in the Jin
Dynasty. Shaped like a crouching tiger, the pillow had four sides painted as
a tiger head with round angry eyes and colorful fur with yellow and brown
colorings. The “back” of the tiger, oval in shape, served as the pillow’s
surface, which is painted in ink with large peony flowers or birds amongst
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
branches and leaves. The images were full of everyday life interest (Fig.
8.93).

   Three common points can be identified in the decoration of black and
white porcelain pillows in the Jin Dynasty: 1. for pillows of all different
shapes, the top surface was encircled following its outline and then theme
images were painted in the encircled space; 2. since the pillows were often
only about 30 cm long, leaving a relatively small area for painting, the
images were mostly simple and concise sketches and small scenery
paintings with common themes being flowers and birds, animals, children
at play, horses, bears and poetry; 3. most pillows had all sides decorated
with floral scrolls of the same style, and a small number with single grass or
with no decoration at all. If these three common points are taken as the
criteria for a large category, a high proportion of black and white pillows
would fall into it. The earliest pillow with year markings that belonged to
this category discovered so far is the Dading Second Year (1162) oval
pillow with bird pattern found at the Guantai second kiln site in 1987. Also
belonging to the category are the Dading Fifth Year (1165) bean-shaped
pillow with the pattern of a sea beast carrying fish in its mouth (Fig. 8.94)
in the Handan Institute of Cultural Relics Protection, the Dading 18th Year
(1178) bean-shaped pillow with chess playing pattern in the Philadelphia
Museum of Art in the US, and the Taihe First Year (1201) bean-shaped
pillow with double ducks in water pattern in the Seikadō Bunko Art
Museum in Japan (Fig. 8.95). The book Pillows Donated by Yang Yongde
Couple contains one black and white octagonal pillow with goose carrying
grass in beak pattern (the Cixian Institute of Cultural Relics Protection has
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
in its collection one such pillow) (Fig. 8.96). The pattern of goose carrying
grass in beak on the pillow is also found in a Taihe First Year (1201) red
and green bowl belonging to a Japanese private collector. The Taihe Fifth
Year (1205) tiger-shaped pillow with brown glaze and black painting in the
Hebei Museum also has a goose pattern drawn in the clearing on the top
surface. Thus, the pillows, often painted with goose carrying grass in beak,
found in the Jin dynasty stratum of the Guantai kiln site could be inferred to
also be from the Taihe era. From the above pillows with year marks it could
be deduced that Jin dynasty porcelain pillows of the same category must be
approximately from the Dading era (or slightly earlier) to the Taihe era
(early thirteenth century).106

   Beginning with the Tongguan kilns in Changsha in the Tang Dynasty,
Chinese potters started writing poems and other texts on porcelain as
decoration to complement the pictures, which is a unique style of Chinese
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
ceramics, a style that was further developed by the Cizhou kilns in the Jin
Dynasty, especially on porcelain pillows as the pillow surface, flat and
large, was perfectly suited to text decoration. Text decoration on porcelain
pillows was very rich and can be classified into the following categories:
1.
   Phrases

Phrases on porcelain pillows are often auspicious words or words to
exorcise evil spirits. One example is the white glazed carved oval pillow
inscribed with “Spring, summer, autumn, winter” unearthed from the Jin
dynasty stratum of the Guantai kiln Phase II site. Pillow contains a black
and white ruyi-head-shaped pillow, a collection of the Museum of the
Nanyue King Mausoleum in Guangzhou. In the ruyi-head-shaped circled
space on the pillow surface two Chinese characters meaning “repelling
ghosts” are written. Thus, the pillow was presumably used to exorcise
ghosts and ward off evil spirits (Fig. 8.97).107 The Tokyo National Museum
has in its collection a Cheng’an Fifth Year (1200) yellow-green glazed
carved ruyi-head-shaped pillow whose one side is embossed with a deer
carrying the character “blessing” on its back. The meaning is “blessing and
good fortune” since the Chinese character for “deer” and that for “salary”
are homonyms. This pattern is also seen on the black and white pillows of
the Jin Dynasty and the unglazed pillows unearthed from the Guantai kilns.
In the collection of the China Cizhou Kiln Museum in Cixian County there
is a black and white octagonal pillow with bamboo pattern and the Chinese
character for “flower.” In the pillow surface area outlined by two lines, one
thick and one thin, a piece of bamboo is painted and above the bamboo is
written the word “Flower.” The pattern is a celebration of a wedding night
because the Chinese character for “bamboo” and that for “candle” are
homonyms, and so “Flower” and bamboo in combination means “flower
candle,” or painted candle, which is used to light the nuptial chamber. The
pattern is an early auspicious image making use of homophonic sound that
appeared on porcelain (Fig. 8.98).108 Other kilns in the Cizhou kiln system
in the same period also produced wares with characters such as “Blessings,”
“Blessings and Virtue,” “Eternal peace for family and country,” and
“Blessing, Virtue, Longevity,” which were mostly used on pearl ground
pillows. The phrases are mostly short, containing only a few characters,
which are mostly auspicious words and words of blessing. At the end of the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Song Dynasty and the beginning of the Jin text appeared mostly on wares
decorated with comb scratching, painting, and black sgraffito. Common
phrases included “Endurance” and “Moral calmness,” with pillows
inscribed with “Endurance” being the most numerous, which was probably
related to people’s mental state given the turbulent social environment of
the late Song and early Jin dynasties. The considerable change from
“Blessing, Virtue, Longevity” and “Eternal peace for family and country” to
“Endurance” was a true portrayal of the social transition from stability and
prosperity to turbulence and poverty.109

2.
   Couplets

A couplet is a pair of antithetical lines written on paper or cloth or carved
on bamboo, woodwork or pillars. Concise, well-organized and coordinated,
they are a unique artistic form of the Chinese language made possible by
the language’s feature of each character having one and only one syllable.
Many folk couplets have rich philosophical meaning and everyday life
interest and are therefore widely used on porcelain pillows in the Jin
Dynasty. For instance, one black and white ruyi-head-shaped pillow
collected by the China Cizhou Kiln Museum in Cixian County, Hebei is
inscribed with “One trellis of green cucumbers, a garden of white and black
beans,” (Fig. 8.99) and a green-glazed black-pattern ruyi-head-shaped
pillow collected by the Hebei Museum carries the words “On the waterfront
wind blossoms age, under the moon dew leaves yellow.” (Fig. 8.100). Most
of these folk couplets were written on pillows by Cizhou kiln craftsmen
who described the scenery that they saw or experienced. Other instances of
such couplets on porcelain pillows include: “The wind blows the bamboo in
the front courtyard, rain beats the flowers in the back courtyard;” “Fish
jump in the drizzling rain, swallows fly in the wind;” and “To appreciate
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
flowers one rises early in spring, to cherish moonlight one sleeps late at
night.” Some of the couplets are famous lines from poems that are revised
by craftsmen. For instance, the “At moonset cry the crows, streaking the
frosty sky, dimly lit fishing boats ‘neath maples sadly lie” (translation by
Xu Yuanchong) by poet Zhang Ji of the Tang Dynasty is modified by the
Cizhou kiln craftsmen to read: “As leaves fall the apes cry, streaking the
frosty sky, by the riverside the fishermen sadly lie.”

3.
  Poems

Many may regard writing poetry an elegant cultural activity for elites to
express their aspirations, ideas and feelings and think that ceramic
craftsmen with little education and little literacy were not up to the task of
writing poetry. Yet in fact poetry is the oldest and most basic literary form
in the world that originated from the production activities of the common
people. Its earliest forms included the labor chants (which later developed
into folk songs) and the sacrificial eulogies of ancient times. It is stated in
the Book of Rites (Liji), Book of Music that “poetry speaks the mind, songs
exercise the voice, and dance expresses feeling: the three spring from the
heart and then musical instruments follow.” Poems, combined with music
and dance, are collectively known as poetry (in Chinese “Shige,” literally
“poem song”). Poetry originated from the common people and is an
expression of their voice and feelings. The words are the plainest language
of the common people and folk craftsmen at the time, and do not inevitably
require a certain level of education. Examples include the five-character
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
poem Old Man on a black and white octagonal pillow in the Linzhou
Culture Museum in Henan and the seven-character poem Ode to
Chrysanthemum on a green glazed carved ruyi-head-shaped pillow in the
collection of the Tianjin Museum of Art.
4.
   Ci

Ci is a type of lyric poem that is sung with musical accompaniment. It
originated in the Tang Dynasty, developed mature patterns in the Five
Dynasties and flourished in the Song Dynasty. Like poetry, ci also
originated from the common people. The many musicians who made a
living in cities by singing, wrote or adapted lyrics containing long and short
sentences based on the patterns of the musical rhythm, and these lyrics, the
earliest ci, gained wide currency with the spread of the music. Still, in the
Tang Dynasty the literati believed these lyrics were not elegant enough to
be regarded as real poetry. It was in the Song Dynasty that ci won the
attention of the literati and refined scholars and became a literary form
equal in status to Tang poetry. Thus, it is not difficult to understand that ci
composed by the common people appeared years earlier than those written
by the literati.
   Due to its folk and popular nature, ci naturally became a source of text
decoration for the Cizhou kilns, which were primarily folk kilns. Potters
chose to write many ci works on porcelain pillows in line with the tastes of,
and thus proving popular with, the ordinary folk due to their easy-to-
understand, simple and natural nature. Examples include the black and
white octagonal pillow inscribed with a Rumengling (tune name, literally
“Like a Dream”) collected by the Cizhou Kiln Museum in Cixian County
(Fig. 8.101) (this particular Rumengling was written by Su Shi in memory
of Dongpo in Huangzhou), the black and white bean shaped pillow
inscribed with a Rumengling collected by the Fengfeng Mining Area
Cultural Relic Preservation Center (Fig. 8.102), the yellow-green glazed
fan-shaped pillow described in Pillow, now in the collection of the Museum
of the Nanyue King Mausoleum in Guangzhou, which is printed with floral
scrolls and beast face patterns on the front, back and two sides, and carved
with Huanxisha (a tune name, literally “Silk-Washing Stream”) on the top
surface in an area encircled by double lines,110 the black and white
octagonal pillow (Fig. 8.103) that has in the octagonal area encircled by
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
slightly inward-arcing broadband and thin lines Pusaman (tune name,
literally “Buddhist Dancers”) by Su Shi written in Xingkai (a style between
running script and regular script),111 and the black and white octagonal
pillow collected by the Handan Institute of Cultural Relics Protection in
Hebei (Fig. 8.104) carrying the work Wuyeti (tune name, literally “Crying
Night Crow”) in Xingcao (a style between running script and cursive
script).112 It can be seen that the ci decorations on Jin dynasty Cizhou
porcelain pillows is extremely rich. Some from ordinary folk, some from
the works of Song dynasty literati and poets, yet mainly reflecting the
aesthetic preferences of the common people at the time, these ci works are
valuable data for examining not only the folk ceramic art but also the folk
culture of the Jin Dynasty.
