   The fifth achievement was the expansion of foreign trade. To meet the
needs of larger overseas markets many kilns specializing in producing
export porcelain sprung up in Fujian and Guangdong, some of which
imitated in large quantities the celadon of the Longquan kilns, the qingbai
porcelain of the Jingdezhen kilns, and the black porcelain of the Jian kilns.
Past studies of ceramic history failed to pay sufficient attention to these
export-oriented kilns, yet with the salvage, excavation and research of
shipwrecks in recent years, many findings in this respect will change many
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
of our traditional concepts and also compel us to reassess the interaction
between Chinese and world culture.

8.7.3 Aesthetic Features of Song Ceramics
The prosperity of ceramics in the Song Dynasty benefited from the
development of an urban economy and culture while the special aesthetic
interest of Song dynasty ceramics came from the aesthetic pursuit of
scholars in that Dynasty. Thanks to the development of urban life and the
prosperity of commerce, porcelain utensils became the main instruments in
people’s lives, including tea and wine vessels, which were also much
appreciated by the literati of the day. As utensils used by the literati for tea
drinking and objects to appreciate when they composed poems, porcelain
wares naturally became vessels conveying their feelings, their ideals, their
tastes and their aesthetic standards. Moreover, in Chinese history, food
vessels were never just food vessels. They were reflections of the etiquettes
and hierarchy of the times and symbols of one’s identity, status and power.
That is why in the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties, food vessels held an
important place among the ritual objects. Later the setup of official kilns
further established their status as ritual objects with a certain symbolic
cultural significance. Such a symbolic significance in the cultural sense led
to the saying “the instrument is the carrier of the Way,” with “instrument”
referring to physical substance and practical objects and “the Way”
referring to cultural connotations embodied in the instrument, things that
belong to the metaphysical and spiritual realm. This is clearly reflected in
the aesthetics of Song porcelain.
   The aesthetic characteristics of the Song Dynasty may be summarized
according to the following aspects.
   The first characteristic of Song dynasty aesthetics was that they were
impacted by literatus thought. From an aesthetic point of view, Confucius,
representative of the Confucian school, believed the nature of humans lay in
their sociality. Thus, he advocated appearance that was in conformity with
nature and the combination of external decoration, namely, artificial beauty,
and internal beauty, or the beauty of nature. The result was a kind of beauty
that was rich, intense and masculine. The representative of Taoism,
Zhuangzi, believed human nature lay in nature, that any appearance added
to nature was superfluous and harmful, and that all sociological
embellishment confined human nature. It was believed that what is natural
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
is intrinsically beautiful and does not need to fit into a certain form. Taoism
stresses nature. In pursuit of beauty, Taoism stresses “authenticity” and
“plainness,” meaning that things should be kept true to their nature and
original flavor, and no artificial polishing or adornment is called for. This is
the pursuit of authenticity, of simple, natural beauty, of plain, quiet beauty.
The appearance advocated by Confucius and the nature held up by
Zhuangzi, one masculine and hard, and one feminine and soft, led to two
realms of beauty. The two schools of philosophical thought have long
influenced the formation of Chinese aesthetics and ceramic styles over time,
with Confucianism taking the dominant position in some dynasties and
Taoism gaining the upper hand at other times.
   Deeply influenced by Confucianism and Taoism, ancient Chinese
scholar-bureaucrats regulated themselves with these two philosophical
systems. They preferred Confucianism when young and ambitious, and
leaned towards Taoism when they had gone through difficulties and gained
a deeper understanding of society. Some of them “cultivated behaviors by
following Confucianism while obtained inner tranquility through
Buddhism.” In some sense, ancient Chinese scholar-bureaucrats represented
the unity of the ethical and the natural personality. In ethics they fulfilled
their obligation of filial piety to parents, were loyal to the emperor, and
discharged their duties to the patriarchal society by contributing to their
families and the country. In terms of natural personality, they enjoyed the
beauty of nature and expressed their feelings through forests, mountains and
rivers to obtain spiritual rest or relief. One corresponded to their job and the
other to their private lives. The unity of these two opposing personalities
was key to the balance of their lives and minds and also the key to the
longevity of the traditional society. Such a unity was particularly prominent
among the literati in the late Tang to the Song Dynasty. During this period,
men of letters on the one hand advocated Confucianism, and on the other
hand followed Taoism and Zen Buddhism in terms of aesthetics and
interests. The spirit of the Song Dynasty was no longer to ride on the back
of a warhorse, but rather to inhabit the boudoir, no longer to occupy the
secular world, but to exercise the mind. The most successful art works in
this period were landscape paintings, love poems, Song ci and Song
porcelain. While the intense, bold and masculine aesthetic style advocated
by Confucianism that emphasized a combination of nature and appearance,
and the simple, authentic and elegant aesthetic style advocated by Taoism
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
that emphasized nature over appearance coexisted, complemented, and
added radiance to each other from the Wei and Jin to the mid-Tang, when it
came to the Song Dynasty, the artistic ideas of the literati almost entirely
leaned towards Taoism and Buddhism.133
    In painting, this change was reflected in the decline in religious
paintings and the relegation of human figure paintings to a secondary status,
giving way to the rise of themes which stressed spiritual comfort and
enjoyment. People’s feelings and sentiments became the subject of arts and
aesthetics. Such attention to feelings and sentiments was in line with the
aesthetic aspiration of Taoism and Buddhism. The most prominent feature
of such aspiration was to understand and experience the beauty of nature.
This experience elevated one above tangible activities and focused one on
the invisible realms of life. Taoist philosophy held a pure spiritual
experience of nature to be the highest and most perfect state of living.
Influenced by such Taoist views, arts in the Song Dynasty transcended
sensual pleasure and artificial decoration to pursue simplicity, archaism, and
plainness, which in turn were believed to embody the most intense beauty
and the strongest flavor. Thus, aesthetic pursuit during the period can be
summarized as returning to the world of natural expression and
experiencing the mysterious unfolding of the inner rhythms of nature amid
silence and aloneness. This led to the artistic standard opposing artificial
ornamentation and in favor of natural interests, which found particularly
prominent expression in the porcelain of the Song Dynasty.
   For instance, the products of the most famous kilns in the Song
Dynasty, the Ge, Ru, Guan (official), Jun and Ding kilns, displayed clearly
the aesthetic preference of the scholar-bureaucrats of the time. Apart from
the white porcelain of the Ding kilns, which featured carved and printed
patterns, porcelain made by all the other famous kilns were solid color
wares with no decoration. Here the absence of decoration does not mean
crude craftsmanship. Rather, it represented a more conscientious aesthetic
of pursuing natural beauty. The Ge, Guan and Ru kilns all produced celadon
decorated with natural crackle glaze. Crackle pattern came from the
cracking of the glaze surface during firing due to different contraction
coefficients of different parts of the glaze. The cracks were probably flaws
that occurred during firing, but craftsmen made use of the defect and turned
it into a type of natural, haphazard and interesting decoration. In Renjianshi
(Worldly Business among Men) and Dechongfu (The Signs of the Fullness
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
of Power) Zhuangzi wrote about a large number of physically impaired,
deformed or ugly individuals who nevertheless are loved by people,
because the people know that physical beauty or ugliness is naturally born,
that beauty does not only mean good looks or attractive decoration, that real
beauty lies in nature, and that natural incompleteness is also a kind of
beauty, perhaps even a more profound beauty. Maybe such a more profound
beauty was what the crackle glaze was seeking at the time.
    In general, the crackle pattern of porcelain produced by the Ge kilns
was the densest and deepest. The cracks were of different depths, the deeper
ones appearing black and the shallower ones appearing pale yellow. Cracks
of the two colors intertwined were called “golden threads and iron lines.”
The cracks of Guan kiln porcelain were sparser and shallower, and thus
were mostly golden in color and were called golden lines. The cracks of Ru
kiln porcelain were even shallower and thinner. Barely visible, they looked
like transparent cracks on ice.
   Ru, Guan and Ge wares all belonged to celadon, yet their glaze colors
were not uniform. While Ru ware was mostly azure and incense ash color,
Guan ware and Ge ware shared similar tones, including light greenish blue,
pale blue, putty color and bluish yellow. The different tones of glaze were
to an extent realized through different body colors, including blackish gray,
dark gray, light gray, and earthen yellow, which gave different shades of
blue to the glaze. It was deep body color that gave Song dynasty celadon its
calm, deep and somewhat mysterious glaze color, a color and feeling that
was pursued by the literati at the time. The Ge and Guan kilns’ adoption of
body materials with a high iron content and deep color resulted in the
phenomenon of “purple rim and iron feet.” Specifically, the high iron
content of the body led it to turn black during firing with a strong reducing
flame, so the thinly glazed mouth rim of vessels somewhat exposed the
blackish purple body underneath, hence “purple rim,” and the foot area,
which was not glazed, turned black, hence the “iron feet.” So, the “purple
rim and iron feet” is also a natural effect that occurred due to glaze
composition and technological requirements, an effect that is in line with
the Taoist aesthetic view that pursued the naturalness and innateness of all
things. Moreover, the Chan Buddhist scripture the Platform Sutra states that
“nature contains all laws and is the largest, and all laws reside in one’s true
nature.” “One’s true nature” transcends time and space, does not require
artificial (external) meddling, and exists by and of itself. Naturalness and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
“inaction” were the ultimate pursuit of both Taoism and Chan Buddhism at
the time and the pursuit was also vividly reflected in the aesthetic pursuit of
Song dynasty porcelain.
   This pursuit also finds clear manifestation in the porcelain art of the Jun
kilns. The Jun kilns belonged to the group of northern celadon producers,
but they introduced iron oxide and small amounts of copper oxide to the
glaze as chromogenic reagents, resulting in extremely varied glaze color
during firing. Some became rose purple, some crabapple flower red, some
pale blue, some sky blue, and some sky blue strewn with purplish red like a
sunset’s glow. There is a saying in China’s ceramic world that “there are no
identical Jun kiln wares.” No two porcelain wares of the Jun kilns, even
fired in the same kiln, were completely the same, because their glaze color
was naturally formed and could not be artificially controlled. This was in
line with the highest aesthetic ideal pursued at the time.
   Another feature of Jun ware was the “earthworm trail pattern,” which
refers to marks on the glaze surface that looks like the trail left by an
earthworm moving through mud. This was actually a defect that occurred
during the firing of Song Jun ware. The glaze layer of Jun ware was very
thick and thus prone to cracking when the temperature was still low as the
kiln heated up. When the temperature rose, part of the glaze with lower
viscosity would flow into the cracks to fill them, thus creating an
earthworm trail pattern, which, like crackled glaze, was a defect formed
unintentionally in the firing process but which achieved a distinctive
decorative effect. This could be said to be an outcome of a combination of
Taoist aesthetic thought and the potter’s wisdom.
    All Taoist ideas can be traced back to the worship of nature. Taoist
philosophy stresses following the natural course of things, praises the
natural and authentic form of things, and advocates showing things as they
originally are. It frowns on forceful intervention, artificial disturbance,
affectation and hypocrisy. Laozi described the Tao as “Pu,” which refers to
a natural state without decoration, and took staying true to nature and
adhering to Pu as his ideal. The natural state then became the highest
standard of beauty as pursued by the literati of later times, and that is how
the saying “the most glorious returns to simplicity” arose. Zhu Xi states:
“Heaven is devoid of sound, color, smell or taste, yet it is the pivot of
creation and the root of wisdom.” (Commentaries on Zhou Dunyi’s Taiji
Tushuo). This is similar to what Laozi states, that “great music has the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
faintest notes.” “Great music” is music without sound, and this is also the
essence of porcelain art in the Song Dynasty. The Song porcelain described
above embodies such simplicity, such plainness, such natural form, such
expression without word, and such music without sound. Even the naturally
formed defects and flaws became beauty. Such is the great beauty and
ultimate beauty. The Taoist aesthetic pursuit is to free people’s thinking
from all shackles so that they may move freely in the broad and boundless
natural realm, to experience the innumerable languages in the wordless
realm. This is an infinite realm, and such infinity dissolves rules, structures,
and all other forms of existence that the human mind can possibly perceive,
so as to gain a sense of a more profound way of being.
   Zhuangzi states: “The ultimate man is one who appreciates ultimate
beauty and enjoys ultimate happiness.” Here ultimate beauty refers to the
profound implications of numerous natural forms in the universe; the
ultimate happiness is to immerse oneself in such beauty; and the ultimate
man is one who is able to appreciate such happiness. I think that of all art
forms in the Song Dynasty, porcelain gave the best expression to such a
spiritual aspiration. The Song Dynasty saw the rise of Neo-Confucianism,
which is described by some people as “Confucianism on the outside and
Taoism on the inside.” This is also reflected in Song porcelain as the glaze
color, texture and aesthetic pursuit of the Song wares favored by the literati
embodied the Taoist spirit, while their shape deigns endeavored to imitate
various ancient ritual objects representing Confucian thought such as
copper and jade ritual objects. The prevalence of imitating ancient ritual
objects was related to the reverence for Confucianism and the popularity of
archaeology in the Northern Song Dynasty. In the late Northern Song
Dynasty, some famous kilns in the north fired tributary porcelain for the
imperial court, mostly by imitating the design of ceremonial vessels of the
Shang, Zhou and Han dynasties, and by the Southern Song, the Guan, Ge
and Longquan kilns still continued the practice. Of course, such practice by
the official kilns in the Song Dynasty was partly due to the fact that the
purpose of Song official kilns’ porcelain production was to replace ritual
objects in other materials with porcelain ones. As for other kilns besides the
official ones, they imitated ancient ceremonial objects on the one hand
under the influence of Confucianism and on the other, were driven by the
guidance of the official kilns.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
The second characteristic of Song dynasty ceramics was the official
kilns’ aesthetic preference for jade. Chinese ceramic aesthetics is related to
mainstream philosophical thought as well as official guidance. In Chinese
history, there have always been two types of kiln: official kilns and folk
kilns. A general rule is that the folk kilns would first create something,
which would finally be recognized by the official kilns and then, under the
lead of the official kilns, the created object would become the social
mainstream. The earliest porcelain invented in China was celadon, which
dominated the porcelain production in China from the Eastern Han Dynasty
to the Wei, Jin, and Southern and Northern Dynasties. While by the Tang
Dynasty, the “southern celadon and northern white” porcelain manufacture
landscape had formed, celadon was still the most celebrated by the people
and the most famous kilns being the celadon-producing Yue kilns and the
most famous porcelain type was the mysterious “secret color porcelain.”
The dominant status of celadon became even more pronounced by the Song
Dynasty. Of the five famous kilns at the time, namely the Guan, Ru, Jun,
Ge and Ding, all were celadon producers except the Ding kilns. In addition,
the Longquan kilns which had the largest production capacity at the time,
the Jingdezhen kilns which were highly favored by the emperors, and the
Yaozhou kilns, all were producing celadon. It was not necessarily official
kilns that first started firing celadon, yet it was official kilns and scholar-
bureaucrats that advocated celadon from the Tang to the Song Dynasty and
it was only through their promotion that celadon production could become
mainstream in the society of the day. That both the secret color porcelain
produced for the royal family in the Tang and Five Dynasties and the
porcelain fired by Song dynasty official kilns were celadon was not only
due to aesthetic reasons but also, and more importantly, because of the
warm, mellow, and jade-like texture of celadon. In his famous Book of Tea
Lu Yu posits that “porcelain of the Yuezhou (越州) kilns is the best” because it
is “like jade” and “like ice.”
   That is to say, the official adoration of celadon from the Tang to the
Song was related to the jade worshipping tradition in China. Ancient
Chinese considered jade as the essence of the sun and the moon, a divine
object. In primitive times, Chinese people used jade to sacrifice to Heaven,
Earth and the ancestors. The ritual objects back in the time of the Liangzhu
Culture were basically jade wares, and it was also recorded in the Rites of
Zhou that “jade is made into six vessels to pay tribute to Heaven, Earth, and
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the four directions. White bi (a round flat piece of jade with a hole in its
center) is used to sacrifice to Heaven, yellow cong (a long hollow piece of
jade with rectangular sides) is used to sacrifice to Earth…” Later, jade
became a symbol of political hierarchy. Officials at different levels wore
jade belts corresponding with different strata while the jade seal was
exclusively used by the emperor. One important purpose of official kiln
porcelain production was to use it as ritual objects in sacrificial ceremonies
in place of jade wares, which explained the pursuit of the jade texture in
porcelain making.
   The jade worship of the royal family and imperial court also resulted in
the personification of jade by the literati and scholar-bureaucrats. Shuowen
Jiezi (“An Explication of Written Characters”) from the Han Dynasty states:
“Jade is the beauty among stones and has five virtues.” The five virtues,
namely benevolence, righteousness, courtesy, wisdom and faith, symbolized
noble qualities in ethics and morality and, used here, are a personalized
description of jade. Fei Xiaotong divided Chinese people’s jade
worshipping tradition into three phases. In the first and initial phase, jade
existed mainly as divine objects for shamans to communicate with Heaven.
In the second phase jade mainly functioned as ornaments that people wore
to symbolize the hierarchical system and to express rites in a civilized
society. In the third phase, jade was still worn as an ornament yet was
associated with moral concepts and regarded as a symbol of people’s virtue
and conduct. These conventions sustained the Chinese people’s love for
jade for thousands of years.134 It is precisely because of the important status
of jade in Chinese traditional culture that porcelain has always been
cherished in China for its jade-like warmth and mellowness, especially
celadon, whose texture and color both are close to that of jade.
   Driven by such aesthetic pursuits, many celadon-producing kilns
appeared in the Song Dynasty. Among the five famous kilns of the Song
Dynasty, all were celadon producers except the Ding kilns which fired
white porcelain. The five celebrated kilns, including the Ding kilns, were all
favored by the royal family either as official kilns directly manufacturing
for the court or as kilns supplying tributary porcelain for the court. Thus,
their products reflected the aesthetic preferences of the royal family.
   The five famous kilns all provided porcelain for the imperial court, yet
it was only the Ding kilns that ceased their tribute work. Ye Zhi gave the
reason in his Notes in Tan Study: “The imperial court deemed Dingzhou
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
white porcelain not proper for use because they had an unglazed rim, and so
ordered Ruzhou to make celadon wares.” There is a similar record in Lu
You’s Notes in Old Scholar Hut: “At the time of the former capital
(Northern Song), Ding ware was not allowed into the imperial palace due to
its unglazed rim, and only Ru ware was used.” Yet was the “unglazed rim”
the only reason that Ding ware was deemed “not proper for use” and “not
allowed into the imperial palace” in the Northern Song Dynasty and why
Ruzhou was ordered to make celadon ware?
   Some scholars believe the unglazed rim would not have been the only
reason. Before adopting the inverted firing method, the Ding kilns had long
been containing greenware with saggers and firing them face up and so the
wares did not have an unglazed rim, and even after inverted firing was
adopted, face-upward firing was not abandoned and was still used for many
wares. Therefore, if wares with an unglazed rim were “not proper for use,”
the undesirable feature should have been easily avoided by firing the wares
face up, and it must be said that it is a bit absurd to abandon a convenient
supplier and instead order the distant Ruzhou to make celadon. Therefore,
to overcome the “unglazed rim” defect, the idea that the Song regime
ordered Ruzhou to make celadon instead of simply asking the Ding kilns to
make fully glazed white porcelain suggests that there was something
undesirable with the tone and texture of Ding white porcelain.135 Another
fact supporting this suggestion was that while some Ding wares had
unglazed rims, the rims were usually delicately edged with gold, silver or
copper. Hence some believe that the imperial palace stopped accepting
Ding porcelain not only because of the unglazed rim, but also probably due
to the aesthetic standards at the time. The Han Chinese regarded white as a
sort of taboo color for it was only used in funerals. Thus, the pure white
porcelain produced by the Ding kilns might have lost favor due to its color.
The rejection of white porcelain was also related to the sacrificial needs of
the court at the time. The establishment of the official kilns in the Song
Dynasty was not to make porcelain to support the royal family’s luxurious
lifestyle, but for the royal sacrificial ceremonies. Although no record of the
requirements regarding the color of ceramic sacrificial utensils has been
found in literature, it is known that the people of the Song Dynasty believed
that “the color of jade is a brilliant green hue,” and that Emperor Huizong
held blue to be “the celestial color.” People in the Song Dynasty valued a
jade-like texture because of their love for jade and valued the blue color
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
because of their respect for Heaven. Thus, “Song dynasty porcelain pursued
the color blue.” Obviously, compared with white glaze, azure glaze is much
closer to the appearance of jade and is more in line with the virtue of
“upholding quality and sincerity” required for sacrificing to Heaven and
Earth. So, it was natural that blue glazed wares became the first choice to be
used in royal sacrifices while Ding white porcelain was abandoned by the
Song court.
    Still another important reason this author believes caused the rejection
of Ding white porcelain by the Song court was that the printed and carved
patterns that were used on most wares to remedy the monotonousness of
their opaque, nontransparent and plain white color rendered the wares
inconsistent with the “pure and uniform” color pursued by official kilns.
Compared with Ge, Guan, Ru and Jun wares, Ding wares bore more
artificial work and were therefore not so in line with the simple, quiet, and
inactive aesthetic pursued by the nature-revering Taoism and Chan
Buddhism at the time. It was because of the popularity of such aesthetic
aspirations and interest among the literati of the day that some folk kiln
products with color painting or other strongly artificial decoration were
considered inferior wares of low taste and suitable only for use by the
common people. Alternatively, they might be export porcelain made for
overseas markets. These ceramic products are not well regarded and in fact
rarely recorded in historical works. For instance, the Tongguan kilns in the
Tang Dynasty were the earliest kilns to create underglaze decorated
porcelain in China and laid the foundation for the later rise of China’s
polychrome porcelains, yet Tongguan wares were mainly exported to
overseas countries and were rarely recorded in historical works. Another
example was the Tang dynasty blue and white porcelain, which was also
rarely touched upon by literature and was also mainly produced for
overseas markets. In addition, the Cizhou and Yaozhou kilns were both
high-yielding folk kilns in the Song Dynasty, and Yaozhou wares were once
tributary wares to the royal house because they were celadon, and Cizhou
wares, with their large output and wide influence, had a broad civilian
market. Still, the products, due to their engraved and carved decorations,
were not favored or appreciated as much by the emperor, the royal family
or the literati at the time as the solid color plain celadon. These phenomena
were all related to the aesthetics of the Tang and Song dynasties.
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
The Song Dynasty was an era of celebrated porcelains. In addition to
the above-mentioned porcelain types, also famous were the yingqing
porcelains of Jingdezhen, the celadon of the Longquan kilns, and the hare-
fur and oil-spot wares of the Jian kilns. All of these famous ceramics
embody the traditional Chinese culture that pursued natural beauty and
interest through the original texture of glaze.
   The third feature of Song dynasty ceramics was the formation of the
aesthetic characteristics of ethnic minorities and of the common people. In
the past, on the subject of Song dynasty ceramic aesthetics, Han centrism
and a focus only on elite culture led to an emphasis on the Han people and
imperial elites and a lack of attention to the common folk and ethnic
minorities, when in fact during the period of the Song Dynasty there were
not only the two Song regimes, but there were also the Liao and Jin, both of
which ruled areas that were much wider than either the Northern or
Southern Song. Although the aesthetic orientations of these ethnic minority
regions were not in the central vision of the Han nationality at the time, they
deeply influenced the ceramic aesthetic orientations in the later Yuan, Ming
and Qing dynasties.
    In China’s history there have been many instances where an ethnic
minority fought with and overthrew the regimes of the Han and established
their own regime. Yet after the military and political victory they did not
strive to eradicate the culture of the Han and strive to promote their own
national culture, but instead tried to integrate their own culture with that of
the Han and even Sinicized themselves. Of course, during such Sinicization
they also retained parts of their own cultural orientation and aesthetic
appreciation. Therefore, they abolished the regime of the Han, but did not
eradicate its culture and on the contrary, continued and further developed
the Han culture. It is for this reason that Chinese civilization has lasted for
thousands of years without a break to become the world’s oldest and longest
continuous civilization.
     It was the same scenario in the Song Dynasty. The Liao and Jin, as
ethnic minority regimes, after conquering vast swathes of Song territory,
did not unilaterally pursue their own culture but quickly Sinicized
themselves and made great efforts to learn the crafts and technologies of the
Han. Before and after the establishment of the Liao Dynasty, it constantly
attacked the central plains where they established new prefectures and
counties with Han people that they had taken captive and named the
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
prefectures and counties after the names of the places where these captives
came from. Many of these Han captives engaged in agricultural production
as slaves or in handicraft work as craftsmen, amongst whom there were
many ceramic craftsmen. These ceramic craftsmen captured by the Liao
were mostly from Ci Kiln Town and the Ding kilns in Hebei in the central
plains since Hebei was in the frontier area of conflict between the Liao and
the Northern Song, and this is evidenced by the heavy influence from the
Cizhou and Ding kilns that can be seen in the variety and characteristics of
Liao porcelain. In terms of shape varieties, there were differences between
the porcelain wares of the nomadic peoples on the prairie and the
agricultural people on the central plains due to their different living habits.
For instance, some special varieties suited to the life of the prairie people
including chicken-leg shaped vases, long neck pots, leather-bag style pots,
and cockscomb pots, were not seen among the central plains wares. Apart
from shape variety, the porcelain of the Liao and Jin were basically similar
to Cizhou and Ding ware in other respects, including decoration methods
and materials such as black and white ware, black background sgraffito
ware, white glazed ware, black glazed ware, green glazed ware and tricolor
ware. The Jin Dynasty, after replacing the Liao, occupied and had its center
in central plains areas which had been traditionally ruled by Han regimes
and at the same time ruled over the entire area east of the Liao River
(roughly present-day Liaoning Province) and part of the southern Gobi
desert. Thus, many famous traditional northern kilns, such as the Ding,
Cizhou, Yaozhou, Ru and Jun kilns, were now under the jurisdiction of the
Jin Dynasty. Yet, after the Jin Dynasty, the Cizhou kilns left all the other
kilns far behind in both output and market share. The other kilns continued
production but were not as prosperous as in the Northern Song period in
both quality and quantity, while the Cizhou kilns featured richer varieties,
more diversified decorative means, and more skilled painting and
decoration techniques. They also generally reached the peak of their entire
development history after the Jin. Nevertheless, though the Ding kilns
declined somewhat during the Jin, archaeological findings show that they
made tribute porcelain for the royal family of the Jin Dynasty and many
kilns imitated Ding ware in the Jin Dynasty. The continued prosperity and
even rise of the Cizhou and Ding kilns in the Jin Dynasty, despite the
decline of other kilns, was in one sense because the porcelain-making
techniques of the Cizhou and Ding kilns once spread to the northern prairie,
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
the homeland of the Liao and Jin, and a traditional liking for the products of
the Cizhou and Ding kilns had developed there. Another reason for their
continued prosperity is perhaps because Cizhou and Ding wares themselves
were in line with the aesthetic tradition of the Liao and Jin. The Liao was a
northern prairie ethnicity and the Jin was an ethnic group that was mainly
engaged in fishing, hunting and animal husbandry in northeast China.
Ethnic groups on the prairie generally favored white. The Jin homeland was
near the Changbai Mountains (“Mountains of Eternal White”) and the
Heilongjiang River (“Black Dragon River”) and so was called “white
mountains and black rivers.” It made sense that Ding wares won the favor
of the rulers of Liao and Jin since both ethnicities liked the color white. The
products of the Cizhou kilns, being mostly black and white with rich
decorative patterns, also accorded with the aesthetic preference of the Liao
and Jin peoples. Though Cizhou wares were not held in high regard by the
imperial court or the literati, they won favor among the general public with
their rich decorative pictures that expressed the common people’s aesthetic
preferences and voiced the folk customs of warding off bad luck and
appealing for blessings in ways that were straightforward, easy to
understand, lively and full of vitality. Such aesthetic characteristics were
quite different from those advocated by the literati at the time.
   During the Jin Dynasty, without a dominant elite culture in the upper
class to play a guiding role in aesthetics, ceramic artworks that were
natural, unrestrained and full of common interest like Cizhou wares
flourished, while celadon-producing kilns like the Ru and Yaozhou kilns,
though still in production, were not as prosperous as earlier. To meet market
demands, from the late Jin Dynasty the Yaozhou kilns started imitating the
white porcelain of the Ding kilns and the black background sgraffito
porcelain and black and white porcelain of the Cizhou kiln system. After
the Yuan Dynasty, celadon declined and was rarely produced in the north.
     If elite culture represents the Great Tradition, then ethnic minority
cultures and folk culture represent the Little Tradition. Generally speaking,
the Great Tradition dominates the Little Tradition with its greater discourse
power. What is recorded in history books is mostly the culture of the Great
Tradition and when reading history we seldom come across descriptions of
cultures belonging to the Little Tradition. It is for this reason that historical
records on the ceramics of the Liao and Jin dynasties are few, and those on
ceramics of other ethnic minority regimes of the same time like the Xixia
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
and those in Dali are even less. In addition, folk kilns with rich and colorful
products and a strong market demand such as the Cizhou kilns were not
ranked in the five celebrated kilns of the time since their products did not
conform to the preference of the elite class and were not selected by the
royal family as tributary porcelain. Yet such folk kilns represented the
direction of the ceramics industry’s future development, just as later
ceramic decorative approaches, including the blue and white porcelain
following the Yuan Dynasty, the red and green porcelain of the Yuan and
Ming dynasties, and the blue and white doucai porcelain and blue and white
wucai porcelain of the Ming Dynasty all developed from the Cizhou kiln
ware of the Song and Jin dynasties.
    In the Song Dynasty, Cizhou kiln-style porcelain was not able to win
the favor of the official arbiters of the aesthetics of the day, and even in the
Yuan Dynasty polychrome porcelain was still considered popular culture by
the elites who disdained the blue and white porcelain of the day. Yet by the
Ming Dynasty, blue and white porcelain had not only entered the
mainstream culture, but it had also dominated the production of the official
kilns of the time. It can be said that it was the Cizhou kilns, a folk kiln
system, that pioneered the development of China’s polychrome porcelains
which became the popular ceramics in both the mainstream and royal
cultures of the Ming and Qing dynasties. In retrospect, the blue and white
porcelain, blue and white doucai porcelain and blue and white wucai
porcelain produced by official kilns in the Ming Dynasty, and the wucai
porcelain, enamel polychrome porcelain and famille-rose porcelain, etc.
produced by official kilns in the Qing Dynasty all originated from the
creation of folk kilns, just as the refined Tang poems and Song ci also
originally came from the common folk. Besides the folk culture, also
deserving of attention are the interactions between ethnic minority cultures
and the Han culture as well as the interaction between China and other
civilizations and nations. If not for the development of Changsha kiln ware
and blue and white ware of the Tang Dynasty, the Cizhou kiln ware of the
Song and Jin dynasties and the blue and white ware of the Yuan Dynasty
would have had no foundation. Changsha kiln ware and blue and white
porcelain of the Tang Dynasty developed, driven by the demand of minority
peoples in northwest China and of foreign markets. The favoring of white
porcelain by the Liao and Jin promoted the production of the Ding kilns as
well as kilns imitating Ding ware. During the Jin Dynasty, kilns imitating
imageKind: Rendered source-page preview; searchable text available below

text:
Ding ware were not limited to kilns in the north; they also included the
Jingdezhen and Fanchang kilns in Anhui in the south. Such imitation
pushed the white porcelain production of Jingdezhen to a peak in the Yuan
Dynasty and won the favor of the Mongolian regime, another prairie people
who also liked white porcelain. The Mongolian regime and the later Yuan
Dynasty established the Fuliang Ceramic Bureau in Jingdezhen to produce
shufu porcelain (also called egg-white porcelain) required by the royal
family, and the production of white porcelain in turn helped improve the
body quality of blue and white porcelain production.
  An examination of the entire history of ceramics shows us that elite
culture and mass culture, Great Tradition and Little Tradition, the Han
culture and ethnic minority cultures, and the cultures of different countries
all developed amidst constant interaction. A non-mainstream culture in an
era might incubate the mainstream culture of the next historical stage.
Without the full development of popular and Little Tradition culture, elite
and Great Tradition culture would not have been born. For instance, the
refined celadon culture originated from the ancient folk worship of jade.
Interaction with ethnic minority cultures and other civilizations and nations
would also bring fresh blood to the development of a culture. For instance,
the ethnic minority cultures of the Wei, Jin and Southern and Northern
Dynasties, the foreign Buddhist culture, and the nomadic culture in the
Tang Dynasty all enriched the variety and decorative techniques of Chinese
ceramics. There will be more such examples in the Yuan, Ming and Qing
dynasties that will be elaborated in the following chapters and readers are
invited to give them careful attention.
